body:
Joshua Tree

My companions and climbing partners for the weekend were to be Steve, Josh O., and Josh G., all of which would be making a long trek from the Bay area on Wednesday. I joined the carravan Wednesday evening, and Josh O. and I arrived late Wednesday night, well ahead of Josh G. and Steve. Hidden Valley Campground turned out to be full, so we proceded to Ryan Campground, where we found a nice slot with a fin-shaped boulder that looked like fun to futz around on. (It was.)

Josh G. and Steve showed up shortly thereafter, and we proceded to sleep like the dead for eight hours.

Thursday: Lost Horse Area

Thursday dawned breezy and perfect. We set out for the Lost Horse area, looking for a couple of moderate trad climbs to kick off the weekend.

Josh O. and I ended up on Roan's Way, listed in the guidebook as a 5.8. Josh happily tied in and headed up the wall, quickly disappearing over a large bulge in the wall.

I heard Josh call down that he'd reached the anchors and was off belay. I tied in, and started to follow up.

I was excited, but this quickly gave way to nervousness. The climbing was smooth going, but I have no trad experience, and I'm used to the short but challenging climbs of Stoney Point, and always on top rope. 30 meters off the deck, with a belayer I couldn't see, I had to stop once or twice to get my head together. I took a deep breath, enjoyed the view for a second, and Elvis left the building. Smooth sailing through the crux, to a surprise at the anchors: this was a two-pitch climb. The guidebook had left that bit out. No biggie. We swapped ends of the rope, transferred the gear back to Josh's gear sling, and he again took the lead, and again disappeared over a ledge several meters above the belay station. The wind kicked up, and I was completely alone, 50 meters up with the wind in my hair, and a spectacular view of the valley west of the wall. Amazing.

40 minutes later, I realized something was wrong. The rope wasn't moving, and my hollers to Josh were getting no response. I figured that he'd reached the sumit (next belay?), but the wind was swallowing our shouting.

Finally, I heard a clear voice from my left: "Josh says he's off belay!" Thank God. Josh G. and Steve had come parallel with me on a neighboring route (Dappled Mare, 5.7), and were able to relay between me and Josh O. It was time to clean the belay station and get moving. We all made a mental note to bring the walkie-talkies with us on our next multi-pitch. (Alas, this would be our only multi-pitch this trip.)

The second pitch of Roan's Way starts with a step onto a slab with very littasdfle for the hands. It's something I've come to expect at J-Tree: the rock is quartz monzonite, and clean, and frictions like a madman. The result is that just about every climb includes a moment (or three, or seven) standing on tiny dishes that your brain cannot believe will hold you. But they're solid, if you keep your weight away from the rock and trust. (As an added bonus, if you don't trust, the same friction that should have held your feet will tear the skin off your knees and arms when you slip.)

Trust I did, and was rewarded with a great second pitch. Fun open-book formations and chiminey-like maneuvers to gain solid feet had me smiling nearly all the way to the summit. Josh had climbed it in his style: solid technique and the balance of a mountain goat, stepping quietly from edge to edge. I climbed it in mine: elbows, shoulders, and backstepping and damn those weak little crimpers. Great fun.

Round Up: Roan's Way

In the Lost Horse area, 5.8, more for sustained 5.7-ish difficulty than hard cruxes. Two full 45-meter pitches. (Tie stopper knots in your ropes, kids!) Solid bolts at the belay, but nothing at the summit. Bring a couple of 20-foot webbing lengths to rig a natural belay anchor, or save a couple of cams; you're going to use all your gear for pro.

Thursday PM: Burger & Beer Dijorno's & Amber Boch

The hike back to earth was more of a down-climb, and time-consuming. All told, by the time both parties had topped out and returned to the foot of the climb, we'd been out for nearly 5 hours. Everyone had expected a single-pitch, so foot and water had been left groundside (a mistake we did not repeat). We ate greedily, and drained the water cache, and decided that we would either cook or shop, but not both. We elected to head into town in search of beer, burgers and a market.

After cruising a little, we finally asked a few locals where we could locate a good burger & beer joint. We were directed to "Time Out", which the locals said didn't have burgers, but did have pizza.

Except that "Time Out" is really more of a dive bar than a pizza joint. The beer selection was Bud, Bud Light, and Amber Buck, and the pizza was Dijorno's heated in the oven. We were tired, wind-blasted, and hungry, and in no mood to argue. Which worked out alright, as the pizza was tasty (but small-- a "large" feeds two people, tops), and the "medium" mugs of Amber Buck we drained were, in actuality quite sizable, and reasonably cheap.

The market (Stater Bros) yielded fine steaks for the Friday night's dinner, as well as ample supplies for the next two days. We planned to spend the remainder of the trip climbing and camping, without having to return to civilization.

Friday: Double Cross, Loose Lady

Friday began with the discovery that a nice stiff wind blowing over the top of the latrine chiminey resulted in a chilly breeze blowing up at you from below. Brr.

Friday was a day of great climbs, but not for me. The cruxes of both Double Cross (Hidden Valley area, 5.8+), and Loose Lady (West of Turtle Rock, 5.9) stopped me cold. Josh O. and Steve had great success with both. Double Cross was, as hoped, an excellent crack line, and Loose Lady was a classic Joshua Tree route: crimpers at best for hands, and smears for the feet. Warm up on a few boulders, remind yourself that the laws of physics don't seem to apply to Stealth Rubber and quartz monzonite, and just go.

Round-up: Double Cross

Hidden Valley area, 5.8+. A 50-meter rope will let you rappel safely to earth from bolts at the summit.

Round-up: Loose Lady

West of Turtle Rock area, 5.9 (bolted). The crux comes almost immediately, the rest is a mental challenge. Power through sketchy feet to the second ledge, then enjoy the J-Tree friction. Our 50m rope was barely long enough to lower off of this one. It doesn't look tall, but it is. If you're going to TR this one (you'll have to have someone lead it to set the anchor) use a 60m rope, and let the leader clean on the way down.

Friday PM: Steak & Potatoes

Pine wood burned at just the right temperature to get our steaks seared outside and slow-cooked inside, and our baked potatoes (placed actually inside the fire) were perfect. Great dinner. And great drinks. Here's the recipe:

  1. Slice 2 oranges, 2 limes, 2 lemmons into a two-gallon jug.
  2. Add two cups of sugar.
  3. Add lots of ice.
  4. Empty a party-sized bottle of tequila into the jug.
  5. Shake the whole thing like a madman until either frost forms on the outside of the jug, or the sugar disolves, or your hands freeze.

My compatriots called it "Yucca". It is potent. We all slept like rocks, having drained 80% of a gallon bottle of Jose Cuervo in under two hours.

Saturday: Wind and Cold

Josh O. reports that there were icicles on our picknick table Saturday morning. I cannot confirm this, as I refused to leave my sleeping bag until later that morning, when my bladder drove me to the latrine. By that time, the iceicles had melted.

The wind from the night before (we hadn't really cared at the time, for some reason, but it was windy) had only picked up, and the temperature was hovering in the mid 40's. The water on the camp stove wouldn't boil, so we headed into town to the "Country Kitchen" for breakfast, hoping to kill a little extra time in the hopes that it would warm up by the time we were ready to climb.

The Country Kitchen sits just opposite the West Entrance to the park, and does a passable job of feeding you. But that's about it. It was busy, which I consider a good sign in restaurants, but the food was iffy, and the service was bare-minimum, and we all agreed that it wasn't as good as the last time each of us had been there.

The weather had not improved by the time we returned to camp, and the forecast was for colder and windier as the weekend went on, so we decided to cut the trip short by a day. We'd had two solid days of climbing, and were ready to head out. Had we just arrived that day, we might have toughed it out, but scratching out another day in that wind and cold just didn't seem worth it. We struck camp in 20 minutes flat, futzed around a bit on the boulders in camp, and headed home.

Epilogue

I'm tempted to do a quick gear review, but as much of the gear wasn't mine, and I have little experience with camping, I don't think I'm qualified. My Mountain Hardware 15-degree sleeping bag stood up like a champ, and Josh O's recommedation of a Therma-Rest Guidelite pad was right on. I like a cushy, warm bed, and that's what I got.

I do, however, recommend a campsite other than Ryan. It's just too exposed for windy weather. You'll be better off at Hidden Valley, which is a bit more sheltered. (Then again, I think we just got the campsite directly into the wind, so moving to the lee side of Ryan's might be workable as well.)
intro: Wow does it take me forever to get around to posting this stuff. I'm just now, on the eleventh of December, posting the trip report and pics taken on the Joshua Tree trip the weekend before Thanksgiving. I'll automate this yet...
title: Trip Report: Joshua Tree Climbing Trip

body:
Okay, so the new look for the site is up. At last. Now I can (theoretically) stop wanking around with CSS and HTML and actually get some work done. On the to-do list:
RSS Feed
I've never done something like this, so it'll be fun. At the end of the day it's just a reformatted main page, so I don't expect significant difficulty beyond finding time to get it done.
Articles
I recently put together a small script to handle backups. This was the first project in quite a while that took me back to "beginner land": Learn a new language, figure out what tools are available, and sew it all together to produce a working program. Lots of fun, and I thought it would make a great basis for a write-up targeted at novice programmers. So, I'll be posting both the backup script and the write-up here at some point. I'll probably keep to the theme of "For Novices", but who knows.
Direct posting of pics from my cameraphone
I have a cameraphone, and thought it would be fun to be able to post pics direct to the site from it. That's what the strange "Today I am..." thing is in the upper right. For the moment, it's static, just a test image. But I'll write a little code to get the pics posted, and index them, and then I can post up-to-the-minute pics there.
Which brings me to the "disclaimer" portion of the evening.

This may look like a blog. It may act like a blog. Hell, it'll even claim to be a blog. But it's not a blog.

My personal web sites have always served primarily as sandboxes in which to try new ideas. My first personal site became a JavaScript wonderland, complete with a "Whack-a-Mole" game featuring 12 Bill Gates heads bobbing up and down. I'd never do that with JavaScript now, and it was kinda dumb then, but it helped me learn JavaScript really, really well. Same thing here. I'll write code to post pictures from my phone, to supply RSS feeds, whatever. Then I'll turn around and use that codebase as the basis to get better at using JUnit, or to try out a new source control idea, or generalize the whole thing and package it for mass consumption. Who knows? The point is: this place is mostly for my own benefit. For the experience of building it.

Lastly: I am not a graphic designer, I am a programmer. The look that you see now is the result of a single afternoon's intensive "Just Get It Done" effort. So, judge not the look of the place. When I start my own company, I'll hire a real live graphic designer to do the page layout and images.

Also: I confess. I used tables to lay out the page. The reason: CSS was just too much of a pain in the ass for such a simple layout. All I wanted was a banner and two columns that went all the way to the bottom of the page. CSS complained, and wouldn't display properly, and yadda yadda yadda. So, in the interest of being able to check "Site Layout" off my list of things to do today, I just went with the tables. My idealism may lead me to tinker some more and try to get rid of them, but they stay for now.
intro:
Okay, so here's the new, and final (for the moment) look for the place. I've left in a couple elements in the site navigation as reminders of what I plan to add next, namely a couple articles, and an RSS feed. And yes, once I get things a little better organized, I'll be posting code here under some kind of Open Source liscence.

I've also linked to Ned Batchelder's excellent explanatory piece on what RSS is. He said it better than I can. Eventually I'll have something meaninful of my own behind that link, but for now I'll just suggest that you visit his blog; he's got a lot of interesting stuff there.
title: Just in time for Feb 29!

body:
I saw a post over on The Fishbowl which kind of echoed my own thoughts. Namely: I just bought $ITEM, and I'm finding it intensely symbolic. For Chuck Palahniuk, $ITEM was a sofa, and I guess for Charles Miller (proprietor of The Fishbowl) too. For me, its a washer/dryer matched set.

I own a sofa, but it's a cheap garage sale one. The washer is hitting a bit harder because of the connotations: I have now invested a non-trivial sum in an object that I have to cart around to future dwellings. Dwellings which I must screen for proper hook-ups and space, which is likely to mean that I'm not going to fit into just any ol' apartment. I'm committed to houses only now. So from here on out, it's rent a house or buy a house, but no more apartments, unless I'm willing to give up a non-trivial proportion of my non-trivial investment.

What all this boils down to is: at 27, I finally have to admit to being an adult.

Anyway, buy and listen to Yo La Tengo's I Can Hear the Heart Beating as One. You won't be sorry.
intro:
Okay, this is going to be a post wholly made of navel gazing. But I figure nobody's reading anyway, so what the hell.

I bought a washer and dryer, and I'm finding this terribly symbolic of growing up, and I remember Chuck Palahniuk saying that he felt pretty much like this when he bought his first couch. Like I said: navel gazing. But I'm not the only one.
title: Buying a Washer and Dryer Set

title: Hair

intro:
There's a rock gym opening in town: Boulderdash in T.O. When I told a particular friend about it, her response was, "Sure, because there's no good local rock." She has a point. Stoney Point, Malibu Creek, and a hundred other crags are within easy driving distance. But much like the reasons why the reasons to love e-books are different from the reasons to love paper books, reasons to love climbing gyms are different from the reasons to love real stone.

Mostly, I'm looking for a place where I can just kind of show up a couple nights a week and find a belay partner. It's about consistency. Getting out three times a month is not the same as getting out three times a week, even if you are pulling plastic. If I get out of work with just an hour of daylight left, there's no way of getting out to Stoney, or even to Lonely Cube, which is on private property anyway, and I had enough of the whole breakin'-the-law! thing when I was a young skate punk. (In case any of my freinds from those days sees this: yes, I was the goody-goody of the group even then.) But these days I see that things like trespassing, trampling greenery, leaving giant chalk stains, etc. just give climbing and climbers a bad rep. All those stickers proclaiming that "SKATEBOARDING IS NOT A CRIME" kind of overlooked the fact that all that hostility came from somewhere. Fringe sports need more community support, not less.

Kinda wandered off there. But I think you get the idea.

So I guess I learned two things tonight:

  1. I still want a local glimbing gym, even though there's plenty of great local stone.
  2. While I was a goody-goody as a kid, I'm now a super-goody-goody. Fooey.
title: New Climbing Gym

intro:
DISCLAIMER: At work, I see these days coming. I have not yet done anything seriously dumb that had any noticible repurcussions for my coworkers. I save the real train wrecks for myself and those I love.
I imagine that people who have seizures, or hallucinate, or have some other mental condition have moments where they can feel it coming on. They feel suddenly cold, or their fingertips go numb, and then POW, they're seeing sharp-toothed pumpkins dancing in the yard. Or something. But they have that moment of, "Dude, no matter what wierd shit happens next, it's not real."

When I catastrophically screw up something as simple as making coffee (we won't get into exactly how), that's my moment. That's the moment where I should resolve not to do anything but read the rest of the day.

But today, I tried to build a computer. And since this is entitled A Project Gone Horribly Wrong, you pretty much know where this is going.

I'll spare you all the gory details. I'm sure your imagination can fill them in.

The Damage:

  • Bought: Wireless LAN card.
  • Destroyed: SuSE Linux (Professional Edition) installation CD #1
  • Destroyed: 1 USB optical mouse.
  • Destroyed: 1 CD ROM drive.
  • Bought: 1 USB wireless optical mouse
  • Bought: 1 DVD ROM drive.
  • Returned: 1 USB wireless optical mouse (for reasons of general suckiness)
  • Returned: 1 DVD ROM drive (because I bought the wrong thing)
  • Bought: 1 USB optical mouse, which rules
  • Bought: 1 CDRW/DVD ROM drive, which also rules
  • Initial budget: $40 and a bottle of Johnny Walker (I traded the Scotch for a case, mobo, and processor to use as a basis for the system. It has nothing to do with this project going completely to hell.)
  • Actual budget: $200 and a bottle of Johnny Walker

Lessons learned:

  • Warning lables are not placed on equipment for my ammusment.
  • Wireless mice just aren't ever going to be as smooth and responsive as wired mice.
  • Double-check everything.
  • RTFM
  • Even after R-ing the FM, some days I'm better off just finishing off a good book than I am trying to build anything.
  • When you think you've double-checked everything, that's your brain trying to mess with you. Double-check everything again.
title: A Project Gone Horribly Wrong

body:
Last night I finally realized what was stressing me out so much: I've become a control freak. Not in the OCD sense, but in the sense that I have a very structured life, and I like it that way. It makes me edgy and irritable when that structure is disrupted.

Stresses of the last couple of weeks (in no particular order):

  • Car trouble
  • Taxes
  • Illness
  • Hectic work days
  • Computer trouble
As of yesterday afternoon, I was managing none of these things especially well. Being sick made me unable to work out, which is a fantastic stress reliever. Pile on the frustration of paying out $$$ to Uncle Sam and the State Franchise Tax Board. The car trouble worked on two levels: it took up my time and energy as I wrestled with the logistics of being without my car for two days, and added to the frustration of having to pay out a lot of my hard-earned cash simply to maintain the status quo. I paid my taxes, and paid for my car repairs, and $1600 later, I'm still right where I was last Wednesday.

Finally last night it dawned on me that I wasn't doing much to help the situation. Every decision I made was short-term. By Wednesday morning I was in full-on self-centered yuppy mode. I rented an SUV because I couldn't stand to spend two days driving the glorified roller skate they call an "economy" car. (And because I wanted to take my bike out trail riding, I told myself.) I declined an offer of coffee from the very nice girl at Enterpise Rent-a-Car in favor of a $4 Starbuck's latte. By the time I got to work, I realized I was wearing the yuppy uniform: dress shoes, khakis, polo, sunglasses. Hell, I had accessorized: Starbuck's cup, cellphone, security badge. SUV. I hung my head, and plotted change.

Starting yesterday evening, I embraced my control freak side, and began my counter-offensive. I pushed the VW dealership for a loaner, and ditched the SUV. I bought a new computer so I wouldn't have to waste any more time fiddling with the old one. My first act at work this morning was to touch base with everyone I was working with, and let them know when I'd have something for them. I asked everyone to submit bug reports over email; no more phone calls. I listed out milestones, and switched projects only at milestones. This radically reduced the ammount of task-switching I did during the day. I called the Doctor and rescheduled the appointment I'd missed on Wednesday because of the car trouble. And I took a rain check on tonight's social activity to catch up on laundry and general housecleaning, and to make sure I get a good night's sleep.

It's not about having less to do. It's about taking control and removing the stress from the system. As of this afternoon, all my projects were humming along toward completion nicely. And though I got my car back tonight, I'd already stopped stressing about it: having a loaner meant that I wasn't paying per day for a rental, and running is as good as riding. A loaner was fine, and I didn't mind keeping it for a few days. And tonight I'm putting together a sweet new micro-ATX system that'll be everything I've wanted in a new computer: smaller, faster, quieter.

Oh, and I got a haircut, which for some reason always chills me out. Magic, I tell ya.

Anyway, the laundry is churning, a backup of my current home directory is being made, and I'm going to use this time to go get a burrito. Ciao.

Oh, and though a lot of how I get through days like this is just my own little systems, a book called Organizing for the Creative Mind has a lot of great suggestions for people like me, who are natually scattered, free, creative thinkers. I used to see organization as an imposed system required by opressive authority figures. Now I use it as a tool to bring more of my crazy schemes into reality.
intro:
My greatest weekness is my tendency to manage multiple projects badly. Notice I didn't say inability. I'm capable of managing my time very well. But if I'm not paying attention, I tend to react to multiple projects for multiple people, well, reactively. And so we all get to the end of the project in one piece, but the general stress level is higher than it ought to be.

This was one of those weeks that tests my abilities: a pretty much constant stream of email and phone calls asking for new features and bugfixes. And since I was in damage-control mode, there were more bugs than usual.

This week, I refreshed my people and project management skills.
title: Management School

body:
The Gear:
  1. MSI micro-ATX mobo w/ integrated sound, LAN, and video.
  2. 1 super-expensive, not-nearly-as-quiet-as-advertised micro-ATX case.
  3. K7 2.6 gig proc.
  4. Sony CDRW/DVD ROM.
  5. Aging, but still perfectly functional G-Force 2 video card. (It's an Elsa E-Razor X or something.)
The OS: SuSE Linux Professional 9.0. Referred to lovingly as Product of die ScheiÃƒÅ¸eland. I will be returning to Mandrake pretty much as soon as they get around to releasing 10.0. I'll buy the combo pack with the stickers, and the dorky Mandrake Linux baseball tee. I will dress in it and dance about and sing their praises because: They have never, in all the time I used their distro, never wasted as much of my time as SuSE has. Moving on.

Okay, so the mobo has integrated video. No big deal. Except that the SuSE installation chokes hard if it can't start SaX2. SaX2 chokes hard if it can't figure out which chip it's supposed to be talking to. And thanks to the good folks at MSI, the mobo isn't smart enough to pretend it has no integrated video in the event that someone plugs in an actual video card.

Now, this wouldn't be so tragic, except that the installation doesn't fail until nearly 45 minutes in. So each and every time you want to tweak a few things and try again, that's another hour or so gone. I have tried maybe 4 or 5 times over the last couple days to get SuSE to install with the vidio card installed, because the last time I had to DL and install video drivers (which, as I recall, was when I got this card in the first place), about half way through the process I decided I'd rather put my dick in a bee hive than ever do it again.

(Before you start screaming: I certainly did not spend five hours watching progress bars. The SuSE installation DVD is really handy: clicky-clicky a few times, hit "GO", and come back in an hour (say, on your lunch break from work) to type in a root password, clicky-clicky a few more times, and return after work to tidy up loose ends.)

Anyway, back to my outrage and bile.

Finally, I decide that having no actual video card is a minor point. I'll concede that the integrated mobo video is probably just as good for things like coding and looking at pictures of nak-- er, um, chess games as is the G-Force. So I just suck it up, instal the whole thing and get it running with the integrated video.

Which worked for the most part, but here's the kicker: my system insisted on using the european keymap, which is sort of allright because all the alphabetic characters are in the right places, except for y and z, which are swapped. But it's really a pain in the ass, because all the non-alphabetic characters have been completely scrambled, which ends up hiding the / character in SHIFT-7, and generally makes it a complete pain in the ass to try to correct the problem.

I reached straight for YaST, which has a handy keyboard-mapping tool. Strangely, this tool told me that I'd already chosen the US keyboard mapping and that everything was fine. Upon clicking "OK", I discovered that everything was back to normal. Except this didn't last. Every time I logged in, I'd have to reset the key mapping.

Fuck. That.

I have shit to do. I don't have any taste for fiddling with something as stupid as keyboard mappings every time I log in.

The work-around is: Tell KDE to use its US key mapping. It'll override your system's (amnesiac) settings, and all will be goodness and light again.

However, now that I've got my video card working (installed it, escaped from the boot sequence, ran SaX2 manually, rebooted, and zowie, it's fixed) the problem seems to have resolved itself. I suspect that the automated patch installation scheme reset some default value somewere, and running SaX2 overwrote it again. Or something. Who knows.

The upside is: SaX2 is a great tool. A quick glance through the man page (use -p option to get info on all detected video cards, use -c N to configure chip N) gave me what I needed to get rolling.

And now, I can get back to lobotomizing my old machine and reconfiguring it to run as a backup server.

However, all this time with computer innards everywhere has brought a familiar quote to mind:

If you made a Venn diagram, there would be two non-overlapping circles, one of which was labeled, "Times when I am truly happy" and the other of which was labeled, "Times when I am logged in as root, holding a cable, or have the case open."

– Jamie Zawinski
intro:
DISCLAIMER: It's late. I'm fried. This will ramble, and often seem to be comming to a point without actually ever getting there. Taking it with any degree of seriousness would be completely insane. Additionally, any and all family members are advised to keep well away. I'm dealing with computers, there will be profanity.

YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED

Just finished the installation of SuSE on my new machine. I'm somewhere between wanting to throw the blasted thing out a window, and wanting to know how Linux has come so far so fast. Many things are far better than they used to be. A few difficulties have yet to be addressed. And that giant sucking sound you hear is the reason I'm writing at all. When all goes well, the story is boring. (In this case, the story is likely to be boring anyway, but that's my fault.)
title: Praise be to Linus, it's Running.

intro:
Now this is a slick solution to the email-harvesting problem:
I am engaging in a little experiment. I built a little perl module which creates magical evaporating email addresses which are only valid for 72 hours. – Everything Burns
What about taking this one step further: a one-off email address that's only valid for thirty minuts or so. Each person who wants to send you an email gets their very own address to write to. If the arrival date of the message matches up with the time interval encoded in the address, the message is passed on to your "real" email.

Maybe another half-baked idea, but worth thinking about. I really don't like either of the usual solutions to this problem: JavaScript obfuscation of your actual address, or presenting the address as an image. Still, that's a lot of code to write when a simple png file is "good enough."
title: Magical Evaporating Email

intro:
Started messing about with the design of the sight again, and came up with this. Not too pretty. But then, I'm not a web designer. I just don't have the patience to deal with something you can't write automated tests for. Broken JavaScript? Gotta manually test it in 4 different browsers. CSS? This article at Position is Everything is extremely informative, and if you're forced (or paid) to worry about pixel-perfect layouts and IE workarounds, is great. But to me it just points out the larger problem: even after all these years, cross-browser compatibility continues to be an issue. WTF? Can't we get a bug-free rendering engine already? Can't we lean on MS to get these things fixed? Why are we forced to commit design attrocities in the name of just getting text to fall where it ought to?

I'm done ranting. Promise.
title: Translucent PNG's!  Wooo!

intro:
My name is Chris, and I hate reading mail.

It doesn't matter how important it is. Envelopes from the bank get recycled without even being opened. Reminders from magazines to renew my subscription go completely ignored. (Though they do get piled on my kitchen counter.) I do everything online. If not for the internet, I'd be in debtor's prison.

So today I finally started going through the acumulated mail. Credit card offers got shredded immediately. Likewise with stuff from the Alumni Assoc. Bank statements got collected and stowed (still unopened) in the appropriate file in my file cabinet.

But the thin one from the State of California, that caught my eye. Inside I found a check for $242.37. My rebate from Gov. Ahnold's decree that I shouldn't have to be systematically sodomized by the DMV every year.

My mom always said it pays to be organized.
title: It Pays to be Organized

intro:
I finally borrowed my roomate's clippers and took the plunge. I was skittish at first, this being my first self-inflicted haircut and all. I kept hesitating just above ear level. Finally, I ran the clippers straight back over the top of my head. No chickening out after that. Any way you slice it, it's tough to keep your dignity with reverse mohawk.

The fear of balding took me by surprise though. There are a couple spots where the hair seems thinner than elsewhere. I'm chalking that up to strange geometry of my noggin. Until this moment, I never worried about losing my hair, or even really understood why guys stress about it. Now I know. That's mortality creeping up on ya. That's the loss of youthful energy, looks, and yes, libido. Patrick Steward be damned, I now suddenly understand the fear behind Rogaine, Viagra, Enzyte.

This is all, of course, insane. I'm 27. No reason to worry...
title: Haircut time.

intro:
A while back, I saw a West Wing episode where the speechwriters, assistants, etc. were trying to come up with seven-word answers to the questions they knew were going to come up in a debate. It was an excercise in clarity.

More recently, I saw a post on dive into mark that mentioned nailing down an idea in ten words or less.

And even more recently, communication has been an issue at work. (More on that in my next post.) I like my coworkers, and they're all intelligent people, but sometimes...sometimes.

So, I have made a rule. The rule is:

When I ask you a direct question, you must answer it in ten words or less, or go to a special jail for dumb people.

Let's see this rule in action!

  1. Me: Can I have a grande non-fat latte, please?
  2. Dude: Sorry, we're out of non-fat milk. Is 2% okay?
  3. Me: Sure.
See how easy that was? Everyone wins, and nobody goes to dumb people jail.
title: Ten Words or Less

Andrei Herasimchuk put together a beee-yootiful little rant over on Design by Fire about the state of documentation in open source projects, the W3C, and a little bit about how some skills tend to be chronically undervalued.

body:
I'm a right-brainer. For me, organization is an all-or-nothing proposition. So I can't just put everything in one place and remember to pay the bill. I have to get all-the-way organized. I must use a system so organized that it is tollerant of my forgetfulness.

Sallie Mae wasn't ready to do that. No pay-by-phone. No automatic debit. And they required that I send in a little "coupon" with each payment, so I couldn't use my bank's automatic bill pay system, which is perfectly capable of mailing out a paper check, but which is certainly not equipped to handle anything as archaic as filling out little coupons by hand. Sallie Mae had locked themselves out of the 21st century, so all the tools that exist to actually solve the problem of my fogetfulness were forbidden to me. I had to muddle along, leaving post-its on my computer screen and refrigerator, and sending email to myself:

#crontab for craser 0 0 20 * * echo "Pay Sallie Mae!" | mail craser 0 0 1 * * echo "Pay the rent!" | mail craser

Which is strangely typical. I've often met resistance from the people who wanted me to "get it together" in the first place. They think I'm going overboard. I can't win, and I've stopped trying. I just do what works for me.

The book Organizing for the Creative Person is great for two things: helping creative types like me (so-called "right-brainers") get organized, and helping the non-creative types ("left-brainers") understand why we have such a hard time doing so. Really, the difference is basic: "Left-brainers" hate spending time searching through a disorganized stack of papers, as it's a waste of time. "Right-brainers" hate spending time maintaining an organized file cabinet, because it's boring. (I have yet to hear of any study on which is actually faster. Scientists seem to assume that being "organized" is the way to go.)

So, to you right-brainers out there: you are not alone, and you are not wierd. But I'm also here to tell you that creating systems to help your day-to-day life will make you happier. Find things that work for you, and don't let other's put you off a system that works. You may find that the left-brainers in your life won't like any system you have. They don't like you being disorganized, and they don't like whatever system you come up with. That's fine. The system only has to work for you.

And to you left-brainers out there with right-brainers in your lives: you can try to help, but ultimately everyone has to find a way that works for them. It may look like a mess to you, or it may seem like the work of an obsessive-compulsive. More likely, it'll make no sense at all. But it's something you have to respect. Stay out of the way, and judge it by the results, not the method.
intro:
The woman from Sallie Mae, my loan servicing company (well, one of them) was concerned. "Well, you're three months overdue," she said.

"I know," I said. "What's the total due?"

"Well, it's built up for three months, so it's quite a bit."

"Give it to me straight, Doc. How much do I owe?"

She took a breath. "Ninety-four dollars."

I laughed out loud. "Can I pay right now over the phone?" I asked.

She was surprised. "Well..."

"And can I pay for three months in advance, so I know I'm safe for a while?"

Now she was confused. I explained to her that cash flow wasn't the problem; I was just forgetful.

She switched into Mom Mode.

"Do you pay rent by check?" she asked.

"Yes..." I answered, unsure where this was going.

"Well, just leave your checkbook and the coupon book in the same place, and that way every time you go to pay the rent, you'll remember to pay your student loans at the same time. See?"

I did indeed. She had children of her own, and they no doubt had never missed a student loan payment. But they were not artists, or programmers, or mathematicians. She hadn't the first clue what it's like to deal with creative people. We're just wired differently, and there's not a damn thing we can do to change that.

I tried to explain. "Well, you see, I'm just forgetful. Can I just pay six months at once over the phone right now?"

"Well, no," she replied. "We need you to fill out the coupon and send it in with your check."

I persisted. "Can we set up a regular direct debit so that it all happens automatically?"

"I'm sorry, no. We aren't set up for that."

And that right there is the problem.
title: Running a Tight Ship

intro:
Okay, so my last entry wasn't completely random. It was triggered by a post on Dive Into Mark which linked to a "life assesment quiz". Kinda hokey, but it's actually kind of interesting.

I've been working hard lately to get my shit together. New clothes have been bought to replace some of the old, a new 250GB hard drive has been installed, and my backup system is complete. (I'm watching rsync copy my home directory to the backup system as I write this.)

Really, it's about clearing the mental clutter. Get the books off my desk, get the CD's organized and moved to a rack, etc. I think this is a large component of one of my favorite hackerly quotes.

Spacial clutter has a way of creating mental clutter. We keep the things near us that are important. When everything's out, and in our way, then everything's important. It becomes really hard to prioritize.

I don't know where all this is going. I just know that I feel a little bit of relief watching all these file names scroll by as rsync backs them up. One problem solved. Not all-the-way solved, but good enough for now. I've hit my milestone for the weekend, and I'm going to leave it at that. I'll think about such things as setting up cron jobs another night. Now I'm just going to eat pizza and read.
title: Organization

intro:
After *mumble* years of debugging various flavors of problems, you get a certain intuition. (Actually, you acquire the intuition much sooner than that. But you learn to listen only later on.) Synchronization bugs, off-by-one problems, user input errors, etc. all have distinctive aromas. But my personal favorite is the "some switch hasn't been flipped" smell. It's the feeling that you're doing everything right except for one simple thing. Forgetting to flip the "uplink" switch on a hub, or forgetting to restart a server after making configuration changes both fall into this category.

These proplems are simple. So once you find them, they're easy to fix. But they do tend to leave you with a mood-wrecking "I'm a dumbass" feeling. You get all the frustration of genuinely difficult debugging, without the moment of triumph that usually makes it worth the effort. You're just left soaking in a puddle of pissed-off, muttering, "But I checked that ages ago..."

So, a lesson to all you kids out there that get to play with Oracle's Application Server: don't forget to flip the switch marked "Auto Login" in the wallet manager.
title: The Unflipped Switch

intro:
I recently ordered a copy of Gentoo Linux. Upon inserting the installation CD, I was confronted with something I didn't expect: a root prompt and a bunch of documentation about how to go about installing Gentoo. It involved copying "stage" files onto magical points on my hard drive, etc.

Now, I read a bit of the documentation, so I am now fully, and repeatedly aware that "Gentoo is all about choice," and yo, I can dig it. Word. But I also think that the first option on any installation media should be a giant button that says simply: "Make it so." It should pick some intelligent defaults, ask the fewest possible questions, and then hum happily along installing the new system. A root prompt and a man page doesn't even come close.

I'm going to give it another try in a few days (maybe), since SuSE continues to annoy me, but I don't hold out much hope: "Mandrake 10 Power Pack" just arrived in the mail on Friday, and I'm willing to bet that their installation procedure is just as easy and excellent as it was the last time I used Mandrake. If that goes well, the only thing driving me to Gentoo will be a glowing recommendation and my own curiosity, with a few technical hurdles in the way. In short, I don't see it happening.
title: Attempted Gentoo

intro:
Once in a while, I get into discussions with family members or friends of friends about this stuff, and I always end up running on and on about details and not properly driving home the main point: piracy would go away if the RIAA and MPAA would embrace the opportunities presented by the 'net.

So this is really just me getting my thoughts collected. I post it here just because now that they're collected, it seems a shame to delete my notes. So, uh, without further ado...

A Few Things the RIAA Must Realize if They Want to Live

Digital Rights Management doesn't work.
Encryption is not a copy prevention tool. It is a use prevention tool. Even with uncrackable DRM in place, large-scale pirates in Hong Kong will still be making copies of your stuff, while my mom will have a hard time playing the CD.
I will not pay the same price for inferior goods.
DRM-encumbered files should be cheaper than the CD.
What you offer must be better than free.
If you offer your customers exactly what they want at unbeatable prices, piracy becomes obsolete. Why wait all night to download a low-quality copy of a song for free when I can pay you a quarter and have a perfect copy in five minutes?
All those dollars you have lost to digital piracy could have been profits riding on your hip.
You've lost sales to piracy, and then paid lawers to try to stop it. You could have made money by offering your market what it wants: cheap downloads unencumbered by DRM. Give us what we want, and everyone wins. Artists, labels, and fans all make out on the deal.

The lessons here aren't new. The Spanish royalty learned all of this four hundred years ago when they realized that their tight-fisted control on trade with the New World was costing them twice. They were being robbed by pirates, and so had to pay for more cannons on their ships, which then got robbed anyway. Once they deregulated the ports, volume rose, prices fell, and piracy became unprofitable. And they made more money than ever before, having cut themselves in on a piece of a much bigger pie.

More recently, bootleged Dave Mathewes Band concerts started appearing, usually going for about $30 per CD. DMB responded by releasing concert recordings of their own, at $15 per double CD. Half the price for twice the music, at album quality. Bootlegs evaporated almost overnight.

The point here is: You see piracy as a threat. In reality, it is simply an indicator of a market demand so strong that both consumers and suppliers are willing to buck the law and endure constant hassles to meet it. You can meet that demand better and cheaper than anyone. You own this market already, and yet you're trying to stamp it out.
title: A Quick Reality Check

intro:
I just finished Kim Stanley Robinson's Red Mars, and I'm floored. I had fallen out of the habit of reading, and wanted something to get back in, something I could read for pure pleasure. Red Mars fit the bill. Just read the prologue in the bookstore. If it doesn't grab you, then you're safe: the rest of the book will not excite you. However, if the prologue does grab you, you're doomed to ripping through three books of great science fiction.

Unfortunately, as always happens with the second book in a great series, I don't have it handy immediately after the first. So I visited three booksellers in search of Green Mars yesterday. None of them had what I was looking for. At the last one, a member of staff asked if there was something he could help me find. Once it was established that they didn't have Green Mars on the shelf, he offered to order me a copy.

When will bookstores learn that the only advantage they have over Amazon is instant gratification and service? If either of those things fails (especialy the "instant" bit), I just walk out and order from Amazon. Why would I wait two weeks and make another trip to the store when I can have my order delivered to my door in 2-3 days, for free?

(For those playing along at home: Yes, Amazon is the chief competition to brick and mortar booksellers, BestBuy, and movie theaters. Invest now.)

So anyway, they didn't have Green Mars. So I got Snow Crash instead. It's cool so far (30 pp. in), but a bit like The Diamond Age in tone and style. There's a depth of technical amazingness that isn't matched by depth of character. Everyone seems like a hypothetical case. (Cryptonomicon is far, far better.)

So anyway, the rest of my list:

  1. Howard Zinn: A People's History of the United States
  2. Tom Robins: Fierce Invalids Home from Hot Climates
  3. John Irving: The Water Method Man
After that, I have no idea.
title: Summer Reading

body:
Most of the rules are common-sense Good Things that are commonly forgotten by the producers of technology. But a couple of them initially struck me as the work of a luddite with impossible demands. The kind of guy who wants everything to Just Work, without having any conception of how difficult that is.

Rule #5: "Good Technology is Simple", seemed impossible. He says:

Simplicity goes hand-in-hand with range of function. Features that you never use get in the way, and they make the product complicated and cumbersome.

Look for technology that does exactly what you want: no more, no less.

This is a tough requirement. Nearly impossible. For two reasons:
  • No two users will want the same set of features.
  • The "simplicity" I like today will be "feature starvation" I hate tomorrow.
So manufacturers have to find the sweet spot between being having a simple interface, and having lots of features. This is a tough balancing act, made all the harder by the fact that even a single user's needs will change over time.

But there is a solution: good interface designers are worth their weight in gold, as they make this sweet spot wider. You can attract high-end users with features without alienating low-end users with a complex interface.

Combine solid interface design with a nice selection of models for different user (is that what they mean by "market segments?"), and you can match the right bit of tech to the right user, and keep them happy for a while until they're ready for the next model up.

But here's where Robin Good goes completely mad, or so I thought. Rule #9:

9) Good technology does what you want it to do. And it doesn't do something else. "Doing what you want it to do" means the same thing as "idiot proof."

[...]

"Doing what you want it to do" is a highly personal thing. If you want your daughter's clothes to protect her from the cold, then her selection of a light chiffon top and an ultra-mini skirt represents bad technology. But if she wants clothes to accentuate her physical features, then the same clothes represent good technology.

Technology is neither good nor bad but the demands of the user make it so. So let's reinterpret this demand into something we can work with:
If you want your daughter's clothes to protect her from the cold, then her selection of a light chiffon top and an ultra-mini skirt represents a poor choice of technology. But if she wants clothes to accentuate her physical features, then the same clothes represent good choice of technology.
Mini skirts and cellphones. It's all the same thing. The key is matching the right tech with the right purpose. Sales staff must be better at guaging a customer's needs and matching them with an appropriate tool.

So, after a bit of squinting at Good's rules, and a bit of work translating them from user-speek to techie-speek, I think we have a couple of good guidelines. And it's spooky at how they match up with the sources of frustration for a great many users. My two suggestions for the tech industry are:

Hire good interface designers, and listen to them.
Interface designers let you enlarge the number of people that a given product can satisfy. You can attract high-end customers with advanced features, while still welcoming entry-level customers with an easy-to-use interface.
Hire good sales people, and get them to listen to your (potential) customers.
Train them to match the needs of the customer to the appropriate tech. This applies just as much to The Home Depot as it does to Verizon Wireless.

Now, back to user speek:

  • Make it as easy to use as possible.
  • Help me choose the right tool for me.

body:
He has many, many detractors. Some say that he has damaged the route after he climbed it to make it harder for others. Some say he never climbed it at all. A recent article in Climbing supports Rouhling's claims. But some detractors still aren't satisfied:
Huber continues, contending that if a person has climbed at the cutting edge, there must then be a track record of his other hard ascents. Huber gestures with his hand: "If Rouhling's level is here," he says, holding his hand at chest level, "and then with Akira it is here" -- he holds his hand at his forehead -- "then there should be many other routes around here." The hand is level with his nose. "Where is this track record?" Huber asks.

And here's where things tie back in with music. During the time that Rouhling was working on Akira, he and his wife had two children, and his wife had brain surgery and nearly died. Rouhling didn't have a lot of time on his hands, and climbed near his home just a couple hours at a time.

I've seen musicians under similar time constraints (or some that just get lazy) do similar things. They work on one really difficult piece and master it, but neglect things like technical etudes and daily sight-reading. At the end of a few months, they can play that Rachmaninoff piano concerto beautifully, but can barely hack their way through The Entertainer.

You don't have to be a great musician to play a difficult piece. There's a shortcut: just learn a certain sequence of notes by rote. This is why you don't progress by mastering a piece of music over months. You become a real musician by mastering many, many pieces in a few days each.

Or, maybe Rouhling's "track record" just isn't in route climbing. If you look at Akira as a V15 boulder problem instead of a 5.15b route, things start to make more sense. Acording to Climbing, Rouhling has done many V14 and V15 problems with "little difficulty." Seems like a fitting enough track record to me.

So, ya know, hey. Maybe all my talk about music is just talk. But who knows?
intro:
A lot of my favorite activities have common threads. Well, yeah, duh. But consider: playing music, climbing, and programming all fuse creativity and structure. The challenge has well-defined rules, but the path to a solution has almost none. So there is a giant leap that happens when you grow beyond knowing the solutions to a few problems, and being good at finding new solutions.

Why am I babbeling on about this? Because of a French climber named Fred Rouhling, who claims that his latest route Akira is the hardest yet climbed by man.
title: Learning One Thing

body:
Clear Channel is in the music delivery business. They have bullied their way to dominance by having a stranglehold on radio stations and concert venues. They make money by being the pipeline from music producers to music consumers.

The so-called Big Five labels, under the umbrella of the RIAA, make money by selling as much music to as many people as possible.

Enter digital distribution.

Labels should love digital distribution. No distribution costs. No middle men. An artist can go from unknown to superstardom in a few days. People can swap mp3s of a song around, and then hit Amazon or iTunes to buy the album. MP3s are to word-of-mouth as a raging PCP addict is to your average fuzzy bunny.

Clear Channel should Fear digital distribution. Fear with a capital F. Digital distribution doesn't just make them weaker; it makes them irrelavent. Nobody needs radio stations when you can put an mp3 in the inbox of a zillion people for free. The pipe from labels to fans is no longer the bottleneck.

But it's the RIAA who's figiting against digital distribution. Clear Channel, who should be screaming bloody murder, is silent.

I think Clear Channel is pulling the strings. They can't convince anyone that they have an inalienable right to make money. But the RIAA can defend "intellectual property", and "artists' rights", and sound, well, downright American!

The labels can't resist. They realize that the market for digital market isn't strong enough yet, that they can't pull an end run. They still need Clear Channel so they capitulate. And so Clear Channel maintains the status quo.

So when the EFF goes after the RIAA, they've missed the target. To fix things, we need to call out Clear Channel for the bastards they are.

Finally, a favorite quote of mine:

"I know I don't know nuthin'. I'm just speculatin' on a hypothesis!" -Chief O'Doole, Miller's Crossing

body:
But, on the statement from CitiFinancial, there is no customer service number listed. Huh?

So I go to the website. The website says to contact your local CitiFinancial office for account inquiries. I do so, using the number on the website, and a nice woman named Debbie informs me that they're "just a branch office" and don't have access to my account. This does not stop her from asking me (twice) for my Social Security number.

I ask her if I should use the 800 number listed on the website. She replies that that 800 number will just connect me to her again, and gives me the right number ot call. It is in fact the correct number, and I'm soon talking to Cherise, who does have access to my account.

But she doesn't speek English. She speeks some kind of institutional secret zaibatsu lanauge that sounds like English, but does not include the words "yes" or "no".

  • Me: I've accidentally overpaid, and I want to have a check sent to me, and I want close my account, please.
  • Cherise: I'll send a request to have a credit issued to you, and you'll receive confirmation in the mail.
  • Me: So, does that mean I'll get a check?
  • Cherise: I've already issued the request for a credit to be issued to you.
  • Me: But what form will that take? Will it be automatically deposited in my bank account? Should I watch the mail for a check? What?
  • Cherise: Sir, as I've said, you'll receive a credit, and a confirmation in the mail.
  • Me: A check in the mail?
  • Cherise: You'll receive a check, sir. Thank you for calli--
  • Me: And the account will be closed?
  • Cherise: I've put in a request, and you'll receive confirmation in the mail.
  • Me: That the account will be closed?
  • Cherise: You'll receive confirmation in the mail, sir.
  • Me: So I'll get a check, and you'll close the account?
  • Cherise: Yes, sir. Thankyouforcalling*click*

Since Cherise hung up on me, I had to call again and talk to Marcus to change my address. Marcus actually used English like a native, using words like, "yep" and "nope", and my favorite: "You'll get a check for $317.57, issued to [new address], within two weeks."

Thus endeth Chapter the First.

body:
I don't feel guilty about this, because the cellphone industry is run by a bunch of monopolistic congolmerates who really don't care what I want to buy. They care about what they want to sell me. So there are only four Bluetooth headset models available in my area:
  • Motorola Wireless Headset HS810 - 98565
  • Sony Ericsson Bluetooth Headset HBH-65
  • Jabra FreeSpeak BT200
  • Jabra FreeSpeak BT250

Even though my primary concern was sound quality, I really wanted an earpiece that I could charge in my car using the charger for my phone. Since I use a Sony Ericsson T616, this meant checking out their HBH-65.

I had to look around for this little baby, and fifteen minuts after I bought it, I understood why no store would carry it: it fell off my ear. The "ear hook" is attached to the unit via a crappy little rubber gasket and post. I suppose the design is meant to give greater flexibility and comfort, but it just falls apart a lot of the time.

Plus, it looks like a prop on Star Trek: all clean design, no personality. Blech. So, even though it uses the same charger as my phone, the HBH-65 gets a big thumbs-down.

Next up was the Motorolla HS810 - 98565. Very light, great design, excellent sound quality, and it stayed securly attached to my head at all times. You can get a Motorolla car charger for this, which is cool. But I often had trouble finding the buttons.

So the Motorolla was good, but the Jabra just had it beat.

Now, for the record: I did not try the Jabra FreeSpeak 250. I only tried the 200. This is becaue while the 250 supposedly has better sound, the 250 costs $145, while the 200 comes in at $99. So, Jabra, if you're out there, here's your killer product: The FreeSpeak 250 with a car charger that plugs directly into the earpiece, for $99. Produce this, and you will conquor all.

Can customers upload their own ringtones?

No. There's an effort by the industry to make people pay for the content on these devices.

It pisses me off every time I read it. Why can't I record my girlfriend humming "You are my Sunshine" and make that my ringtone? Because, "there's an effort by the industry to make people pay for the content."

But the stupidity at Danger runs thick and deep:

If you're a developer, how can you develop software for the Sidekick?

We're Java compatible, and we have a software developers kit. People with Java programs can tweak them and port them over to run on our platform, using Java or J2ME. We're just getting started but trying to reach out to the independent developer community. A lot of the new games and applications being launched by us now are certainly all coming from third parties.

What about allowing developers to create user-installable applications for the Sidekick?

Not user-installable. We're a gatekeeper in that sense. They use our developer kit, they reach an agreement with us, and then through us they can have access to our user base.

They want to be the "gatekeeper", charging a toll every time a developer wants to write software for their platform. Now, acording to the interview, Danger's handsets compose "1 percent of T-Mobile's installed base". One percent! For a software developer, it's enough of a turn-off that this platform comprises less that 1% of the total mobile platorm market. A licencing fee is basically a great big "GO AWAY" sign. They're counting on the built-in capabilities of the system to sell the units.

So if I buy a Sidekick or Hiptop, I can pretty much count on Danger squeezing me for every penny they can. No third party software will be available, and I can't roll my own. And it'll only connect via T-Mobile. No WiFi.

Why would I want one of these things again?

Okay, so I had a little time this weekend, and I wanted to play with a couple of things that I haven't had much of a chance with yet: JSP custom tags, and regular expression support in Java. I even had a nice project to use them with: URL-to-Action mappings in Struts, and URL generation in JSP's.

For instance: The action that retrieves a list of entries from the database by section (weblog/articles/galleries) is called SectionListing. So, the URL generated by Struts' link custom tag looks something like: 

http://dreadedmonkeygod.net/home/SectionListing.do?section=articles
This is fine, until I scrap Struts. So really, when I have sections, I want them to be represented in a URL like this: 
http://dreadedmonkeygod.net/home/articles
Much nicer. So, simply put: I wanted to use the full power of regular expressions to map URLs to Actions. I wanted to be able to say 
s/.*\/(\w+)$/SectionListing?section=$1/

Now I can. It's implemented as a Filter, and while it has some serious issues, it works well enough for me to start using it here.

Anyway, I already know of a couple places I need to put the new link-rendering custom tags in (That was the second thing I wanted to learn, remember?), so I'll be going back over the site double-checking everything.

Bottom line: old (*.do) URLs will continue to work for the forseeable future, but I will make no effort to preserve them accross framework transitions.

Not that anyone links to this site anyway. Bleh.

Project Censored reports that Fox News ordered Jane Akre and Steve Wilson to present false and misleading information as fact. They refused, and were fired.

intro:
The web app I'm working on today has two shipping forms: One is a general-purpose shipping form that handles U.S. and international addresses, and has been tested and stable for years. The other is a simplified form custom made for a particular customer.

On Friday, the customer told us they wanted to be able to input international addresses.

No problem! Re-use the existing international form, rewire it to work with the customer's specific needs, and be done with it.

Right?

No.

Because of time pressure, we're going to tweak the custom shipping form so that users can enter non-U.S. countries. This will take a day to complete, and another day to test and debug.

Now, we all know what's going to happen next: the customer is going to try to ship something to, say, CANADA, and notice that there's no way to specify the province. So we'll tweak the form again, taking another day to tweak, test, and debug.

We will go on adding one feature at a time, taking far more time than just re-using the existing intl. shipping form would have, and ending up maintaining two pages that do the same thing slightly differently.

You hear that Mr. Anderson? That is the sound of inevitability. It is the sound of your death. -Agent Smith, "The Matrix"

It's like Sysaphus, but instead of a boulder, we have cruft. We build like crazy under horrendous time pressure, only to find at the end of three years that the product of our efforts needs to be torn down and re-written, but faster this time.

So here's my question: is this inevitable? Are we as software designers and programmers forever doomed to saving a day now by spending a week later?

UPDATE: I've just been informed that in the event that users actually need to use the form to ship to international addresses, they'll be instructed to cram the province name into the second line of the street address. Heaven help you if you live in an apartment in Canada, for we will be unable to enter your address into our system.

*sigh* ... deja vu.

intro:
I went into Barber Volkswagen this evening to get a simple piece of information: what is the interest on the financing available to me to buy my car? (I'm coming to the end of my lease.)

I talked to a salesman named Joel, who is too good a person to be in car sales. Or at least working at Barber Volkswagen.

Joel said that I'd have to get that information from the Finance Manager. No problem. But I had to wait to talk to the finance manager, and when the Finance Manager found out that I hadn't bought my car there, the wait just got longer. After 45 minutes of waiting for the answer to a simple question, I witnessed this scene:

A young salesman came in and told the FM that there was a guy who'd bought a car, and wanted to surprise his wife with it. He wanted to park it on the lot for half an hour, a bring his wife by for a "test drive", and just never come back.

"Eh?" said the FM, "That doesn't make any sense. Did he buy it here?"

"No," said the salesman.

"No way. That's crazy. Let 'im park it somewhere else! Why should we let him park his car here? Tell him to piss off."

Well, the customer had walked in just in time to hear that last bit, and got pretty angry. As it turns out, he had bought the car there just the day before. But here's what really floored me: the FM still didn't want the guy's car on the lot. He said to him, "Why should I agree to that? You already bought the car!"

When the customer informed the FM that he'd be taking his new car elsewhere to be serviced, the FM finally changed his tune, but too late. Mr. Customer stormed out, leaving all the salespeople staring at the FM.

I picked up my keys and wallet and stood up. The FM looked at me and said, "Hold on a sec, I'll get you a contract."

"Nevermind," I answered. "I'm getting hungry, so I'm gonna take off."

"That's it?!" the FM asked.

"Yup. That's it."

I looked at the nice salesman who'd been chatting with me for the last 45 minutes, just trying to keep me happy and grab a few easy comission bucks. "Sorry man," I said, "but he needs to be nicer."

All the FM had to say was, "Sure!" and he'd have had two happy customers. Instead he had a shouting match in the lobby, and lost two customers for that dealership, and I suspect that the other guy will likely never buy another VW after that. I wouldn't.

On the way home, I realized that it might have been fun to tell the FM that I'd walk if he didn't help the guy surprise his wife. But at the time I was just too floored by what an asshole the guy was.

So yeah. Avoid Barber Volkswagen in Ventura. The salesguys are all young and green, which tells me that they've got some serious turnover, and the Finance Manager is a loathesome human being, which tells me why. I'm going to call up my guy at the other dealership and get the papers set.

intro:
Okay, so I said it. Here it is again: EMACS sucks.

EMACS on Windows has its find-file function correct your capitalization as you go, which is great. But it's still bound to a two-keystroke command. So I'm going to go home and make EMACS as I like it. I will rebind C-o to find-file (who needs open-line anyway?), and modify find-file if I can to be case-insensitive.

Hey, what do you know. Two minutes of Googling and here's the necessary mumbling for my .emacs file: 

(global-set-key [?\C-o] 'find-file)
(setq completion-ignore-case 'on)

So yeah, EMACS sucks. The good news is that it only takes two lines of code to make it rule.

Which reminds me: A while back, some friends and I came up with a three-tier system for judging everything. At first we only had two tiers:

  1. Sucks
  2. Rules

But then we realized this wasn't granular enough. So we revised it:

  1. Sucks
  2. Doesn't Suck
  3. Rules

And really, that's as much as I've ever needed. It applies well to software. If something sucks, my job is to make it rule. If it merely doesn't suck, then it goes on the Wish List, and I eventually get to make someone smile by making it rule as well.
title: EMACS Sucks

intro:
Okay, so I'm a coffee snob. Not so much that I'll turn up my nose at even instant coffee, but enough that I know that Starbucks is not the paragon of gormet coffee that most people seem to think it is.

The story so far: my office has just-okay coffee. Not bad, but not great. It's fine. But some of the folks here in the office have decided that double-strength is the way to go. They just double the measure of grounds in the coffee maker. Which means that instead of just-okay coffee, I get a bitter, acidic, worthless cup of undrinkable snot.

I remembered reading an article a while back that stated that the time to brew should be about 4-5 minutes for best extraction. This is true for all beans. It's not the measure of the grounds, or the extraction time that should control flavor; it's the beans and roast.

I finally remembered where I read all that: it was in an article by Natalie MacLean, linked from Girlhacker's Random Log. But if you follow the original link to the article:

http://www.nataliemaclean.com/articles/coffee.html

The article is gone. Too bad. Lost in a redesign, it seems. Why do people feel so free to just ditch old material when they redesign, when presumably the earlier version of the site drew its success from that content?

So anyway, I guess I'm a Web snob too. Once you put a bit of material on the web, people link to it. The URL shouldn't change. So that's why I'm chasing down all the links on DMG generated by Struts' <html:link> that end up looking like blahblah.do?a=1&b=17, and replacing them with custom-written tags such as <dmg:sectionlink> that generate URLs like sections/weblog. Then I just map section/(\w+) to ListEntries.do?section=$1, and I'm done. Next time I write a web app, I just look and see what URLs I need to support, and away I go. So here it is in a nutshell:

Just as procedure declarations are interfaces to your code used by other programs, URLs are interfaces to your site used by other sites. Change them at your peril; 404s piss me off.

Enough! I have actual work to do.
title: Fight Link Rot!

intro:
Okay, so I'm finally going to do what everyone's been telling me to do since I was seven: get an organizer, and use it.

(And don't even start about how I should get a PDA. As far as I'm concerned, the personal day planner is still paper's killer app.)

Trouble is, I'm having trouble finding a good one. Nothing quite meets my (admittedly strict) criteria. And this is important. I can't fudge, or I'll have just wasted my money. I've tried this "getting organized" thing before, you see, and failed every time.

So here are my requirements:

  • Leather. I kill anything softer in weeks.
  • No "luxurious" squishiness. Thin cover. Fuck status symbols, I'm going to have to carry this thing.
  • Size: 8''x5''
  • Loose leaf. I'm going to be adding/removing pages at a frightening rate.
  • Loop for pen.

In a nutshell, I want something as close to my molskine as possible: 8''x5''x¾'', thin covers. I'm not going to get it, but that's the ideal.

That's the cover. Here's what I'm going to put inside:

  • 1yr calendar, 2 pages per week.
  • Ruled pages (otherwise blank) for making lists.
  • Color-coded sections of to-do lists:
    • Blue A: Calls to make.
    • Blue B: Emails to send.
    • Green: Actionable items. (There will be several of these, grouped by context or project: HOME, ERRANDS, AUTOMATED BACKUPS, etc.)
    • Yellow: Items I'm waiting for. (Loan papers from VW, etc.)

The calendar is a snap, but I can't find colored section dividers. And just forget about finding a leather binder at a reasonable price, let alone made to my specs above. This is crap. I'm going to cruise by Staples or something on the way home, and see what they have.

body:
Obviously this is taken from other people's work. However, I had to do some work of my own to put this whole process together, based on the instructions other people provided for slightly different situations. Thanks to other wiki contributors, mailing list participants and other random people whose stuff I found by googling.

This is a thorough walkthrough geared towards the very newbie user. Yes, I know some stuff should go unsaid. Also I wanted this to essentially be a shell script. I've done this on two identical machines now, one with a Rev. B card and one with Rev. A2. I will be doing this on about 5 more identical machines in the next week, and I'll update if I come across a Rev. A1 card.

Note that this CVS source grab was around 26 May 2004. Hopefully nothing will break in the future!

Fresh install of Mandrake 10.0 Official, Download version (i586, 3 CDs). My procedure was to put the entire machine together (including the DWL-G520) and install Mandrake, completely ignoring the card through the entire install process but still having it in the machine. (Mandrake will prompt you on bootup if you've added some new hardware.... I think this screwed me up once when I tried to configure the wifi card through Mandrake's automated procedure. Then again, it might have just been voodoo.) Then, after installation, I run through the following.

1) retrieve madwifi driver source: 

cvs -z3 -d:pserver:anonymous@cvs.sourceforge.net:/cvsroot/madwifi co madwifi

2) switch to root! 

su

3) install linux kernel source from CD (Install CD 3): 

urpmi kernel-source

4) install wireless tools (Install CD 1): 

urpmi libiw wireless-tools

5) create link madwifi will require to compile: 

ln -s /usr/src/linux-2.6.3-7mdk/ /lib/modules/2.6.3-7mdk/build

6) install madwifi: 

cd madwifi
make clean
make
make install

7) create /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-ath0 : 

echo "
STARTMODE=hotplug
DEVICE=ath0
BOOTPROTO=dhcp
NETMASK=255.255.255.0
ONBOOT=yes
WIRELESS=yes
WIRELESS_MODE=Managed
WIRELESS_ESSID=(your ssid here)
#WIRELESS_ENC_KEY=(your wep key here)
WIRELESS_RATE=54M
WIRELESS_IWPRIV=mode 3
MII_NOT_SUPPORTED=yes
" > /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-ath0

NOTES ON THIS STEP:

a) for ssid: put "any" if the machine will be using many access points and/or your AP brodcasts the ssid.

b) If you use WEP, put the WEP key in there and uncomment that line (delete the #).

c) The hotplug might not be necessary, but it works. I'm not sure what the opposite of hotplug would be. Static?

8) change permissions on ifcfg-ath0 (not sure if it's completely necessary but hey, we want all the scripts in that directory to look the same, right?): 

chmod 755 /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-ath0

9) put "'alias ath0 ath_pci'" into /etc/modules.conf and /etc/modules and /etc/modprobe.conf. (I think only one of these is really necessary, but I'm not sure which one. /etc/modules is likely unnecessary.) 

echo "alias ath0 ath_pci" >> /etc/modules.conf
echo "alias ath0 ath_pci" >> /etc/modules
echo "alias ath0 ath_pci" >> /etc/modprobe.conf

10) run depmod depmod

11) Now I usually reboot, although it should work by running "ifconfig ath0 up" or some such. Make sure your wireless router or access point will give out a dhcp address! (I was going nuts the other night trying to get this to work before I realized that the router had hung up and needed to be rebooted.) Also you will want to unplug your wired ethernet so that you can make sure it's all working.

intro:
For a long time, I've wanted to embark on a study of history using Scotch Whisky as a point of departure. Sort of like that Connections series, but starting each episode from the same focal point: Scotch.

For instance, Scotches produced on the coastal islands in Scotland typically have a more "peaty" taste; the farther inland you go, the less they peat the malt. Why? I haven't done much research on this, but I believe the root of the phenominon is that distilling was illegal in Scotland for most of the 17th century. (16th? 15th?) My guess is that something about the peating process makes hard to do on the sly. Maybe it's the time it takes to properly peat a malt, maybe it's the smoke itself. Whatever. The point is: if you're on an island, you know that you're going to see the King's men coming, so you can pretty safely produce Scotch whisky the way God intended: with plenty of peat. But if you're in Edinburg, you'd better keep a low profile, and keep to quietly distilling in the back woods with a minimum of signal fires.

That's my theory anyway. It'd be interesting to see if I'm right.

And it might be fun to do the same thing with coffee. For instance, bags of whole bean coffee are a modern phenomenon. INeedCoffee.com says:

The development of canned coffee was initially considered a luxury and more valuable than the whole bean coffee we value today. It was a convenience to have it roasted for you and then to be able to do nothing more than open a can, measure and brew. Due to poor and lengthy shipping methods, this actually provided an improvement in quality for most consumers.
So Starbucks's emergence isn't coincidence. Until you can ship the beans wherever you need them in perfect condition, you can't even think about tapping into people's laziness and snobbery; they can get better coffee in a big-ass can from their grocery store for two dollars.

The same innovations in shipping (trucks, refrigerator cars) that made local butchers extinct brought you that charred vaguely coffee-ish swill from Starbucks (or a taste of heaven in your kitchen if you buy your beans from a local roaster).

(Now, I'm writing this with a cup of Starbucks coffee in my hand. You're just going to have to reconcile that with the above on your own.)

Anyway, all I'm saying here is that Scotch whiskey and coffee both have long histories, and it would be really interesting to research all the ways in which they've influenced and been influenced by the world around them. But who's got the time? So the best I can do for now is the occasional Google search for "Scotch whisky history".
title: History of Beverages

intro:
Paul Gram has posted an excellent essay on why programmers are so damn touchy about copyright and civil liberties issues, and why legislators should be paying attention. An excerpt:
Why are programmers so violently opposed to these laws? If I were a legislator, I'd be interested in this mystery-- for the same reason that, if I were a farmer and suddenly heard a lot of squawking coming from my hen house one night, I'd want to go out and investigate. Hackers are not stupid, and unanimity is very rare in this world. So if they're all squawking, perhaps there is something amiss.

All I can say is thank God somebody finally said this so well. I've been trying to express this idea for years, to skeptical response.

It may be cool to be a programmer these days, but there are still no cool programmers. We're still odd outsiders who obsess over things our relatives are barely aware of. So when we get worked up over something like copyright, the same old pattern asserts itself. Just like when we talk about movies, or games, or Robot Wars, they tune us out, and make a mental note that copyright is "one of those geek things." So, if we really want to be heard, we're going to have to get off our asses and agitate a bit.
title: Paul Graham on Hackers and Civil Liberties
