intro:
Okay, I'm skeptical about whether the following quote is totally accurate, but if it's even close...

Anyway, here's the quote:

In the summer of 2002, after I had written an article in Esquire that the White House didn't like about Bush's former communications director, Karen Hughes, I had a meeting with a senior adviser to Bush. He expressed the White House's displeasure, and then he told me something that at the time I didn't fully comprehend -- but which I now believe gets to the very heart of the Bush presidency.

The aide said that guys like me were ''in what we call the reality-based community,'' which he defined as people who ''believe that solutions emerge from your judicious study of discernible reality.'' I nodded and murmured something about enlightenment principles and empiricism. He cut me off. ''That's not the way the world really works anymore,'' he continued. ''We're an empire now, and when we act, we create our own reality. And while you're studying that reality -- judiciously, as you will -- we'll act again, creating other new realities, which you can study too, and that's how things will sort out. We're history's actors . . . and you, all of you, will be left to just study what we do.'' -Ron Suskind, for the New York Times

I wonder if that can really be the way it happened, but it's still scary. And it pretty much answers all my questions about how W. can be so blithely sure of himself. He believes the world will realign itself around his will (or maybe His will?), sweeping aside previous complications. it goes along way toward explaining how the current administration can, over and over again, brush aside objections and doubts and inconvenient facts.
title: Empire

intro:
I've decided that Cory Doctorow is saying the things I'd like to say far more eloquently than I ever manage to say them. Which makes sense, because he's, y'know... a writer.

This time he's on about digital video recorders and why getting one from a store just doesn't make sense. Well, technically he's on about why market forces can't act against DRM. Anyway, here's the nutshell:

When he bought the media centre, it did the thing he wanted it to do with the shows he wanted to do it to: it's like buying a VCR to record the World Series, taking it home and satisfying yourself that it works. It worked.

Then, months later, it stopped working. He could no longer record his favorite shows. Why? Well, because the cablecaster decided to remove a right from him. -Cory Doctorow

Which states so beautifully what I've been trying to articulate to parents and friends for years. I won't pay money (up front, and monthly) for a product that will stop working in ways that are important to me whenever the manufacturer wishes it.

Seems to me that the only way to inflict a little "market force" damage is to build your own DVR. I've also seen a few pop up recently that are more like VCRs: just record from TV and burn to DVD. It may be that one of those will fit the bill. Time to do some research.
title: I'm going to stop talking now.

intro:
Slate contributor Andy Bowers has a great write-up on how to get SUV's off California streets. Yes, it's extreme. But if you drive a small car in L.A., you know that something's gotta give.

The nutshell: many big SUV's (Hummers, Suburbans, Escalades, Excursions) exceed the 6000 lb. dividing line between light and heavy trucks. As such, their drivers qualify for tax breaks, and the trucks themselves are exempt from efficiency and safety regulations that govern regular passenger vehicles. But crossing that 6000 lb. mark also makes it illegal to drive these trucks on many CA streets.

So, if we can get the local authorities to enforce the laws that are already on the books, we can start clearing these monsters off the roads. The same owners that claim state and federal tax breaks by classifying their SUVs as "work vehicles" should also be constrained by the regulations on "work vehicles".

I favor regulating big SUVs for the same reasons I favor banning assault rifles: there is no defensible reason to own either one.
title: SUV Kryptonite

"Sure. I can watch DVDs on my computer. It's illegal, but I can do it."

"Because I'm playing it on an unlicenced player that is (legally speaking) cracking the copy protection in order to play the movie. A kid in Norway actually wrote the software, and they tried to put him in jail for it."

Megan McArdle at Instapundit reports that HP has refused to supply her with the necessary drivers for her mother's HP Officejet 5510. intro:
When you go to the polls today, don't forget to ask for a paper ballot. There is plenty of good reason to believe that the electronic voting machines are neither secure or accurate. The EFF is already reporting that voters in at least half a dozen states are having trouble:
Voters discovered the problems when checking the review screen at the end of the voting process. They found, to their surprise, that the machines indicated that they voted for one candidate when they had voted for another. When voters tried to correct the problem, the machine often made the same error several times. While in most cases the situation was reportedly resolved, many voters remain uneasy about whether the proper vote was ultimately cast. Meanwhile, voting experts are concerned that other voters are experiencing the problem, but failing to notice that the machine is indicating the wrong choice on the "summary" screen.

If you're not convinced that paper is the better option, check out the EFF's page on E-Voting.

I want everyone's vote counted today. Pretty please, with sugar on top, vote on paper.
title: VOTE ON PAPER!

For the last few months, I've known that this election would be close, but been in denial as to what that meant: a large percentage of the voters in this country want that treacherous little freak in charge.

Of the Presidential electon of 2000, Dick Cheney said:

"From the very day we walked in the building, a notion of sort of a restrained presidency because it was such a close election, that lasted maybe thirty seconds. It was not contemplated for any length of time. We had an agenda, we ran on that agenda, we won the election--full speed ahead."

Oh. So it's like that.

I'll be stepping up my donations to the ACLU, the Access Fund, and the EFF.

This isn't a case where we don't know what to expect. We know exactly what we're getting. It's time for those of us in the "reality-based community" get realistic about that. So it's full-court press time. Write letters. Donate. Call your Congressmen. Vote. That maniac has 51% of the vote, four years to play in, and no intention of governing from the middle.

I had hoped to write this morning:

Kerry to Bush: "Pardon me, you're in my seat."

Instead, all I can come up with is:

We lost the election. Full speed ahead.

intro:
Okay, so I got impatient last night. Once my computers were set up, I sued to root, and typed in: 
iwlist ath0 scan

This netted a single, gloriously open access point. No encryption. Hell, it even had "default" as the SSID. No worries. Just check my email, post a couple of pics here (after checking the bandwidth to make sure I'm not slamming anyone), then hit the sack.

But no. Oh no, my friends.

I hopped over to ifcfg-ath0, and quickly removed the WEP key and changed the SSID to "default", then typed ifup ath0. And that's where things went wrong.

It turns out that this configuration caused a kernel panic. Everything just stopped. So I rebooted, and got another kernel panic. Booted into fail-safe mode, disabled ath0, and rebooted again. Too late. dmesg reports that 127.0.0.1 couldn't be set up, which I'm guessing is indicative of a completely fubared networking stack. And I couldn't start X.

So it's time to reinstall.

The moral to the story: This is what you get for trying to mooch bandwidth. Karmic vengence is swift and terrible.

The other moral to the story, kids: If you're making configuration changes to your machine, go slow. Baby steps. When you change a network interface configuration, set ONBOOT to no. That keeps you in control. And always have a value for the WEP key, even if it's "". I suspect this was the cause of the kernel panic.

So anyway, dinner with friends tonight, then reinstalling. (Which is exactly how I like to spend my evenings.) I have no interest in figuring this out tonight. I just want my machines working.
title: Well that's what you get.

intro:
Quick disclaimer: I know exactly dick about computer security. So this is just a jumping-off place for my next project.

I'm in my new apartment, and I'm setting up the wireless network. The general plan is to have two access points:

  • 802.11g private access point accessible only to my own machines.
  • 802.11b public access point for visitors, and freeloading neighbors.

Now, once I set this up, I want it secure (duh). So, I need to do the following:

Secure the g network against any and all intruders.
This seems fairly straight forward: MAC address white list, WEP, and non-broadcast SSID. Also, ensure that machines on b network cannot access g network.
Secure the b network against configuration changes, while still allowing open network access.
The plan here is just to have a basic access point with no WEP which broadcasts an inviting SSID. But that puts an aweful lot of pressure on the HTTP authentication which protects the router's adminstration control panel. I remember reading somewhere that HTTP auth. is fairly easy to circumvent, so I'll have to do some more research and see what I can do to lock things down a little better.

More on this when I get rolling.
title: Cracking into Wireless Networks

Prominent on my "heavy rotation" playlist is Beolach. I'm not going to embarass myself trying to describe it, and thankfully I don't have to. You can hear Beolach for yourself here. Especially check out The West Mabou Set.

intro:
The "Intellectual Property Protection Act" is legal sausage: all the undigestible bits from other defeated bills repackaged as something supposedly tastier. It tries to outlaw such nefarious practices as gasp! skipping commercials, and makes no distinction (as all other copyright law does) between accidental and willful infringement. It's a stupid, stupid law. (See also Lawrence Lessig's post on this bill.)

Public Knowledge has an action alert set up where you can let your congressional representatives know your concerns about this law. Here's my letter (salutation and, er... end thingie omitted):

I write to you today to ask that you oppose the omnibus "Intellectual Property Protection Act," both as a whole and in its parts, and respectfully urge you not to support this bill.

I'm a software developer, so I have a dog in this fight too. If the code that I write is pirated, I'm out of a job. Just like all the authors, actors, screenwriters, musicians and artists out there, keeping Intellectual Property protected is vitally important to my livelihood.

The growth of digital music's popularity has spotlighted issues like digital piracy and digital rights management or DRM. DRM has no future: it antagonizes customers while doing nothing to prevent large-scale organized production of high-quality counterfeit product. DRM does not prevent copying; it prevents honest customers from making fair use of digital content.

I applaud Congress and those industries who have sought to address the difficulties of preventing piracy in the digital age. This topic must be discussed if the creative industries are to thrive. But this act serves to reinforce eroding business models in the music and movie industries at the expense of technolgy companies. The answer to the MPAA and RIAA's woes is evolution, not legislation.

If H.R. 2391 is enacted into law, American companies will be reduced to having their lunch money stolen by foreign manufacturers unencumbered by the need to ask Hollywood's permission to include a fast-forward button.

There is too much in "The Intellectual Property Protection Act" that harms market innovation and my rights as a consumer. For the reasons above, I respectfully ask that you oppose H.R. 2391.

Go voice your opinion.
title: Intellectual Property Protection Act

body:
I have now joined the rest of the planet in having a working BitTorrent client. I tried (I really did) to get the original Python client running ages ago, and again last night, but it would only run in "headless" mode. GUI mode coughed and died every time, and I don't know enough about Python to diagnose the problem. All RPM dependencies have been resolved, etc, and the thing still blows chunks. Ick.

So while I was mulling over how to address that issue (which, really, was minor; I have no problem writing a quick wrapper script), I went back to the BoingBoing post about How to never miss an episode with BitTorrent and RSS. The HOWTO page recommended the Azureus Java BitTorrent client. Azureus rocks. Installation was dead easy.

Incidentally, I'm underwhelmed by all the Python-based projects I've come in contact with. I've already mentioned my trouble getting BitTorrent's GUI client working. And I suspect that Straw is just a practical joke. From the Straw home page:

Requires PyGTK, libglade 2.4, gnome-python 2.0, Berkeley DB 3 or 4 and their Python bindings, ADNS library and the corresponding Python binding are highly recommended for smoother operation, but Straw will work without them.

If you were previously running 0.21.2 or older, you also need mxDateTime to convert the straw database to the new format.

I take the above to mean: "Python was absolutely the wrong choice of language for this project, but we got it working anyway by writing a bunch of glue code." Yes, this assessment is completely unfair. Many people seem to like Straw, so I'm probably just missing something.

So who knows what the deal is with this. I'm actually keen to get Straw working, so if I manage it (I did take the time to make sure any and all Python support/development libs were installed when I re-installed last), I'll post about it here. I said once before that I've learned to like frustration, as it means I'm about to learn something. With Straw, I am very, very frustrated.

Anyhoo...

Tonight I wallow in self-pity and write code to automatically detect when my iRiver has been plugged in and auto-sync with my music directory.

intro:
I just want one thing to go right. Actually, no. I want everything to stop going wrong.

Halloween, my car has a rock thrown through the back window.

I have this fixed, and and my local insurance rep tells me that the cost of the rental car is not covered at all. He is wrong, and I now have to submit my bill to get reimbursed.

(Also, while my back window is being replaced, I ask the mechanic to check the battery and alternator, as the car's been slow to turn over. He reports that the contacts were just dirty, cleans them and charges me $60 for the labor. This will come up again later.)

Nov. 6, my car window is broken again. I wisely decide to deal directly with State Farm Insurance, bypassing my local agent. Everything's covered, including the rental car, and they greenlight $2200 in repairs and cleaning for my Jetta.

Two days after taking the car in to be fixed, the mechanic tells me that the car will be ready that night. I leave work early, drop off my rental car, and go to pick up my car. It is, in fact, not ready to be picked up, and will not be for another week. I go back to Enterprise and get another rental car.

In the meantime, I have to move into my new place, using a tiny rental car, and requiring my parents' help. They can't help but try to run things. So Instead of them helping me move, I help them move me. Stress, stress, stress.

Small irritation: I wait around for three hours on the 13th for a tech to come set up my cable modem. The tech does not show.

When my car is finally ready, I double check with the mechanic: I pay my $250 deductible, and they bill State Farm, right? Well, under normal circumstances, yes. But State Farm has decided to mail me a check. Which has not arrived yet. So the car is ready, but I can't pick it up, because I don't have $2200 lying around. The check arrives two days later.

When I drop off the rental car, State Farm declines to cover any of the cost, since I "already dropped off the rental that's attached to this incident." I'm still trying to straighten this out.

When I do get my car back, the cleaners have missed a spot. It still smells like egg inside.

In the meantime, I've started swimming again, which is great. But it starts another sinus infection. I wait a few days, but when the infection moves into my chest, I go to the doctor, who prescribes Biaxin, an antibiotic. The cure may be worse than the disease: I'm hungry all the time, but food is disgusting for a good 8 hours after I take the pills. After three days of this, I'm just taking it on faith that this will get me healthy faster than just waiting would have.

After work today, my car had trouble starting. Battery's weak. But it does turn over, and I go to pick up a friend for a dinner party in Encino, after calling the host and verrifying that he has jumper cables so we won't get stranded. The only spot remotely near her place is in front of a fire hydrant, but (famous last words) I'm just going to be a minute. Of course, once I've parked, the car will not start again. We take her car to dinner.

So, four days after picking up my car from the shop, and just three weeks after both the battery and alternator were specifically checked, my car will not start. Battery's completely dead. When we get back from dinner, we try to push the car to a new spot, but cannot because I'm parallel parked, and I'm not strong enough to push the car up away from the curb. So, I am now stuck parked in front of a fire hydrant. I may be ticketed overnight, and there's nothing I can do. The note I left on my car reads: "Battery is dead. Please have mercy."

When I get home, the lightbulb in my bedroom lamp burns out. Since I just moved in, I have no spares. But my phone is now charging.

So tomorrow, I get to call AAA to get a jump for my car, then deal with the dealership and have a new battery put in. And if they can fix my car quickly, I get to go argue with my insurance agent and get all my reimbursements straightened out. So yeah, I'm calling in sick. I'm cleaning up this mess once and for all.
title: I'm just going to rant for a bit.

intro:
As noted yesterday, I thought that something in the "read entire post" links was causing posts to be noted as "updated" by feed agregators. That's exactly what's happening.

The reason is that I'm using a subclass of Struts' html:link tag to generate that link, and the link tag automatically inserts a session ID at the end of URLs, like so:

http://yaddayadda/archive/221;jsessionid=af-fmvZ6KHJe

Every time the agregator visits this page, a new Session ID is generated and appended to the URL. So every time the agregator visits, it looks like I've changed that link, so the agregator flags that post as "updated".

I should have a fix for this in tonight.
title: Found the Bug

intro:
Just hopped from Everything Burns to JWZ's post about his new Roomba. This ammused me:
It doesn't follow any kind of easily-discernable pattern when tooling around the room, so it's kind of hard to guess how long it'd have to run before there was a statistical likelihood that the whole room had been vacuumed. There might be some spots it never found, but I'm not sure. (It's a Heisenvacuum!)

Why it doesn't build a map, I have no idea. Reminds me of a web demo I sat in on for a product that advertises itself as a general purpose file conversion tool for getting flat file, XML, and EDI data into your database. The trouble is that it was originally written strictly as an EDI processor, and so has to convert everything to EDI before it can process it. So if your trading partners want to do some kind of funky file format that doesn't map to an EDI standard, you're hosed. Why not just build a general-purpose mapper and be done?1

Same with the Roomba. Seems easy enough to keep track of the places you've been, the layout of the room, and especially store the location of the base station. The first thing a robot ought to be able to do is find its way home.

Anyway, Popular Science did a pretty good round-up of the robo-vacuums a while back. Looks like none of them are really ready for prime time, but hey, we're moving forward.

1. To be fair, they seem to be embarking on a serious effort to re-work the product, and the reworked sections seem very strong. In a year or two they should have a rockin' piece of software.

While checking out options for my new A/V setup, I stumbled on CinemaNow.com, which offers legal movie downloads. Very cool. But, being a Linux guy (and a firebreathing DRM hater), I have to make sure that I'll be able to actually watch the movies. So I go digging through their FAQ and hit this:

Q: Can I watch on a Mac?
A: No. Unfortunately, you can not currently watch any of the PREMIUM or PAY-PER-VIEW films. This is because of a compatibility issue with the Digital Rights Management (DRM) we use to securely deliver our content.

So they're willing to summarily ditch all non-Windows users, a fair portion of the early adopters out there. Not smart.

And their selection bites. So they can't take advantage of the long tail. Really not smart.

So it looks like Netflix is still the way to go for this kind of thing. Which is sad, really.

This tour through two of Japan's top console gaming stores almost makes me wish I were into video games again. Two stores, both world-class console gaming hotspots, within 100 yards of each other, crowded with gaming geeks of all stripes. Game geek Nirvana. Kinda makes me wish I were into that stuff again, just to enjoy that energy. I used to sit for hours mastering all the moves for SNES version of Street Fighter II, and happily spend entire Saturdays working my way through Super Mario Bros. 3.

The problems: cash and time. I hate when a serious (and continuing) dollar investment is necessary to enjoy something. That's part of why I got out of Magic: The Gathering. And I've long since abandoned comic books. Hearing the word "mint" in any sense other than "mint chocolate cookie" (Mmm...cookies...) makes me cringe.

I can't wait 'till Netflix gets it together and starts offering games. I've been eyeballing a used PS2 for a while, but I just can't bring myself to spend $50 per game. (Then again, all my favorites are either in the $10 bin or are actually PS1 titles.)

Anyway, the stores are jaw-droppingly cool. Stores here in the US just don't seem to ever hit this level. About the closest I've seen is Golden Apple Comics in L.A. (Forbidden Planet in London was kick-ass.) I love the over-crowded store that has everything. And two-story shops are just kick-ass, no matter what they're selling.

I grabbed my ankles that one last time, but it gave me plenty of incentive to try fixing a busted blinker myself. Turns out it was extremely easy. Not even a replacement part needed.

Evil Tim helped me get the headlight assembly under control, and once we popped the blinker light out, it was obvious what was causing the problem: one of the contacts on the bulb was fried. Well, almost fried. Tim cleaned off some of the corosion, and the bulb started working again. Should last long enough for me to order a replacement.

The downside: I'm a dumbass and forgot to write down the part number while I had it out. It is not the same bulb that the manual at Kragen indicated. So I may end up popping out the bulb again just to get a look at the part number. Annoying, but not cause for gnashing of teeth or anything.

intro:
When I got home last night, I spent a little time reading, and then decided to spend some time thinking and writing. It started like this:
Okay, since I'm in a self-examining kind of mood, and since I'm exactly the kind of drama queen to examine myself in public, I'm going to steal a page from overworked & underf*cked, which is about the funniest blog I've seen, and go through someone else's list of vaguely introspective questions.

Now, the good news is that overworked & underf*cked is genuinely the funniest blog I've seen in a while. I think the last one that made me cackle like this was a "diary" on Kuro5hin, back when I used to hang around over there.

The other good news is that despite being a drama queen (in my own small quiet way) I did not actually post. It was neither especially entertaining nor enlightening, and some of what's there is pretty personal, and not really fit for public viewing. I have my faults, same as anyone, but I know when to keep the self-analysis to myself.

But, since I took the time to write it, I might as well run it up the flagpole, so to speek. I've snipped out the saucier bits and put them in a laquer box by my bed.

intro:
Earlier, Cory Doctorow took issue with Wired Magazine's "soft on DRM" position. Chris Anderson, Editor-in-Chief of Wired Magazine, responded. And now Doctorow has completely evicerated Anderson's argument that a "realistic" attitude is necessary re. DRM.

All of that makes great reading. But Cory's punchline is my favorite bit:

WARNING: THIS DEVICE'S FEATURES ARE SUBJECT TO REVOCATION WITHOUT NOTICE, ACCORDING TO TERMS SET OUT IN SECRET NEGOTIATIONS. YOUR INVESTMENT IS CONTINGENT ON THE GOODWILL OF THE WORLD'S MOST PARANOID, TECHNOPHOBIC ENTERTAINMENT EXECS. THIS DEVICE AND DEVICES LIKE IT ARE TYPICALLY USED TO CHARGE YOU FOR THINGS YOU USED TO GET FOR FREE -- BE SURE TO FACTOR IN THE PRICE OF BUYING ALL YOUR MEDIA OVER AND OVER AGAIN. intro:
Chris Anderson, author of my latest favorite article, has put up a rebuttal to Cory Doctorow's post on BoingBoing calling Wired "soft on DRM".

As a small note in that rebuttal, he makes an argument that I've heard over and over again in defense of DRM: that the success of the iPod is evidence that the public doesn't mind DRM so much.

I disagree. I think that the iPod has succeeded because it's a beautiful tool that supports the most popular digital music format: the MP3. I think that the vast majority of storage on the iPods around the world is used to hold DRM-less MP3 files.

Now, this is just my theory. I'd love to see hard data that would disprove/support it. I have a few questions to start:

  • How much music (in GB) has the average iTunes customer purchased?
  • Would that fill an average iPod?
  • What does that say about why people buy iPods?
title: iPod's success proof of DRM acceptance?

11:20pm EST... +190. Cliff called Evil Homer. It's a made up game in a variation of Stud and Chicago. The lowest spade in the hole chops the pot with the high in a seven card stud format. However, the only change is this... the Jack of Spades is the Evil Homer card. If you get that as one of your down cards, before the last round of betting, you have to jump up and do the Evil Homer dance. Afterwards, you are able to remove cards from your opponents hands. You select one card you want to get rid of... say you pick Aces... and everyone that has an ace has to muck it and only use the rest of the cards in their hand.

One of my buddies used to invent games while he was sitting in class all week, and we'd try 'em out on Friday night. Man, that guy was inventive. He had one called "Pyramid Scheme" that was great fun, but we all forgot it over one summer, so it's lost to time. (Too bad, too. I bought a couple of CDs with my winnings from that semester.)

intro:
After a week of suffering with knots in my back and a stiff neck that wouldn't resolve itself, I finally broke down and got a massage, and I'm really glad I did.

Not only was she able to release the tension in my neck and back, she also helped with my knee. I'd told her I'd been running, and when I mentioned some knee trouble, she immediately went looking for and found the muscle in my let that's probably causing it. I didn't fully understand, but apparantly there's a line of muscle and tendon that runs from the base of your spine over the top of your hip and down the outside of your leg. Tension in that system can cause problems with your knee properly distributing force. (Or something like that. There were a lot of terms I'm going to have to look up in Gray's Anatomy.)

Anyway, she worked on my hip, my leg, and my back and shoulders, and reminded me to stretch regularly. In other words: I went in hoping to get my neck fixed, and got my knee righted for free.

We also talked about a lot of other stuff, which I why I mention any of this at all. There are a lot of negative associations with massage. People think it's new-age fru-fru bullshit. People think it's sexual. People think it's for the yacht and polo crowd. None of this is true. Massage therapists are healers. This is why every team on the Tour de France has a massage therapist on staff to work on the riders. This is why insurance companies will cover chiropractic adjustment and massage after you get in an auto accident.

I think mainstream doctors have much to learn from these people. In all my years carrying stress in my neck and shoulders, only one doctor has recommended massage. The rest just push codine and muscle relaxants and get me out of the office. The best doctors (and I'm finding my collection) recognize that they can be more than mere technicians.
title: Healers

I'd forgotten about Ned Batchelder's article about Deleting Code. It's a topic that's near and dear to my heart. Less code translates directly into fewer bugs.

Over the weekend, I deleted a bit of DMG: the "Sections" implementation. I used to assign each entry a Section and a Topic. (It hasn't been visible for a while; the last remaining vestiges were the "Galleries" links in the sidebar and a few admin functions that were only visible to me.) No more. It's gone. And I don't mean "gone" in the sense of "invisible to the user." I mean gone. All related code, columns and tables have been removed completely. grep -i section `find . -name "*.java" -name "*.jsp"` returns zero rows.

Tonight, as an experiment, I'm moving all "attachment" images into the database. Having them stored in a directory within the web app is a mistake, and having them in a directory outside the web app is only marginally better: I'd rather have all content in one place: the DB. I'm curious to do some benchmarking and see what effect it has on disk usage, performance, etc.

I spent most of this weekend helping some friends of mine move into their first house, which was great fun. All in all, this was a very smooth move. Pro movers for the furniture, friends for the small stuff, and much fun was had by all. But it stilll got me thinking (being a geek) about what could be done to make the next move go even more smoothly.

We spend a lot of time asking/answering the question, "Where do you want this?", so that's an obvious bottleneck. Others were more subtile. I have let my hatred of repetitive labor guide my judgement. Some of the things that would have been really handy:

  • A color-coded map of the new house. (Kitchen is blue, den orange, etc.)
  • Cardboard boxes (lots of them) in bright colors to match the map. (All the orange boxes go in the den!)
  • Colored sticky tags for furniture. (The stickum should leave no residue when removed, even after getting rained on, baked in the sun, etc.)
  • Boxes pre-packed with dividers to hold glasses, plates, and other breakables. Also, preformed boxes to hold CDs, DVDs, and LPs.
  • Boxes with padded sides to hold things like DVD players, receivers, speakers.

So the end result, ideally, is that you have just about everything packed ahead of time. On the day of the move, you pack up your bedclothes, bathroom, refrigerator contents, etc. When the movers arrive, you hand them each a colored map to the new abode, and then you're free to handle items like, "How are we going to get your California king bed into the upstairs bedroom?" rather than being a traffic cop all day.

I'm sure someone, somewhere has already done this, but I haven't seen it.

And now, it's lunchtime.

So anyway, after that (and a couple cups of coffee), I was feeling pretty good, and decided to get about moving gallery images for this site from the filesystem to the database. I hit my milestone for the night (storing and retrieving images) and then checked the clock: it was nearly 2am, and I have to be awake and at work in seven hours. What did I do? I warmed up my coffee, and responded to a few emails that I needed to get to. I'd nearly forgotten how relaxing late-night hacking can be.

So anyway, I can now attach any file I want to any blog entry, as long as the file is under 16MB. It can be a jar file, a jpg, a pdf, whatever. It's way better than cramming things onto the disk. (Though I have zero information on performance.) And it'll stop the problem of images getting lost when I update the web application that runs this site.

Originally, I put uploaded images on the disk where the web server could get at them. The simplest place seemed like a spot under the web app that runs this blog. I realized that the images would get blown away every time I uploaded a new version of the web app, but I really didn't worry. "I'll be careful," I said.

Now, whenever you find yourself saying, "I'll be careful each time," that's a sign of trouble. Humans are bad at being careful each time. Sooner or later we screw up, so it's good to have a warning signal to let us know we've made a mistake. But in this case putting in the warning system would be more work than fixing the problem properly, so I let it go. I just didn't feel like fixing it at the time. intro:
Okay, so it's been a while since I used XML and XSLT, but I'm starting a project using XML, so I have to get my act together (again). I'm doing the quick refresher with O'Reilly's XML in a Nutshell, which is excellent. But as everything comes back to me, I find my self thinking, "Oh, right. Now I remember why this sucked." Here's a great example: On page 171, we note that some XPath functions can accept any number of arguments:
For example, concat("a", "b", "c", "d") returns "abcd".
Nothing new there. I file away the concat operator in my memory banks in case I need it. Then I see:
id('p342 p4567') indicates both Alan Turing and Richard Feynman's person elements.

So, concat() takes multiple arguments, but id() takes just one, which then has multiple values parsed out. WTF?

I'd prefer the following:

id("p342", "p4567") indicates both Alan Turing and Richard Feynman's person elements.

This is a small thing, but stupid inconsistencies like this grate on me. Wasn't someone watching the big picture, making sure some kind of sanity prevailed? Guess not.

Yes, this is my "this language should have been strangled at birth" moment. I'll get over it. I did last time. I do every time I learn a new language. It's part of the learning curve. I hereby resolve not to let XML, XSLT, and XPath get swapped out of my brain ever again, or I may actually strangle someone.
title: Purest Stupidity

For the purposes of demonstration, here's the relevant snippet from my RSS feed: 
<item>

  <description>
  <![CDATA[ 
        File Under: mlp
        <p>
        <a href="http://www.crypto.com/papers/safelocks.pdf">Safecracking
        for the Computer Scientist</a>
  ]]> 
  </description>
  <pubDate>Fri, 14 Jan 2005 10:22:55 PST</pubDate> 
  </item>
<item>

And here's the relevant XSLT snippet: 

<xsl:template match="item">
 <div class="entry">
   <div class="title">
     <a href="{link}"><xsl:value-of select="title" /></a>
   </div>
   <div class="entrymetainfo">
     Posted <xsl:value-of select="pubDate" />
   </div>
   <div class="entrycontent">
     <xsl:value-of select="description" disable-output-escaping="yes" />
   </div>
 </div>
</xsl:template>

This works using the org.apache.xalan.xslt.Process XSLT processor, and using IE. I see:

Cool Paper on Safecracking and Locks
Posted Fri, 14 Jan 2005 10:22:55 PST
File Under: mlp

Safecracking for the Computer Scientist

But it does not work in Firefox. I get the contents of the description tag dumped onto the page as a litteral:

Cool Paper on Safecracking and Locks
Posted Fri, 14 Jan 2005 10:22:55 PST
File Under: mlp <p> <a href="http://www.crypto.com/papers/safelocks.pdf">Safecracking for the Computer Scientist</a>

According to this page, which repeats thoughts I've seen elsewhere, this is a known bug in Firefox:

The [template] is using the disable-output-escaping attribute, which adjusts how an XSLT serialiser should output a document. However, firefox is not using an XSLT serialiser -- it passes the result tree directly to the layout code.

Well...meh.

So, at the end of the day, I can't get what I want. My grand plan was to have an XSL stylesheet for my RSS feed that made it look just like the rest of the site, with header graphics, sidebar, everything. (This is primarily a learning excercise, remember. So why not go crazy?) But I guess I'll just have to settle for a human-readable warning that "You've wandered backstage, kiddo."

Or maybe it's time to start contributing to the Firefox project.

intro:
One morning, a rider knocked on the smithy's door. "I need a new shoe for my horse, and hurry!"

The smithy usually made nails. He had a gig that helped him make them faster than anyone else. He could make a thousand nails a day.

But he had no such gig for shoes. He could only make two horseshoes a day.

After a moment's thought, the smithy realized that if he built a gig to help make shoes, he could make ten shoes in a day. But building the gig would take all day, and the rider was impatient.

By lunchtime, the shoe was made and the rider was off, and the smithy returned to making nails.

The next day, the rider needed another shoe for his horse. And again the smithy spent half a day making the shoe.

This continued until the smithy had made four new shoes for the rider's horse. Each time, the smithy decided it was easier to spend half a day making a shoe than all day building the gig, plus an hour making a shoe.

Had he spent the first day making the gig, he could have made all four shoes in just half a day more. (And spent the other half making five hundred nails!)

He was too foolish to see that a rider who asks for one shoe will eventually need three more.
title: The Smithy and the Horseshoes

intro:
Dave Shea has posted a quick note on the trade-offs between Redundancy and Dependency when using CSS.

I've made the choice in my own CSS templates to code for redundancy. As Shea says, it's usually easier to maintain, and I hate that moment where you realize a given element is being unintentionally affected by some other rule. Which rule? No idea. I haven't seen a tool yet that lets you select an element in your HTML page and see what CSS rules apply to it, in what order. That would rock.

(Admittedly, it's been a while since I used anything besides EMACS or Dreamweaver to write HTML. I tried Bluefish a while back, but found it so sluggish it was unusable. Maybe it's time for another look.)

But I digress.

My other weapon against unmaintainability is really simple: smart class naming. I define class names and IDs to very closely match the data they represent. I'll never name a class something like smallred. Instead, I'll call it something like formadvice or footnotewarning.

Of course, my favorite solution goes like this: Even though browsers ignore tags they don't support, that doesn't mean those tags shouldn't be eligible to be styled. Unrecognised tags should behave like a <span> tag with no attributes. I ought to be able to invent a <posttitle> tag, and then have a rule like this in my stylesheet: 

posttitle {
  display: block;
  font-size: 1.2em;
  font-weight: bold;
  border-bottom: 1px solid #555;
}

That'd be pretty cool. But I'm sure it breaks some theory somewhere, so it'll never happen.

And again, I digress.

I really have no idea where this is going. I'm going through a phase where I'm really thinking about "how nice it would be if..." or "how this really ought to work is...", rather than "what tools exist to...".

Okay, I'm done.

Wait, no. I really like the way del.icio.us uses bookmarked JavaScript scriptlings to post links. I will definitely have to build something like that for my quicklinks section. (Actually, no. I think I'm going to scrap "quicklinks" in favor of just having that feature be "Powered by del.icio.us", like my blogroll is "Powered by Bloglines".)

Okay, now I'm done.
title: Redundancy vs. Dependency

intro:
Ned Batchelder points to a post by Ian Bicking which discusses the subtleties of catch-all exception handling. Ian notes that "just catching everything" is considered an anti-pattern.

Their discussion of the topic is more than ample; I won't bore you by repeating their thoughts.

I offer a warning, however. Novice programmers (and a few high-priced consultants) should note the following code, and remember it well: 

catch (Exception e) {
    return null;
}

To paraphrase O-Ren Ishii: The price of writing code that ignores exceptions and returns null is I collect your fscking head.

Are we clear on this? Good. Carry on.
title: More on Trade-Offs

intro:
I ordered a really great living room set about two months ago. The sofa and accent chair arrived promptly, but I'm still waiting for an ottoman and chair.

The store called a couple weeks ago, said the chair was in, and scheduled a delivery. Instead of a chair, I got an ottoman with no feet. (I refused delivery.) The delivery guy said the chair was backordered until the 27th, but a nice lady working the telephone line happily scheduled a Jan 22 delivery for the chair and the ottoman (even after I reminded her that the chair was backordered). When I went to the store to make sure that everything would arrive, the guy there straightened everything out. I'll have my chair and my ottoman on Feb 6. (I hope.)

I also ordered a couple of counter chairs a month ago (from a different store). They were supposed to take 7-10 days to arrive. After two weeks, I called the shop, who told me that they'd written down the wrong part number. I went to the shop, showed them the catalogue I'd ordered from, and proved that they had the right part number. They said that my chairs would arrive in a week.

Two weeks later, I stopped in to raise hell and see where my chairs were. They were in the back of the shop, waiting. "Didn't you get our call?" they asked.

No, no I didn't.

I take the chairs home, and put them together. Well, I try to put them together. The parts are so badly made that I have to do a little shoving just to get the bolts to line up. And then I notice that several of the pieces simply don't fit, and never will. They're cheap chairs, sure. I don't expect Ethan Allen. But I do expect Ikea.

(By the by, my Black & Decker cordless drill laid waste to all it surveyed. I had the chair together--as much as possible--in about two minutes.)

So I take the chairs (one assembled, one in pieces) back to the store. The sales woman tells me, "Oh, I'll have our guys look at it. They're very good; I'm sure they'll be able to--"

"No", I say. "I'd really rather just get a refund."

Now, somebody explain this to me. Is this par for the course with furniture stores? Why are the smartest people working for these places the delivery guys? Why the hell aren't these guys promoted? All the "blue collar" folks I've talked to in the process of getting my apartment set up have been models of professionalism: smart, capable, and on-time. But the call center folks, dispatchers, distributors, etc. have all been brain-dead.

So anyway, yeah. Tomorrow I go shopping for counter chairs again, so maybe sometime this year I can stop eating off my computer desk.

A while back, Chris Anderson argued that the success of the iPod is evidence that consumers don't mind DRM. (Michael Gartenberg has argued similarly.) I disagreed, hypothesizing that the number of DRM-protected AAC files played on iPods was insignificant next to the number of MP3s.

Robert X. Cringely's column from Jan 27 seems to support this hypotheses:

Apple has sold 250 million songs to date and has sold 10 million iPods. That's 25 songs per iPod...

Last I checked, I had something like 2200 songs on my 20GB MP3 player. That's a landslide of non-DRM music making its way onto players. A scant 25 songs hardly constitutes consumer acceptance of DRM.

Wired News reports that whoever's running Napster is a moron.

Actually, Wired didn't say that. At least, not as bluntly.

Napster has launched a new service that'll let users download as many songs as they like for $15 a month. The songs expire thirty days after you stop paying Napster's monthly fee. All that stuff you downloaded? Gone. All that money you spent? That's gone too. If you want to be able to burn those tracks to CD, you'll have to pay the regular rate of $1 per track.

Screw that. I'll order the CD used from Amazon for $8, and skip the DRM.

intro:
I'm going to submit this to Cool Tools, but I thought I'd post it here first.

Product: Timbuk2 Messenger Bag

Available at: Timbuk2.com

I've had my bag for 9 years. I have the "Deedog" model, from back when they still gave the bags names. Now they just come in S/M/L/XL. It has survived 4 years of all-day, every-day college use and 4 years of civilian life. It's been through rain and snow, it's been dropped in the mud, stepped on, run over by bicycles, and chewed by dogs, and still looks almost brand new. This thing is indestructible. I take it on every plane trip I go on, and every time I do, someone asks me about it. "Dude, cool bag. Where'd you get it?"

Oh, and even after nearly a decade of being loaded with heavy stuff, the strap is still stiff and distributes weight nicely. Fully loaded, the bag still feels light. I've carried books, computers, clothes, even groceries for miles in complete comfort.

And the whole thing is designed to stow securely on your back for bike riding. The length of the main strap can be adjusted, and there's a secondary strap that clips under your left arm to keep everything in place. (Check out their "How to Wear" page for the visual aid.)

After I got my bag, both my roommates were impressed enough to buy their own, and as far as I know, all three of us still use them regularly.

The Timbuk2 website lets you build your own bag, including colors, fabrics, accessories, and whether you want a right- or left-handed bag. (Handedness affects where the adjustment handle for the main strap is.)

I haven't tried any of the accessories they offer, but if I get the Powerbook I'm eyeballing, I might just have to spring for a quilted laptop sleeve.

This bag has not only kept me satisfied for nearly a decade, it's kept me from even considering another bag. If I didn't already have one, I'd be jealous. If, somewhere down the road, this bag gets lost or stolen (I'm convinced it'll never wear out), I'm just going to head right back to Timbuk2 and get another one.

intro:
The technique is really, really simple. The basic idea is that you find a domain that you want to impersonate, say www.paypal.com, and you substitute out one or more of the letters for a letter from another language that looks just the same, but has a different binary representation. Here's the example from the Shmoo Group's description: 
http://www.pаypal.com/
To a computer, this is totally different from www.paypal.com. But what you see is: 
http://www.pаypal.com/

This "duplicate" name can be used to obtain SSL certificates, which makes this really scary.

Acording to the official notice, this seems to affect all major browsers except IE. There is no known workaround for Opera or Safari.

The (cribbed from BoingBoing) workaround in Mozilla/Firefox is:

  1. Goto your Firefox address bar. Enter about:config and press enter. Firefox will load the (large!) config page.
  2. Scroll down to the line beginning network.enableIDN -- this is International Domain Name support, and it is causing the problem here. We want to turn this off -- for now. Ideally we want to support international domain names, but not with this problem.
  3. Double-click the network.enableIDN label, and Firefox will show a dialog set to 'true'. Change it to 'false' (no quotes!), click Ok. You are done.
  4. Go check out the shmoo demo again and notice it no longer works.
title: Nasty New Phishing Attack

intro:
John Gruber has posted an excellent analysis on why Napster To Go is just dumb.

What really caught my attention, though, was an angle I hadn't thought about.

Since the iPod dominates the player market, any music download service is going to have to work with the iPod. The only workable way to do that is to offer straight, DRM-free MP3 files.

So let's say I want to offer a music download service. The RIAA won't play ball without DRM, but DRM locks me out of the iPod market. The only way to go is to court the indy labels who might be willing to treat digital distribution the way it ought to be treated: a superior option to both iTunes and piracy.

Everyone's watching the majors. I wonder what the indies are up to?
title: John Gruber on Napster To Go

intro:
I used to get sick maybe once a year. But over the past six months or so, I've had real trouble staying healthy. I've gotten sick again, and again, and again, and again. It seems that every time I get back in my groove, I get knocked down again.

So I'm rethinking the L.A. Marathon. I'm putting it where it really ought to be: second priority, behind getting healthy and staying healthy. I'm just getting over this cold. I slept thirteen hours Friday night, and 12 hours Saturday night, so my body clearly needs the rest. I'm not whole again yet. And the race is just three weeks away. So I'm going to call my friend who I was going to run with and let him know I won't be running that Sunday, but I'll be there to cheer him on and hang out with everyone at the finish line.

This time next year, I'll be at my target weight, running like I know I can, and stronger than ever. But right now I'm starting from square one again. A weekly routine of two short runs, two trips to the gym, never more than 45 minutes. The first month is dedicated solely to getting back into the rhythm of working out. No hard stuff, no pushing my limits.

I hate this. When I registered for the Marathon, it seemed a little crazy. I wasn't sure I could do it. Then, as my weekly runs stretched out from five miles to seven, to nine, and more, I felt better and better, I realized that 26.2 miles was a reachable goal. I knew that when the day came, I could keep putting one foot in front of the other for as long as it took.

But now I have to acknowledge that a Marathon on March 6th is out of reach. I might be able to finish in a kamakaze dash, but I'd just end up sick and in pain. I have to re-lay the foundation that all those double-digit runs were built on. So I'm going running tonight: three miles, slowly. Target time is 35 minutes.

I'll keep y'all posted.
title: Rethinking my Priorities

intro:
I used to get sick maybe once a year. But over the past six months or so, I've had real trouble staying healthy. I've gotten sick again, and again, and again, and again. It seems that every time I get back in my groove, I get knocked down again.

So I'm rethinking the L.A. Marathon. I'm putting it where it really ought to be: second priority, behind getting healthy and staying healthy. I'm just getting over this cold. I slept thirteen hours Friday night, and 12 hours Saturday night, so my body clearly needs the rest. I'm not whole again yet. And the race is just three weeks away. So I'm going to call my friend who I was going to run with and let him know I won't be running that Sunday, but I'll be there to cheer him on and hang out with everyone at the finish line.

This time next year, I'll be at my target weight, running like I know I can, and stronger than ever. But right now I'm starting from square one again. A weekly routine of two short runs, two trips to the gym, never more than 45 minutes. The first month is dedicated solely to getting back into the rhythm of working out. No hard stuff, no pushing my limits.

I hate this. When I registered for the Marathon, it seemed a little crazy. I wasn't sure I could do it. Then, as my weekly runs stretched out from five miles to seven, to nine, and more, I felt better and better, I realized that 26.2 miles was a reachable goal. I knew that when the day came, I could keep putting one foot in front of the other for as long as it took.

But now I have to acknowledge that a Marathon on March 6th is out of reach. I might be able to finish in a kamakaze dash, but I'd just end up sick and in pain. I have to re-lay the foundation that all those double-digit runs were built on. So I'm going running tonight: three miles, slowly. Target time is 35 minutes.

I'll keep y'all posted.
title: Rethinking my Priorities

intro:
I have two tech support stories today. This is the first.

My dad was moving some stuff around in his home office, and accidentally unplugged a few power cords, which were connected to the DSL modem and wireless router. When he plugged everything back in, his laptop couldn't connect to the net.

So he calls up Yahoo SBC (the DSL provider), and asks for a hand getting things up again. The helpful techie walks him through the process of hooking up an ethernet cable to his laptop and configuring it to talk directly to the DSL modem. Further, the techie tells my dad that the 802.11g router will have to be completely reconfigured, and that my dad will have to talk to Netgear for help with that.

So the Netgear 802.11g router is now effectively a dead stick. Unnecessarily so, as we'll see.

At this point, my dad calls me and fills me in on what happened, and asks if maybe I could come by a little early for dinner on Sunday to get things fixed up properly. No problem, Dad.

I arrive for dinner, and go through the Standard Operating Procedure for this situtation:

  1. I unplug the 802.11g router.
  2. I unplug the DSL modem.
  3. I plug in the DSL modem, and wait 20 seconds for it to settle.
  4. I plug in the 802.11g router, and let it settle.

Once I did that, happy thoughts started appearing on computer screens throughout the house: "Connected to Office Network. Signal Strength: Excellent."

My question is: how come the techie didn't try this right off? Five minutes, and you're fixed.

So I showed my parents the process above, which I hope will be helpful. I even unplugged everything all over again, which kind of freaked them out ("No! You just got it working!"), but I find that really doing the whole thing breaks down their fear of breaking stuff. So hopefully they're not only aware of what to try when something like this happens, they'll be comfortable actually doing it.

So, um...yeah. That's tech support story #1.

I've been that way all my life. I can get the basics verbally, the details visually, but to really grok something I need to tinker with it (debate and discussion count as tinkering). I think this is a big part of why I'm in computers: they're a tinkerer's wonderland.

...thou canst not Plumb its [UNIX's] Mysteries by mere Study but must become One with it through Practice. The true Way to the Knowledge of the Source is not the timid and footling way of the Student, but the Divine Foolery of the Hacker. body:
The Trouble

The Trouble started when I noticed that "request URL" that my code here on the server sees isn't necessarily what was actually requested by the browser. If you use dreadedmonkeygod.net as the domain name, the server still thinks you asked for www.dreadedmonkeygod.net.

You can see this in action here. See? Your browser thinks the url is:

http://dreadedmonkeygod.net/home/cookies.jsp
But the server thinks the URL is:
http://www.dreadedmonkeygod.net/home/cookies.jsp

And this is a Problem Because... ?

Normally, this is not a problem. Server code shouldn't care what server it's running on, and mine doesn't.

However, while I don't care what the host name is, I do need the server and the browser to agree on what the host name is. Whatever they agree on is fine, so long as they agree. Pointing your browser to dreadedmonkeygod.net will cause trouble, because the server still thinks you're talking to www.dreadedmonkeygod.net.

The support tech explained that this is due to the way that the server handles virtual hosting, and there's really no good way to fix it.

(While I suspect that this is, in fact, fixable, I respect his judgement that it's not worth the time it would take to fix it. I pay a rediculously small fee for their hosting services, and I suspect I'm the only customer who has noticed the problem.)

So the problem won't go away; I have to deal with it head-on. The crux of the problem, very specifically, is that I need the host name in the <base href> tag in the header of every page to agree with the host name in the actual request URL1.

The Workaround

So, there are several ways to make the base tag and the actual request URL agree:

  1. Don't specify a host name in the base tag. That should work for my purposes. But it doesn't. All the links on the pages work correctly, but links to stylesheets do not, for some reason. I'm not inclined to spend an evening reading up on the subtleties of of the base and link tags, so I looked elsewhere for a solution.
  2. Write the base tag using JavaScript, which runs on the client, and will have clear access to the actual URL of the page. Not a bad idea, but text-only browsers tend to choke on stuff like this, so I gave it a pass.
  3. Write a quick five-line snip of JavaScript to ensure the client is looking at www.dreadedmonkeygod.net, since that's what the server is going to see anyway. (They need to agree, so I'll make 'em agree.)
  4. Go through all my templates and insert absolute URLs, then implement some kind of hackery in my blog entry logic to convert relative links to absolute ones on the fly. Ick.

I ended up going with #3. If you view source on this page, you'll see a little script tag that imports funnelhost.js, which just bounces users looking at dreadedmonkeygod.net over to www.dreadedmonkeygod.net. Simple.

My first thought was to soft-code everything. Have the JavaScript look like this: 

var w = /^www\./;
if (!w.test(window.location.hostname)) {
	var nh = new RegExp(window.location.host);
	window.location.href = window.location.href.replace(nh, 
          "www." + window.location.hostname);
}

That way, I stay completely independent of what the host name is. I simply say, "Make sure there's a www on the beginning of the host name."

But the problem is specific to my current hostname and provider, and I thought the solution should be as well. So I made the check specific to dreadedmonkeygod.net: 

var oh = /^dread/;
if (oh.test(window.location.hostname)) {
	var nh = new RegExp(window.location.hostname);
	window.location.href = window.location.href.replace(nh, 
          "www.dreadedmonkeygod.net");
}

The benefits of this come into sharp clarity when I test my site code at home, where the URLs of all these pages start with http://localhost. I don't I don't want my idiot JavaScript bouncing me to http://www.localhost. I want it to silently stop working and stay out of the way.

The Moral of the Story is...

The over-arching lesson is that software design is about far more than just "what works". It's a long, long series of trade-offs. My ISP doesn't want to fix the hostname mismatch problem because they feel it's not worth their time. I put my workaround in a snip of JavaScript hanging off the main template because that lets me contain the solution to this problem in one single file, rather than making several design changes in the rest of the system.

But remember: all of this is because this was originally viewed as a small problem. A problem not worth spending time resolving. And yet look how hard I had to think in order to avoid writing a little code to work around the host name mismatch, then a little more that has to be compatible with that work-around, and so on. This is how pearls are made: small acretions wrapped around a single grain of sand. Before you know it, you have a giant wad of work-around code that's making your system unmaintainable. Suddenly that grain of sand doesn't seem so small. And if you have two small things to work around, heaven help you when they collide.

This is why I bothered tech support with this in the first place. I know how these things go. It's worth at least trying to tackle the root of the problem.

Footnote

1. In case you're wondering, the base tag is there so that relative links to stylesheets, images, and other pages work correctly no matter what the URL of the page is. For example, a blog entry might appear on the main page at

http://www.dreadedmonkeygod.net/home/

or as an individual "archive" page at

http://www.dreadedmonkeygod.net/home/archive/346

That blog entry can simply link to archive/37, and that relative link will work no matter what, because of the base tag. The same logic applies to page templates and image and stylesheet links. They can appear in pages at any URL and their relative links will still work. (I won't go into why I prefer relative links in templates.)

I'm just getting up to speed on the whole ChoicePoint fiasco. QDN hit this on the head:

...the truth of the matter ... is that a group of criminals managed to create fake businesses and then set up entirely valid accounts with ChoicePoint in the name of those businesses, and then obtained the information about consumers via those accounts.

Had ChoicePoint immediately sent letters to everyone potentially affected, I might be able to give them the benefit of the doubt. But it looks like ChoicePoint has decided to keep quiet and hope that those victims outside California simply don't notice. What kind of todler logic is that? "If I don't tell Mommy I broke the lamp, maybe she won't know it was me."

I invite the executives at ChoicePoint to mature past the age of three. When you screw up and put people in danger, you tell them, and you try to put it right.

I can't help wondering: Why is sensitive personal information for sale? Is it even possible to really protect myself when all my personal information is already out there in the hands of half-wits?

And now, if you'll excuse me, I'm going to go check my mail.

intro:
Okay, so yesterday was a premature w00t!.

Er, a premature \/\/00+.

Either way, I had to take the pillows back. They were like rocks. This is the second set I've returned. First, I got the "Extra Firm", which were nice, but too thick. These were the "Firm" ones, and were perversely harder than the "Extra Firm" ones. Today I looked around for "Mediums", but they didn't have any. Not one.

So I headed for Macy's to see what they had. Success! Firm pillows that are really wonderfully comfortable! I know, because I lay down in the store to try. And when I stood back up again I kind of freaked out some poor woman on the other side of the duvet shelves.

So anyway, I get up to the check-out counter, and the woman says that if I get a Macy's card that I'll end up getting like 20% off. Since I'm buying a lot of stuff, I figure the savings are worth going through the trouble of closing the account tomorrow, so I go for it.

After I've filled out the little form, and clarified my address and phone number, she asks me to tap my social security number into the touch-pad.

"Is this really necessary?" I ask.

"Oh, don't worry," she says. "It's just so they can verrify your identity. Nobody else will see it."

"Uh, you're aware that thirty five thousand people had their records sold to criminals a couple of months ago, right?"

"What?"

The other salesperson confirms my story.

"Well," says the first woman. "I can't process your application without it."

I think about the risks, I think about getting $35 off my purchase, and I give them my soc.

And they turn down my application.

So yeah. I won't be doing that again.
title: I fell for it.

American Library Assoc. President-elect Michael Gorman has posted a rambling diatribe criticizing blogs, among other things that annoy him.

He says:

A blog is a species of interactive electronic diary by means of which the unpublishable, untrammeled by editors or the rules of grammar, can communicate their thoughts via the web.

And he just goes on from there, mouth foaming, eyes rolling, putting bloggers in their place. It seems he's upset because the unwashed masses are going and, and... writing! And they're doing it without professional supervision!

Hell, handcart, blah, blah, blah, etc.

The church said the same thing about the printing press, and they were just as wrong. Welcome to democracy, Mr. Gorman.

Michael Gorman comes across as a small man, hurt and angry that an ugly, populist movement is overtaking his beloved libraries, cathedrals of learning, that were never properly appreciated to begin with. An angry anti-blog op-ed piece doesn't warrant much attention on its own merrits. Only Gorman's post as the head of the ALA makes this worth mentioning. The online community shares too many goals with the ALA to let a rift open between us.

Denying blogs their due respect is myopic at best. The heart of writing is communication. Where there is connection, there is value, no matter how poorly spelled. Just ask any parent with their child's finger painting on the refrigerator.
title: Who's Michael Gorman?

intro:
SearchSecurity has posted an interview with ChoicePoint CISO Rich Baich, who, astonishingly, says that the recent theft of 145,000 personal records "is not an information security issue."

This guys is so full of shit, I can't believe it. He says:

We worked with (authorities) and did the right thing disclosing the breach where a lot of companies may not have ever disclosed this. A lot of companies may not have ever disclosed this. Our vision is to make a safer, more secure world through the responsible use of information.

But as the editor of the interview pointed out, "ChoicePoint initially disclosed the theft only to Californians, as required under the state's breach notification act." Only after a public outcry were all 145,000 victims notified.

Baich blames, of all people, the media for the bad press this has generated. He says the frenzy presesents "a negative impression that suggests we failed to provide adequate protection."

But ChoicePoint did fail to protect the public. From ChoicePoint's website:

In a time when mouse clicks take the place of handshakes, and decision times are down to seconds, it is becoming increasingly important to know who you are doing business with. You need to be confident that a business is legitimate and protect your company's assets and reputation. ChoicePoint offers several cost-effective solutions to screen companies and business partners.

ChoicePoint couldn't even protect themselves.

Baich says that the theft was accomplished by an individual who, "circumvented our customer credentialing process by providing fraudulent documents, like business licenses, and became an authorized customer; i.e., the fraud." That's not the media's fault, and splitting hairs about what kind of breach this was does nothing to help ChoicePoint's reputation or the public's security.

Baich seems to be making the case that this was fraud, rather than a "computer hack". That's splitting hairs. Any security expert will tell you that the weak link in many security systems isn't technological, it's social, or personal. The fact that the thief used social engineering to breach their security doesn't mean that ChoicePoint couldn't have seen this coming. It means that ChoicePoint didn't take security seriously.

Rich Baich is a moral cripple who keeps trying to sell the notion that the breach wasn't ChoicePoint's fault, or that it isn't as serious as we think. He never learned to be a man. When you screw up, there is only one acceptable course of action: Apologise, and tell the people you've wronged how you plan to make it right, and why it won't happen again. Period.

This whole fiasco started because ChoicePoint is bad at what they do: verrifying identity and providing background checks. It's time for them to admit that.
title: ChoicePoint Unrepentant, Unforgivable

intro:
As mentioned a few weeks ago, I decided to put my health ahead of running in the L.A. Marathon on Sunday. I've had a few ups and downs since then.

As of last Sunday, my longest run since kicking my cold was aboout 5½ miles. I knew that unless I was able to hit about 12 miles by Thursday (tomorrow), I'd never be able to finish.

So I set out for my run on Monday evening hoping I could hit about 9 or 10 miles, and get in position to do 12-15 on Thursday.

As it turns out, I did 11 miles at a nine-minute mile pace, for a total time of about 1:40. This included a big-ass hill in the middle, and plenty of extended gentle slopes. I felt great.

I felt great, that is, until I tried to walk after getting out of the shower. My knee was in pain.

I guess 11 miles of pounding took its toll, and I was limping the rest of the night. I'm not talking about "a bit of an ache", or "some soreness". I'm talking about sharp pain if I stepped on it wrong. Not good.

So my lungs and my legs are ready. But my knee needs some professional attention. I'm afraid that running 26.2 miles on it would leave life-long scars. I don't want to walk with a cane ever.

So yeah. After finally coming up with the goods, after getting healthy, staying patient, staying focused, eating right and listening to my body, I'm sidelined by my problem knee. This sucks. Especially considering that this kind of thing is really treatable.

So, there's only one thing to do: treat it, get 100% again, and crash the Dan Diego Marathon in June.

And yes, I still want that Iron Man for my 30th birthday.
title: Officially Dropping the Marathon

In that case, you'll be shunned in favor of A-List celebrities Antonio Banderas and Carlos Santana. (From Spain and Mexico, but they speak spanish, so it's cool, right?) They'll do a flamenco version of your song, which is bizarre, since Flamenco is a Spanish style completely foreign to Uruguayan culture.

So yeah, it's easy to understand why Oscar winner Jorge Drexler is a bit annoyed.

At the Academy Awards on Sunday, instead of giving his acceptance speech, he sang an quick a-capella version of his beautiful song. In so doing, Drexler delivered a "'bofetada sin mano,' which means 'a slap without a hand,' a dignified act of revenge," which I find incredibly cool on two levels. First, he had chutzpah to "slap" the movie industry and the wit to do it like a gentleman. Second, I'm pleased that this kind of social sparring is still alive and well somewhere in the world. We seem to have lost the notion here in the U.S.

intro:
The whole idea of Lent is that you're supposed to give up a staple of your daily life. Something that you feel you "need" to get through your day. The idea is that after 40 days of not having coffee or caffeine, I'm supposed to realize that the coffee I "needed" to get through my day wasn't important at all. I have realized the opposite: it is important.

It's as important to me as running, working out, or seeing my friends. They're all coping mechanisms. And right now, I'm not coping especially well. With a busted knee keeping me sidelined and my no-coffee Lenten vow in effect, I have no outlet for my stress, so I'm forced to cut it off at the source.

And I think that's part of the reason my training lately has been sporadic. I keep getting sick, and injured, because I'm using excercise as a coping mechanism rather than as a way to improve my body and my life. I ran too far, too soon, because I needed to blow off steam, and end up missing the event that I've been training for since last July.

Getting sick once happens. Getting sick over, and over, and over again doesn't "just happen." It means I'm not taking care of myself. Time to fix that.
title: You Gotta Go to the Source

intro:
I had my MRI scan last night. There are now hi-res images of my left knee... well, somewhere in the world. I asked about getting personal print-outs or electronic images on CD, but they're a serious medical facility, and don't do That Kind of Thing.

But the very nice lady at the front desk pointed out that they are my records after all, and I can borrow them any time. So, once they're done figuring out what's wrong with my knee, I'll borrow them for an evening and make scans of the whole thing.

The whole procedure was remarkably boring. I just had to lay very still with my knee in a "coil", and get slotted in between two giant blue hockey pucks. Keeping still was the main thing, and they had Norah Jones playing, so I just kind of dozed for most of the time.

Afterward, I got to look at the images (the nurse was really cool-- she got a kick out of how interested I was in the whole thing), and I have to say, that under all my skin and fat, I am badass. My calves in particular look really cool, all striated and knotty.

I am continually floored by modern medicine, and my access to it. I wonder how much time and energy this MRI visit will save me over my lifetime. Will I avoid needing a cane later in life because this will steer my doctor toward the correct treatment now? Without this, would I have had to give up ever running a marathon?

I remember reading that there are something like 10 MRI machines in all of Canada, and that if you want access to one, you have to schedule it weeks, if not months in advance. I'm sure this isn't the whole truth, but there are regions in the world where having a refrigerator is a big deal, nevermind an MRI machine. I wonder if Doctors without borders needs a programmer...
title: MRI Report

Add to this a report at MSNBC that outlines just how frequent errors are in ChoicePoint's database. One woman reported that she found numerous errors and omissions in her 20-page dossier.

And it gets better. A second customer reports:

"I asked the guy at ChoicePoint how I can get these errors fixed," she said. "And he said they can't."

She was told that she'd have to contact each of over 100 businesses with whom she had (or hadn't) done business and get them to correct their records.

Bruce Schneier says:

I have no idea why ChoicePoint has decided to tape a huge "Please Regulate My Industry" sign to its back, but it's increasingly obvious that it has. There's a class-action shareholders' lawsuit, but I don't think that will be enough.

Once upon a time in this country, corporations had to re-apply for their very existance every year. If they were found not to be acting in the public interest, they were disbanded. Seems like a good time to resurect that practice, hmm?
title: ChoicePoint: Errors, Omissions, and no Accountability

intro:
A lot has been said about Exception handling. Joel Spolsky prefers return codes, Ned Batchelder disagrees, and so on.

But even when Exceptions are used, they're often used badly. I've seen far too much code in my time that "handles" an exception by simply returning null. 

try {
  ...
}
catch (Exception e) {
  return null;
}

In other words, "If anything goes wrong, lie about it and hope nobody notices." (Yes, I've mentioned this before.) I'd like to refer to this flavor of problem as "code maturity", but that already means something else.

Jim Shore's column Fail Fast makes a great case for agressively singnaling problems immediately when they occur: when you find a problem, scream about it now, when it's easy to track and fix. Good stuff.
title: Fail Fast
