Back when I was a music student (lo, those faraway days...), I was playing worse every week. I was unmotivated, cutting classes, and not practicing. I was burning out, and my teacher realized it. (He's an amazing tubist, and the best teacher I've ever had on any subject, but I won't mention his name here. God forbid a Google search for his name should land anyone at a story about me burning out under his tutilage.) Anyway, yeah. He saw what was happening-- I was steadily losing interest in the tuba, and in being a musician, and my playing was suffering as a result. He did two things: he put me in the jazz band, and he handed me a new horn. And it nearly worked.

As Ottmar Liebert says, "a wonderful instrument like this is a great challenge to a guitarist to improve oneself." Very true. The desire to live up to the quality of the instrument you're holding is a powerful motivator.

As it turns out, I wasn't meant to be a musician after all. I'm much happier as a programmer than I ever was as a music student. Maybe that's because I was a classically trained musician, rather than persuing a career in jazz. Nowadays I listen to jazz recordings and want to play along so bad... I pick up my guitar and pick along for a few choruses, but I still don't make the time to really practice, or find a teacher. So I guess I'm still not "meant to be" a musician.

If you're reading this, and if you're a musician living in Camarillo, CA, email me and let's get together and play some duets or something. Any and all ages and instruments welcome.
title: Musicians and Their Instruments

intro:
Back in college, my friends and I had a great system for categorizing movies: the good/bad system. It worked like this: There are four tiers of movies:
  • Good Good
  • Bad Good
  • Good Bad
  • Bad Bad
A movie like Miller's Crossing is a brilliant film, and was meant to be so. So it falls neatly into the "good good" category.

Something like Chopper Chicks in Zombietown, on the other hand, lies at the other end of the spectrum. It's a crappy movie, and was never really intended as serious film, so it's a "bad bad" movie.

With me so far?

John Carpenter's Vampires was never inteded as high art, but it's a fantastically fun movie nonetheless. It's a prime example of a "good bad" movie. Blood of Heroes lives in the "good bad" gategory, and I've often opined that Rutger Hauer is the king of good bad movies.

Oh, I should mention that none of these categories has anything to do with whether you liked the movie. (Though liking a bad movie can help elevate it to "good bad" status.) Moving on...

That leaves us with "bad good" movies. These are art films that are unwatchable, and duds like Waiting to Exhale and Somersby. (Though I usually like Jodie Foster.)

Now, like I said: none of this has much relation to how much you actually like a movie. It's really more a description of flavor than of interest. So my friends and I put our heads together, ranked our favorite movies, and decided that if you actually put the above categories in decending order of how much we liked them, you'd get:

  1. Good Good
  2. Good Bad
  3. Bad Bad
  4. Bad Good

"Good good" movies are obviously the best. But we put "good bad" movies just behind. (You can think of "good good" as synonymous with "good film", while "good bad" means "good B movie".) "Bad bad" movies come in third by virtue of sometimes being "so bad they're good", while "bad good" covers all the Merchant Ivory-wannabes that end up just being unwatchable pretentious crap.

Where this leaves Sneakers is anyone's guess. I say its lack of pretention puts it in the "good bad" ballpark, while certain friends assert that the cast elevate it to "good good" status. So yeah, the whole good/bad system isn't totally scientific.

Anyway, I think this may help explain why bad movies typically do better at the box office: if you set out to make a bad movie, some will love it, and some will heckle, but everyone has a fair shot at a good time. If, however, you aim higher, you'll either have an Oscar winner or a complete failure, so the stakes are higher, and the odds of success lower.

Anyway, just thought you might be interested.
title: Good Bad Movies

body:
It just kept telling me, "Sorry, I can't help you right now." So I headed across the street to the supermarket, and tried to buy a box of granola bars so I can get cash back. No dice there either.

So I headed out. I had about an hour drive ahead of me, so figured I had time to get on my cellphone and get this worked out with WAMU customer service and stop off at an ATM on the way.

But customer service explained to me (at 4:45 on a Saturday) that my card had been cancelled and a new one mailed to me. Why? Because an "unnamed vendor" had a security breach, and my account information "may have been exposed". Where was the new card mailed? My old address, of course.

So, today, I get back on the phone with Washington Mutual. "The card was canceled for your security, sir," they tell me.

I explain that if they're going to cancel my card, I'd like a phone call at the very least. The CS rep explains that well over one hundred thousand customers were affected, and that notifying them all by phone simply wasn't practical.

So I tell the rep that I need to update my address, cancel the new card that was just mailed, and have a new one mailed to my current address.

He says that if I change my address over the phone, there's a 30-day waiting period before I can request a new card over the phone.

I tell him that I'll just go to a branch office, and take care of the whole thing there.

He says that if I change my address at the branch office, then they can't order a new card for 30 days. I have to either use the phone to update my address, and then go to a branch to order a new card, or the other way round.

Lovely.

ChoicePoint has a breach, so Washington Mutual cuts me off. And now I have to jump through hoops to regain access to my own money.

So here's my to-do list:

  • Get a new card for my account.
  • Move all my accounts to the local credit union.
  • Find out how to remove all my records from ChoicePoint's database. (I'll do that via email, so y'all can read about it.)
  • Find out who gave ChoicePoint my bank account information, and halt all dealings with them immediately.
  • Write letters to my Congressmen urging them to hold corporations directly accountable for breaches like this. They must be properly motivated to implement strong security.
[Update 2:02pm] Just visited the local branch. Not only was my change of address not yet processed, but the rep on the phone was completely wrong about the waiting period. I can go into any branch, ask for a new card, and change my address. So this is what I did.

Disturbingly, all I had to do was present the old card. No photo ID was required.

intro:
Jason Kottke points out some recent research which finds that humans are actually only able to hold about 3 or 4 things in their head at once. After that, our brains start dropping things. (We get around this by breaking a system into manageable chunks.)

This is why programmers need a quiet, study-like atmosphere to do their work. We are frequently holding the maximum possible number of variables in our heads. Interruptions or distractions make it extremely hard to do our work.

And it sheds a lot of light on why software is built the way it is. Programmers routinely deal with systems of many, many elements. We have to break them down somehow. So we have scoping rules, and abstractions, and "Best Practices" that balance the human need for simplicity with the system's innate complexity and need for flexibility.

I've heard global variables denounced as instigators of unreliablity. The more variables you have in scope at a given moment, the more possible states there are for your program at that point, and the harder it gets to test that all those possible states lead to correct behaviors.

However, the same is true for the programmer: the more variables are in scope, the less likely it is that the programmer will be able to modify the program easily. (He has to consider all possible states!) Subroutines are a way to "pre-chunk" your code so that another programmer will be able to read it. This is why variable and especially method names are extremely important-- they're the built-in Cliff's Notes on what your program does.
title: Remember Three Things

I had a physical therapy session on Wednesday, and got some more very encouraging information. The Chondromalacia may be present, but it's minor. The real cause of the problem is a tight IT band, which is pulling my patella out of its proper channel, causing it to rub over bits of my knee that it's not supposed to. According to the physical therapist, I should make a full recovery and be able to return to distance running soon, provided I do my daily stretches and excercises.

body:
ChoicePointe's first email:
From: consumer.center@choicepoint.com

Thank you for contacting ChoicePoint. We have received your request to opt out of ChoicePoint's Direct Marketing Services database. In order to process your request, please reply with your full name and current address.

No, I'm not interested in "opting out" of anything. I want ChoicePoint to forget anything they ever knew about me. So here's my reply to their first email:

Thank you for your prompt response. Just to clarify: I want ChoicePoint to delete any information that you currently have about me. Will this email accomplish this, or is there further action I need to take to make that happen? Christopher Raser [address omitted]

ChoicePoint's second email:

From: CorpMktg.Communications@choicepoint.com

ChoicePoint was recently a victim of organized fraud, and we understand this news may be cause for concern.

A very small number of criminals posed as legitimate companies in order to gain access to personal information about consumers. When the fraud was discovered, access to information was immediately discontinued and the authorities were notified.

ChoicePoint has acted quickly to address the circumstances that led to the unauthorized access, and we are committed to our core principles of working to create a safer, more secure society through the responsible use of information while ensuring the protection of personal privacy.

We have sent letters to affected consumers whose information may have been accessed. If you did not receive a letter from us, you have not been affected. You may also contact ChoicePoint us at 1-877-547-2518 to find out if your information was potentially affected.

If you have not received a letter but are still concerned, here are some actions you can take to help protect yourself from misuse of information.

If you think you have been the victim of identity theft, you should place a fraud alert on your credit report by contacting any one of the three credit bureaus listed below. As soon as one credit bureau confirms your fraud alert, the other two bureaus will automatically be notified to place fraud alerts on your credit report, and all three reports will be sent to you free of charge.

The above is a complete crock. Verrifying trustworthiness of companies and individuals is what they do. The notion that ChoicePoint is "committed" to "ensuring the protection of personal privacy" is provably false. And noting that it was a "very small number of criminals" is just impertinent. I really don't care how many theives were involved. I care that 145,000 people's records were compromised.

I'll be calling the above number (1-877-547-2518) and talking with a ChoicePoint rep to see what's what. More on that when I get around to it.

intro:
I bumped into a posting on Neil Gaiman's weblog in which a high school senior asks about comics as literature:
I am a high school student senior doing a term paper on the status of comic books as legitimate literature, and I would be ever so greatful if you would express to me your thoughts on graphic literature's impact on western culture and conventional literary thought. How do you, as a comic book writer, feel comic books are regarded by the conventional literary community? How do you feel comic books should be regarded?

I wrote that same paper as a junior in high school, and seeing this post made me realize just how much I've changed since then. If I'd had it to do over again, I'd read The Great Gatsby, then go out for pizza. I'd get an A.

The reason: English teachers love literature. They love it so much that they want to share it with kids. And usually what they love is Austin, or Hemmingway, or Falkner. Asimov, Herbert, Heinlein, Robinson, Bradbury, these are authors favored by Chemistry and Physics teachers, not lovers of Literature. They're generally good people, but in the end they're not much different than fans of any particular genre.

Conventional litterary thought is severely biggoted against new forms. Neil Gaiman ought to know: he won a World Fantasy Award for the Sandman issue "A Midsummer Night's Dream", and what happened? They changed the rules so that comic books couldn't win after that. And that's how comics are treated by fantasy authors, who ought to have some understanding of being dismissed by conventional wisdom.

So yeah. I'm kind of past arguing with my high school English teacher. It's not worth my time. I just wish I could share that lesson with Ally, the kid who wrote to Neil Gaiman. Quit tilting at windmills, kid. Just give 'em what they want and get out. It'll free up your time to explore on your own terms, and you'll have the grades to go wherever you want.

At least, that's what I learned in English class. Pity, isn't it.
title: Quit tilting at windmills, kid.

From: consumer.center@choicepoint.com

Thank you for contacting ChoicePoint. We have received and are processing your request to remove your information from our Direct Marketing Services database. You will receive a follow-up letter in the mail that provides more information about the Opt-Out process.

While your information will be removed from our Direct Marketing Services, you should understand that ChoicePoint processes many types of transactions for businesses, government agencies and non-profit organizations. These include screening services such as pre-employment background checks and inquiries in connection with applications for homeowner's insurance, auto insurance or an apartment lease.

While this information will be removed from our direct marketing services activity, it will not be removed from our general database. We, of course, cannot remove information from public records just as consumers cannot remove public data about themselves from county courthouses and other public records databases.

We will continue to include such public data in information products we provide to government, businesses and non-profit groups that use these products for legitimate purposes such as detecting and preventing fraud, performing legal due diligence, locating criminal suspects, finding missing children, screening volunteers and managing business risks.

We are continuing to strengthen our customer credentialing and other security processes to limit access to these information products to those who have a legitimate use for the data. ChoicePoint does not distribute information to individuals, such as when a family hires someone to work in their home, without the individual's permission.

If you would like to learn more about the public records that ChoicePoint's customers use to make decisions, visit www.choicetrust.com.

Thank you,

ChoicePoint Consumer Center

Here's my response:

I understand that information cannot be purged from public records. However, my bank account and credit card information are certainly not matters of public record. Please delete this information from your databases.

After sever emails, you still have not answered my two original questions:

  1. How do I determine who gave ChoicePoint my bank account information?
  2. How do I get ChoicePoint to delete all records you have regarding my bank accounts and credit cards?

I look forward to hearing the answers to these questions.

I'm sure this is going to go nowhere. I'll go get them on the phone in my copious free time.

And let me just point out the pomposity of mentioning "detecting and preventing fraud" and "performing legal due diligence" as one of the services supported by their databases.

intro:
I think I've just found the worst-designed website ever. It's downright user-hostile.

It's the website for Metrolink, Los Angeles's commuter rail system. Let's start with some basic things for usability testing:

  • How do I print a map of the whole system?
  • How do I locate the Metrolink stations closest to my origin and destination?

But there's more that they could have done. Wouldn't it be nice to enter a starting address, a destination time and address, and get back a schedule of how to get from A to B on time? The MTA's website does this. Why was this feature left out?

But they didn't even get that far. The Tickets & Fares page is a mess. I can click on a heading under "Tickets & Passes" to find out the definition of, say, a 10-Trip Ticket, but if I want to find out how much that 10-Trip Ticket will cost, I have to go back to the Tickets & Fares page, and click on the Fare Chart. But even that doesn't give me enough information. I still have to figure out how many "zones" I'm traveling through, so I have to go back again to the Tickets & Fares page and click on the Fare Zone Map. In short, the information I need in order to choose a ticket type and determine the price are spread across three pages, none of which are interlinked.

Oh, and the whole site displays in a tiny 800x450-pixel window, no matter how big your browser is. And if that weren't annoying enough, they then waste now-precious screen real estate on giant navigation menu buttons and cram the map down even smaller.

But the map is useless amyway. It has no streets. If you want to know exactly where a Metrolink stop is, you have to click on the line that stop is on, then on the stop itself, then on a link to Yahoo! maps.

Fer crying out loud. This site is just painful.

Maybe I should send 'em a resume.

In case you're wondering: Yes, I did manage to figure out how to get to work in the morning using the Metrolink. Downsides: I either have to bring a bike, or walk a total of nearly 3 miles. And it costs $8 per day to ride the thing if I get a $170 monthly pass. No wonder nobody's riding this thing.

So yeah. I'll be sitting in traffic with the rest of y'all.
title: Metrolink's Web Page Sucks

intro:
Finally, finally, someone has called bullshit on all the self-absorbed navel gazing going on in writing about hacking over the last few years. ESR had a great point with The Cathedral and the Bazaar, but then he started talking about "What is a Hacker?", and things kind of went downhill from there.

Not that I really noticed. I (and everyone else) just kind of nodded along, thinking, "Yeah, I am pretty cool, aren't I," and much coolaid was consumed. We were all convinced that the world was changing, that nerds were the new jocks, and that we'd all be driving Feraris and dating Anna Paquin by next year.

But in his essay Dabblers and Blowhards, Maciej Ceglowski has singled out Paul Graham for dishonorable mention. (Disclosure: I have warmly quoted Graham in the past, and will continue to do so where I agree with him. But in this case I can't help but feel that Ceglowski has a point.) Ceglowski said:

Great paintings, for example, get you laid in a way that great computer programs never do.

Yep. There it is. Smart may be sexy, but programming never will be. Then again, an ex of mine once leaned over my shoulder and corrected my HTML. Hot sweaty geek lovin' ensued. (On hindsight, I think the HTML was fine. The geek lovin' had more to do with me having owned several cats than her knowledge of table layouts: I know what it means when the cat bats at your newspaper.)

Sometimes you don't realize how stuffy a room has gotten until someone opens a window. Many thanks to Ceglowski for doing so.

intro:
Okay, so the last remnants of the old "Quick Links" system are gone, replaced by del.icio.us.

And I've just about finished incorporating Tiles into this place. Or, as much as possible, given Tiles's horrible limitations. It's the same problem I had with Struts Templates, but inside out. With Tiles, I couldn't nest inclusions. With Tiles, I can't nest inserts.

In other words, I can't insert one tile into a slot in another. At least, not if I want to pass parameters. There's no way to say, "Format this blog entry as HTML, then insert that into the main content area of the page layout." Nope. Can't be done.

And page-specific sidebars were a pain in the ass: they have to be coded as separate JSPs, which makes for a brittle linkage with the main content, and extra files to maintain.

Yes, I'll be looking into coding my own templating system. In my copious free time.

But I can't shake this feeling that there's just something I'm missing. I just ran across the flush attribute that appears in just about every Tiles tag, and flushing was exactly what my app server was complaining about. No time to really check this out tonight. More tomorrow.

[Update 4/21/05] Turns out my intuition was right on the money. Ten minutes of playing with the flush attribute solved all my ills.

intro:
I've been reading Coder to Developer, and thinking a lot about the software development process. And at the end of the day, I think I have a pretty clear idea of the kind of tools I really want.

The ideal solution: integrated bug/feature request tracking, source code control, and IDE. For the purposes of this discussion, I'll use Bugzilla, CVS, and NetBeans.

Here's how the workflow would go:

  1. Select a bug from the Bugzilla database to work on.
  2. Edit.
  3. Commit. All edited files are tagged with the Bugzilla ID number of the bug that I fixed. Bugzilla database is updated to reflect that I've commited a fix, and edited files (and versions) are noted.

At the end of the day, CVS commits and Bugzilla bugs should be cross-linked. I want to be able to find all edits done for a particular bug or feature, and I want to see what bug a particular edit is associated with.

I have seen that this can be done. Who knows, maybe Bugzilla already does this, or NetBeans already has a plugin available to do this.

Or maybe I should write one.
title: CVS/Bugzilla Integration

intro:
Looking for info on integrating CVS and Bugzilla, I found Derek Anderson's definition of CVS/Bugzilla Ingegration:
CVS/Bugzilla Integration (def): Automatically updating bugs in Bugzilla with commit log entries from CVS. Adding to a CVS commit log text along the lines of "bug #45, bug#46" would append the log to the comments of bugs 45 and 46.

Pretty close, but still too much manual labor. If I have to rely on myself to manually tag commits with bug IDs, the system is going to fall into disuse. The whole idea is to set things up so that my development system keeps track of things for me.

So I'll keep looking.
title: CVS/Bugzilla Integration II

intro:

Maybe I'll give it a shot when I get home tonight, and see what happens.

intro:
Simon Brunning has a few thoughts on Joel Spolsky's revival of Hungarian notation.

I'm with Simon: I sometimes annotate variables this way, but it's more part of the variable's name than some kind of add-on shorthand. If I have a string that I need to check out before I parse it as an int, I might write something like: 

String qtyParameter = request.getParameter("qty");
// Do some input checking...
int qty = Integer.parseInt(qtyParameter);

Then again, that's just me. I like my code to look like English as much as possible. I use single-letter variable names and abreviations only were it's completely obvious what I'm talking about. And even then, I usually have some kind of comment explaining each abbreviation. (ex. qty = 'quantity')

And here's my own personal WTF-style double take for the day. Found this burried in some data access logic: 

if (quickCheckOut == null 
    || (quickCheckOut != null && quickCheckOut.trim().equals("null")))
{
  //...

I guess the programmer just wanted to be extra thorough.

Oh, and I once had a programmer try to tell me that there are no bitwise AND and OR operators in Java. This is complete bunk. The | and & do exist, and do perform bitwise operations as you'd expect. However, in Java they're also overloaded to work on boolean operands, but they just don't short circuit; they evaluate both operands, no matter what.

So now you know.

TGIF. Have a great weekend, everyone.

intro:
On most of the machines at work, administrators have instituted a "Three Strikes" rule: An account is disabled after three failed login attempts. As a new member of the team, (AKA the FNG), I keep tripping over this.

The usual sequence of events goes like this:

1st Attempt
Try my own password by reflex. Login fails. I realize my mistake immediately.
2nd Attempt
Try password $foo. Login fails. I say to myself, "Whups, must have been a typo."
3rd Attempt
Try password $foo, very carefully. Login fails. I've got the wrong password. And the account is disabled.

I remember reading an article ages ago about how a "Three Strikes" policy was misguided, and just forced people to write down their passwords and stick them to the edge of their monitor.
title: Password Security: "Three Strikes" Rule Sucks

intro:
Timbo and I headed out to Stoney Point over the weekend to take another run at Maggie's Farm. Neither of us expected to get it, but we had fun trying. While we were there, a guy happened by with his two kids.

The father was really cool at first. Very friendly. He's a climber himself, and we chatted about trips and so on for a few minutes. Then he took an appraising look at Maggie's Farm and said, "Wassat, about 5.8? 5.9? You young fellas should have no trouble!" Maggie's Farm is an overhanging 5.11a/b. He looked dubious when I told him this.

Every time I'd fall, he'd say something that started with, "Oh! I see! You just need to..."

And every time I'd fall, he'd jump back to the start of the climb to fondle the rock for a minute or two, while I stared at the back of his head, and waited for him to get out of my way. I tried to be polite. I'd listen to his ideas and say, "Okay, lemme give that a shot," and then stare in frustration as he continued to stand at the base of the climb.

After a few repetitions of this routine, he stood directly behind me as I was getting ready to climb. Remember: Maggie's Farm is overhanging, so when you fall off it, you pendulum out from the wall a good six or eight feet. He had watched this happen many times already, yet was standing right on the spot where I'd probably be cannonballing through in a few seconds.

"Uh, you may want to move, man," I said.

He replied cheerfully: "I'm good."

"Not if I fall, you're not." I made a mental note never to climb with this guy.

He just looked confused. My belayer had to clue him in: "He's going to swing right into you, dude." He looked startled and quickly stepped out of the way.

And when I did indeed peel, he started up again with, "You need to get your foot up there..."

I was getting testy. "How about we put you in a harness?" I said.

"Just trying to help you here, son."

"I know. But every climb looks easy from the ground."

One of his kids asked, "Are you going to climb, Daddy?"

"No," he replied with a fatherly smile, "I don't have the right shoes."

After a few more minutes (and plenty more free beta), he took his kids and wandered off.

I'm not sure what the lesson here is. I'm not sure there is one. I guess what I wanted to say to that guy is that I wish he'd be a little more mindful of the people around him. His kids wanted to move on ("Can we go now, daddy?"). I wanted to climb. My belayer wanted to climb. And yet he was totally focused on what he wanted.

Anyway, the 5.9s at Stoney are too easy these days, and the 5.11s are too hard to be really fun. I need to scan my So. Cal. Bouldering Guide and track down some nice meaty 5.10s for my partners and I to sink our teeth into next week.

intro:
Ottmar Liebert just posted a quickie mentioning a matter near and dear to musicians everywhere: finding an instrument case tough enough for air travel.

Now, if you play the clarinet, or the trumpet, this isn't a big deal. But I play the tuba, which cannot be carried onboard a plane. When I was in the tuba studio at IU, air travel damage was a common ailment, and after any break, (summer, hollidays, spring break) we'd all compare notes on who had what case, and whether their horn had survived the trip home.

Ottmar Liebert says, "I think what the baggage handler wants to destroy s/he will destroy... no matter how strong we think the case is."

Absolutely true. A friend in the tuba studio had an Anvil case. It was steel reinforced with giant metal knobs on the corners, and casters so you could move the thing. It looked like something Metallica would take on tour. (Hell, they very likely do.) With a tuba inside it must have weighted 100 lbs. easy. Anvil cases are renouned as "bulletproof".

Unfortunately, even the mighty Anvil wasn't enough to withstand a fifteen foot fall out of an airplane. It fell off the top of the the luggage conveyor onto the tarmack. Damage was minimal, but the point is clear. You can pay extra for oversized luggage and special handling. You can get the badassest case on the market. But nothing is really going to protect your instrument from the carelessness of airline baggage handlers.

Some desperate musicians have gone so far as to buy additional seats in which to place their instruments. However, airlines have evidently stopped this practice, for reasons unknown.

And there's a popular urban legend that's been circulating for years about a baritone sax player who claimed that he was carrying an oboe so he could carry it on. (As the story goes, "Oboe" was on the list of instruments approved for carry-on. "Baritone Saxophone" was not.)

This is just one of the issues I'm happy to have left behind when I gave up serious musical study.

intro:
This is a rant, but it's short.

CVS lets two people work on the same file, and automagically merges changes as long as they don't conflict. You and I can edit the same file at the same time, as long as we're editing different parts of the file.

But if we're working on the same parts of that file, somebody's going to get screwed, and nobody gets any warning. You commit your changes, and everything's fine. Then I go to check in mine, and discover that you beat me to it. I have to re-do several hours of work.

This is what's known as a "CVS Conflict" and I've heard a lot of people (including Mike Gunderloy, author of the excellent Coder to Developer) say things like "CVS collisions sound scary, but it's not that tough to just get the latest and re-do your edits, and really this almost never happens."

Horse shit.

I have edited seven files since this morning. Now that I'm preparing to commit my changes, I discover that five of them have conflicts. Yesterday it was two out of six.

CVS may be great as long as there is only one developer, or as long as the developer-to-files ratio is low. But for Java web applications it sucks utterly.

Why? JSPs, that's why.

JSPs make up a small subset of the files in a J2EE web app. And since just about every back-end change eventually ripples through one or more JSPs, developer activity is funneled into one area that's perpetually in motion. Collisions are going to happen.

</rant>
title: CVS Sucks

intro:
Josh has put up a post that did make me chuckle, in that "I've been there" kind of way. He's talking about reproducable test cases. Reminded me to link (again) to How to Report Bugs Effectively.

Today was spent in the throes of a full-team debugging effort, which raised some issues with the current development infrastructure. In short, we're outgrowing current communication and tracking methods.

No way to add visibility to debugging effort.
We can't keep anyone "in the loop." Our "bug tracking" system is just a Trouble Ticket system. So if you're not the requestor or the asignee, you're S.O.L. No observers allowed.
Insufficient Status gradation for bugs.
Bugs go through a variety of stages, but it's usually something like:
  1. Reported
  2. Assigned
  3. In Progress
  4. Resolved (Fixed / Will Not Fix / Duplicate / etc.)
  5. Closed
A system that supports only "In Progress", "Suspended", and "Closed" just doesn't cut it. How do you mark an item that has been fixed, but not yet QA'ed and moved to production?
No integration between Trouble Ticket system and CVS.
Tying off change requests / bug reports to individual edits would be awesome. Yesterday a coworker came to me and reported a bug that wasn't a bug. He'd found some changes where I'd removed a feature, but couldn't figure out why I'd done it.
Frequent, difficult-to-resolve CVS collisions.
I've talked about this already, but I suspect that certain properties of J2EE architecture make CVS unsuitable as a source control tool for our team.
Far too many, "we'll just have to be careful" statements.
Humans are bad at being careful. That's what computers are for. I'm going to start compiling a list of all the things we're supposed to remember to always / never do.

As part of today's group effort to QA a batch of recent changes, we compiled a list of known bugs, which was sent out via email. When the development team end-runs around current bug tracking, you know there's a problem.

We're also in serious need of automated testing. Many of the bugs we squashed today were regressions, that would have been caught immediately by an automated test suite.

The moral to the story? I don't know. I keep suggesting ways to make our lives easier, but nobody seems to be interested yet. I'm going to do a presentation on JUnit in a week or two, and see if that gains any traction.

I guess I'm just fed up with doing things the hard way. I'm having a hard time accepting that the tools we have are fine when I know that there are tools out there, free tools, that are great.

I've had several people on the team reply to my suggestions, "But is this really that big a deal?" Not individually. But pile up enough little annoyances and inefficiencies, and you get nothing done.
title: Test Cases, Debugging, Communication

intro:
This is the "family recipe" for oatmeal chocolate chip cookies. No, no raisins, no nuts (though I may try that). Chocolate chips. Trust me. These are the only cookies that I've had people at work pester me to make again. My regular chocolate chip cookies are gone shortly after lunch. These don't make it past 10am.

Okay kids, get your ovens heated to 350°, and collect the following:

  • ¾ cup shortening
  • 1 cup brown sugar (I prefer dark brown)
  • ½ cup granulated sugar
  • 1 egg
  • ¼ cup of water
  • 1 tsp vanilla extract
  • 1 tsp salt
  • 1 tsp cinnamon
  • ½ tsp baking soda
  • ½ tsp ground cloves
  • 1 cup flour
  • 3 cups quick-cooking oatmeal
  • 1 cup Nestle semi-sweet chocolate chips
Mix thoroughly shortening, sugars, egg, water, and vanilla, then stir in remaining ingredients. (I strongly recommend adding them in the order I've listed them above.) Drop dough by rounded teaspoons onto greased baking sheet. Bake at 350° for 12-15 minutes. Remove immediately from baking sheet, and store in tight container.

The best way to know when they're done: they're no longer shiny on top. They'll still be soft, but will firm up when they cool. If you overcook them, they get really, really dry, so watch for that magic moment. That said, it's better to overcook than undercook- they're better a bit crispy than simply mushy.

intro:
Okay, so I did the life ones, and now I'm remembering all my programming rules of thumb. Here ya go:
If you type something twice, you're wrong.
(Credit to Scheme jock Eric Hilsdale for this wording.) Any time the same code appears twice, that's bad. If that code is a subroutine that's been cut and pasted, you need to refactor. If it's a common idiom (ex. try/catch/finally), then it should be a macro. Doing repetitive tasks are what computers were invented for. Free up human processing time for solving new problems.
Data duplication is the root of all evil.
Similar to the first rule, but more focused on data representation. If you have a bit of data expressed in two places, you have to spend time ensuring they stay in sync. The duplication will be a source of bugs, and a drain on your time, and your program will be more complicated because of it. Pre-calculate, cache, or agregate data only after careful consideration, and only for performance reasons; it will never make your program easier to maintain.
Name your variables well.
Someone is going to have to read your code later on. That someone is usually you.
Never return null.
The contract of most methods implicitly states that the method will return something useful. null is almost never useful. If you're method may return null, consider checking for this and throwing an exception instead.
Fail fast.
When something's wrong (empty result set from the database, no network connection, unparseable user input) don't think, don't hesitate, just throw an exception. This makes debugging easier, and leads quickly to more robust code.
Fix bad code as you find it.
A lot of project managers out there will tell you that you shouldn't be spending your time re-writing code. Your job is to make money for the company by writing new code. This is true. But it's also true that bad code costs money in wasted developer time. Use your best judgement.
Don't be careful. Be bulletproof.
Whenever I hear anyone say, "We'll just have to be careful to...", I know that somewhere down the line, someone will forget to "be careful", and I might have to come in at 2am to fix the problem. Anything you have to "be careful" about should be automated.
title: Programming Mantras

intro:
In putting together my list of programming rules of thumb, I realized how many of them are implicit arguments in favor of automated testing.

It seems to be a disease of small software shops (or departments) that automated testing is seen as an unnecessary luxury. Testing is done by hand, usually by developers "banging on" the latest build. There's a lot you have to be careful to remember to test. As the number of cases grows, so does the number of missed test cases, and the number of problems that make it into "production" builds.

In this environment, code can only get worse. Refactoring doesn't happen because the testing required would be time-consuming, and find only a fraction of the bugs introduced. An attitude of "don't touch that, it works" sets in, and new features are bolted on the side. So the whole thing gets worse and worse, and nobody's allowed to fix it.

Automated testing is the answer to all of this. Even massive code changes can be undertaken with confidence-- the test suite will make sure everything still works.

body:
Lord knows my teachers did everything possible to make me hate reading. Endless classics. Serious fiction. Anything involving adventure was not Literature. Science Fiction was right out. (Worse: The A I got on my project for Dune was used as evidence against me. "See! You can do the work, you just don't apply yourself! Why don't you try harder! nag, nag, nag...") The things that thrilled me were labeled childish. "You can't read science fiction the rest of your life. You have to read some real literature too."

Thank God my mom loved reading, and kept me interested. She was always keeping books around the house, and putting things in front of me, without any pressure. Sometimes it was Dragonlance books. Other times it was Catcher in the Rye.

To this day, I like Science Fiction, because it gets my imagination fired up. And I like nonfiction, because true stories are more compelling. If I do read fiction, it's because it's really, really good. Nobody gets to tell me what I should read any more.

If a boy is reading, that's good. Don't punish him for reading the "wrong things," or try to "help him enjoy real literature." Nobody puts Harry Potter on the same level as Hemmingway. But that's not the point. Harry is great because it's a joy to read.

Anyway, now I'm just ranting. Go check out the Guys Write for Guys Read.
intro:
Wow. Just read an interview over at Bookslut interview with Jon Scieszka, of the Guys Write for Guys Read project. He's trying to put together supplementary materials and resources to get more boys into reading. Here's the nutshell:
I think we've sort of ghettoized kids -- and boys, in particular -- for so long that it makes them feel bad about their reading choices. I knew plenty of little guys when I was teaching second and third grade, that nonfiction was their favorite reading. I had some little guys who would just learn everything about submarines and the World Wars. And that was some really spectacular information, and you know what? That's what we use in real life, too. We should be helping kids learn how to filter information better.

Well put.
title: Guys Write for Guys Read

intro:
Decloak Software has posted a screed on why CSS is bad, and they'd like you to receive it as an example of why simple is better, and why you ought to do business with "common sense" people. But the article is really just a display of hopeless stupidity.

Their reasons for dismissing CSS as an accessibility tool are hilarious. By their logic, the only obstacle to a disability-friendly website is that screen readers are too stupid to ignore spacer gifs.

He thinks the problem is that the required alt attribute isn't appropriate for spacer images. The real problem is that he's still using spacer images.

So why should I care about what this knucklehead has to say? Because he is the prototypical knuckleheaded, if-it-ain't-broke-don't-fix-it developer. They love to talk about how NASA spent millions developing a ball-point pen that worked in zero-G, while the Russians just used a pencil. (That story is false, by the way.) They take every opportunity to ignore problems, or work around them, rather than fix them. They all think this is something to brag about. They never quite grasp that having a workaround in place isn't the same as not having a problem.

And they all believe that bug-ridden, brittle, late software is simply a fact of life as a developer.

I worked on several projects where a move to semantic markup & CSS was avoided, while serious developer time was spent on making all fonts consistent. If you think moving to CSS is expensive, try not moving to CSS.

It's long been a truism that no project is cheap, fast, and good all at the same time. More and more, I believe that building software the best way we know how will produce all three. This is part of why I want to start doing freelance work: I don't need the money, but I want to run a few projects at 12, and see what happens.
title: If You Think Education is Expensive...

The web is having a good har-dee-har about DRM proponent Michael Gartenberg getting so fed up with the DRM on his MS Reader files that he cracked MS's DRM and converted the contents to DRM-less PDF format.

It's times like this that I have to wonder, what exactly did Gartenberg think was going to happen when companies started including DRM in their products?

Gartenberg has the wrong attitude on DRM. He says:

If you're a Linux user, you don't get to use iTunes and iTunes music. If you're a Mac OS user, you don't get to use Yahoo music, Napster to Go or Rhapsody or any of the MSFT Janus stuff. There's nothing new here.

Gartenberg is missing the point. I'm really not that upset that there's no iTunes for Linux. I am pissed off that even if I buy songs from iTunes legally, it's illegal for me to convert those songs to MP3 format so I can put them on my non-Apple player.

Let me say that again: In practice, it is illegal to play iTunes music on non-Apple players. DRM is not about copyright. DRM is about customer lock-in.

That's the lesson that Gartenberg fails to learn here. MS doesn't care about Gartenberg making copies of those files. MS wants him to keep using MS Reader.

intro:
Earlier this week I (and thousands of others) bombarded our Senators with faxes, emails, and phonecalls about the proposed Broadcast Flag. This morning I received a reply from Senator Dianne Feinstein.
June 24, 2005

Mr. Christopher Raser [address snipped]

Dear Mr. Raser:

Thank you for writing to me about the digital broadcast flag. I appreciate hearing from you.

I feel strongly that we must prevent the theft of copyrighted works, and that includes digital television (DTV) programming. As we move forward in the digital age, it is increasingly easy for unauthorized copies of copyrighted works to be made and illegally distributed. Over-the-air digital content is the easiest to pirate.

As we contemplate the use of new technologies to protect copyrighted works, we must pay careful attention to ensure that a balance is struck between competitive protections and individual consumer interests. It is important to allow for the continued fair use of copyrighted material, even while we seek to stop unauthorized reproductions from being illegally distributed outside the home and over the Internet.

Again, thank you for writing. Please know that as the Senate considers legislation of the broadcast flag, I will be sure to keep your views in mind. If you should have any questions, please feel free to contact my Washington, DC staff at (202) 224-3841.

Sincerely yours,
Dianne Feinstein
United States Senator

http://feinstein.senate.gov

Further information about my position on issues of concern to California and the Nation are available at my website http://feinstein.senate.gov.

http://feinstein.senate.gov/issue.html.

She seems to get it. I love that she specifically mentioned balancing fair use with protections for copyright holders. That's awesome.

But Senator Feinstein also says that, "Over-the-air digital content is the easiest to pirate." This is plain untrue, and I worry about where the balance will be struck if media companies continue to use piracy fears as cover.

DRM is not about copyright. DRM is about locking consumers in, and competitors out.

I'm thrilled at the Senator's response. I honestly didn't expect such a quick and topical reply. And the Senator clearly understands the trade-offs involved. My faith in government grows every day.
title: Senator Feinstein on Broadcast Flag

intro:
Damn. Engadget should know better. It's one thing to be balanced, it's another to grant a voice to people who are full of shit.

Yesterday's Clicker colum, written by Stephen Speicher, is entitled "In Defence of DRM". The crux of Speicher's argument is this:

If you can get past your visceral negative reaction, you'll quickly see that DRM has actually brought consumers more advancements than restrictions. In truth, the hatred of DRM is a product of its own success; without the added options which DRM brings to the table there would be little to rebel against.

Let me get this straight: If DRM wasn't so cool, people wouldn't hate it so much. Riiight.

DRM hasn't "given" us anything that wouldn't be an order of magnitude better without it. If iTunes sold DRM-less MP3 tracks, I'd have spent a year's sallary there already. As it is, I simply can't play iTunes music on my non-Apple player. And this isn't specific to iTunes; any DRM-protected track is useless to me.

Speicher's point is that without DRM, we wouldn't have had anything at all. I disagree. Cory Doctorow said it well:

And honestly, there may be some powerful bozon emitters in the halls of the RIAA companies, but does anyone really believe that the record industry will just take its ball and go home at this point?

And Speicher seems unclear on Fair Use:

...Fair-Use grants the end-user the ability, when possible, to enjoy the benefit of copying for personal use.

No. Fair Use grants the customer the right, always to copy a recording for personal use. The crux of the problem with DRM is that it's simply not possible to balance Fair Use rights with DRM. No software can distinguish between "I'm stripping the DRM in order to play this iTunes song on my non-Apple MP3 player" from "I'm stripping the DRM in order to email this song to all my friends!"

And yes, I saw Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc on West Wing, and I've been dying for an excuse to use it. I feel so smart now.

As you can see, there's not a lot left. It is not getting easire to pirate copyrighted works. Digital broadcasts are no easier or harder to pirate than anything else. intro:
Here at work, we have several rules regarding passwords:
  • Passwords must be 8-10 characters long
  • Passwords must contain at least one number
  • Passwords expire after 30 days
  • Passwords cannot be re-used
  • Three successive failed login attempts results in the account being disabled on that machine.

And the kicker here is that most of the development tools we use do some kind of auto-login. When you try to connect to the database, they'll automatically provide your Windows username and password. This is intended to be handy.

But what happens when you connect to a database you haven't worked on in months?

The first thing that happens is that your "helpful" database client tries to use your current Windows login. Since the last time you used this database was more than 30 days ago, this login is wrong. So you've got STRIKE ONE against you, and all you did was open your database client.

You ask yourself, "When was the last time I worked on this server, and what was my password at the time?" So you take a guess. And it's wrong. Yes, always. STRIKE TWO

Now you have one guess left before your account is disabled, and you have to call the help desk and admit that you, a professional programmer, can't remember your password, even after three tries. What do you do? You guess again, usually with about a 50/50 shot at getting it right.

So 9 times out of 10, you end up playing a game with the computer. The game goes like this:

You have one chance to guess which old password you used. Hint: It's not $OLDPASS.
Password: _

My solution: I use the same password for everything, and it's on a post-it on my monitor, with an expiration date and list of all the machines it applies to.

Actually, no. It's under my mousepad.
title: Three Strikes Rule

This is a great idea, and much needed. Right now I'm going back and forth with Amazon about my Homunculus CD, trying to determine whether my disc was DRM-afflicted or just defective. (Is there a difference?) Part of the problem is that there are no pertinent markings on the case.

intro:
A couple years ago I attended a bachelor party for one of the guys on the hockey team. I caught a ride back with a couple of guys I'd been talking to, both techies on the entertainment end: one a game programmer and the other a special effects guy.

At one point the special effects guy asked me, "So, Chris, where do you think the 'net is going? What's next?"

Data fusion, I said. Climbing websites that combine geographic information with route data to help you plan a weekend trip. A Zagat guide that lets you do Google Maps-like searches: "I want a Thai restaurant within 5 miles of 93010 for $15-$20 a plate with great date atmosphere." That kind of thing. Integrating information from various websites to form a more useful fusion.

They kind of shrugged, then went on for the rest of the night talking about video on demand, computer-in-the-living-room stuff, and ignoring my notions of data synergy. I admit it: I felt dumb, like I'd been asked what I wanted for dinner and answered that in 2035 people will eat cruelty-free food grown from stem cells rather than harvested from dead animals.

But when I saw Google Maps fused with Craigslist to present apartment information, and Flickr integrated into weblogs, and del.icio.us, and RSS, I knew I'd been right.

Cringely seems to agree.

Here is what Web 2.0 WILL be, in my view: a new way of structuring Internet businesses around published APIs, Application Programming Interfaces. New companies will spring up that simply glue web-based APIs together. For example, Google Maps plus accident reports for insurance companies, or Amazon plus eBay plus Froogle for purchasing departments.

Hell, that's what the sidebar on this site is about: integration. Quick links powered by del.icio.us. Blogroll by Bloglines.

I want to build a dating site like this. Match + Google Maps + Zagat + Flickr + Ticketmaster.

But yeah, I guess video on demand happened first.

I didn't realize at the time that I was forseeing portals reinventing themselves. I didn't think about blogs. I didn't think about social networking sites (which still suck, by the way).

On Tuesday I was asked to identify the files that I'd edited since our last deployment to production. Any time I'm asked to "figure out which files I edited", alarm bells go off. It's a symptom of a badly broken development process.

And the week started out so well...

So that settles it. I'm using the Joel Test to screen future employers. Specifically the following questions:

  • Do you use source control?
  • Can you make builds in one step?
  • Do you have a bug database?
  • Do programmers have quiet working conditions?

And I've added a few of my own:

  • Do you use automated testing?
  • Is there an in-house graphic designer?

intro:
EFF is covering some of the first post-Grokster bullying going on.
"We're hopeful Slingbox will incorporate technology that will respect copyright," said Dean Garfield, vp and director of legal affairs at MPAA. "You don't have the authority to retransmit license work without negotiation or authorization."

This is getting scary. I was apalled when cellphone makers refused to let customers use MP3s as ringtones because "There's an effort by the industry to make people pay" for unique ringtones.

Now, even TiVo had better pay up.

"Even if you take it at face value that it is a one-to-one transmittal device, I don't think it will be very long before some hacker in Cupertino posts on the Web the way to modify it, the way they modify a TiVo, that turns it into something that can be tapped by 50 people," Franks said.

Get ready to fork it over, kids. We're all going to be paying more for devices that do less.

What really pisses me off about this? All the techies saw it coming. All the business guys saw it coming. All the lawmakers saw this coming. The only people too stupid to see the damage this would do were the United States Supreme Court.
title: Inevitable Fallout from Grokster Ruling

intro:
Just checked out a post by one of the interns working for Joel Spolsky this summer. He mentions that he spent ninety minutes figuring out that some automated email he was generating was being rejected by Yahoo! because it contained a link to http://localhost/aardvark.
So basically I spent around 90 minutes tracking down a problem that doesn't even matter because the production site will obviously send emails that link to copilot.com, not localhost.

Oh, so you think this was a waste of time, eh?

Not so. This should teach you about shortcuts, proofreading, and blind spots in your testing procedure.

It's never possible to say "this won't be a problem in the real world", because trust me: the real world will throw more problems at you than your test environment, not less. You must make as few assumptions as possible about what the "real world" will be like. When you uncover one, it is rarely wise to dismiss it.
title: Mindset

intro:
I've railed for years about how legislators and judges are, for the most part, frankly unqualified to work on technology law.

Donna Wentworth at Copyfight seems to agree.

And I have further evidence that education might be a good idea. Richard Posner, in his analysis of the Grokster ruling, says:

For example, copyright owners who wanted to be able to sue for contributory infringement might be required, as a condition of being permitted to sue, to place a nonremovable electronic tag on their CDs that a computer would read, identifying the CD or a file downloaded from it as containing copyrighted material.

Judge Posner seems to have overlooked that professional programmers sometimes go home and program for fun. And with some programming skills and a little time, getting around restrictions is a simple matter. (For an especially lucid explanation of why this is so, see Chapter 2 of Hackproofing Your Network.)

Prof. Ed Felten also points this out, and proposes that we need to educate judges on the basics of how computers and the Internet function. With the RIAA, MPAA, and countless other entities actively trying to muddy the waters, it becomes especially important that judges be able to clarify matters.
title: Educating Judges

intro:
As many of you know, I've been having knee problems over the last year or so. I've been to a doctor, a massage therapist, had an MRI scan, and taken a few months off running.

And yet after my hike yesterday, I'm in pain again. It's the same symptoms. Tightness in my ITB, and a hot, tight feeling on the outer side of my left knee.

And yesterday, as I was enjoying my lunch and flipping through the latest Runner's World, I noticed a story on fixing gait problems. One of the well-known problems cited in the article: ITB Friction Syndrome. One of the contributing factors is a narrow gait, which fits; all my shoes have scuff marks on their inner sides from rubbing together as I walk/run. The magazine suggests a couple of gait-correction excercises to help with the problem.

Now, I'm not going to take a magazine article as gospel. But I'm now completely convinced that I need a doctor with more expertise in sports-related injuries. If this is a common problem among runners, it shouldn't have been this hard to diagnose. MRI? The massage therapist heart "runner" and "knee" and headed straight for my ITB. My doctor ordered an MRI and three weeks of physical therapy, and I'm nowhere close to being able to go for a run.
title: Sports-Centric Medicine

I've been preaching so much about the Joel Test that I figured it was time to put it into action at home. I've enacted various parts of it at work, but because I was fighting company culture most of the time, it turned out piecemeal. I introduced the folks at my old job to Bugzilla. A coworker brought in JUnit and Ant. Source control has always been present, but I've never seen it used especially well. And only the newest of new projects employed the full stack of development tools.

So it's time to get used to running "at 12" at home, so that I can better bring it to work. Or at least as close to 12 as I can get at home. There are few questions that simply don't apply. Here are the ones that I want to do something about:

  • Do you use source control?
  • Can you make a build in one step?
  • Do you have a bug database?
  • Do you use automated testing?
  • Do you have automated backups of all changable files (Including IDE config, routers, etc.)?

(That last one isn't strictly a development-related goal, but it does help my sanity.)

These are all very doable. I got CVS running tonight. Tomorrow is two projects: Bugzilla and Ant. If I'm not totally burned out on Sunday afternoon, I'll aim for bring in some JUnit tests, but since this is a web app, I'm going to have to look into Cactus or something else to test the presentation layer.

So I guess in the end, I'm trying to run my home development environment at 5.

intro:
Slept in on Saturday, then headed for the climbing gym, where Timbo and I discovered that Boulderdash was hosting California Climbing Challenge finals.

Within about thirty seconds of walking into the gym, one of the staff grabbed us and put us to work as full-time belay bitches. The competitors ranged in age from 11 to 45, and I learned something from each and every one. The first girl up was so smooth, just made her decisions and went with 'em, no energy wasted hanging around.

I belayed from about 2:30 'till 5:30, then spent some time just watching the bouldering rotation. After a quick hop up the street for a quick burger, Timbo and I finally got to try our hand at the competiton climbs. Everything was harder than the competitors made it look, but the first two climbs were great fun. The setters seemed to take sick pleasure in making the last hold on several of the climbs a sloper.

And the "bonus" climb that I'd belayed all afternoon was nothing but slopers. Very cool-- you don't see that very often in gyms.

The whole atmosphere reminded me of the early days of skateboarding, when you'd show up at the skate shop on a Saturday, and there'd be a couple pros and most of the local badasses running a launch session, and 50 or 60 people all watching or doing tricks of their own on the fringes of the crowd. When I see Prana t-shirts I have flashbacks to Vision Street Wear, and I think I finally understand the feelings of everyone who wants the sport to stay small.

Spending time with great musicians always elevated my playing a bit. Watching world-class climbers up close was the same way. Afterward, I found myself climbing differently, and finishing climbs on the first try that might have pitched me last week.

Funny how all my favorite experiences lately have been ones that I just kind of stumbled into while heading somewhere else...

intro:
Last week I mentioned that the next version of Windows will contiain video-hobbling DRM, and that MS is aparently trying to slip this in under consumers' radar.

Now the consortium behind the HD-DVD spec is aiming for the same thing: a digital "imprimatur" meant to verrify that the disc was produced by a licenced authority. From Freedom to Tinker:

The AACS documents avoid giving a rationale for this feature. The closest they come to a rationale is a statement that the system was designed so that "[c]ompliant players can authenticate that content came from an authorized, licensed replicator" (p. 1). But the system as described does not seem designed for that goal - if it were, the disc would be signed (and the signature possibly revoked) by the replicator, not by the central AACS organization. Also, the actual design replaces "can authenticate" by "must authenticate, and must refuse to play if authentication fails."

Like Prof. Felten, I hope that consumers will notice the stupidity of this, and vote with their dollars.
title: HD-DVD to Require Permission to Play

I'm all for having some kind of official taxonomy for naming items in a library. But I haven't met one yet that doesn't convince me it would be easier to just go search the stacks.

I remember being a music student trying to find, say, recordings of Bach organ music. You can't just type in "Bach organ concerto", because you'd get sheet music, writings about, and maybe, burried somewhere on page seventeen of your search results, the reference number of the CD you're looking for. So you have to clarify. You want a concerto for organ by Bach, and you want a recording. So you have to use "auth: Bach +snd key: concerto" or some such garbage.

On the other hand, I can type, "our house, in the middle of our street" into Google, hit "I'm feeling lucky", and find myself with complete lyrics and album info for "Our House" by Madness.

See the difference?

I know someone who's getting her Master's in Library and Info. Science. I'll ask her why libraries suck.

And I have a particular complaint about Indiana University's IUCAT library search system. It's great and all (especially since it let me find my recital recordings in about three seconds), but I can't permalink to the catalog entry that has the info I need. (This is as close as I could get.) If I want that record again, I have to search for it again. Dumb.

body:
In the case of looking for recital recordings, I wondered why the IU library system would hang on to an archaic search syntax when Google seems to have proven that a few well-chosen keywords will almost always get you what you want.

And trying to describe car parts led me to think about the futility of devising a system to describe all possible mechanical components.

And so, I started thinking about tags, and I thought about keyword searches, and I thought about libraries. I thought about libraries of tagged car parts whose descriptions could be searched by keyword. And I realized I ought to talk to an expert.

So I did. I had an interesting talk with a friend over the weekend about all this.

First and foremost, I wanted to know why libraries typically have such difficult-to-use search functions. It took me 45 minutes to find a recording of a recital that I played in.

Software design is all about trade-offs, and it seems that libraries have different priorities than Google, and so make different trade-offs. Libraries are interested in precision and completeness above all else. So their search syntax is a language designed to let users describe with great acuracy exactly what they're looking for.

"Fiction by Isaac Asimov that was published in periodicals between 1954 and 1961."
"Fiction which Asimov co-authored with Arthur C. Clarke"
"Scholarly work by Asimov on the subject of Chemistry"

All of these are subtilly distinct searches when expressed simply as keyword sets. But they're radically different when expressed in the language of a proper library catalog search system.

So okay, I'll buy that. There's a power and precision to library searching that Google can't match. Additionally, each work is scrutinized by an expert and associated with various keywords and subjects by that expert. So even a book that never usese the word "evolution", but that does talk about development of species, would turn up under the subject heading of "evolution". And that's cool.

But you can't do that for the Web. It's too big, and it changes too fast. It's relatively easy to keep up with every book published in the world in a year. Someone, somewere read it and stuck it in the Library of Congress. But the Web? That's hard.

So it's not that Google is all that great, it's just that Google is the best we can do for the Web. And that's part of why it's sometimes hard to use Google for research. Unless you know the right keywords, you're hosed. Nobody has read the material and cross-referenced it with likely search terms. If the author used "sufferage" instead of "women's right to vote," you'd damn well be searching for "sufferage."

I get that power and precision are good. But the user interfaces to most library search systems suck. And not just a little. So there's work to be done there. Google is doing great things in UI work, so there's a natural partnership there. (Well, duh. But you know what I mean.)

And I think that the trade-off between precision and searchability is a false one. What annoys me most about library search systems is the guessing game aspect. Search for that Bach fugue, and a cantata won't be included in the returned data.

Oh, and another thing: folksonomies. Not sure how that figures in. Really, I don't think it does.

As for categorizing car parts, I have no idea. I may have to start with the Wikipedia tonight and surf until I find something useful, then go talk to an expert again.

intro:
Had a run-in with the XHTML spec last week, and wanted to post it here in case I need it again.

I had an image in a table, and for the life of me couldn't figure out why the browser (both Firefox and IE, if I recall correctly) were inserting a three-pixel margin at the bottom of the image. (The image was in a table cell by itself, and those extra three pixels were stretching the whole table out of alignment.)

For the life of me, I can't locate the page where I found the solution, so I'll just explain it again here.

The XHTML spec says that the bottom of an image should be lined up with the baseline of the text. No text? Doesn't matter. The browser will still throw in some space under the image as if there were.

To fix the problem, apply the following style to the affected image: 

img {
    vertical-align: middle;
}

Between this, my superscript issue, and all the other stuff I dump in here just so I can search for it later, I'm starting to think that some kind of personal knowledge base might be a good idea. Hmm...
title: XHTML and Images

intro:
Shit.

I took the train to work this morning, which always puts me in the mood to get a shiny new 12'' Powerbook, so I can hack on my way to work in the morning. And I've got a bonus coming up, so the free cash may actually materialize to put said shiny new Powerbook in my hands.

But the first thing I see when I get to work this morning is a post on BoingBoing linking to a Wiki page about about Apple is putting DRM into OSX.

This really, really sucks, and basically means that I won't be buying that Powerbook.

Why? What's so horrible about "Trusted Computing?" What's the problem with DRM?

The problem is that DRM (Digital Rights Management) and Trusted Computing have nothing to do with preventing copying. DRM is a tool for enforcing customer lock-in.

Trusted Computing potentially makes it illegal for me to open my own files, written by me on my own computer, with a program I wrote.

Let's say I write a screenplay in MS Word for Mac OSX. Microsoft might see fit to mark every Word document so that it can only be opened with Word. Trusted Computing would make the OS refuse to open that file with EMACS, or OpenOffice, or even an older version of Word. And it would be illegal for me to break that restriction.

My data is my life, and I won't keep it in a strongbox that someone else has the keys for. Cory Doctorow

Slashdot is also on the story.
title: Apple OSX to Incorporate DRM

intro:
By now everyone's heard about the boy who was killed after taunting another boy after a baseball game.

I keep hearing about how terrible it is for the boy who was killed. And it was. I feel for his parents, and his friends, and for the boy who killed him. It's a terrible loss, and I wouldn't wish it on anyone.

But I don't hear much about what it took to make the attacker pick up a bat.

By one account, the victim outweighed his attacker by 100 lbs, and after taunting and shoving the other boy, asked, "What are you going to do about it?"

If my kids are ever bullied, I'm going to show how to use a roll of quarters, and tell them, "If he comes at you again, just make it cost him. You don't have to win to make him not want to mess with you again. There are worse things than suspension." Bullying is about power, and the only way to regain your dignity once a bully has taken it from you is to take it back.

There's a great scene in Good Will Hunting where Will and his friends attack a guy that used to beat up Will when he was a kid. Most of my friends don't understand that that fight isn't about revenge. It's about Will saying, "You have something that belongs to me." Win or lose, Will is able to stick up for himself like he couldn't as a boy. That's what that scene is about.

So when a bully asks, "What are you going to do about it?" and gets a bat to the head, well...

To paraphrase Chris Rock: "I'm not saying he should have killed him... but I understand."
title: Bullying, Baseball, Tragic Consequences

body:
First, the clippers.

About a year ago, I got myself a barber's hair clipper. I was tired of spending $20 on a hair cut every three weeks to keep my hair as short as I wanted it. It was a $35 investment that has since paid for itself ten times over.

Anyway, it turned out to be a great idea. Yes, my mom doesn't like my haircut. It's tough to get the back just right, and I can tell you from experience that it's a bad idea to cut your own hair when you're angry.

Anyway, I've become pretty good at getting things trimmed the way I like, and thought I'd pass along a few tips.

Start with the larger guards and work down.

I start with a #3 guard to trim everything. Then a #2 for the sides and back, and finally finish the back, temples, and behind the ears with the #1. Final cleaning up along the back of my neck is done with a razor.

Keep a vacuum handy

Hair's going to go everywhere. Don't even hope for tidiness. Just clip away, and vacuum up the mess later. (And make sure to put your toothbrush away before you start. *cough*)

I was serious when I said hair would go everywhere. Vacuum again, and make sure you check on top of the medicine cabinet, along the tops of cupboard doors and drawers, etc.

Don't cut your hair first thing in the morning.

Give your hair a quick wash or just throw some water in it and dry it off. Get it standing up normally before you start, or you'll end up with strange irregular patches sticking up here and there. I learned this on a Sunday, so I just trimmed up that night and only my family was the wiser.

For God's sake, don't tell anyone.

For months, I didn't mention to anyone that I was cutting my own hair. Not that it was any big secret; it just didn't come up. I even got a couple of compliments.

But as soon as people know you cut your own hair, they tend to scrutinize a bit, and they're pretty free with the comments. My favorite so far: "Wouldn't you be happier letting a professional do it?"

Okay, so that covers the clippers. On to shaving.

Ages and ages ago, I went looking for a Better Way to Shave. (I even posted about it.) The Kid Glove Shave Gel is awesome. But I've found a better option.

At the suggestion of an old college bud, I tried shaving the way my grandfather would have: shaving soap and a brush. And it's great. Extremely close shave, happy skin, and that light, clean smell too. And I can skip the metro-priced $12 shave gel in vavor of a $1.29 cake of shaving soap.

So what's the upshot of the whole thing? No idea. Just thought I'd share. Happy Monday, everyone.

I had an appointment with Dr. Kvitne this morning, and it went extremely well.

In about five minutes he found everything that my GP, an MRI specialist, and two physical therapists took weeks to figure out, and spotted the runner's knee, which the others missed.

The guy's a rock star.

The rundown: runner's knee in both knees, and bad ITB friction syndrome in the left. I'll have to ice both knees every night and after any physical activity, and undergo about two months of "agressive" physical therapy. He says I'll be black and blue from my calves to my hips after the massage. Fun.

But the net result is that I should be able to start running again in October, which is great news.

Dr. Kvitne seemed surprised that I was willing to drive 90 min. to see him, but to me it was a no-brainer. Having a specialist look at the problem, and getting real answers makes all the difference. If I'd seen him in March, when all this started, I'd be running already. If I'd seen him before that, I might have been able to run the marathon.

intro:
When I was a kid I used to play a lot of bumper pool during the summers. I was mad for it. Every weekday I'd just hang out at the local community center from the time the day camp let out until closing time. I got pretty good, nobody in the neighborhood could beat me. It ruled.

Except that when I left, I'd still be thinking about bumper pool. I'd hear the doorbell, and think about the best way to carom off the wall, into the hallway, through the living room, and hit the front door. It was like that old Donald Duck cartoon about billiards and geometry; everywhere I went I saw angles and reflections.

Sometimes the same thing happens to me when I've been coding too much. I went into the breakroom yesterday looking for a knife to cut some cake with. I started with the row of cabinets above the counter. As I was working my way down the row, a coworker said, "Dude, the knife is in one of those drawers." I kept searching the cabinets, thinking, ah, so I'll find it on my way back, and optimize the pattern next time.

"Dude, drawer," he repeated.

I finally snapped out of it when he reached into the drawer and handed me the knife. "Have you had your coffee yet, man?"

I thought for a second, and decided that I'd rather plead stupidity than total nerdspace immersion.

"No," I said. "Good idea."

Engadget has been hosting Stephen Speicher's "The Clicker" column for a while. Speicher's never been any genious, but his latest The Clicker is just jaw-droppingly stupid:
Hash it. Encrypt it. Do what you like, but make sure that the file only plays if it's been unaltered. I agree; that's not an easy problem. However, it's really no harder than completely locking down the file. This of course would mean you would need to produce closed-source tools for all the major operating systems, but this could be done.

It seems that all the best-informed, most lucid writers on this topic are heavily anti-DRM. I agree with their stance, but I'm wary of the echo-chamber effect. I'd love to hear from some other perspectives. But those perspectives have to acknowledge the technical realities of DRM implementation, or they're just hand-waving.

Engadget is an outstanding venue for discussion of DRM. It's too bad that Speicher isn't delivering the kind of well-informed discussion that might help align consumer and content-owner interests.

I recently met with a physical therapist about my knees, and nearly the first thing she said was, "Have you considered giving up running?"

No, I haven't. And I won't. Here's why:

Eskimos hunted killer whales with sealskin canoes and spears. North American natives played games of Lacrosse that spanned days, and miles. And I've met 60-year-old men who are still badass climbers, runners, swimmers, and bikers.

I have a hard time believing that I've put my body through anything like what native peoples did. I have no trouble at all believing that I tried too much too fast, or that I didn't stretch enough, or didn't eat right, or that I have poor form.

So no. I'm not giving up running or anything else. I'm going to rest and learn, and become stronger and smarter than I was.
