intro:
I've been pulled by conflicting forces lately, and they've all surrounded one decision: Do I buy a 12'' Powerbook?

First, I'll cop to the pure geeky technolust charge. Yes, it's shiny. But there's more than that. I want to play with the latest toy so that I can be there when it becomes a tool. It's the same instinct that drove me to spend beer gaming money on a copy of JavaScript: The Definitive Guide back when I was in college, and not yet even a Comp Sci student.

Mobile computing is What's Next, and the time is finally ripe to jump in and see what's going to shake out of that. Some may argue that laptops and Treos and PDAs have been around for years. But they're all functioning as a stand-in for some less gadgety item. PDA's replace leather and paper day runners. Laptops are just portable desktops. What we carry with us has changed. But the way we use it hasn't. Yet.

The reason I got excited about Plazes is not because it's some stupendously snazzy web app that I'll use every day. I really haven't touched it since I mentioned it a few days ago. I got excited because it's an app that doesn't even make sense if it doesn't run on a mobilie device with a 'net connection. Now we're cooking.

But then, the buzzkill of fiscal responsibility kicks in. A 12'' Powerbook is over $1600 with tax, and that's a lot of money to spend when I really should be shedding credit card debt.

And one of my goals this year is to spend less time at the computer, not more. Last weekend I took a traditional-style climbing class in Idyllwild. I loved being disconnected.

For the last couple of weeks, I've been talking about getting a Powerbook. But it's just not going to happen until I pay off my other consumer debt. I still owe $1500 on one credit card, and $3500 on a credit account that's not accruing interest until next year. So I'll get that down to manageable levels before spending my cash on The Next Thing.

But damn, it's shiny, innit.

Our guides/instructors were Bob Gaines (Saturday), and Erik Kramer-Webb (Sunday). Both were fantastic teachers-- I have more new knowledge packed into my brain than I'm even aware of. I'm sure the next time I go climbing I'll use a few techniques I leared last weekend, probably without realizing it. After two days doing something, a new technique isn't new, it's just the way it's done.

Suicide Rock lies at the end of a 45-minute uphill hike. If you're like me, and live at sea level, remember to pace yourself. It's not a long trail, but you start at 6000ft. of elevation, and climb to about 6700ft. And bring plenty of water. I was fine on Saturday, but underestimated my needs on Sunday, and ended up having to conserve a bit in the afternoon. No problems resulted, but being a bit thirsty is no way to try to enjoy a day in such amazing country.

Saturday started with a lecture on basic safety, leading techniques, and gear types, followed by a "simulated lead" up The Hernia (5.8).

I got my first adrenaline kick when a nut pulled a couple meters below me, leaving me well into groundfall territory. I could only think oh, shit as that red stopper ran merrily down the rope. Then I realized two things: 1. I'm on toprope. 2. I'm standing at a giant fscking cam placement. So I just cursed my carelessness in forgetting to set the nut, and sank the cam.

The rest of the climb went without incident, with Bob jumaring up a fixed line next to me and coaching me on my placements and technique.

Once everyone was back on the ground, we did an hour or so on some very basic self-rescue techniques, and a workshop on anchor building. Bob was amazing. No filler in his lessons; everything's important. And he accepted our inexperience with the patience of Job.

The plan for dinner was so simple: cook the steaks on the portable grill and the potatos in the campfire, then chow down, drink beer, and sit 'round the campfire.

Of course, this was not to be. The copious juice from the steaks extinguished the coals under them, leaving us with half-cooked steaks and not enough coals to finish the job. And since we'd planned to sit around the campfire later, I'd started the wood fire in the "fire pit" side of the pit, not the "grill" side. So we had no choice but to try to move the camp fire.

Of course, this just put the campfire out too.

So, there we are with raw potatos, undercooked steaks, and no fire. Things took a while to get going again, and most of the potatos were lost in the process. Some were accidentally peeled by falling logs, others made it to the table only to be returned for more cooking. In the end we had overdone steaks for dinner, sans potatos, with beer to wash it down.

Rather than try to fill our bellies with Cheez-Its and jerky, we finished our beers and decided to walk into town and find a coffee shop or something where we could get some snacks, and hot drinks, and relax for a while.

Upon reaching the road into town, Darrell pointed straight across it and said, "how 'bout we take a short cut?"

"I don't think that goes where you think it goes, Dude. 'Downtown' isn't that big," I said.

We took the "short cut" anyway, and ended up about half a mile east of the town center. We were a little out of our way, but we discovered two really interesting things:

  1. Idyllwild, CA, Pop. 34, has a skate park, which struck me as progressive.
  2. They also have a Greek restaurant where you can get date shakes. I've never had one, but Darrell seemed pretty excited.

Having filed that knowledge away for later, we wandered over to the Java Lounge ("Your coffee and tea experience!"), which advertised "live music". Looked good from the outside, but there were a bunch of people sitting around using laptops, and the "live music" was a guy playing slightly atonal renditions of Celine Dion standards on a keyboard.

As we sat on the deck watching bugs circle the streetlights and sipping lukewarm lattes, it became very clear to us that Jo An's is the place to be on Saturday night. Hell, some girls had actually "woo"-ed at us as they drove that direction, so hey, y'know.

Unfortunately, it was 10pm, we'd been up since 6am hiking and climbing, and we were too pooped to karaoke. On hindsight, another drink (or three) might have helped turn us back into party people, but as it was we just finished our coffee, grabbed a snack at the mini-mart, and headed back to camp to crash.

And all was blackness and quiet until 4am the next morning, when our neighbors started bickering about how to put their pop-up trailer back in "trailer mode". I cursed them unto three generations, and tried to get back to sleep. But this was difficult for several reasons:

  1. The ground at our site was sloping. Move a little bit, and you'd slide downhill an inch or two. Roll over, and you had to inchworm back onto your pad.
  2. It was pretty damn cold. Weather.com reports overnight temperatures at 64°. This is a lie, and I have the sniffle to prove it. (I was toasty in my mummy bag, but Darrell reports chattering of teeth in his square flannel thing.)
  3. The moon was full, and dawn was close. Too bright to sleep.

So we shook the sleep out of our eyes, broke camp, and headed into town for breakfast, hoping to score some (reportedly delicious) blueberry pancakes at The Bakery. This was not to be. The Bakery opens at 8am.

So we headed over to Jan's Red Kettle cafe for omelettes (decent) and biscuits (outstanding), and then met up with our guide Erik Kramer-Webb.

Sunday's class was more of the same, with a simulated lead on Breakout (5.6). Later on in the afternoon we had some fun on The Bunny Slope (5.10 slab), which was great fun. Erik TR'ed it with ease, but Darrell and I both escaped to the right up the Breakout crack section. I can't wait to get back there and give it another go.

While we played on The Bunny Slope, some poor climber had stalled out just below the tree on Flower of Higher Rank. After what seemed like ages of struggling, she managed to reach the tree and set up a belay. Her partner quickly joined her there, and we thought he'd lead to the top, but eventually they both retreated, leaving some really un-tempting sling/biner booty on the tree.

A word to the wise: Flower ain't no 5.9.

The retreating climbers ended up working on a nice slab next to our afternoon hex placement workshop, and we couldn't help but notice that the girl who'd struggled on FoHR was extremely cute. Though I wanted to, I thought it would be in poor taste to stare, and my descretion earned me nothing but trash talk from Erik and Darrell for "giving her the cold shoulder." Next time, I'm going to shamelessly hit on any woman nearby, so that my friends can witness the train wreck that usually results.

This was a great trip-- I've had more fun in my life, but I learned an aweful lot, and realized I have an aweful lot yet to learn. I'm decent with a regular backyard charcoal grill, but the portable model gave us some trouble, so I'm tempted to get one and practice cooking over it so that I can put a proper meal together next time. And I also think that for just a two-person trip, camping just isn't that much fun. For less than 4 people or so, I think you're better off just getting a cabin.

Darrell and I have agreed that the next step is to get comfortable on some sport leads, then do a guided climb up Tahquitz, which features some long, easy routes we can use to get our act together under adult supervision.

But for now, I'm holding off on putting together a rack. A set of draws should be plenty for a little while.
title: Trip Report: Suicide Rock Trad Class

intro:
I love brain teasers. But it really burns me when the question turns out to have a problem.

In this case, I'm talking about the 1960 Popular Science Puzzle posted to BoingBoing yesterday. In an update to the solution, a reader starts his comment with, "Here's why I think the answer to the 1960's puzzle is bullshit:"

And I agree. Here's the puzzle (dmg copy):

The census taker, placing one weary foot after another, climbed the steps and rang the bell. "How many people live here?" he asked the person who answered the door.

"Three," was the prompt answer.

"And their ages?"

The reply startled him: "The product of our ages is 225, while the sum is the same as the house number."

The census taker looked up to check the number he had already noted on his tally sheet. "Hmm," he said, "I need to know one more thing: Are you the eldest?"

"Why, yes," the person said. And the census taker, cheered at the novel answers, smiled as he wrote down their ages and walked away.

Now, here are the clues gleaned from the above:

  • There are three ages: a, b, and c
  • a + b + c = house#
  • a * b * c = 225
  • The census taker knows the house number.
  • The census taker didn't know whether the speaker was the oldest.

Now, I quickly factored 255 as: 1 * 3 * 3 * 5 * 5 = 255. And there are only so many ways to multiply those factors together into three ages. My hand-scribbled list has slashes through it, so I pasted this one from BoingBoing:

  • 9 + 5 + 5 = 19
  • 15 + 15 + 1 = 31
  • 15 + 5 + 3 = 23
  • 25 + 9 + 1 = 35
  • 25 + 3 + 3 = 31
  • 45 + 5 + 1 = 51
  • 75 + 3 + 1 = 79
  • 225 + 1 + 1 = 227

Now, the census taker knows the house number, and still needs more information to narrow the possibilities. There's only one sum ("house number") that leaves any ambiguity, and that's 31. So we're left with two possible age combinations:

  • 15 + 15 + 1 = 31
  • 25 + 3 + 3 = 31

Now, we know that the census taker didn't know whether he was talking to the oldest. So my thinking is: If the census taker is talking to a 1- or 3- year-old, he knows he's not talking to the oldest. If he's talking to a 25-year-old, he knows he is talking to the oldest. So he must be talking to a 15-year-old.

So the people in the house must be 15, 15, and 1.

Nope. The thinking of the people who wrote the puzzle is this: There exists an "oldest", therefore he can't be talking to a 15-year-old twin. And if he were talking to a 1- or 3-year-old, he'd know he was not talking to the eldest. So he must be talking to a 25-year old.

So, basically, the authors of the puzzle accept the premise that the census taker might be a moron who can't tell a 25-year-old from a 15-year-old from an infant or toddler.

So yeah. The question is flawed.

This is a big part of why I like tavern puzzles so much: there's no way that anyone can hand you the puzzle wrong.
title: The Trouble with Brain Teasers

I did a very, very little bit of climbing over the weekend. And it sucked.

My feet and balance are fine, but after essentially a month off from climbing anything harder than 5.8, I have no core strength, I feel weak and heavy. I tried to climb a sequency 5.7, and couldn't do it. Seriously. Not, "I fell the first time." No. I fell three times and gave up.

Crap.

Since I've been my doctor's orders preclude walking, running, climbing, etc., and since I had a little strain in the tendons in my hands (from climbing, natch), I've basically been sitting on my ass for the last month. It is horrible, and I'm getting restless enough that I'm going to try swimming.

By now you know as well as I do what's going to happen next: I'm going to get a sinus infection.

So I'm taking a Claratin now, and I'll be adding an extra milti-vitimin at the end of the day, and hoping that I can burn a few calories in the pool tonight.

And I might try a Yoga class. I have to do something...

intro:
Some half-wit at the credit card processing company forgot to get the handshaking right. You know who you are. You got a B- in EE101, because you didn't understand handshaking. You didn't pay attention when they taught about transaction management.

I bet you swallow exceptions, you neanderthal.

Here's what happened:

  1. Point-of-Sale system submits request to charge my credit card.
  2. Your server responds "OK", and charges my card.
  3. P.O.S. system never gets reply, displays "ERROR".
  4. Cashier says, "Hmm. Lemme try again."
  5. P.O.S. system submits request to charge my credit card.
  6. Your server responds "OK", and charges my card.
  7. P.O.S. system never gets reply, displays "ERROR".
  8. Cashier say, "Sir, there's something wrong with our credit card system. We can try again on your next visit."

Later, I discover that I've been charged twice.

So, to all of you out there hiring programmers, and thinking (or not thinking) about the relative cost of hiring a half-wit v. a Rock Star, add this on the "liabilities" side of your equasion. Poor programmers incur horrendous wastage of resources because they don't know what they're doing.

I swear, I'm going to make so much money some day teaching corporate coders how to do their jobs...
title: Communication Breakdown

intro:
On Monday I took a friend's recommendation and called 1-800-CONTACTS. I gave them my eye doctor's phone number, and let them know I just wanted another pair of whatever I had last time.

I waited on hold while the service rep called my doctor. When she returned, she said that my doctor was on vacation until Sept. 7, and that they couldn't obtain the prescrition until then.

So this morning I call my optometrist's office to try to straighten things out. He is indeed on vacation until the 7th, and they can't provide the prescrition until then. I ask if there's a way around that, since I'm just trying to order contacts. She says that the prescription isn't written down.

What?!

After two minutes of excruciating discussion, we establish that yes, my prescription is in my file, it's just not written on a little prescription paper, so she can't let me use it to buy eyeglasses or contacts.

Evidently, since that prescription is more than a year old, the doctor has to be there to sign off, and since he's on vacation, I'm screwed. They cannot provide the prescription to the contact lens service. And since it's more than two years old, I must come in for an exam before he'll sign off.

Say what? It's written down in my file, and it's been stable for years. I'm wearing glasses that are five years old. And I still have to jump through a month's worth of hoops every time I want new glasses.

Fine. When can I come in?

The receptionist says that since the doctor's on vacation, his schedule is pretty crowded for the next couple of weeks.

I say I understand, and can I please have the first Tuesday or Thursday morning he has open.

The receptionist suggests a Wednesday afternoon.

No, I strongly prefer a Tuesday or Thursday morning.

No, a Friday morning won't work.

No, not Monday either.

No, a 10am doesn't count as "morning".

Finally, she books me for 8am on a Tuesday morning.

Three weeks from now.

There has to be a better way to do this. And in three weeks, me and the good doctor will talk about how I can get new glasses and contacts without a month lead time, and without him sidestepping applicable regulations.
title: What Century is This?

intro:
This is why I don't use UPS voluntarily any more:
THE RECEIVER WAS UNAVAILABLE TO SIGN ON THE 1ST DELIVERY ATTEMPT. A 2ND DELIVERY ATTEMPT WILL BE MADE
I went to UPS's website, which used to let you change the shipping address, but evidently doesn't any more. I found these instructions, which mention buttons that don't exist: Delivery Change Request Instructions
  1. From the UPS.com homepage, select Tracking.
  2. Enter a UPS InfoNotice Number in the Tracking Number field.
  3. Select the Track button below the New Tracking Numbers input fields.
  4. Select the Detail button on the Tracking Summary page.
  5. Choose the Delivery Change Request button on the Tracking Detail page.
  6. Select a Change Delivery option and complete the associated form.

I thought that maybe the buttons are only available to registered users. After all, you don't want just anyone being able to enter a tracking number and having everything shipped to them.

So I registered. I tried to use "craser" as my username, but that's been taken. So I used another name. I tried again to use the instructions above, still no dice.

So I called. And waited on hold. And talked to Steve, who assures me that they'll bring my package to my workplace tomorrow. I asked him to make sure they bring it to the front desk, not the receiving dock.

Except I know they will. Why? Because you don't have to be a half-wit to work at UPS, but it helps.

By the way, the stupidity over there has leeched into the advertising department, who clearly haven't mastered American English idioms. While I was on hold, a cheerful recorded voice reminded me to visit UPS's website, which can be used from anywhere, allowing me to be "so close, yet so far away."

And yes, they're still inviting me to find out "what brown can do for me."
title: UPS = Useless Piece of Sh!t

Ask them to explain why they think something is right, and they fall back to simple insistence.

title: Grammar

intro:
Okay, people. We need to get this handled. Can we please display am/pm information on all clocks at all times? My coffee maker has a little "AM" that's visible only when the clock is set for an AM hour. My alarm clock has a little light next to the "PM", which is doubly unhelpful: if I'm setting the clock in the dark, I just see the light, and not the "PM". (Or was it "AM"?) And if the clock is set for AM, the light is just off, which just leaves me wondering.

I hereby request that digital clock manufacturers feature a positive indication of both "AM" and "PM" status. I should never be in doubt as to what time is being displayed.

And for all you numbskulls out there that love to say things like "if you want to know what time it is, just look out the window!" I know perfectly well what time it is. I want to know what time my coffeemaker thinks it is.

I am tired of having to spend an extra ten seconds every time I set an alarm to double-check that I got the am/pm right.
title: AM/PM

intro:
I'm having one of those weeks. Monday started out with a coworker wisecracking about my relaxed interpretation of the dress code, then I find out that my credit card got double-charged to the tune of $270 extra.

My effort to order new contacts became an ordeal, and UPS inflicted their stupidity on me Wednesday and Thursday, and I'll have to deal with them again this week. Joy.

I took my car to get serviced, and while they remembered to fix my busted air conditioning and turn signal clicker, they forgot about my right rear brake light. And the replacement steering wheel stem controls don't have a cruise crontrol button.

Last night the neighbors kept me up from 12:30 to 1:45am watching some gladiator movie at full blast with the windows open. I called security at 1:10, but if they ever showed I have no idea. At 2:00 I finally reset my alarm from 6:30 to 7:30, took a Tylenol PM and crashed.

But the fun just doesn't stop. Oh no.

I awoke to hammering this morning at 7:10. Turns out a cleanup crew was in the apartment next door, and needed to, I dunno... hammer something on the other side of my bedroom wall.

I got up, barked at the cleaning crew, and stopped by the manager's office at about 7:50. A helpful gentleman reminded me that the office doesn't open until 8am.

So I called on my way to work. The apartment manager helpfully informed me that city ordenance allows crews to start work at 7am. I told her that painting, vacuuming, etc. are reasonable, but hammering on my bedroom wall really doesn't give me that warm, fuzzy, "my landlord loves me" feeling.

I told her that general noise is more and more of a problem, and that it's not just one apartment. I asked, again, that security make the rounds around 11:30pm, and try to remind people to close their windows.

Tonight I dig up my lease papers, and find out when I can leave.

Of course, all of this is a field of poppies compared to the clusterfsck going on in Louisiana. Just forget I mentioned any of it.

1. cd into the working directory.
  2. Make sure there's no version of the deleted file in the current directory.
  3. cvs login (You'll enter a password, and henceforth be able to run commands.)
  4. Run cvs status DeletedFile This'll show the current version. Here's my output: 
    ============================================================
File: no file DeletedFile          Status: Up-to-date

   Working revision:    No entry for DeletedFile
   Repository revision: 1.1.2.2 /path/to/working/directory/DeletedFile,v
   Expansion option:    o
   Commit Identifier:   f98431f3a44310e
   Sticky Tag:          b20050607 (branch: 1.1.2)
   Sticky Date:         (none)
   Sticky Options:      -ko
   Merge Form:          (none)

    The part that we're interested in is the "Repository revision". We'll need this later to tell CVS which version we want to restore.

  6. cvs update -r 1.1.2.2 DeletedFile U DeletedFile
  7. cvs commit DeletedFile

intro:
I ran across an article on my company intranet this morning on the Right to Repair Act (HR 2048). When the DMCA was passed, I wonder if Congress had considered the impact on the auto repair industry. From Aftermarket.org:
The Issue: Modern cars and light trucks contain advanced technology that monitors or controls virtually every function of the vehicle including: brakes, steering, air bags, fuel delivery, ignition, lubrication, theft prevention, emission controls and in some cases, tire pressure. Car owners and independent shops must have full access to the information and tools necessary to accurately diagnose, repair, or re-program these systems. This information and equipment is necessary to ensure vehicle safety, performance, and environmental compliance. Vehicle manufacturers are making access to such vital information increasingly difficult and costly to obtain for the independent aftermarket and its customers.

In other words, you ought to have the option of taking your car to an independent shop. But if the company that made your car decides to "protect it's intellectual property" and deny information and tools to independents, you're screwed.

This doesn't mention the DMCA specifically, but reading between the lines, I think it's pretty clear. Copyright is used over and over again to do things that have nothing to do with copyright, such as preventing third-party manufacturers from making replacement printer cartridges, or even refill old ones. It's been used to lock out disabled users: you can't make an out-loud text reader if you're not allowed "unauthorized" access to the text.

You'd think that the automotive industry was far, far removed from the concerns the Recording Industry Association of America. Not so. The truth is that "Intellectual Property" is being used in many industries as a tool to eliminate competition and force customer lock-in.
title: Ripples of the DMCA?

intro:
My knee is not healing well. I took a 15-minute walk last night, and it hurt. And it stayed tight the rest of the night. I stretched, I iced it for 20 minutes, and still it ached when I got into bed.

I'm starting to think that my physical therapist is a quack.

I told him about the walk, and he said, "Well, then you can't do that. You have to start out on the eliptical, or try a three-minute walk."

Whatever I do, he says it's too much. When I started with him, I could walk quickly for half an hour, and feel okay as long as I stretched. Now a 15-minute stroll around the block leaves me in pain.

I used to leg press 450lbs. Now I feel strained getting up a flight of stairs.

And I'm having a hard time seeing what a massage, stretching, and ice three mornings a week is really going to do. Shouldn't this be coupled with some kind of gait retraining?

When I asked him, "So what's the plan for getting me out of here?" He hand-waved it away, saying that we need to let things progress. I'm going to press him tomorrow on the expected timeline for something like this. When should I be able to walk for 20 minutes? When should I be headed back to the gym, and what excercises should I be doing?

At the moment, it just feels like things are coasting. The Doctor talked about "agressive" therapy, that I'd be "black and blue" on the outside of my leg from the massage, and that he'd be "floored" if I wasn't running again after a month of therapy.

And after two weeks, my physical therapist says I should "try a three minute walk?"

Time for me to get things in gear again.

intro:
I admit I didn't spend this weekend remembering the shock of four years ago. I decided on Friday to turn off the television, and avoid the 'net for a few days. I checked email, but that's about it. I worked on the code that runs this place. But I avoided the news.

I woke up late that morning. I slept through it. I got up, cursed my badly-designed alarm clock, and started to get dressed. Geoff called, stuttering.

"Have you seen the news?"

I said I hadn't.

"Then you don't know?"

"Know what?"

"You don't know? You haven't seen the news?"

"I don't know. What's going on?"

"Turn on the news."

"Geoff, I don't have cable."

"So you haven't seen the news?"

"No. Tell me what's going on."

"The United States has been attacked. The World Trade Center is gone, and the Pentagon was hit."

My feet were standing on the warm spot on the carpet by the window, the light coming through the vertical blinds from the living room. It was a beautiful morning.

Since I've been sidelined, I've been thinking about how to keep a log of daily runs once I get back into the habit. I've considered all the basics, (date, time, distance, pace, etc.), but some dude named Dave seems to have it nailed. He's evidently built a way to automatically upload time, heart rate, and GPS information to his blog, which then uses the Google Maps API to create a map of the run.

See for yourself.

This is extremely cool.
title: Geek Running

intro:
I've been chewing through The West Wing on DVD over the last few months. I hit the end of Season 4 at a full gallop, and ran right into the Season-5-isn't-available-yet wall. After waiting for six weeks for WB to get their act together and realize I need my fix, I hit up my favorite P2P service, and 18 hours later had The West Wing Season 5 on my hard drive.

I remember catching the Season 5 premier when it aired years ago. I made time for it. I was living with my parents at the time, and I sat down especially to watch the season premere.

And it sucked. I think I let my dad change the channel after half an hour or so.

Warren Ellis posted to the Bad Signal mailing list (dmg copy) about this very problem:

The biggest shock is the quiet. No-one has anything to say. No-one is funny. No-one is smart. Brad Whitford and Janel Moloney look choked. Alison Janney wanders around like someone stole her purse. When they do get to talk, it sounds like someone swapped out their brains over the summer. Suddenly none of them are any good at anything. The Secretary of Defense appears to have a whole different personality.

Secretary Hutchinson isn't the only one. Leo isn't listening to any one. Donna barely knows Josh. C.J. can't talk, never mind Toby or Will, who have all the poetry and inspiration of an extra value meal. Three seasons ago, Josh schooled his psychiatrist, then delivered the punchline: "I report to Leo McGarry and the President of the United States. Do you think I'd walk into this meeting without knowing exactly who you are?" This season he debated with a NASA scientist, saying, "I prepare even for the meetings I don't want to be in." But I just watched Josh fall apart in the Oval Office and get his ass handed to him by an intern.

I was watching the extras on the Season 4 DVD set the other night, and Sorkin was talking about the scene where Amy asks Donna, "Do you love Josh?" He said that the first two scenes in that episode with Amy and Donna are notable for the things that aren't said, and that the audience has to trust you to go somewhere with that. Sorkin delivers. Every time.

John Wells seems to have missed the previous four seasons worth of storylines and character development. Nobody is acting like themselves, and that breaks the audience's faith in the characters. When Will takes the fall for leaking sensitive documents, the audience is supposed to know, right that second, that it was the Vice President who actually leaked them. They know this because Toby's judgement is clouded by his resentment of Will leaving, and because Will simply wouldn't leak the documents, and has a track record of falling on his sword. That scene is suppoed to build tension, because we know that the next scene must be a confrontation between Will and the V.P.

But we don't. We just conclude that the writer decided to make Will a dumbass this episode, and then we have to endure the tedium of Josh Malina and Richard Schiff desperately emoting at each other for another fourty seconds.

Dammit, why does every character remind me of a bobble-head?

And what's happening in the California 47th? And wasn't Toby's wife about to get sued? Where's Jordan Kendall? And what the hell is up with the casting? What is this, The Love Boat?

And jeezus, they just completely wasted Glen Close. Glen Close.
title: The West Wing Season V: Adrift in the District

intro:
Well, it looks like the Marathon isn't going to happen. I sat down and did the math last night.

An agressive training schedule would have to start with three-mile runs at the beginning of October. At the moment, I don't think that's realistic. I'm fine to walk for 20 minutes or so, and I'm now clear to do an easy bike ride for 10-15 minutes, or eliptical machine for 10 minutes or so. Building up from that to 26.2 miles is no small thing. Most 4- or 6-month training schedules are predicated on an existing base of regular running. I'm starting from my couch.

Bottom line: pushing too hard is what got me here in the first place. I won't make the same mistake again. So tonight I go home, take a ride around the block, then ice my knee and read up on Google Maps.

What's making me crazy is that whenever I say "the Marathon isn't going to happen", everyone says that I should have a better attitude. When I say I'm committed, I get nothing but admonishments that I shouldn't push too hard.

So, I'm going to keep a positive attitude, and not push too hard, and we'll see what happens.
title: Next Year

My ideas are part feature creep and part interface design, but none of them are out-of-this-world crazy. Maybe that's a problem. I don't know. And I don't think I will know until I use the app.

I've already started building a project that uses the code for this blog to build a personal knowledge base. I'm tempted to build it out with tools like those for Backpack, and several of my own design, and see if it can become something more.

So this'll be a real test of my programming chops. Can I build a fast, smooth, easy-to-use web app that my dad might use? And can I do it without just reinventing Bugzilla?

So I may just have to pick up that used iBook I've been eyeballing. $550 for a G3 with WiFi? Deal.

intro:
I was at business dinner a few weeks ago. Dinner was winding down when the woman across from me asked, "So, how do I get back on the freeway from here?"

I answered: "You turn left onto Ventura right here, and the onramp is right down there on the left. You can't miss it."

She looked doubtful. A coworker chimed in. "No, no. Go right, and head toward Calabasas. Take a left over the overpass, then a right up Ventura, then take the onramp on your right."

I pressed on. "Seriously. If we were out front, you could see the overpass."

200 yards vs. a winding, 5-mile path from Woodland Hills back through Calabasas. Guess which one she picked.

Dinner broke up, and the ladies headed one way through the parking lot, and the guys the other. I looked at one of the other guys and said, "Nobody ever listens to me!"

"Yeah, dude. Where's the love?" he said.

"I'm plenty loved. Now I want fear and respect."
title: Nobody Ever Listens to Me

intro:
A couple weeks ago, I was a bit irked at my optometrist's unavailability.

Well, he's officially fired. The short version of today's events is: I broke my glasses, and after two conversations with my optometrist's receptionist during which I probably made things harder than they needed to be, it was established that since my prescription is out of date, they would not be providing replacement anything until I came in for an exam. So, instead of being able to pick up some new contacts on the way home, I had to scramble around and find a repair shop.

A coworker recommended Gabe's Frame Lab on Owensmouth just north of Sherman Way. The guy there was awesome, and had my glasses fixed in about five minutes, for $35. (Note that the address for that Google Maps link is not exact. It just points to the right spot on the map.)

So I'm no longer blind. But I'm sick of my eye doctor's extortion. I'm having an emergency, and I've been wearing the same prescription for the last 5½ years, and yet my optometrist is saying, "well, come in and pay my examination fee, and we'll set you up."

And, just to top it off, the receptionist promised me at 3pm that the doctor would call me back and try to straighten things out. It's now 5:15, and I haven't heard from him.

So I'll go on Tuesday morning, and get my new specs (and a backup set), and then I'm going hunting for a doctor that'll return my calls.

Update 01/02/08: This FAQ page at 1-800 Contacts.com says that the "by law" one-year expiration date on prescription is a minimum, not a maximum, and that eye doctors can issue more relaxed expiration dates if they see fit.
title: I'm Firing my Optometrist

intro:
Well, after a couple of months of hemming and hawing, I realized that I really oughtta, well, shi-- er, fish or cut bait.

So I fished.

I'm typing this on my new toy, a 12'' Powerbook. After realizing that $1500 just wasn't going to happen, and that an iBook was going to be horribly underpowered, I settled on a used machine. I paid $950 for a 12'' G4, which is perfect. Plenty of power (though I think I'm going to upgrade the ram from 256MB to 1G), and it'll do everything I need from a portable machine.

And it's Unixy to boot. Already I'm finding that there's a certain comfort level there. I just updated the /etc/hosts file to include the various machines on my home network, and I'll be writing a few scripts to perform various things like syncing with my desktop machine, etc.

There are a few things that I wish were easier. At home, I use a Happy Hacking Keyboard, and at work I've mapped the CAPSLOCK key to Ctrl, so I'm really, really used to having the Ctrl key right there under my left pinky. Already I'm tired of trying to save something in emacs and just getting AXC typed into the buffer.

I found this helpful page with plenty of tips for a UNIX geek trying to get comfortable on a Mac. Unfortunately, that page looks to be fairly dated. It recommends using dumpkeys and loadkeys to modify keybindings, but I can't find either of those utilities anywhere. Do they still exist on Tiger?

Anyway, I now have a perfect platform for testing some of my wacky ideas about where the web is going, and what kind of code I want to write next.

And it's shiny.

I'm housesitting for a family while they're away on vacation (bad guys: I still return home most afternoons and evenings), and I've really enjoyed having pets around. I love cats and dogs, but due to the small size of my apartment, and the long hours during the day that I'm out, having a cat or dog of my own just isn't a good idea. So yeah, it's been nice to have "rental" pets for the last week.

Except, I grew up with sane cats. Unemotional, stable, loving cats. Yeah, they might give you a warning swipe with the claws when they didn't want to be petted any more, but they were always well-behaved.

But I've learned something lately about cats that don't get to go outside: they get neurotic as hell. At the moment, the cat in this house is pissed because I didn't let him sleep on my bed last night. (Seems to be his favorite spot. I often find him in here when I get home at night.) He's running around all wound up with unfocused anxiety and general agressiveness. Bad for cats, and bad for houses where delicate items have been put on shelves. They're out of the reach of little hands, but they tend to be tempting targets for angry cats looking to knock some stuff over.

So Moogie got up on the headboard of the bed, and knocked off a glass jar. No breakage, fortunately.

After I kick him out and shut the door (and double-check that I haven't left any glasss on the kitchen counter), I hear a crash from the next room. Everything seems to be in order; I can't tell what was knocked over. (But the cat looked good and guilty, so I know something fell.)

Anyway, this has basically reminded me that I really don't want a cat after all.

And why am I posting about this at 12:30am on a Friday night? Because I'm just getting a kick out of posting from my bed. Very cool. I'm getting used to this "laptop" idea.

intro:
Okay. I want something fully understood before I go on: I hit this phase with every new programming language and UI I learn. It's that sweet sour spot where I've used the thing enought to know that I hate, but not enough to know about all the stuff I'll eventually love. It's the point where my usual ways of doing things (which are shaped by other languages/UIs) collide with a different mentality.

At the moment, I kind of want to throw OS X out the window and install Debian Linux or something.

Alt-Tab

Alt-Tab switches between applications, not windows, so if you have two Firefox windows open and want to Alt-Tab back and forth, well, it sucks to be you. I'm told that Cmd-~ swaps between windows, but I'm not happy about having to adjust my muscle twich memory around what kind of window I'm looking for. I think it's crap that instead of just hammering on Alt-Tab to get to another window, I have to stop and ponder a moment: "Is the window I'm looking for a member of the same application as the one I'm using, or is it a different one?"

Clicking the dock doesn't necessarily open a new window.

When I click the dock icon for, say, Firefox, it's because I want a new Firefox window. But if I already have Firefox running, it just transferrs focus to that application. The net result is me swearing at the computer. "No, a NEW one, you imbicillic machine! If I wanted the EXISTING one I'd have used Alt-Tab!"

Alt-Tab doesn't restore minimized windows.

This makes sense when you think of Alt-Tab as switching between applications, not windows. You don't want all those minimized email drafts jumping onto the screen all at once. But I've already weighed in on the wisdom of that.

Closing Windows Doesn't Close the App

Not sure who's responsible for this, but they should be shot. Here's my thinking: Windows are the user interface for the app. When I close the last window, the app effectively has no UI. Why keep a UI-less app around?

This is especially annoying when I try to Alt-Tab to an app that has all it's windows closed. The exchange usually goes like this:

  1. Alt-Tab to Firefox
  2. Get blank screen. WTF?
  3. Click the Firefox icon in the dock.
  4. Again, nothing. Erg...
  5. Finally manage to focus on Firefox app, and hit Cmd-n for a new window.
  6. Hit Cmd-d to select the address bar, get "Bookmark This Page" dialog. Motherfucker!

In the end, an operation that usually takes me about 2½ seconds ends up taking the better part of a minute, because I have to stop and second-guess years of muscle memory before each and every operation. It's about as comfortable as a three-legged sack race.

Okay, that's it for now. In general, I'm really happy with my Powerbook, but when I just want to cruise through writing a couple emails, posting here, etc., it's really, really annoying.

Wait, wait, no. One more thing. Tabbing through a form skips non-text entry fields. Dumb.
title: OS X Rants

intro:
Maybe I'm perverse, but I still see technology (any kind) as a labor-saving exercise. I don't think in terms of the things I can do because I have a laptop/mp3 player/cellphone, but rather the things I don't have to do because I have these things.

I've been kicking around this post idea for a while, and today Jason Kottke posted about his cellphone usage, and so I'm finally getting to it.

I rarely go CD or DVD shopping any more. I have Amazon for that. Fine prices, free shipping. Why deal with BestBuy's lack of selection?

I don't rent DVDs either. I have Netflix, which charges a very reasonable monthly fee, and delivers straight to my mailbox.

Because of these things, I go to the movies only as a social event. (Previous rant.)

I don't think about what CD's to put in my car, or take on vacation with me. I have a 20GB mp3/ogg player. I can take nearly my entire collection.

I don't watch TV. I have Netflix, a DVD player, and BitTorrent for the things not yet available on DVD. (I'm currently working my way through seasons 5 and 6 of The West Wing, which I'll buy as soon as they're released.)

I don't line up every snapshot perfectly. I snap a dozen shots, and delete the ones that don't turn out.

I also don't pay for film or developing, either.

I don't worry about paying my bills on time. They're all set up via direct debit. (Gas and Electric included!)

I don't have a land line for my phone any more. I never miss it.

I don't have to go home to check messages or email. Cellphone and laptop cover all the bases, anywhere I go. (I'm finding it extremely easy to locate an open network and bum some bandwidth whenever I need it. Plus I have a T-Mobile/Starbucks WiFi account for emergencies. Haven't used it in years; it's in pay-as-you-go mode, costing nothing, just sitting and waiting in case I need it.)

And yet, I don't find that I get any more done.
title: Decisions I Don't Make Any More

intro:
I've long since filed "english-like syntax" under CONSIDERED HARMFUL. I've found that it makes it harder to learn a language. Here's my favorite argument as to why voice-recognition will never be suitable as a general-purpose input method:
Have someone else sit at your computer for five minutes and tell them what to do. "Open my documents. folder...", etc. Presumably, a human being is the best possible translator from English to mouse click, but this is still an insanely frustrating excercise. And a computer is going to do even worse.

English is an abstraction, and it will leak.

Observe the core of John Gruber's essay on english-likeness:

The idea was, and I suppose still is, that AppleScript's English-like facade frees you from worrying about computer-science-y jargon like classes and objects and properties and commands, and allows you to just say what you mean and have it just work.

But saying what you mean, in English, almost never "just works" and compiles successfully as AppleScript, and so to be productive you still have to understand all of the ways that AppleScript actually works. But this is difficult, because the language syntax is optimized for English-likeness, rather than being optimized for making it clear just what the fuck is actually going on.

Well put. I'll go further.

Any computer language requires the user to understand how the computer will take what you say, and figure out what you mean. English-like syntax widens the gap between syntax and meaning, and so requires the user to know more about the parsing process, not less. Since syntax is almost never the bottleneck in learning or using a programming language, english-like syntax just makes the easy part a bit easier, and the hard thing much, much harder. That's a bad trade-off.

And if you feel (as I do) that learning some hobbled pidgin language is actually harder than learning, say, C or Python or Scheme, then you've made everything about the language harder. Ick.
title: English-Like Syntax

intro:
Why is it that nobody in the software world wants to actually tell you what they're selling? Some are awesome. From page 1 of the Ant manual:
Apache Ant is a Java-based build tool. In theory, it is kind of like make, without make's wrinkles.

Outstanding! Ant gets extra credit for being clear and concise at the same time. Usually, open source docs are either extremely clear, but very long (think man pages), or terse and cryptic (think man pages).

The very first text on JUnit's homepage:

JUnit is a simple framework to write repeatable tests.

Perfect. Nine words.

Now for the bad. Let's check out Bugzilla:

Bugzilla is server software designed to help you manage software development.

Wow. Totally useless. True, but useless. And the list of features isn't much better:

  • Optimized database structure for increased performance and scalability
  • Excellent security to protect confidentiality
  • Advanced query tool that can remember your searches
  • Integrated email capabilities
  • Editable user profiles and comprehensive email preferences
  • Comprehensive permissions system
  • Proven under fire as Mozilla's bug tracking system

Well, that last one is sort of wandering in the right direction. But seriously. When I show this to my boss, and I have to talk about why we should use Bugzilla instead of just sending emails to each other, I'm a fool if I mention an "optimized database structure."

Don't get me wrong; I love Bugzilla. I use Bugzilla. But when you're dealing with something as abstract as software, you absolutely must have a ten-word followup to "$PRODUCT is..."

Thank you, that is all.
title: So, What is It?

intro:
Good to know: older versions of Java made a point of being backward-compatible. No more. 1.5 bytecode won't run on a 1.4 jre. You can still develop using the latest JDK, though. Just pass the following arguments to your compiler: 
-source 1.4 -target 1.4
Now, can anyone guess why I was up later than I planned on Monday night? That's right! Because instead of the runtime detecting a version mismatch, it throws a ClassDefNotFoundException, so I spent an hour tearing apart JAR and WAR files to make sure everything was getting included, and double-checking classpath settings and chasing down possible server-related issues. Not sure what made me think of a possible version mismatch, but there you go.
title: JDK 1.5 vs. JRE 1.4

intro:
I caught Nine Inch Nails at the Hollywood Bowl last night. Amazing show. There are no words.

(Incidentally, I'm going to refer to NIN as "he", since it's really "Trent Reznor and his Touring Band", rather than a proper group. No disrespect to the band, though: everyone was a fantastic performer.)

I was hoping that this wouldn't be just the "With Teeth" tour, and it isn't. I think just about every album had at least one song featured. Reznor introduced Reptile: "This is an old favorite." Lots of old favorites in this show.

And the stage show was unreal. The Bowl is a big place, and I can't even imagine the energy and planning that go into energising an audience, some of which are more than 150 yards away. By far the best show I've ever seen.

I was surprised to see political commentary as part of the show, but it fit, and it was extremely well done. Nice Adbusters-style juxtaposition of images, and in the end the point was extremely clear. I'm going to fumble the wording a bit, but: We secure our own prosperity through violence. A more nuanced essay would be nice here. Is this violence necessary? Are we really so spoiled? Don't we balance the force of our will with generosity of our heart? Doctors Without Borders, the American Red Cross, the Peace Corps, the staggering sums we give in foreign aid.

But, really, no. Not when I see a woman with a gun to her head.

So yeah, the show was un-fscking-believable. But what I'll carry with me (and what I hope others in the audience will as well) is a sense of the necessity of helping the world. It is not a sin to be comfortable. It is, I think, a sin to be complacent.

So I'm off to the gym. I've been whining long enough about how I just can't get excited about working out until I can go back to 100%, but I think it's high time to just get over myself and start rebuilding. I'm no good to anybody if I can't get my own ass off the couch.

intro:
It was the cover of the September 2005 issue of Runner's World that made me buy it: "Best Tips Ever: 25 Proven Ways to Train, Eat, Race, and Stay Injury Free"

I sat at home that night, knee wrapped in a cold pack, and picked out all the things I'd done wrong. The list grew, and I realized that not only was my injury unremarkable, it was nearly inevitable.

So here's the list of all the time-honored running rules that I broke.

The 10% Rule: Increse weekly training mileage by no more than 10% per week.

I jumped from 3 miles to 5 miles to 8 miles over and over again. I didn't know when to quit. I thought that my body would get over it and get back into form if I just "pushed it a bit."

The 10-Minute Rule: Start every run with 10 minutes of walking and slow running, and do the same to cool down.

I took the first mile easy, but I shunned cooldowns, and neglected stretching. Stupid. Looking back, the happiest, healthiest period in my running life over the last few years was when I was living in Ventura: a twice-weekly 7-mile run, starting with a very easy, meandering mile through the neighborhood, and followed by 10 or 15 minutes of stretching. That's how to stay healthy.

The 2-Day Rule: If something hurts for two straight days while running, take two days off.

I let my knee worsen for weeks, pushing out ever farther (and breaking The 10% Rule to boot).

The Conversation Rule: You should be able to talk in complete sentences while running.

Again, I followed this in Ventura, and forgot it later. I don't run with a partner, so I don't know whether I could hold a conversation. But I set my heart monitor intentionally low.

The Refueling Rule: Consume a combination carbohydrate-protein food or beverage within 30-60 minutes after any race, speed workout, or long run.

I'd run, then shower, then get take out, then drive to a friend's house, then eat. Too much time.

The Don't Just Run Rule: Runners who only run are prone to injury.

This is my big one, I think. I stopped doing any weight training. Just after I started running regularly, weight training cured me of a tight left calf (which has not returned).

At my most active, I was weight training Monday and Wednesday, swimming, running, rock climbing and playing hockey. I had one rest day a week: Friday. Yes, there were times when I pushed too hard. But cutting back to two rest days a week usually put me back in gear.

While I was trying to train for the marathon, I ran, and I climbed. That's it. And both sports are plagued by overuse injuries.

The Long-Run-Pace Rule: Do your longest training runs at least three minutes per mile slower than your 5-K race pace.

I'm not sure what my 5-K race pace is, but I know that I was pushing the tempo on long runs, a big no-no.

So, what's the end result of all this? I've learned a lot. Go slow. Get my heart monitor back out, and set it so that it'll keep me from trying to push too hard. Cross-train: get in the weight room twice a week. Warm up, cool down, and do my stretching. Eat something shortly after a long/fast run. Don't try to run too far too soon. Set my heart monitor even slower for weekly long runs.

And if it hurts for two days in a row, take two rest days, warm up, stretch, and pamper my joints.

Okay, that's it for tonight. I'm off to the doc in the morning.
title: Doing Everything Wrong

intro:
I had a follow-up visit with my knee doctor this morning. After five weeks of physical therapy, I'm still not much improved, and he agrees that my therapists don't know what they're doing.

I trusted them because they came highly recommended, and because the reason I'm injured is that my sense of what's "reasonable" or "light excercise" is out of whack. I trusted "experts."

Typical morning:

  • 20 minutes of hot pads on my knees
  • 10 minutes ultrasound massage
  • 10 minutes massage
  • 10 minutes stretching
  • 5 minutes very easy leg work: weighted front leg raises.
  • 10 minutes waiting for someone to come tell me what to do next.
  • 10 minutes on the eliptical cross-trainer
  • 15 minutes ice and electrical stimulation

Now, there are a few problems here: none of this is agressive enough to really fix an injury. It's fine for people recovering from a knee surgury, but I don't need recovery, I need a cure.

Also, they were stretching me before I did any excercise. They were stretching me cold, first thing in the morning. This ran against what little I know, but I went with it because, y'know, they're the experts.

So I'll be doing light workouts and stretching on my own. On my own recognisance, I'm going to find a physical trainer, and I know an excellent massage therapist that can help with stretching out my ITB. (It's a tough muscle to stretch on one's own.)

And if I'm not making progress in a month, the Doc wants to see me again.

So I have a timeline, a plan, and backup from my doctor. Outstanding. I'm at the gym tonight, leg pressing... 30lbs or so. *chuckle*
title: Knee Update: Firing my Physical Therapist

I'm aching for a good storm. One that lasts a good week and soaks everything. So I may just have to treat myself to a weekend away somewhere snowy. A quick trip to Oregon, maybe.

itbs.info links to a great page on solutions for ITBS, with some really excellent advice. Just about everything they're talking about jibes with what I've found to work, and the philosophy that I'm more and more convinced is the right one for treating non-acute sports injuries: start by strengthening the affected area, not by "pampering" it and "letting it heal".

And I'm tempted to try something like an ITB Compression Wrap. So, I'm off to the local exercise equipment store to get a foam bolster (used to do some stretching/self-massage) and maybe a compression wrap.

Current status: My knee is doing much better. It's changed from being exceptionally tight to being really loose and popping all the time, which is very typical of me when I start loosening up (I've seen this before with my kees, hips, and shoulders, and consider it a very good sign). So, I'm working my hamstrings and calves, and stabilizing muscles, stretching religiously, icing, and it should be stable in a week or two.

In any event, my knee itself has completely stopped hurting. The "discomfort" has moved from my knee into the the muscles of my leg, which is awesome.

And getting back in the gym (and climbing harder again after getting my finger problems worked out) has me sore all over. Good sore. I almost feel like a human being again.

So far, so good.

Incidentally, I just love that feeling of throwing for a hold, and not knowing what it'll be like when you get there. Feels like flying.

intro:
I'm reading through an essay at devloper.* on the Factory Chain pattern, which aims to reconcile tensions between the Gang of Four's Factory pattern and generics in Java 1.5.

As I'm reading through the example code, I see: 

public static Blah getBlah() {
    try {
        // Create a new Blah object
        return blah;
    }
    catch (Exception e) { e.printStackTrace(); }
    return null;
}

Great. The old "if anything goes wrong, return null and hope nobody notices" pattern.

I took a C++ class a while back, and the instructor loved to pick "clever" names for variables when he created example code. At one point, he had an object of type Class, and named it mate, so that he could type: 

Class mate = new Class();

Ha! Awesome! Puns make code more readable! Good grief.

It's all just example code. But when you're teaching, you should strive to be even more readable, more instructive than usual. Poor exception-handling practices and arbitrarily-chosen variable names don't help with that, and its inexcusable when doing it right is no more trouble than slacking.
title: Poor Practices in Example Code

Rodeo Drive proper is about two blocks long, bounded at the north end by Santa Monica Blvd, and Wilshire at the south. It's surrounded by various upscale shops and cafes that couldn't get real estate on the Drive itself.

I was there shoe shopping. Steve Madden has destroyed men's shoes, and you have to head for the stuffiest of high-end shops to find classic designs these days. So I was at Brooks Bros.

I got what I needed. But the whole thing left me a bit unsettled. Rodeo Drive is the point on the planet where the ley lines converge, giving the abstract "tumor of American consumerism" physical form. The teeth and claws are out, and the casualties are everywhere.

Plastic women stepped around homeless men to buy $4000 handbags. I did the same to find Cole Haan and Brooks Bros. Men and women older than me smiled and softly stroked my ego, congradulating me on my first visit to such a prestigious store. Do you feel like a million dollars?

Meanwhile, the asshole across the room is acting like a spoiled seven-year-old, all but stomping his Ferragamo-shod feet.

People are dying in Pakistan and Mexico and Louisiana, and some dude is trying to tell me I've "made it" because I shop at his store.

Nobody within a mile seems to have any perspective, and I can't help wondering if I'm losing it too.

So if you'll excuse me, I'm going to go find places to donate money to good causes. AIDS Project Los Angeles. Doctors Without Borders.
title: Do You Feel Like a Million Dollars?

intro:
No, no. Not me. Some other guy. His name is Stephen Downes and he kept a log of installing ruby on rails from scratch.

It's amazingly thorough, even covering the bit where he kind of guesses about which archive to download from the project archive, (".zip is probably a Windows archive, .tgz must be Linux (not sure exactly what .tgz is but it's probably like .tar.gz). What the heck is .tgz though?")

This is exactly the kind of thing that the open source community needs more of. Over and over again I basically guess my way through installing and configuring some piece of software, all the while cursing the documentation, which often leaves much to be desired: "This can be configured by tweaking the appropriate setting." Which setting? Which config file? Does the server need to be restarted for this to take effect? Where can I find more information on configuration?

Anyway, this reminds me that I wanted to do a write-up of installing and configuring a complete development environment at home. Still stalled on that. (Priorities, you know. Like watching The Butterfly Effect. Bah.)

So yeah, I'll read Stephen's write-up, both as as a lesson in good doc writing, and as prep for installing Ruby on Rails myself.

intro:
Bruce Schneier has a nice article in Wired on making developers responsible for software security.

Executive Summary:

  • Software is insecure because the costs of bad security are paid by the customers, not the manufacturers.
  • Making producers responsible changes this balance, and will make good security worth while for manufacturers.
  • Making individual developers laible will not change the balance, since manufacturers still aren't responsible for the costs of bad security.

As usual, Schneier is right on here. Worth a read.
title: Developers Responsible for Code Quality?

intro:
Tim Wu's essay on Google Print finally nails it. It avoids the shrill zealotry of lefty copyfighters and the misguided protectionism of the Authors Guild.

The nutshell of his argument is an analogy between authors' control of their books and landowners' control of their land:

Imagine how terrible maps would be if you had to negotiate with every landowner in the United States to publish the Rand McNally Road Atlas. Maps might still exist, but they'd be expensive and incomplete. Property owners might think they'd individually benefit, but collectively they would lose out-a classic collective action problem. There just wouldn't really be maps in the sense we think of today.

Nicely put.

Go, read the whole thing.
title: Tim Wu on Google Print

intro:
Okay, so I bought a coffee maker. An expensive one. On sight, at a yuppy-bait kitchen store in an upper-middle-class Los Angeles suburb. I had it comin'.

But of course, I didn't see it comin'. I just walked in, thinking, I bet they have good ones here, and said, "Wow! A timer, an insulated carafe, and a basket that looks really easy to clean. Goodbye old and busted, hello new hotness!"

The first thing, the first thing this coffee maker did was overflow water all over my kitchen counter. This is because when the water level indicator on the base reads "10" (which should be fine, since this is a 10-cup coffee maker), that's actually more water than will fit in the carafe. So the damn thing overflowed. Bah.

The next thing it did was make me an incredibly weak cup of coffee. Jumping Jeebuz on a pogo stick, what the bloody hell is wrong with drip machines these days? I had (and my parents now have) a perfectly serviceable little Braun drip machine that cost me something like $25 bucks. And every $120+ machine I've ever bought has been a disappointment.

So, now I'm doing my research. I have three things I want in a coffee maker, and all are critical:

  1. Must make good coffee. (Duh.)
  2. Must have an auto-on feature so it'll run automatically while I'm getting up in the morning.
  3. Must be easy to clean.

Amazingly, only one drip machine measures up, according to Consumer Reports: the Capresso 440.05 MT-500. It's kinda pricy, but at this point, I'll pay a king's ransom for a decent brew in the morning. (Plus, skipping the coffee shop in the morning will pay for this in no time.)

And, as if CR's endorsement wasn't enough, even CoffeeGeek.com likes it. So the bit of trash on my counter will be going back to the store tomorrow night, and I'll be seeking out the new new hotness.
title: New Hotness

intro:
I returned the new old and busted, and traded up to the new new new hotness. I took it home last night, gently washed all its loose parts in warm soapy water, and gave it a "dry run" with just water.

All good.

For the first time in history, "10 cups" on the base matches the actual capacity of the carafe. Outstanding.

And holy crap is the water hot. As it should be.

So, I dried it off, refilled the reservoir, and set the timer to brew me a pot this morning. Now, consider: The grounds sat all night in a damp filter, and I actually poured the coffee about 40 minutes after it was brewed.

And the coffee was very good. It'll be better when I fine-tune the proportions and actually use grounds that haven't been sitting in my cupboard for a month.

So yeah, we happy. I'm stopping by Bent... On Coffee on the way home. I've been cheaping out with grocery store beans lately. Now that I have a machine that'll let me actually taste my coffee, it's time to restock with the good stuff.

intro:
Sometimes it's amazing how much is available online. Papa John's Pizza lets you order whatever you want over the web. You can have it delivered or pick it up, from any one of their stores. Great stuff.

And then there's Baja Fresh.com, where their menu is burried behind a page detailing their philosophy of fresh food, etc. Yes, I click on "Menu", and they respond by telling me that "one thing that distinguishes Baja Fresh from everyone else is our commitment to freshnesss." Good for you. Now, can I please look at the menu? Once you get to the "menu", it's further subdivided by type of food. Salads are on one page. Burritos on another. Tacos on a third. If you're ordering for a group of friends that all want different things, you're going to be doing a lot of jumping around.

There's no excuse for not madly shoveling your product onto a cusomer's screen as fast as possible. When they click "Menu", give them the menu, and give them the whole thing. They can ponder your philosophy of fresh ingredients and quality service later, once they're not hungry any more.

And then there's 24hr Fitness. I've been doing a lot of jumping around town the last few weeks, and it would be nice if I could go to any club I want. I remember that they were offering that for just $3/mo a while back, so I thought I'd hop online and check it out, and maybe upgrade my membership.

No dice. From their FAQ:

I want to upgrade my membership, what is the cost?
The cost for an upgrade varies from club to club, and any one of our sales counselors at 24 Hour Fitness would be happy to explain the prices and give you a tour. You can find a club near you by using our Club Finder

Wow. So, here, online, is a note telling me that they're not smart enough to integrate their website with their membership database, that I might be paying a higher membership fee because of my zip code, and that they'd rather let a salesperson pressure me than simply give me the information I've asked for. I'm in awe of their disregard for common sense customer service. Hell, the reference to their "Club Finder" should be a hyperlink, but of course it's not.

Bottom line: I'm visiting their website in the hopes of giving them more money every month, and they're saying they'd rather have me talk to a salesperson. Stupid.

Over and over, and over again, I try to find what I'm looking for in a company's website, and instead of giving me what I want (which is usually really simple), they want to tell me about how they're working harder than anyone else to make me happy, or how their dedication to quality and service distinguishes them, blah, blah, blah.

Corporations still suck at using the web. Everyone's all a-buzz about AJAX and Web 2.0, but the fact is that suits still don't really grok the web, and still ignore the good avice of their technical staff. And their technical staff still thinks the website should mirror the database structure, and nobody is listening to the HCI consultants and UI designers.
title: Major Companies Still Suck at Using the Web

  • ¾ cup peanut butter

  • 1 ¾ cups whole wheat flour (see note)
  • 1 teaspoon baking soda
  • 1 cup golden raisins

In a large bowl, beat peanut butter, honey and sugar with an electric mixer until creamy. Add egg whites, milk, oil and vanilla; mix well. Combine oats, flour and baking soda and add to the peanut butter mixture. Mix well. Stir in raisins and peanuts. Cover and chill at least 30 minutes.

intro:
I mean, when your profits aren't growing fast enough for Wall St, what else are you gonna do, right?

Damien Katz pointed to Business Week's interview with SBC CEO Edward Whitacre. Whitacre had some scary stuff to say:

How concerned are you about Internet upstarts like Google (GOOG), MSN, Vonage, and others?

How do you think they're going to get to customers? Through a broadband pipe. Cable companies have them. We have them. Now what they would like to do is use my pipes free, but I ain't going to let them do that because we have spent this capital and we have to have a return on it. So there's going to have to be some mechanism for these people who use these pipes to pay for the portion they're using. Why should they be allowed to use my pipes?

The Internet can't be free in that sense, because we and the cable companies have made an investment and for a Google or Yahoo! (YHOO ) or Vonage or anybody to expect to use these pipes [for] free is nuts!

Um... Mr. Whitacre, my parents are SBC customers. Are you telling me that you're going to cut them off from Google unless Google pays your ransom? Are you smoking crack?

This is exactly the kind of thing discussed in Dr. Ing. Barbara van Schewick's paper on network neutrality (dmg copy).

What Mr. Whitacre is talking about doesn't add value to the product. He isn't bringing something new to the market. He is threatening to cut the legs out from other companies unless they pay for protection.
title: SBC Tries Protection Racket

"Dude, I'm pretty tired, so I don't think climbing's gonna happen. L's coming over and we're going to do movie night, and I figured we'd go climbing tomorrow."

"No can do. I can climb Saturday, though. Sound good?"

"Oh, uh... allright. Maybe. Call me later this week."

Timbo just experienced what I call "Priority Whiplash": the shock that seems to aflict my friends when they try to push my schedule around and discover that they're just not going to get to see me for a week.

Here it is in black and white. Weekday priorities:

  1. Gym: weight loss and knee therapy
  2. Sleep: physical recovery, stress management
  3. Social Life
  4. Personal Stuff: reading, cooking, coding

If I'm going to get healthy again, I need two days of cardio per week, and two days of weights and stretching for my knee. It's not going to happen on weekends, so that means I have one free weeknight per week. If I use it up early, I'm comitted to working out on Friday. And if I have plans for Friday, I can't come out and play until then. I'm not just being anal, and I'm not being anti-social. This is about getting healthy again.

I used up my "one night" last night for Halloween. Gym tonight, climbing tomorrow night, gym on Thursday, then cardio on Friday. That's life, and everybody's just going to have to wait.

Yes, this is one of those, "if you're my friend, you'll understand" moments.

intro:
Had my first session with the personal trainer ("Bart") at 24hr Fitness on Tuesday.

I told him I'd been working out there for more than three years. I told him I'd worked with a trainer before, and knew the program. I told him that I ran regularly for three years, and was training for the L.A. Marathon. And I told him that I'm trying to recover from a knee injury.

He showed me how to do ball squats. Aaawesooome!

Afterward, we were putting together a schedule for the next eight weeks or so, and I had to try four times to get him to fully get his mind around "Mondays and Thursdays at 7pm." He still wanted to spot-check each day. "So, Monday the 5th at 7?... So, Thursday the 8th, at... 7? Monday how 'bout... Monday the 12th at 7?" I wanted to strangle him.

My dad's been working with a trainer who just retired after years with the L.A. Lakers. I'm giving him a call immediately.

A couple years ago, I trained there with a guy named Scott, who was, as far as I'm concerned, the God of personal training. He convinced me he was worth the money by kicking my ass with nothing but a Swiss ball and a bungee cord. We set goals that I thought were agressive, and then blew right by them. Without supplements. He went on to chiropractic college, though, so I'm outta luck trying to find him now.

It looks like Scott was the exception, not the rule. I talked with the Fitness Manager last Monday, and laid out my hard-earned cash. I told him that I was available Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday after 6pm. I got a call from a trainer on Thursday, and discovered that he had no idea what my schedule was like, and that he couldn't make it to any of the times I was available. He said another trainer would call me in a couple of days.

Nobody called.

So I talked again to the Fitness Manager, who was surprised to hear that there was anything amiss, and directed me to one of the trainers, "Matt". I had to keep Matt under controll- he wanted to talk all about the Five Components of Fitness and all the rest of the sales pitch, and remind me about how important nutrition would be, nevermind that I really just wanted to keep the ball rolling toward getting me a trainer and a weekly schedule.

Matt hooked me up with "Bart", with whom I had my intro session last night, which is where this little story started.

Bottom line: back to the doctor on Monday, and I'll be calling around to physical trainers and therapists over the next couple of days.

Here we go again...

intro:
I saw my knee doctor this morning. I think I've reached the end of what he can do for me.

We went through all the diagnostic steps again: range of motion, where does it hurt, etc. He concurred that not much progress has been made, and said that it might take another six months for me to get back in shape. (At this point, I kind of feel like he's pulling these numbers out of his ass.)

I asked for some physical therapist recommendations, and reminded him that things had gone really badly with Sports Motion Physical Therapy. He said he'd find me a few other places.

When I got out to the front desk the nurse handed me a prescription that directed me to (wait for it!) Sports Motion Physical Therapy. I objected gently, and said that I'd been there, and had a terrible experience.

The nurse seemed skeptical, and printed up a new prescription sans specific therapist. I pressed for a recommendation, reminded him that I'd had trouble finding a good therapist, and he handed me a list of every physical therapist they refer people to. I had to push to get him to narrow down the list for me.

So I now start over again with a list of names, none of them new, and a phone, and I start calling around and trying to get someone to listen to me.

Oh, and the parking garage is not free, despite clear signs saying "Parking for Kerlan Jobe Center." This morning I forgot this, and was surprised to hear the attendant say, "That'll be $4.00." I backed up, parked the car, and limped to the nearest ATM. When I returned, he ran my ticket again: "That'll be $5.00."

WTF?

While I was getting cash, the meter was still running.

So yeah, I'm having a lovely morning.

Merry Chistmas.

intro:
A federal judge has ruled that "Intelligent Design" has no place in science classrooms, (PDF of the ruling) and that's a good thing. The wheels of our judicial system turn slowly, but they do turn, and mostly for the better.

Ned mentions that he isn't sure that expelling I.D. from the classroom is a good thing; that teaching students not just about biology, but also about the political and philosophical context surrounding the teaching of evolution.

I agree. I think that it's worth discussing philosophy of science and teaching students not just about the rules of biology or chemistry or physics, but the rules of Science. What they are, why they're important, and how they keep us honest.

I think Ned misspoke when he said that he wasn't sure it was a good thing that I.D. has been legally expelled from the science classroom. In the true tradition of the internet, the comments are full of pedantic ninnies taking Ned to task for being "duped," or "missing the point," or other such nonesense.

Bah!

Here's what I think Ned was talking about: Science teachers can use the imposed recitation of the "I.D. Disclaimer" as a jumping-off point for discussing what science is, and what it does for humanity. It would be a nice way to turn the tables on the Intelligent Design camp. True.

But it's clearly vital (and I'm sure Ned understands this, I'm just kind of of on my own riff here) that we reject Intelligent Design's right to be in Science classrooms. It's not science, it's Creationism re-worded to try to end-run around Constitutional prohibitions against religion in public schools, and deserves to get slapped down hard.

I have friends and family that are religious. I'm annoyed that zealots such as those pushing Intelligent Design continue to either a) display their shocking ignorance or b) engage in dishonest debate in an attempt to game the system, and bring down the reputation of smart, wise, thinking people of faith everywhere. Crap like "Intelligent Design" is the reason so many thinking people believe that faith and intelligence are mutually exclusive.
title: Intelligent Design Suffers Legal Defeat

intro:
The W3C CSS Validator says that my style sheet has problems. Ick. Not sure why I didn't think to check this before, but there it is.

Among the outstanding issues:

  • Orange is not a color value. Who knew?
  • You're not allowed to use negative values for padding. (i.e. padding-bottom: -3px)
  • I haven't fully specified all colors. For instance, I have a "color" attribute for the body tag, but no "background-color". I beg your pardon.

And let's just not talk about the results of validating my markup. See? I even called it "markup." I can't commit to a standard even here. HTML 4.01 Transitional? Strict? XHTML 1.0?

The problem there isn't the templates, it's the content. Even if all my templates validated as XHTML 1.0, the content wouldn't. I have to go back and put </p> tags in, etc. And I'm sure as hell not going to validate all 850+ entries. No way, Jose.

So yeah, this is just another personal reminder posing as a blog entry. I did warn you that this place would be useless until '06.

Ta.
