intro:
This panorama of suburban sprawl near San Ramon, CA, looks exactly, I mean exactly, like most of the neighborhoods where I live. I've lived with this so long that I've moved past the "Why are we replacing millions of acres of beautiful countryside with houses?" tragedy, and just want to know the asking price and the going interest rate.

For people who still haven't quite grasped what's happening in the housing market in california: houses like these, shoveled in cheek-by-jowl, typically go for between $600k and $1M, depending on the neighborhood.

In order to afford the average house in CA, you need a household income of $94k. Only making $75k? Sorry. Better learn to love apartment living. And forget retiring: you'll never retire. Rent is too high; you'll never get your monthly expenses low enough. (Everyone who could've retired while still paying $1600/mo. for their two-bedroom has long since moved into a house.)

Yes, a cool million will get your a pastural suburban paradise, with a 45-minute commute ($150-$200/mo. in gas), homowners' association dues near $300/mo., and a Blockbuster, a Chilli's, and a Borders within three miles, and four Starbucks within shouting distance.

And, yes, I still want it. I want a garage full of steel shelves holding climbing, camping, hockey, and cycling gear. I want crown molding and a teeny back yard perfect for barbecuing but without the need for serious maintenance.

I want my American Dream. But even as a well-paid 29-year-old professional with (relatively) low debt, I can't get there. Nope. Last I checked, I could've gotten myself a whole $250k from Countrywide Mortgage, and that's simply not enough. The math is cruel.

It's not that a $250k house isn't "good enough" for me. It's that there simply isn't anything for sale at that price. It's like looking for a two-thousand-dollar new car.

So, while the world looks on in horror at the flatpacking of American life, I can't help but press my nose to the glass, wondering if I'll ever be able to live there.

intro:
Ned and Joel are at it again. It's a replay of their exceptions-vs.-return-codes cage match a couple years back.

Basically, Joel laments that kids are getting Comp Sci degrees without having to master pointers or recursion, and Ned points out that they're learning about exceptions and object orientation, which are just fine for typical programming work these days.

This reminds me of a story...

On about the third day of my first programming job, I got handed some JavaScript to debug. It was one of those standard web forms that double-checks that you filled in all the required fields before letting you submit it. In this case, the JavaScript that was supposed to be doing the checking wasn't working.

When I got my mitts on the source code, it was immediately evident what was going wrong. At the bottom was the following code: 

document.YoyoForm.onsubmit = validateForm();

I quickly removed the mistake... 

document.YoyoForm.onsubmit = validateForm;

...and checked the JSP back into source control. My coworker came in and wanted to know why the original code was wrong.

I said, "'validateForm' with the parentheses means the result of running that function. 'validateForm' without the parens means the function itself. We don't want to run the function and use the result as the event handler; we want that funcion to be the event handler."

He stared for a few seconds, then said, "Say that a different way."

He was a C++ coder, so I talked about void pointers to subroutines. No dice. I tried discussing the difference between having a vending machine and having a candy bar. Still no good.

It was that conversation that convinced me that most of his code would be crap. And I was right. Exact meanings and subtile distinctions were lost on the guy. Everything he wrote almost worked. He'd hammer on the same JavaScript or Servlet class for days until finally he'd say something like, "I have to work on $BIG_PROJECT, can you wrap this up for me? PLZTHX."

I belive he's consulting now.

So, Joel says we need some way to separate the men from the boys, and pointers and recursion are good for that. And he's right. The good programmers I know have zero trouble with these concepts, and the bad programmers I've worked with almost invariably do not understand them well. The very worst deride them as ivory tower navel gazing.

I believe that Computer Science majors should go through hell. We don't need more programmers. We need more good programmers. Bad programmers don't simply have a lower value than good programmers. They get in the way. They have negative value. Add a crappy programmer to a team, and they will make the team less productive for a while, and then everything will return to normal as the rest of the team cuts off the dead weight. When I move from one apartment to another, I don't need a soccer team of seven-year-olds. I need three strong guys and a truck.

HOWEVER.

Deriding Java as "not difficult enough" and pointing to Scheme as the answer is kind of silly. Scheme can be taught to half-awake students in half an hour, and is capable of acrobatics that will melt your brain in the most wonderful ways. (Some smoke up, I work through The Little Schemer. S'all good.)

The problem with using Java to teach undergrads isn't that it's easy, it's that it's bad for teaching. It's meant for industrial application, not toy projects. Have you seen the source code for Hello World in Java?

Bottom line: I think Ned is perceiving a false dichotomy here. Joel's central point holds true: Deep knowledge of programming is vital to be(comming) a good programmer, and Java is a poor language for either teaching or assessing depth of programming knowledge. I'll buy that.
title: Are You Ready to Mumble?

Okay, so one of my New Year's Resolutions is to get my personal information organized. This applies to dmg as well.

I'm hoping to have a few updates ready in the next couple of weeks, including a complete cleanup so that every page will validate as HTML 4.01 Strict.

In the interest of cleanup and general orderliness, here are a few links that you might find helpful in thinking about a website redesign, and good guidelines for making sure that a redesign gets you where you want to go.

W3C Validation Service
The tool for checking your work.
Cool URIs Don't Change
Short essay on thinking about how URIs should be designed, and provides some great guidelines on how data should be organized. I've put a lot of the ideas in this essay into practice.
Choosing a DOCTYPE
Handy rundown of the differences between HTML, XHTML, Strict, Transitional, etc.
HTML 4.01 / XHTML 1.0 Reference at W3 Schools
Quick reference, accessible from just about anywhere.
Semantics, HTML, XHTML, and Structure
Excellent intro article on semantic markup. I've gotten nowhere with arguments for semantic markup based on making life easier for me, the programmer. So here's my new pitch: Google.

Tell Google what your site is about, and Google will tell potential customers what your site is about. The first thing a reputable search engine optimization service will do is tell you to make your pages standards-compliant and machine-readable. There's a reason for that.

And with that, I bid y'all good evening. Until we can all live the Real Simple life, we'll just have to settle for a cleaner, simpler Web.

Next episode: Chris cleans off his kitchen counter. Be afraid.

public Customer getCustomer(int custId)
    throws DataAccessException
{
    Connection conn = null;
    CallableStatement call = null;
    ResultSet rs = null;
    
    try {
        conn = getConnection();
        call = conn.prepareCall("CALL GETCUSTINFO(?)");
        call.setInt(1, custId);
        rs = call.executeQuery();
        if (!rs.next()) throw new DataAccessException("No customer found with id \"" + custId + "\"");
        return populateCustomer(rs);
    }
    catch (Exception e) {
        throw new DataAccessException("Error finding customer with id \"" + custId + "\": " + e, e);
    }
    finally {
        try { rs.close() }
        catch (Exception e) { log(e); }
        
        try { call.close(); }
        catch (Exception e) { log(e); }

        try { conn.close(); }
        catch (Exception e) { log(e); }
    }
}

private Customer populateCustomer(ResultSet rs)
    throws SQLException
{
    Customer cust = new Customer();
    cust.setCustId(rs.getInt("CUST_ID"));
    cust.setName(rs.getString("NAME"));
    // ...etc.

    return cust;
}

intro:
I've bitched about password policy before. But this time there's a new twist.

See IBM security policy dictates that if you don't log into an account for 5 days, that account is automatically disabled. This effectively means you must log in to every account you have at least twice a week. Once a week is only every 7 days, and that's not often enough.

While this may be workable for civilians, it's hellish on developers. I have six accounts on various machines, some of them used very, very rarely. But when I do use them, it's vital that they work.

So, last night, I ran the weekly catalog update. (Don't even start with questions about why it's not real-time.) The basic flow of our update is:

  1. Copy data from our main database to "staging tables" on web database.
  2. Slice and dice "staging tables" and insert data into web catalog db.

You see where this is going, right? Right.

When the update program tried to log into our main database to copy over the updated catalog, it used my login. But since I hadn't logged into the main db in the last 5 days, it couldn't get the new "staging tables".

Normally, this shouldn't be a problem. The update process should fail, and produce some kind of output indicating that it couldn't retrieve the new catalog data from the main database.

But, of course, that's not what happened.

Instead, it failed silently, wrote an explanatory message to the log, and carried on parsing and loading the old staging tables. The net result is that no error message was displayed, and it took about the right ammount of time to run. The only reason anyone realized there was a problem is because some small bit of new data didn't get updated, and we started looking into why.

So, we have two interacting stupidities: IBM's magical expiring passwords, and some programmer's habbit of ignoring return codes. Result: I stayed home last night babysitting a no-op instead of going climbing.
title: Three Strikes: The Revenge

Buy enough $4 lattes on the way to work, and you have trouble making your rent at the beginning of the month.

body:
Here's the whole thing, archived here because I refuse to lose this beautiful story to link rot:

I'm walking down Glenwood and admiring my new lobster-claw gloves. They form a Vulcan salute -- two fingers, two fingers, thumb -- that make them warm yet dextrous.

I'm also reviewing the debate I've just had with a fellow cyclist regarding a rider's responsibilities vis-a-vis red lights and stop signs. His thesis was that if cyclists obeyed the rules of the road, drivers would be inspired to follow suit. My counterargument -- that he was a fantasist and an apologist -- was as inarticulate as it was ineffectual. It is only later, in the townhall of my mind, that I am a master debater.

And I'm thinking about the cyclist who was killed this week in Bucktown. I'd seen him at Critical Mass but never knew his name until now. Isai Medina. He rode a homemade chopper bedazzled with blinkies, and he always had a smile to share. That's the chopper for you: It sucks the mean out of anyone. Wednesday night he was standing on Western Avenue when a car hurtled onto the sidewalk, killing him. It was a freak accident, but it has nonetheless made me sad and angry.

I'm walking and admiring and reviewing and thinking when I see a car barrelling down the cross street. I step into the crosswalk, defiantly enough to say, "Piss off and slow down, 'cuz I'm not afraid of you," but hesitantly enough so that I can ditch in case the driver doesn't see or doesn't care.

Which he doesn't. He breezes through the stop sign and turns in front of me. His window is inches from my nose when I scream, "Gonna stop or not, asshole!?" Then I reach up to flip him not one but two middle fingers of righteousness.

Except I can't. The gloves. The lobster gloves. All I can do is wag two claws of powerlessness.

--Decisive Moments

intro:
BellSouth has declared war on content providers:

BellSouth Corp. confirmed Monday that it is pursuing discussions with Internet content companies to levy charges to reliably and speedily deliver their content and services.

SBC CEO Edward Whitacre threatened to try a protection racket a while back, but I thought he was just blowing hot air, and that saner minds would prevail. I mean, he wasn't serious about trying to charge both the drivers and Ford for the use of his toll roads, right? He did understand that he'd be degrading his own service, and that it was already just DSL, right? And that he'd be hurting his own customers more than he'd be hurting Google... right?

Well, evidently Whitacre and BellSouth are that stupid.

So, there's only one way to handle a bully: kick his ass immediately. Give him the fight he doesn't want, and can't win. So I'm completely behind Jeff Pulver:

Given the market power that Google has today, they are more relevant to the Internet community than BellSouth. Given that, if I were running Google today, I would choose to implement a BellSouth Boycott and stop offering access to Google to BellSouth customers and would start advertising Cox Cable service on any requests that came from BellSouth customers in their regions. I'm willing to wager that by Q3 2006, BellSouth's DSL group will feel the effects of their grave error in judgment.

So, let's see it, Google. No head fakes. No lip service to resolving things peacefully. Put SBC's nuts in a vice, and do it today.
title: Dammit, Can Everyone Please Stop Being Moronic?

intro:
My right hand has been cold the past couple of days, and the thumb in particular has been a touch numb, as if I'd been bowling. (Bowling is hell on my thumb, for some reason.) I didn't think much of it, since it's pretty chilly out (for CA), and I wasn't moving around much. But I finally paid some attention when I headed out for lunch. After a 15-minute walk to a local lunch joint, my left hand was toasty, but my right was still cold. I squeezed a "stress ball" for a couple of minutes when I got back to my desk, but it still wouldn't warm up.

So I started poking around, and found a really tender spot just below my elbow along the top of my radius. A little stretching and massage, and my hand warmed right up. Fine now.

So what the hell was it cold for? I've been working with rubber bands to try to balance out the grip strength I've gained from climbing. Really, I need to get back to the gym and start regular resistance training again, but since I haven't been able to make that happen, I've taken to wraping a rubber band around my fingernails, and gently pushing outward. Two minutes on one hand, two on the other, and I should be done.

Except, I saw Chronicles of Narnia on Sunday, and took my rubber band with me, and forgot to moderate. So the muscles that open my right hand got a serious workout with very little follow-up. Dumb. I should have had L take a look at my forearms last night, but that'll have to wait until next week.

So, once again, the lesson is: GO SLOW!

(And, in case anyone's wondering, the other trouble in my forearms that emerged last week has evaporated. Like it never happened. There's nothing wrong with my arms a few trips to the gym won't fix. That's not to say I'm not sitting straighter, and typing more lightly these days...)

intro:
Tools can be the stealthiest of traps. In this case, I'm talking about Outlook. We use it here at work to schedule just about everything. It's great.

Except Outlook was designed by idiots. From the MS Support page for Outlook reminders:

If the appointment date and time is in the past, the Reminder check box is not selected by default. If the appointment date and time is in the future, the Reminder check box is selected by default. This behavior is a design feature of Microsoft Outlook; there is not a user interface to change this behavior.

No big deal, until you combine it with this (also from that help page):

If you open your calendar and click Actions, and then click New Appointment, to create a new appointment without first selecting the desired time on the calendar, a new appointment form appears that has the appointment time occurring in the past. Therefore, the Reminder check box is not selected by default.

And I've verified that the Reminder check box doesn't magically check itself once you alter the time for the appointment to be in the future. In other words: regardless of your personal configured default, all appointments will have reminders turned off unless you physically click on a time in the future first. And this is, acording to Microsoft "a design feature of Microsoft Outlook; there is not a user interface to change this behavior."

What's worse: when I (possibly inadvertantly) create an appointment without the Reminder box checked, that carries over to you: when you accept the appointment, it'll have its reminder turned off for you too, no matter what you'd prefer.

Now, I found out all of this today, after missing a meeting yesterday. I've set my default reminder. I set the reminder for the particular meeting I missed. But when the meeting got rescheduled, the reminder got cleared. So even after making two attempts to let Outlook know that Yes, dammit, I want to be reminded about this, it still left me out in the cold.

Bottom line: there are so many quirks that undercut this important user preference that it ends up merely providing a false sense of security. Not to provide me with a way to alter this behavior is a highly questionable decision on Microsoft's part.

Okay, I've ranted. I feel better. I'm going to go find a solution now.
title: Outlook Reminders

intro:
A couple of weeks ago, I got an automated voicemail message from my doctor (or, really, some service he hired) inviting me to a meeting at a local hotel to discuss "changes in his practice." I ignored it. I have zero interest in spending an evening dedicated to... what, exactly? No info there. "Changes in his practice." Hmm.

I just got a call from a human being again inviting me to this meeting to "discuss changes in his practice."

"What is this meeting about, exactly? What changes?" I asked.

"There will be some changes in the doctor's practice, and he's having a meeting to discuss them."

I perservered: "Uh huh. But, what's going on? This is all pretty vague, and I'm inclined to just ingnore the whole affair. If he's retiring, I'll make an appointment with the new guy. Will he still be accepting patients?"

"After the meeting there will be a question and answer session where you can ask whatever questions you like, sir."

Okay. Thanks.

So I call the doctor's office. A nice lady there explains to me that there are going to be some "changes in his practice" and that there's a meeting to discuss them.

She asks if I got the flier. My kitchen counter is kind of a mess, and I actually open my mail like once a month. It's anyone's guess whether I got the flier. Probably. But the important point is that I haven't read it, and don't know what the meeting is about.

So now I'm supposed to get a call from a "patient advocate" to talk with me about the meeting, and I'm just about ready to skip the whole question and just go to the meeting.

It's times like this that I wonder whether there's something wrong with me. Does everyone else really read everything that drops into their mailbox?

I mean, 90% of what's in my mailbox is junk. 9% is completely ignorable: slips from various people informing me (for my files) that I've paid them in full, etc. 0.9% of the stuff that actually requires some action on my part is duplicated online somewhere. I pay everything electronically.

And that leaves 0.1% that is actually important and isn't online. 0.1% is well below my error rate for sorting mail. I'm sure I mis-file more than one letter in a thousand. It's just not in me to scrutinize 2000 pieces of mail and make sure I find the 2 that acutally matter to me. They either get thrown away with the junk, or misfiled with the stuff that requires no action.

Bottom line: it's a smarter use of my time to spend 30 minutes on the phone with my doctor's office than (collectively) 2 hours (5 min * 6 days * 4 weeks) sorting mail.
title: Communication Skills

intro:
A quick list of decisions I've made that people seem to think are/were unreasonable, or explain otherwise mysterious behavior on my part:

Homework
If I know I get A's on all homework assignments and exams, it makes no sense to do all my homework, when I can do half my homework and still get a B.
Assignment Books
It makes no sense to spend the time to write down all my assignments and only do half of them, when I can simply try to remember them all, forget half the time, and achieve the same effect.
Procrastination
One day of broken bones is better than weeks of bruises. HOWEVER, I've outgrown this, mostly. As an adult, I have far more control of how I spend my time. I have the job I want, and do what I want with my free time. When it comes to tax time, however, I start everything on April 12th. The extra two days are because I know I'll need to pick up another form or something that'll take an extra day. (This is less of an issue with everything now available online.)
Reading my Mail
It takes two hours per month to sort my mail and find the 0.1% of it that I actually need to pay attention to. It takes far less than that to iron out the mistakes that result from ignoring my mail.
title: Trade-Offs

intro:
In addition to infecting their customers' computers with malware, Sony BMG stole code that was written by "DVD" Jon Johansen and licenced under the GPL. In his blog this morning, Jon discusses a converstaion with a lawyer regarding possible legal action against Sony BMG.

Johansen's lawyer says that it'll be hard to impose any kind of penalty. U.S. copyright law only provides statutory damages for works copyrighted within the U.S., and actual damages are difficult to prove, given that it's the GPL and Johansen didn't plan to make any money off the code anyway.

So it seems that the biggest obstacle to the GPL's enforcability has nothing whatever to do with its legal bulletproofness. Rather, since there's no money involved, violations draw little more than a yawn from our legal system. No money, no damages, quit yer bitchin.

I'm weary of the notion that the only worthwhile persuit in this life is wealth. It's coded into our legal system, social, and political systems, and it's rotting us from within.

Thought for the day: "At either end of the economic spectrum, there lies a leisure class." Which end is easier to get to?
title: DVD Jon Mulls Legal Action Against Sony BMG

Cory Doctorow reports on a presentation by Microsoft's Amir Majidimehr, Corporate VP of the Windows Digital Media Division, in which Majidimehr basically said that the purpose of MS's new licencing scheme for drivers is to reduce the number of driver vendors to a managable level.

I can see how this would help reliability. But I know a lot of programmers who grew up writing toy code on their Windows boxes, and device drivers are a particularly interesting area for a lot of hackers. Making new things work is really, really satisfying stuff, and a perfect way to get young programmers thinking about software design.

But Microsoft would, evidently, prefer that young programmers get more comfy with Linux or BSD device drivers. Stupid.

I learned my (admittedly meager) graphics skills on Adobe Photoshop. I learned to program with HTML and JavaScript, and did my undergrad work on Solaris and Linux, using EMACS and make and Java. So, with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Java, what do you think I do for a living? Yep: J2EE web development.

So, if nobody grows up writing Windows device drivers for fun, what's going to happen to the quality of Windows device drivers in the long-term? MS is cutting off their supply of programmers that "speak Windows drivers like a native."
title: Microsoft Starving its Young

intro:
After a failed creating of a new instance of IBM's WebSphere, this error was displayed in the UI:

Error: There was a problem creating the database. Error: Instance was not created. Please correct the error before retrying.

The only line in the log was:

There was a problem creating the database.

The only line. In verbose mode.

I'm more and more convinced that IBM subsists on marketing and corporate enertia alone.

There's a Tragedy of the Commons here: the cost of making good software is IBM's to bear alone. But the cost of making crappy software is spread across all their users. The key is to keep that cost spread thinly enough that it's still cheaper for customers to stick with IBM than to roll their own.

As open source frameworks continue to blossom, IBM is going to have a harder and harder time justifying these massive licencing fees.

intro:
I'm not a practicing Catholic, but I do observe Lent. There are a couple of reasons for this. First, the spirit of living a spartan life is a breath of fresh air after a year of consumerism and complication. It's a time to pause between Fry's runs and ask, "Do I really need an LED-illuminated USB hub?"

On a more spiritual level, Lent is about something different every time. Two years ago, I tried giving up coffee, and failed. I realised that I needed to take better care of myself. So over the next year I made progress (in fits and starts).

Last year, I was able to give up coffe. I had a headache for four days, but I managed to stick with it. And learned something new: I was using coffee as a stress outlet. Instead of actually doing something about the source of my stress, I was venting it through exercise and coffee. Not healthy.

After a couple of weeks hating my job, and having no way of venting that frustration, I got a new job. It took no time at all, and I got the raise I knew I deserved.

Point being: Lent is not about suffering or self-deprivation. It's about giving up one crutch or another (or trying), and seeing what happens. There's no telling what it's about until you either give up your crutch, or fail to give it up.

This year, I'm giving up sweets. No soda. No cookies. No chocolate.

Why? Because sweets are my most effective tool for self-sabotage.

Lent is not about giving up something you'll be glad to get back. It's about giving up something you enjoy, but that you'll be happier without.

Lent is about purification, about clearing away of worldly complication. It's not, not, not about suffering.
title: Lent

intro:
This post has been changed from its original version. To my utter astonishment, Michael Reardon actually read this post, and emailed to help straighten out a few facts I'd gotten wrong. I have corrected my errors to the best of my knowledge and ability. Where errors remain, they are mine alone.

If what I've written here has fueled the controversy over Reardon's accomplishments, my most sincere apologies go out to Mr. Reardon and to everyone else involved.

After work last night I headed over to the local REI to check out Michael Reardon's slideshow "No Strings Attached", so called because of his notoriety as a free soloist.

(Non-climbers: "free soloist" means that he climbs without ropes or safety gear of any kind.)

There's been a lot of controversy surrounding Reardon, and after last night, I think see why.

I really got the feeling that the Michael Reardon phenomenon is really the result of something completely alien to climbing: hype. Reardon clearly respects the traditional ethic of keeping free soloing on the low-down. It's tough to believe when you see him in Rock and Ice striking rock-n-roll poses, but from what I saw last night, it's the truth. From what he said last night (and every word sounded credible) he tried to keep his solo of Romantic Warrior quiet as long as he could, but word got out. Not through the usual grapevine, but simply because there were witnesses. A couple of guys saw him do it, and that was that.

That's not to say that Reardon's a quiet guy. Anything but. And that's the burr under so many people's saddles. He put it really well last night: "If someone asks me a direct question, I'm not going to lie." And by now, I bet the guy gets a lot of direct questions. So he's really got two options: pull a Howard Hughes and shun the media, or answer the question. Being who he is, he figures it's more honest and in the spirit of climbing to answer the question. Fair play to him.

So now the genie is out of the bottle. The magazines all eat this stuff up, because everyone wants to read about this amazing guy out there pushing the limits of human capability. And so the stories get published, and the doubters come out of the woodwork.

Last night was no exception. There was a guy who went on and on about how there's no way that Reardon could have soloed a route that Bachar had to bail from, and why did Reardon make a movie about himself, which wasn't that good a movie anyway, and any of this stuff could have ben faked, and that doesn't really prove that he did the thing... The guy went 'round and 'round. It was like he got on the merry-go-round and couldn't get off.

So, it's this perfect storm of a guy doing amazing stuff, an "adventure recreation" industrial machine trying to generate interest, and a bunch of guys that react badly to the hype created by the climbing press, and come down on Reardon.

Me, I'm just more and more reminded of the adolescent days of skateboarding. The cult of cool is rising, with stories in the climbing mags about knuckleheads who've totally screwed up their lives, but are "Texas's hottest new 5.14 climber" or whatever. I've heard that you don't hear very often about a free soloist falling. That's true. But that's not because they're "hardmen", it's because they know when to back off. Kind of like "being right is usually a function of keeping your mouth shut when you might be wrong," being a successful free soloist may be a function of going home when you feel like you might fall.

Which brings me round to Reardon himself. I respect the guy. He put it better than I ever could: "I can't describe the process, I can't describe the rewards." Very true. One thing I've learned about climbing, about Lent, about just about anything that really matters: you don't know jack untill you've done it.

Reardon makes a choice I would not. He has a wife and child, yet continues to risk his life climbing. The rewards to be gained from a solo climb may be immense, but they are individual. The risks are shared by everyone: the climber, his family, the local rescue service, and the climbing community at large. Every dead climber hurts us all.

So, just so I have this written down: The heckler last night asked why Peter Croft had to get plucked off "Equinox" at Joshua Tree, which Reardon says he soloed. Reardon said something like, "Yeah, totally. I was surprised by that too." Evidently, Croft attempted the route, a long finger crack, on a really cold day, in new shoes, and just decided it wasn't going to happen.

The bottom line is that the slide show did inspire me to start leading again. I got my gym certification (I just passed a test that shows I know how not to die), then got sidetracked by injury, flaky partners, and a general reluctance to get back on the sharp end. So we'll see if Timbo can pass his test tonight, and go from there.

Update 2/16/2006: A Few Corrections, a Few Thoughts

What I got wrong:

  • I originally stated that it was John Bachar that bailed from Equinox, which is wrong. The climber being discussed was Peter Croft.
  • I also said that Reardon claimed to have onsighted Equinox. I got things garbled. Reardon did solo Equinox, but did not onsight it, and he never said any different.

In case anyone's interested, I've saved the original text of this post here.

Okay, with the errata out of the way, a few thoughts:

I'm not a journalist, editor, economist, historian, or stenographer. What I've written here is just my late-night musings on fame, media, personality, hype, industry, tradition, and the strange synergistic forces that come into play when they collide. intro:
Ugh. Went in feeling strong, feeling confident. Something got into my head on my second warmup climb, and I just couldn't shake it. Constantly double-checking my tie-in knot, overgripping, the works.

So, basically, it was a really bad night for me to try to help Tim with his lead test. I passed mine weeks ago, but haven't lead since, and getting back on the sharp end felt strange enough without the goblins in my head whispering about blown feet and juggled clips.

Tim strived mightily, but ultimately failed his test-- I think we were on the hardest "5.9" in history, a strange, off-balance thing involving a "natural" arete that, ultimately, neither of us could get up on lead. I was moving well up until the third bolt, then the goblins returned with a vengance, and every move was scaring the crap out of me. When I realized that my hands had very little strength in them, and I wasn't going to be able to pull over the lip above me to the next bolt, I just lowered off. Ugh.

So, Timbo spent the rest of the night analyzing all the reasons he failed, and I just kind of threw myself up every 9 and 10 I could find, beating myself back into shape. I've been moving well lately, but my contact strength and endurance aren't too great, and my confidence is thus, well, impaired. Ick. It's fine to get out on lead confident that you can make the next moves, but it sucks being out there totally convinced that there's nothing but a whipper waiting for you.

Yes, leading is a head game.

Anyway.

The similarities between climbing and music continue to abound. As a musician, it's very easy to get into a groove of doing the same warmups, the same exercises, the same solo pieces for long periods of time. Focusing on learning a particular piece is a healthy, necessary thing. But if you stay in that groove too long, it becomes a rut. First you plateau, then you start losing ground.

I think a similar affliction has struck me and Timbo: we climb the same 10-15 routs all the time (seasoned with other things once in a while), and so we're very strong there, but put us on something new, and we flail. Tim thinks this theory is crap, but I'm going with it.

If you're a musician, you slay this nasty beast by sight reading every day. Warm up, then play something you've never seen before straight through. No stopping, even for the most horrendous mistakes. Sometimes it's a train wreck. But over time, you rebuild your core skills as a musician: the ability to read notes on a page and turn them into music. If you've got the time, the absolute best thing you can do is "perfect" a one-page piece in a single sitting, like this:

  1. Sight read straight through, no stopping.
  2. Go back and take a few minutes (no more than 15) to work up those sections that gave you trouble. If you managed to get through a section, don't work on it. Return only to those sections that you could not sight read.
  3. Play the whole thing through again, no stopping.
  4. If (and only if) you feel like you can really nail the whole thing, go over the trouble spots one more time, then play it again. But only do this if you're confident in moving beyond the notes.

So for the next few weeks at the gym, I'll take one or two shots at a route, then move on. And no backing off or calling for tension. No calls to my partner that "it isn't going to happen." Hangdog, sure- after a fall. Surrender, never. Pull or peel.

When I was an undergrad, I was in a class where the teacher went on about the security problems in Windows, and how the Windows Registry was a poor implementation. "The irony here," he told us, "is that the Registry solves a problem that isn't new, and has several known good solutions. It is your responsibility as a programmer to understand this, and to seek out known solutions to the challenges you encounter."

So I can't help but grind my teeth when I see this in the tutorial for displaytag: 

<%
      Connection con = ...; // just open a connection

      Statement stmt = con.createStatement();
      ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery("SELECT * from table");
      RowSetDynaClass resultSet = new RowSetDynaClass(rs, false);
      stmt.close();
      con.close();
      request.setAttribute("results", resultSet);
%>

      <display:table name="requestScope.results.rows" />

And this in CSS tutorial: 

.redtext {
  color: #FF0000;
}

In writing a tutorial, you have assumed the mantle of Teacher. You have a responsibility to adhere to common Best Practices. Either make your example code unimpeachable, or advise the student that you are taking a shortcut you don't recommend in general practice.

I'm just annoyed because I've had to work with too many coders who have taken these ill-advised lessons to heart. I have to struggle with them to keep the code readable, maintainable. And in the end, after I've spent countless hours refactoring, rebuilding, and debugging their code, and generally doing their job for them, they always say the same thing: "See? I told you we'd be fine."

Grrrrrrrrrrrrrrr...

Evangelist Ken Ham smiled at the 2,300 elementary students packed into pews, their faces rapt. With dinosaur puppets and silly cartoons, he was training them to reject much of geology, paleontology and evolutionary biology as a sinister tangle of lies.

"Boys and girls," Ham said. If a teacher so much as mentions evolution, or the Big Bang, or an era when dinosaurs ruled the Earth, "you put your hand up and you say, 'Excuse me, were you there?' Can you remember that?"

I only watch TV while doing something else: eating, folding laundry, or pedaling. TV is a time sink, so I reserve it for when my hands are busy but my mind is bored.

A few years ago, I packed everything I owned into four large cardboard boxes. I handed the boxes to UPS, and I boarded a plane for home.

And then I went through hell trying to get UPS to actually deliver those boxes. Their reps broke promises. They obfuscated. They contradicted each other. They lied. And no, nobody ever called back when they said they would. (Or at all, for that matter.)

So, here's how you keep them honest: take notes. I Will Teach You to be Rich has posted a handy customer service notes Excel file to help you do this. I speak from experience: when you can say who told you what and when, it really cuts the options they have to make you go away. (Which is really what they want: they figure it's cheaper to lose your business than to make you happy.)

The trouble taking notes is worth it, if only for the silence that happens after they say, "Well I don't know who told you that," and you reply, "Well, Devon told me that. His rep. ID is 4851, and I talked with him yesterday at 4:22."

So, there are two morals to this story: never ship anything UPS if you can avoid it, and take notes every time you talk to a service rep on the phone.

intro:
Digg pointed to this CSS Tutorial. It's a wonderful tutorial. Just about the cleanest, clearest CSS tutorial I've ever seen. Really great stuff. But they've fallen into the old trap of badly-named examples: 

.greenboldtext{
  font-size: small;
  color: #008080;
  font-weight: bold;
}

Now, the author did include a disclaimer:

The reason I named it "greenboldtext" is for example purposes, you can name it whatever you want. Though I do encourage you to use selector names that are descriptive.

No mention of semantic markup, even implicitly. No hint that naming classes based on how they look is a bad habit.

So, to put my money where my mouth is, here's my version:

Let's say you want to have links to other sites look different from links within your site. Classes are perfect for this. Define two classes: 

.externallink {
  background: #ffa000;
}

.internallink {
  background: #33aa33;
}

Now, when you have a link to somewhere else, you use the .externallink class: 

<a class="externallink" href="http://www.google.com">Google</a>

And when you have a link to another page on your own website, you use the .internallink class: 

<a class="internallink" href="resume.html">my resume</a>

The rule of thumb is: Use classes to label what something is, not how it looks. Giving classes names like "greenboldtext" or "reditallics" is a bad habit to get into. Names like "externallink" work no matter what you want the link to look like, but names like "orangebackground" don't make much sense when you deside to use a purple underline instead.

Okay. A tech writer I'm not. But it works well as a proof of concept, eh?

What makes the example more of a mystery is that CSS classes are used really well within the tutorial itself. View the source of the pages, and you'll find great semantic markup throughout. I understand simplifying for the sake of example, but in this case, I fear they may be giving novice web designers a bad habit that'll stick with them for years, and make their life harder in the process.

Variable names matter, kids, even in turorials and classroom examples.

I've also emailed the author of the tutorial to offer my suggestion. I don't know whether that makes me "that guy" or not. I mean well, anyway.
title: More Bad Examples

I ran on Monday night. About ¾ of a mile, in about 10 minutes. More of an easy bounce/shuffle than a real run, but I'm pain-free, and that's huge.

When I say "bounce/shuffle", what I mean is: imagine jumping rope. Your footfalls are mostly on the balls of your feet, not the heel. Same thing here, execpt I'm bouncing from foot to foot, moving forward as I go. Or, you can think of it as if I were running barefoot. Either way, the main thing is: foot strike is all on the balls of the feet, with an especially bouncy gait to re-train my leg to absorb shock and rebound.

I incorporated some of the research I've done, and essentially did a modified fartlek workout: very slow, easy stuff for 3 or 4 minutes, then 30 seconds of flat-out. The important thing: form. My left leg still isn't good at absorbing shock, so I really had to concentrate on keeping everything smooth, keeping my footfalls at an even tempo.

So yeah, I'm feeling positive. Hoping for another "trot" tonight, if I have time.

Oh, and chalk up for me under "Lessons Learned." I felt really good toward the end of my run, and considered going for the full 1½-mile loop around the neighborood. But, I remembered that new workouts do unexpected things, and headed for home. I'm glad I did: my calves aren't used to that kind of sustained effort, and are a bit sore. (Good sore, though.)

intro:
Okay, there's a reason I'm re-connecting my cable modem after a month. I'm not doing it just because.

Before I disconnected, I (and several guests) had noticed that there was an open WiFi signal accessible from my apartment. I used it for email for a few days when I first moved in (and didn't yet have a connection of my own), and have been leeching a little here and there over the last few weeks.

People keep trying to tell me that this is "stealing". I disagree. I agree that it's morally questionable (more on this later), but stealing? No. This is not "like walking into their house if the front door is unlocked," nobody's privacy is being violated. This is not "like hooking my hose up to their faucet," nobody's paying extra because of me. And this is not stealing. They still have their bandwidth, and their ISP still has their money. Nobody lost anything. But this wordplay is just pedantic. The bottom line is that I really shouldn't be doing this unless they intentionally left the signal open.

As to that. Well, I kind of figured that there's so much know-how about securing your home WiFi signal that if it's open, you probably intended it to be open. I evidently overestimated the tech savvy of the general population.

See, the signal is wide open. The SSID is "linksys", and there's no encryption enabled. Which is why I figured it was intentional. I might do the same if I wanted something for guests to use, or just didn't care if neighbors were able to get online through my connection.

But a few nights ago, while I was trying to connect, I kept having DNS issues. I could ping the access point (192.168.1.1), but packets were not making their way to the outside world. Wondering what could be the problem, I speculatively tried logging onto the admin console on the router. (I know.) The login was still the default setting. Username: admin. Password: admin.

I am now forced to acknowledge that they are not "nice neighbors", they just haven't configured their router, and I'm probably not welcome.

So I had two options: try to figure out which of the 15 apartments within fifty feet of my desk was home to the signal, or just re-activate my own damn internet connection.

So Adelphia's on the way to hook up my connection again, and I'll be setting up my old 11b router as a "friendly neighbor" access point, with some kind of SSID that makes it clear that casual users are welcome, and zero access to my local network.

intro:
So, well. Ahem. Looks like the goodwill Adelphia earned is rapidly evaporating.

Here's the timeline:

  • Thursday: Talk to Adelphia rep to get reconnected. She's awesome, arranges for a tech to come out on Saturday to connect my cable modem.
  • Saturday: I sit home from 1pm on. At 4:45 the tech arrives, discovers that he doesn't have the key for the cable box. So we agree that he'll return on Monday while I'm at work to connect the wire, and in theory I'll be good to go once I restart my modem and router. I (foolishly) sign his work order indicating that all is well. I offer to hand over the $30 installation check, which the tech refuses: "I don't take any money. It'll just show up on your first month's bill."
  • Monday 2:00pm: Due to a freak alignment of the plantets, I'm home from about 2pm on. Since it's raining, I decide to stay in and read, figuring that if I'm here to let the tech in, we can finally get everything squared away.
  • Monday 5:15: The tech has not showed up. I call Adelphia Customer Service, who say that I'm listed as "Installation Complete", and that they haven't received my $30 installation fee. I explain to them what's happened. The rep says, "Oh, you want tech support." I wait on hold. I tell my story again to the Tech Support guy. He tells me that since the installation never really happened, I'll have to talk to Sales. I wait on hold.

    Sales tells me that an emergency tech should be out sometime tonight before 10pm. I start to talk about scheduling something for Tuesday, but the rep assures me that a tech will certainly be at my apartment in the next few hours, and I'll finally have my net connection. I try to remind the rep that I won't be available during the day on Tuesday, and he repeats, "Don't worry, I'm sure someone will be out there tonight to take care of you."

  • Monday 10:15: Still no tech. I call Adelphia again. An automated message informs me that my installation is scheduled for between 8:00am and 12:00pm on Tuesday. I repeatedly hit 0 to machete my way through voicemail to an actual human.

    I tell the Customer Service rep what's happened. I tell him about Saturday. I tell him I've been on the phone for an hour this evening. He says that there's nothing noted on the account about an emergency visit tonight (Monday), and that installation is scheduled for tomorrow. I explain the situation with, y'know working for a living, and he says that he'll request an emergency tech for Tuesday evening after 6pm, and informs me that it's crucial that I answer my cellphone tomorrow when they call to confirm.

So far, I've spent 1½ hours on the phone, and spent 4 hours of my weekend waiting for their tech. And I still have no net connection.

My next course of action will be to borrow my dad's bolt cutters, remove the padlock from the cable box, screw in the cable myself, then call tech support and have them hook up the networking end. This all started because the tech didn't have the key...
title: Adelphia: Still No Connection

Your weekly long run shouldn't comprise more than 30% of your weekly mileage.

intro:
Beautiful stuff from Alex Papadimoulis:

A client has asked me to build and install a custom shelving system. I'm at the point where I need to nail it, but I'm not sure what to use to pound the nails in. Should I use an old shoe or a glass bottle?

How would you answer the question?

a) It depends. If you are looking to pound a small (20lb) nail in something like drywall, you'll find it much easier to use the bottle, especially if the shoe is dirty. However, if you are trying to drive a heavy nail into some wood, go with the shoe: the bottle will shatter in your hand.

b) There is something fundamentally wrong with the way you are building; you need to use real tools. Yes, it may involve a trip to the toolbox (or even to the hardware store), but doing it the right way is going to save a lot of time, money, and aggravation through the lifecycle of your product. You need to stop building things for money until you understand the basics of construction.

Not only does he nail this phenomenon beautifully, he goes further, and points out that replying with answer b generally has the opposite of the intended effect: you are labled "unhelpful" or "anal" or, "negative" or in his words, "a curmudgeon." And in the end, some other person in the room (or mailing list, or discussion board, etc.) will camly, quietly, and "helpfully" answer a.

Answer C

Unfortunately, Alex has done exactly the same thing in a different forum. Just like the "shoe vs. bottle" question has a third answer, so does his "enable vs. smackdown" question.

The reason that people say answer b is curmudgeonly is because, well, it is curmudgeonly. Tone is everything here. Nobody likes to be smacked down, no matter how richly they deserve it, and once you've pissed someone off, they simply stop listening.

On the other hand, if you calmly, supportively, explain that their question is rooted in a design that could be better, and here's how grown-ups do it, two things happen: the person who asked the question will actually listen, and they will realize that you spared them a much-deserved smackdown. And now you've taught them two things at once.
title: Curmudgitude vs. Hackery

intro:
The past few weeks, I've managed to catch snips and scraps of This American Life on NPR. Every week it's something different, and every week I'm sorry to have to get out of my car and go pick up my groceries or whatever.

This week, I couldn't get out of the car.

This American Life covers Guantanamo Bay

I remember hearing that we were offering large rewards in Afganistan for terrorists and taliban fighters, and thinking, "What's to stop these guys from feeding their families for the next decade by turning in their neighbor?" It looks like exactly that has happened.

No hearing. No trial. No evidence. No way out.

Nobody who knows this is wrong has the power to help. Nobody that can help believes that it's wrong.

I remember my classes on South American history. I remember all the coup d'etats, all the disappeared people, all the horrible things that happened there, brought about by people who believed they were protecting their country. People who believed that, like fighting fire with fire, they were fighting evil with evil.

And every time I see W get up there and explain to us why the law doesn't apply to him, or why the "POWs" at Guantanamo Bay don't deserve legal protection, or why he won't outlaw torture, or why judicial oversight is unnecessary, I can't help but think of those dictators of the past, who ravaged their people to protect the country, and so rotted their country from within.

Where civil rights and the balance of power are eroded, corruption and incompetance flourish.

Halliburton. Katrina. Guantanamo. Domestic surveilance.

And that's just what we know about. The President has repeatedly refused to be sworn in when testifying before congress. He reserved the right to lie to us.

WTF happened to my country?
title: Guantanamo Bay

Just for grins, here's the workout I did. Unless otherwise noted, sets were 15 reps, with no rest between sets within a circuit. And yes, the names will only make sense to me. My blog, my rules.:

  • (Warm Up) Two circuits of:
    • push-up to side plank (8)
    • ball twists (16)
    • rubber-band side steps (12 forward, 12 back)
  • Two circuits of:
    • soccer throws: straight arms, pull a cable over your head
    • cable shot-put
    • cable "lawn mower starts"
  • Two circuits of:
    • dumbell chest press on swiss ball
    • dumbell shoulder press (no ball)
    • ball dumbell rows
    • ball push-ups
  • Two circuits of:
    • squat/lawn mower (stand & pull, then squat and release)
    • walking lunge
    • windmills
  • Two super-sets of:
    • sitting calf press
    • standing calf press
  • Warm Down: 5 minutes on the bike
  • Stretch:
    • calf stretches
    • standing hamstring stretch
    • sitting hamstring stretch
    • groin stretch
    • ITB stretches
    • spread-leg sitting groin/hamstring stretch
    • one-leg hamstring/calf stretch
    • back roll-over stretch (shoulders and toes on the ground)
intro:
Hit the gym last night, on my own recognisance for the first time since January, I think. Felt awesome. I've re-established my ability to kick my own ass in 45 minutes. Everything involved multiple muscle groups, and everything got my core working, whether I was doing bending/twisting moves or just push-ups or soccer throws.

My favorite new exercise:

  • Start in push-up position with your hands on two dumbells (I used 22.5lbs, YMMV), and your feet slightly more than shoulder-width apart.
  • Do a push-up.
  • At the top of the push up, row one of the dumbells.
  • Put the dumbell back on the ground, and repeat the sequence, alternating dumbells.

I only remembered to try this one after I was already through most of my workout, so I really didn't have a chance to get into it properly. I think I managed about four reps. But that was enough to see the value here. Great stuff.

Tonight I jog, ride the bike, and stretch.

intro:
MobileTracker reports that movie theater owners are hoping to jam cellphone reception in theaters.

"I don't know what's going on with consumers that they have to talk on phones in the middle of theaters," John Fithian, president of the National Association of Theater Owners, told the ShoWest conference in Las Vegas.

I'm with them on jamming the phones. But this is just a tiny piece of the problem. Theaters used to be the first, best places to see movies. Today, I have Netflix, and for less than the cost of one night at a movie theater, I have a steady stream of movies mailed to me. No schedules, driving, parking, lines, coffee-less concessions counters, commercials, bathrooms, or bad seats.

Theater owners don't need to reduce the reasons people stay away, they need to give us a reason to leave the house. ArcLight Cinemas gets this.

The theaters where I live have split into two camps: the big-ass multiplex near the freeway is a madhouse of 12- to 17-year-olds, and the smaller art house theater and Roxy cultivate an upscale atmosphere that keeps kids away. Managers are visible, and in suits, ushers are over 18 and wear uniforms. The Roxy has, since it re-opened about a year ago, become the only place in Camarillo that my friends and I will see a movie.
title: Movie Theaters Still Not Quite Getting It

They took a cameraman along, and did video diaries, and created something really amazing: Long Way Round. This is what reality TV was supposed to be.

The series aired as just 7 episodes, the last one being little more than a highlights reel from their trip across North America. My friends and I were left breathless. What? That's it?!

In yet another wonder of entertainment industry brain damage, the complete, 10-episode series has been released on DVD in the UK, and Canada, but not in the US.

But, of course, you can find Long Way Round at Amazon.ca.

I'm sure there's a catch here somewhere. I'll just have to try ordering the thing and see.

intro:
I've been using a diet- and activity-tracking website for about a week now, and I'm lovin' it. But there are some things that are driving me crazy.

The biggest thing is (pum-pum-PUMMMMM!) interface. Too many tabs. To many sections. It's clear they didn't do any usability testing, or really think through the flow of using the site. I wonder if the programmers working on the site actually use it. Dogfooding would go a long way.

I see several big improvements that could be made with little or no programming, and a couple that might require a bit of work, but would radically improve ease of use. And I see nothing I couldn't code myself.

In short, the tool that I've been designing for myself kicks my current service's ass.

Normally, I'm all about features. But a diet site is different. Everyone's going to have the same features. You've got to win on ease of use, and completeness of pre-configured food items.

See, dieters are already motivated. They'll put up with a clunky interface because, dammit, they want to get into better shape. The life goal trumps the momentary urge to stop clicking.

But entering items into a food log is a chore. Users may be willing to use a site with a clunky interface, but the longer they use it, the more the interface will wear on them, and they'll jump ship as soon as another site comes along that lets them track their fitness level in under 5 seconds per log entry. They can return from lunch, click-clickety-click, and then get back to those TPS reports.

And, there are plenty of features that I'd love to see in a site like this.

So, I'm tempted to build it. I'm really, really tempted. I know a designer who's perfect for this. Clean, friendly, fast. And I've got the coding skills. Who knows... maybe this could be something.

So yeah, I've avoided mentioning them here. I don't want them stumbling over this (what company doesn't Google themselves once in a while?), and taking my advice to heart before I have a chance to blindside them.

Built-to-Flip, here I come.
title: Interface

intro:
In a staggering disregard for public safety, the U.S. Agriculture Department plans to test fewer cows for bovine spongiform encephalopathy, aka "Mad Cow Disease", reports Forbes. Yes, they've found three cows with BSE in the US. No, they're not going to go looking for any more.

Why? Because they don't consider testing for Mad Cow a safety measure. From the article:

Despite the confirmation of a third case of mad cow disease, the government intends to scale back testing for the brain-wasting disorder blamed for the deaths of more than 150 people in Europe.

[...]

Agriculture Secretary Mike Johanns pointed out testing is not a food safety measure. Rather, it's a way to find out the prevalence of the disease.

I'm with Consumerist here when I say, WTF?

I can only speculate that Mike Johanns has already been infected.

Update 3/24/'06: BSE can only be detected in cattle older than 30 months. Since most are slaughtered at around 20 months, testing all slaughtered cattle will not keep BSE out of human food supplies. More here.
title: Mad Cow Tests to be Scaled Back

intro:
Wow. I'm really annoyed now. I was listening to NPR last night on the way home from work, and got some more information about the whole Mad Cow thing.

I was initially shocked that after three confirmed cases of bovine spongiform encephalopathy, aka "Mad Cow Disease," in the U.S., the Agriculture department was scaling back testing, mysteriously claiming that testing for BSE is "not a food safety measure."

Last night's story on the radio was about a Creekstone Meat Packing, who want to test all slaughtered animals for BSE, so they can re-establish shipments to Japan, which banned U.S. beaf after the first confirmed case of BSE. But the U.S. Agriculture Department has forbidden Creekstone to do so. I was, again, shocked.

But NPR, being NPR, got the bit of the story that Forbes left out.

It turns out that BSE can only be detected in cattle more than 30 months old. Since most cattle are slaughtered at around 20 months, tests performed on them will always be negative, regardless of whether the cattle are diseased. So, testing all slaughtered cattle will just create a false sense of security.

Kudos to NPR for including the Agriculture Department's reasoning. And shame on Forbes for leaving it out. This is too important to screw up, and if our government is going to make sensible desicisons, they're going to need an informed public.
title: Mad Cow Update

intro:
As a web programmer, I get a lot of feature requests for "simple things." And as a web programmer, I have the job of explaining why "just putting a selection list right there" will take three weeks.

A great example of this is my effort to enable comments on this site. It sounds so simple: visitors to the web site can enter some text in a little form, and have that recorded as a comment.

Yes, that part took about an hour. It's everything else that takes time.

Say what?

See, I can't just have a little form for comments. I need to think about spam, vandalism, security, and storage needs.

Spam is the biggest issue here, so I have to do research into spam screening services, build a moderation queue, decide on policies, and make sure the whole thing isn't going to make me vulnerable to cross-site scripting, or cram the storage capacity on my database account.

At this point, your average office worker is waving their hands, saying, "Woah! Woah! This is a low-traffic site! We don't need industrial strength protection! Can't we just have the receptionist screen the incomming comments?"

No. Bad plan. If we do that, I have to build the same tools anyway. And since they're now aimed at a non-technical audience (the recptionist), I have to make them friendlier and more fault-tolerant. They'll need features like "undo." And then I'll have to spend time teaching the receptionist to use these tools, and answering questions on the phone when the receptionist gets confused. And the receptionist will have to spend an hour a day just reading comments on our website.

Suddenly spending the extra week automating the process looks pretty good, no?

Yeah. Looks good to me too, since I'm the receptionist around here. I don't mind clearing out the odd raving manifesto, but I will not spend a single hour of my already-short-enough life deleting Viagra adds one-by-one.

And once we have comments, each blog post should have an RSS feed for its comments, and the form should have spell-check, and we need to make sure nobody can put HTML in the comments.

So yeah, this is taking some time. Time spent so far: three hours. I've been busy with other things.
title: But Can't We Just...

intro:
A while back, CBS reporter Mike Kirsch did an investigative piece on intimidation tactics used by Florida's Broward Police Department to prevent people from filing complaints against them.

In evident retaliation, the Broward Police Benevolent Association issued a BOLO ("Be On the Look Out") on Kirsch, posting his picture and personal information on their website.

What is normally referred to as a BOLO or Be On The Lookout by police - a bulletin announcing a criminal who is wanted - was being used by the Broward PBA to show Mike Kirsch as a wanted man. The website went on to show Kirsch's personal driver's license information.

When CBS4's attorney's [sic] wrote a letter to the PBA, they took down the BOLO, only to put it back up days later with his personal information such as home address deleted.

This is why I have a problem when authorities want to forcibly install surveilance cameras on private property, or use error-prone "watch lists".

We have a government built on checks and balances. Why has it become politically taboo to insist that those limits on power stay in place?
title: Police Abuse of Power

intro:
Dammit. I really should have learned by now to start small. Do a couple weeks of 90-minute, moderate hiking.

Looks like I may have overdone it a bit on my Sunday hike. I've got a bit of pain and inflamation in the underside of my foot, just in front of the heelbone. Looks like I've got plantar fasciitis.

Causes of plantar fasciitis include:

  • Repeated and forceful stretching or pounding (on a hard surface)
  • Tight calf muscles
  • A sudden increase (more than 10% per week) in the intensity of a workout or sports activity

That's a big 10-4.

So I'll tape it up tonight while I'm packing up my stuff, stretch, do towel crunches, apply the RICE principle (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation), and see if that helps.

I'm learning here is that cross-training is vital to intense physical activity. It's so easy to have the muscular strength and endurance to put your body thorough stresses that your connective tissues simply aren't prepared for.

And it's becomming obvious why starting a new activity should be done with care: I have the leg strength and cardio endurance to climb long, steep trails. But doing so put new stresses on my feet. I'm not surprised that it's my left foot that's showing the strain: I've been favoring it for a year. It's weaker than the right.

I swear, when I finally get back in shape, I'll be halfway to certification as a physical therapist.
title: Plantar Fasciitis

Dear Representative Gallegly,

I am writing to voice my support for the Voter Confidence and Increased Accessibility Act (HR 550).

Just so I don't lose this list. Features to be added to DMG:

  • Comments (real soon now...)
  • Trackback (ditto)
  • "next" and "previous" links on entries and images
  • Archive: calendar-based browsing
  • Searching: also display list matching/related tags
  • Searching: greater flexibility/accuracy. Outsource this to Google?
  • Tags: list of all tags, find entries and attachments by set of tags
  • Improved database transaction management.

A brief note about that last one, in case any J2EE people are reading: I've chosen to use a POJO-style data access layer, and my hosting service doesn't allow server-level configuration, which means connection pooling isn't an option (I've tried configuring at the app level; still no dice). This leaves me hand-coding the connection and TX management. Rollbacks and error handling are currently handled within the data access objects, but this results in the possibility of some database changes being committed and others rolled back within the same HTTP request process, leaving the database in an inconsistent state.

I've coded carefully to avoid this happening, but you know how I feel about "being careful".

Yeah, a lot of the restrictions on the part of my hosting service are kind of bogus, but they're dirt cheap, and in the end I have a far more portable web app running my blog. At the moment, there are zero server-dependent features, which I like.
title: To Do, More on Being Careful

Looks like I'm going to do without TV for another year at least. Why? Because I'll be living in a north-facing apartment.

Stupid but true. Satellites, dishes, digital signals gliding through the universe, all for naught because my windows face the wrong direction.

I thought we'd have this worked out by now. You know, plug it in and it just works. Instead, I'm dealing with azimuth/elevation tables and trying to ballpark where I can put the dish to get a signal.

And, y'know, my landlord has a few rules about how crazy I can get in persuit of Must-See TV. No messing with the plaster or the railings. No poles. I haven't seen the actual language yet, but I get the idea: On the patio, no shenanigans.

So: I won't pay $75/mo for cable, and satellite is a non-starter for technical reasons.

I was talking with my dad the other night about the push to require cable and satellite providers to offer a la carte channel options. He mentioned that this undermines the ability of new channels to get into the market: if you're unknown, nobody's going to order you individually. And if nobody orders you, you can't grow your audience. You're locked out.

Fair point. But there's nothing stopping providers from setting up "batches" of channels that can be bought together. ("Geek Channel Bundle", or "Sports Fan Bundle", etc.) And I have little doubt that the "basic package" will contain a bunch of channels bundled together that subscribers get for free.

And on the upside, Adelphia could finally bring in people like me, who really, truly, just want the local stations, CNN, Comedy Central, and HBO. I won't pay $75/mo for 200 channels, but I'll pay $25/mo for the 7 I actually watch.

Besides: the Net is going to change everything. If television providers want to live through the next 20 years, they're going to have to make a few changes.
title: The Way of the Future

intro:
A friend and I were talking last night about health insurance, and it's shift away from its original purpose: to spread costs of health care among everyone, so that everyone gets the care they need, and so that serious illness isn't a financial catastrophy. Instead, insurance companies work on an actuarial model, trying to make sure they turn a profit on each individual.

Here's the quote that tied it all together:

We as a society have made a concious decision to pay a human cost for our economy.

There's a great New Yorker article on this, which I encourage you to read.

Gina, a hairdresser in Idaho, whose husband worked as a freight manager at a chain store, had "a peculiar mannerism of keeping her mouth closed even when speaking." It turned out that she hadn't been able to afford dental care for three years, and one of her front teeth was rotting. Daniel, a construction worker, pulled out his bad teeth with pliers. Then, there was Loretta, who worked nights at a university research center in Mississippi, and was missing most of her teeth. "They'll break off after a while, and then you just grab a hold of them, and they work their way out," she explained to Sered and Fernandopulle. "It hurts so bad, because the tooth aches. Then it's a relief just to get it out of there. The hole closes up itself anyway. So it's so much better."

The economics of health care have led us here. The results are undeniable: companies make more money by taking only the "good bets." I'm a prime example: I'm 29, exercise regularly, eat well, have no history of serious illness (though there is a history of cancer in the family), and I work a cushy office job that caries virtually no risk of injury. Yet I was denied health care recently because of my knee injury. To get coverage, I had to be "symptom- and treatment-free for 12 months."

I shudder to think what my situation might be if I didn't have a job that offered benefits, or couldn't afford them.

So, on that note, I'm making national health care a voting issue, and I'm making a dental appointment.
title: Human Cost

intro:
I took the plunge last night, and showed up for the Krav Maga class at Chatsworth Karate.

My plan was to check out the intro class, but (unsurprisingly) I read the wrong day's schedule off the calendar, and ended up arriving an hour early-- just in time for the intermediate class. After a quick chat with the instructor, I borrowed some gloves and joined the class.

We started with about 5 minutes of bag work, then did mostly ground stuff. Kicks from defensive positions, escaping from having someone on top of you, etc. I got paired up with a guy who was about 6'4'', and huge. I'd guess about 280 lbs, but I really have no point of reference. Think of the quintesential SWAT team member, and you've got the idea.

So Mr. SWAT has me in a headlock, and I get the roll right, moving him onto the ground and putting me on top. But, he's not letting go on the headlock. I do the wrong thing: instead of going for viscious rib and kidney punches, which makes your opponent want to let go, I dig in my elbows and try to heave my way out of the headlock. I get more leverage, he squeeses a little tighter, and something in my neck pops. So today I have a stiff neck, and I won't forget the rib shots again.

I was tempted to stick around for the intro class, but I could already feel my wrists and abs getting sore, and I've learned to start slow with new activities, so I headed out and grabbed some dinner.

I'm glad I did: I can barely type today because my wrists are so shaky, and I'm going to be really sore tomorrow from all that ground work: full body workout.

I noticed a couple of things. First, the instructor talked about twisting your body with every punch (at which point I had visions of Pai Mei talking about Chi). I'm noticing the same thing in climbing: your greatest leverage comes not from your shoulders, but from your abs. A twisting/row motion will get you far more control, and a much longer reach, than trying to do a pull-up.

I was also struck by how close you have to be to someone to strike them. Probably not news to anyone else, but it surprised me.

And yes, my left leg has considerably less explosive strength than my right. Time to start some easy plyometric stuff in the weight room.
title: Krav Maga: Day 1

I got the whole thing on my GPS unit, so hopefully I can introduce a little Google Maps magic and give you an overhead view of the whole thing.

It was chilly and breezy, so I got to try out my new rain shell. It's becoming clear that I just sweat too damn much, and need to work out a system for staying warm and dry in cool/cold weather. Yesterday I wore a long-sleeved dri-fit top under my rainshell, and had serious condensation issues, even with all vents open and the front zip around my belly button. It's not that the shell doesn't breathe, it's that I just sweat like a madman, and it seems to have more to do with my core temp than with the outside temp. Bottom line: with the shell, I was cold and damp, without the shell I was freezing.

This tells me two things: a soft insulating jacket might be a better approach for hard hikes in cool weather. I should save the rain shell for more moderate efforts or actual rain.

It's also likely I boxed myself in: I got good and sweaty before removing the rain shell, at which point the wind was wicked on my sodden shirt. Maybe if I'd started out with just the dri-fit, it could have kept me warm and dry until I got up high enough for wind to be an issue.

Clearly, more research is called for. :)

Finally, one programmer's spouse had enough, and broke the story anonymously, for fear of retalliation from EA. The result was a class action lawsuit on behalf of all the programmers that EA had screwed over the years.

The programmers have won. EA will pay $14.9 Million to coders who worked for them, reclassify many salaried employees as hourly so that they can claim overtime, and move deadlines from Mondays to Fridays in an effort to encourage a normal five-day work week.

intro:
Oh, baby. People, we need to do better here. Web forms suck, and I suspect they're a major reason more people don't use online services.

I just donwloaded a JDBC driver from IBM's support site. Before I could download, I had to give them my company's postal address. What possible impact does that have on downloading a JDBC driver? No idea. But that's another rant for another time.

The real problem was that there were multiple required fields (marked with red asterisks), and I missed a couple on my first run through the form. (I didn't sleep well last night, if you must know.) So when I submitted the form, expecing a download page, I got... the same form again, with a message in red at the top: "The information you have entered is invalid. Please try again."

So I double checked, got one of the missing fields filled in, and submitted the form. And again, was met with "The information you have entered is invliad. Please try again."

Which field did I miss? Invalid how? Bad formatting? Missing completely? What? No clue. "Invalid. Try again."

And just as I thought I was about to finally get the files I needed to do my job, I clicked "I comfirm" (as opposed to "I cancel", are the folks at IBM native English speakers?), and got:

Missing required fields.

You must agree to the terms of the license before you proceed

message code: 52e

Only at IBM would "message code: 52e" be considered handy information for the user. As it turns out, you have to both click the little "I agree" checkbox and click "I confirm."

I feel a little like the kid digging through a twelve-foot-high pile of manure: "There's gotta be a pony under here somewhere!"

Error conditions are not errors, they are opportunities for clarification, for dialog with the user. I used to live in an apartment building with the street adress 805, which happens to also be a local telephone area code. I'd get into a lot of frustrating exchanges:

GUY: Address?

ME: 805--

GUY: No, your address.

ME: Yeah. 805--

GUY: No, sir. I need your street address.

ME: I live at 805 Paseo Ponderosa...

GUY: Oh! Oh, okay.

ME: ...apartment 231...

The guy's reponse was the equivalent of just yelling "ERROR!" Things migh have gone much more easily if he'd just let me keep talking. Or clarified with, "Sir, are you sure that your street number is 805?"

Anyway, I'm tempted to go home tonight, fix a few bugs, then start work on a set of custom tags for better handling of form input errors. Maybe something like Netflix's little word balloon pop-ups. Floating error messages that specify the problem, and point right to where it's happening. They'd all appear immediately when the user hit "submit", and disappear as the problems were fixed. Clicking "submit" before they were cleared would pop the user back to the field that needs fixing.

Yep. In my copious free time.
title: Web Forms

intro:
My climbing partner and I were working on a pinchy, balancy climb that went up the spine of a loose open book formation. It was like trying to climb up a series of charcoal briquettes. While I had to lower off after a few attempts, my partner nailed it fairly easily: he kept his form, stayed close to the rock, and moved his feet first. Textbook climbing style, if executed with an individual flair.

I tried again, duplicating his foot sequences and balance moves... and flailed hopelessly before lowering off again.

The problem wasn't my technique. My problem was that I'm quite a bit bigger than he is. He could fit easily into the open-book, but I couldn't. I kept banging my elbows, and had to lean away from the rock in order to give my knees enough space to get my feet up.

Last night, I'd learned my lesson, and skipped my failed attempt to duplicate his sequence. Both my partner and I stemmed and counter-pressured our way up a devious 10a/b in the corner, but with completely different hand and foot placements, and a completely different last move. Another open book route. He went first, and dispatched it after some struggle. As soon as I set hands on the route, he started with the beta. "Dude, your left foot needs to be up higher. Wait, no, you're..." I ignored him, and smoothly stepped through the opening moves into the second section of the climb. "Oh. Dude. You did it different from me."

Yeah. That's the beauty of this: what works for you won't always work for me, and vice versa.
title: My Way
