intro:
By now everyone has seen the video of UCLA cops using a taser on a handcuffed student. It's been covered in The Daily Bruin as well as most of the major news outlets. I'm not sure I have anything to offer the discussion. Mostly, I'm just appalled that a weapon introduced as a means of self-defense and subduing violent suspects has become a tool for gaining "compliance" from detainees.

Do they use knives, guns, punches or kicks to get someone to stand up? Then why is a taser acceptable? And it seems strange to me that you'd inflict a paralizing jolt of electricity on someone you wanted to stand up. It's been noted that after the first jolt, it's likely the student was physically unable to stand.

And, at the very end, you can hear a student in a white t-shirt asking for the name and badge number of one of the officer. The officer tells the student that if he doesn't go away, he'll be tased too.

MSNBC reports:

"Any student who witnessed it was left with an image you don't want to remember," said a witness who asked not to be identified.

When asked whether the student resisted when officer attempted to escort him from the building, the witness said, "In the beginning, no. But when they were holding onto him and they were on the ground, he was trying to just break free. He was saying, 'I'm leaving, I'm leaving.' It was so disturbing to watch that I cannot be concise on that. I can't just say that he was willing to leave. He had his backpack on his shoulder and he was walking out when the cops approached him. It was unnecessary."

ABC News reports that a UCPC sergeant told a reporter that the student wasn't injured: "If he was able to walk out of here, I think he was OK."

Is that ever not the point. The point here is that a student who forgot his ID card, and was (if slowly) doing as he was told was repeatedly tasered, and then arrested.

As far as I'm concerned, all of these cops should be fired from the force, and serve time in prison. Campus police tasering an essentially cooperative student is unconcionable. Refusing to identify themselves once the student was handcuffed and removed from the building was suspicious. And threatening another student for asking for their identifying information shows a complete disregard for their responsibility as peace officers.

What disturbs me most is that at every point, the officers escalated the situation first. The student was leaving, and an officer grabbed him by the arm. The student asked the officer to let go, and another officer grabbed him. He started to struggle, and they tased him. At no point did they try to hold him down and cuff him, or restrain him by means other than the taser. To me, that shows that they're simply not qualified to be officers. They were unable to judge the necessary level of force, and relied entirely on their weapons to control the suspect, even though they were in very little danger.
title: UCLA Cops Taser Student

intro:
Okay, I think we've all heard this one: "Since your body is more efficient about burning fat at lower exertion levels, walking actually burns fat faster than running!"

This is complete bunk. But like every convincing bit of BS, it's based on some truth.

When walking, a greater percentage of the calories you burn are drawn from fat, compared to the same caloric burn when running.

Just by conincidence, I happened to run and walk the same route on two different days this week. Let's look at the data. (I'm rounding the numbers just a hair: I actually ran the course in about 22 minutes.)

  Running Walking
Time: 20 minutes 40 minutes
Total Calories Burned: 375 375
Fat Cal. Burned: 206 225
% Cal. Burned from Fat: 55% 60%

Wow. Look at that! I burned an extra 20 calories of fat by walking instead of running! Woo!

Well, yes and no.

Look at how much time I spent walking: 40 minutes. So, I spent double the time for that extra 20 calories. And it's not really extra. I just burned fat instead of, um, other stuff. (Glucosamine, I think?)

Suppose I'd run for 40 minutes, the same time I spent walking. The numbers would look like this:

  Running Walking
Time: 40 minutes 40 minutes
Total Calories Burned: 750 375
Fat Cal. Burned: 412 225
% Cal. Burned from Fat: 55% 60%

Same percentages, huge differences. In the same time I can walk two miles and burn 375 calories, I can run four miles (at a very modest pace, I might add) and burn double the total calories, and 83% more fat, and strengthen my heart and lungs.

Bottom line: a 20-minute run is going to do way more for you than a 40-minute walk.

So why was I walking instead of running last night? Because I trashed my legs on Sunday, and they haven't recovered yet.
title: Lower Your Heart Rate, Burn More Fat?

intro:
I tried a bit of a culinary experiment tonight, and I'm very relieved that it came out okay. Well, better than okay. It was great. But I was pretty worried there for a bit.

I decided I wanted breaded chicken breast for dinner tonight, which is perfectly reasonable, until you consider that I've never made breaded chicken, and I refuse to fry any food I cook at home. I figure that I eat pretty badly when I go out, so I should eat healthy stuff (more or less) when I stay in. The only way I've seen breaded chicken made was to pan fry it.

So, I googled for "breaded chicken breast oven", got a half dozen recipes, and triangulated.

Here's the result:

Preheat oven to 400°, and gather:

  • 1 egg
  • 2-3 Tbsp bread crumbs
  • 2-3 Tbsp flour
  • 1 chicken breast (boneless, skinnless)

Put the flour and breadcrumbs each in its own shallow dish, and beat the egg in a bowl. Roll the chicken breast in the flour untill nicely dusted (no caking!), then dip in the egg, and let the excess drain off. Last, roll the chicken breast in the bread crumbs. (Again, no caking!)

Cook the chicken covered for about 45 min. (Your cooking times, and mine, will vary.) The breaded coating should be crispy and golden, and the chicken will be tender and should be cooked through.

Since I don't have a proper pan with a lid, I improvised using a small cast iron frying pan and a lid from one of my pots. It worked great.

All in all, I'm really happy with how easy this was, and how it came out. Five minutes prep, then 45 minutes cooking, and it's done. Tender and juicy throughout.

Oh, and as a personal touch, I added a bit of cinnamon to the breadcrumbs, which added lots of aroma and just a little flavor to the dish. Next time, I think I'll try some garlic salt, and just use egg whites instead of whole eggs.

Update: I made this again last night, and found that the chicken was overcooked at 45 minutes. I suspect that it was still partially frozen the first night I made this dish. The more I cook meat, the more I think using a meat thermometer is the way to go.
title: Oven Breaded Chicken

intro:
My magnets arrived over the weekend, and I have to admit that I radically underestimated their strength.

I ordered several ¾-in cubes. Once they stick together, I have to use pliers to get them apart. Not only will they hold paper on my refrigerator door, they will hold pots and pans to my refrigerator door.

These little suckers are dangerous.

If you're just looking to stick stuff to your fridge, skip the big stuff. Use the ½-in disc magnets. You'll need to glue them to something, but that can be a fun little art project for Sunday afternoon. My order came with a tube of sample magnets, so I got a couple of these for free, and retrofitted a couple of souvenier magnets I had lying around. They're now securely holding a large map of Yosemite to my fridge door.

Discs the size of a nail head are powerful enough to hold several photos. Smaller pinhead magnets will hold a single photo.

So, yeah. I went a little overboard. But this has led me to a new project. A while back, some friends and I were musing on the posibility of a gaming table with a coat of ferrous paint on the table itself, and magnets attached to strategic game pieces. No more problems with pieces falling over or people bumping the table. Everything stays put!

I was originally worried about cost and feasibility. But it's only about $20 for 200 of the right magnets, which should be more than strong enough to do the job, it looks like it might be a go!

After the hollidays, though. Right now, I'm far too busy baking cookies and listening to The Chipmunks.

Wicked night tonight. Krav is like doing wind sprints for an hour. The last 20 minutes of class are much more technique oriented, but the first ten are hell, and the thirty after that are really about maintaining power and technique in the face of a rising tide of oxygen debt and muscle fatigue.

I'm moving my feet much better, but still badly, and my jab has lost its power. My left hook continues to improve, though, and my endurance is much better.

We also did some work on deflecting punches, which was really valuable. It took all of three seconds (1) to see that I'm not keeping my elbows tight while throwing punches, (2) see why this makes them child's play to parry and (3) correct the problem, which I've probably had since I started.

Gotta get to class more often. Just not enough days in the week.

intro:
I never would have believed this if it didn't come from the L.A. Times, but there it is. Sape Gangs ("Sape" is French slang for clothes): groups of men who take pride in dressing head-to-toe in top shelf designer duds.

They don't carry guns and rarely brawl, but occasionally they invade one another's turf, dressed to the nines, of course, in what they call a "Defi de Sape," or fashion challenge.

Think "West Side Story" meets "Zoolander." They flash labels, not knives.

"If we see them walking down our street, we run home, change into our best and come back out to prove that we're not nobodies," said Willy Biselele, 28, a leader of the 100 Years War.

The winner is the team with the most expensive or rarest collection. One recent standoff was televised by a local station.

On the one hand, I'm in wonderment at the fantastic and bizarre variety of human culture. On the other, I see men with no future trying to pretend for a little while. The crash is going to be hard on them.
title: Sape Gangs of Kimshasa

intro:

Alienated punks, picking up computers, menacing society.... That's the cliched press story, but they miss the best half. Punk into cyber is interesting, but cyber into punk is way dread. I'm into technical people who attack pop culture. I'm into techies gone dingo, techies gone rogue -- not street punks picking up any glittery junk that happens to be within their reach -- but disciplined people, intelligent people, people with some technical skills and some rational thought, who can break out of the arid prison that this society sets for its engineers. People who are, and I quote, "dismayed by nearly every aspect of the world situation and aware on some nightmare level that the solutions to our problems will not come from the breed of dimwitted ad-men that we know as politicians."

Chills, I tell ya.

intro:
Okay, I'm just going to say this once, and get it overwith, because every damn time I read Bruce Sterling's blog, I feel the need to let this out.

Why the fsck does one of the most interesting thinkers out there have the LEAST READABLE BLOG ON THE NET!?!?

I'm serious. None of his URLs are actual links. His own thoughts are encased in (((multiple parentheses))), as if that makes it easier to sort his words from others', and the whole thing reads like a dumb text braindump of his research material. And doesn't he just love throwing in giant digital camera pics and screenshots that just slide right on over the right-hand margins.

And that's if you're looking at the version hosted at Wired. If you're reading it via RSS on, say, Bloglines, you are hopelessly screwed, since all those huge images just mean that you end up with paragraphs two feet wide.

Man, the guy is brilliant. And I'm on board with the idea of a blog that' sjust a braindump of what he's thinking/reading at the moment. But Cheeeee-RAAHST it's so much god damn work just trying to read this thing.

(Chris pauses to bang his head on the table.)

And I have yet to see an explanation as to why it is this way. I get it when Warren Ellis writes from his mobile, or when Marc Cuban just can't friggin' type. But Sterling's a writer for crying out loud, so we know he can type, and he's publishing this stuff in Wired, which ought to be the most bleeding edge tech-savvy rag on the planet, next to 2600.

So, Bruce, WTF is the problem?! EH?

Okay. I'm done.
title: Beyond the Beyond

intro:
Very, very quiet weekend. Chilled at home on Friday night, climbed with Timbo Saturday, and though it pained me to miss the incredible fall weather this afternoon, I spent most of today cleaning and going through my backlog of snail mail.

And I've been thinking hard about what I want to do next year. For the last few years, I've had some kind of psychic paralysis about making plans. But looking back, I wish I'd followed through better. When I got in gear, great things happened.

But now that I'm starting to come out of that and think ahead about what I want, I realize I'm going to have to make some hard choices. I want to join my family for the semi-annual camping trip. (Well, really we just rent a cabin and go hiking and canoeing and play flashlight tag for a week. It's awesome.) And I also want to do a two-week NOLS backbacking class. And I want to keep being involved with the ALC. And I want to get back to Indiana and see my friends from college, many of whom have started families since I was there last.

I can't have it all, and I'm going to have to make some hard choices. And all of those choices are going to ripple from next year all the way back to how I spend my time right now. So, I guess, unbidden and unexpected, the time has come to figure out what will make me happy, and go get it.

The big stuff is hard, but the small stuff is easy. I want one- and two-night camping and climbing trips. I want to get my mountain bike out more. I want to head into the mountains and go hiking in the snow. I want to go skiing. I want to revive "Movie Night." I want to stop eating fscking cookies and brownies until I weigh less than 180 lbs. And I want to spend less time watching TV, and more time talking on the phone.
title: Planning Next Year

intro:
I have no idea how I avoided mentioning this until now, but it seems that there will be no fourth season of Deadwood. David Milch and HBO evidently couldn't strike a deal for any regular episodes. Milch wanted a full season to wrap things up, while HBO was prickly about the budget, and proposed an abbreviated six-episode season. However, a deal has been patched together allowing the series to "end the show with dignity": two two-hour movies will air sometime next year.

Which is a crap solution, if you ask me. I'm disappointed here. These are great characters, and they deserve great endings. I don't care about resolution. Nobody knows what happened to Little John after that last arrow to determine the place of Robin Hood's grave. But the story of Robin Hood needs that arrow, and Deadwood needs Al Swearengen to die. Evidently the real Swearengen died penniless and ailing, in a fall from a freight train.

Tell me that isn't a beautiful last shot.

Maybe we'll still get to see it. But with just four hours to cover the last year of Deadwood, I wonder if Milch will have time to make it count. I'm terrified that we'll get an ending like The Gangs of New York, with all the previous story rendered irrelavent in a few minutes of fog and historical sweep.

But if anyone can, Milch can. Here's hoping.
title: Farewell, Deadwood

intro:
There's a great piece in the L.A. times on the current state of the United States Anti-Doping Agency (USADA) and the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA).

As a fan of all kinds of sports, I'd always assumed that Anti-Doping rules were strict but fair. But the L.A. Times article uncovers deeper flaws in the system than I ever could have imagined.

From the L.A. Times:

Tests for banned substances may be performed only at one of the 34 labs around the world accredited by WADA. Athletes are not permitted to have their samples tested at any lab outside the agency's system. The rules also prohibit WADA labs from doing any tests in defense of an accused athlete.

The rules also assume that all tests are performed perfectly. Evidence to the contrary is not available to athletes.

I believe that a strict system is needed to keep sports clean. But it's clear that the WADA and USADA have lost all perspective. The system needs an overhaul. Outside evidence should be admissable, so that athletes can put blood and urine samples in escrow for later testing in their own defense. Arbitrators should have more leeway to determine appropriate penalties, so that athletes who neither intended to take nor benefitted from banned substances don't have their Olympic dreams dashed.

The L.A. Times article mentions several cases where even the arbitrators handed down suspensions "with a heavy heart", because the rules didn't give them the leeway to do the right thing. How can WADA officials still believe that their system is fair?
title: The State of World Anti-Doping Rules

intro:
Since this is a whole blog entry about this, and since it isn't starting with "I installed Ubuntu 6.1 over the weekend," you know this is going to be a rant. Today has not gone well in general, and it's not improving.

I'm currently trying to install Ubuntu. And it's behaving very badly.

The first sign of trouble was that you can't just install straight from the DVD. It insists on bringing up a pretend desktop, on which is an installation application. Fine. But the installation app's window can't be resized, and is bigger than the desktop, leaving the "back" and "forward" buttons hidden under the lower taskbar. Dumb.

I clicked on random buttons until the installation wizard appeared over the taskbar, making the buttons accessible, and continued trying to install.

I tried to get it to use my existing partitions. That seemed to go fine until I had to assign mount points. But every time I try to confirm my mount point choices and go to the next page in the installation wizard, it just barfed up a warning: "No root partition." I double check that I've assigned one of the reiserfs partitions to /, and click again. No dice.

I hit "back" a couple of times, and see two options: "Erase entire disk: IDE master (hda)" or "Manually edit partition table." I have a Win2k installation on hda1, so erasing the entire disk isn't an option, unless I want to install two OSs today. Nope. So again I try "manually edit partition table", and again I hit the "No root partition" error message. Feh.

I hypothesize that my partition arrangement is confusing it for some reason, so I go back to the partition editor, and simplify: hda1 is for Win2k, hda2 is a 2GB swap partition, and hda3 is /. I click "Forward", and things start to get scary: the hard drive is making read/write sounds, and I see a progress bar that's moving slowly. I realize that Ubuntu, "Linux for human beings" has just made my existing Linux install unusable, without warning, and well before any "INSTALL" button has been clicked. Double feh.

No problem. I'll just assign / as the mount point for hda3, and all will be well. Nope. "No root partition."

At this point, I'm stumped. I have an unusable Linux installation, all my data is gone (I have an up-to-date backup, naturally), and Ubuntu still won't install.

Whiskey. Tango. Foxtrot.

So, I'm going to try installing in "text mode", an option I saw on the original boot-up screen. We'll see if that works better.

Resetting.

Pick "install in text mode."

Um, it's trying to auto-detect my keyboard layout, even though I told it not to.

Okay, I banged my forehead on the keys, and it realized it wasn't going to get any Russian characters out of me. Back to the "Detect keyboard?" screen. I choose "No" again.

Hmm. It seems to think it can auto-configure WiFi access. This should be funny...

Yep. It thinks that "Your network is probably not using the DHCP protocol. Alternatively, the DHCP server may be slow or some network hardware is not working properly."

Or, you twit, I might have access control turned on. You don't know the network name or the key. Everything's working fine.

Hm. A "Configure network manually" option. Sounds promising.

GAH! It wants an IP address. I had hoped it would ask for a network name and WEP key, but no. I forgot we're working on the ASS-umption that the networking gear is broken.

Okay, I'll disable the security on my router ever so briefly...

Nope. I guess despite the "wifi0" label it gave my NIC, it still doesn't know that it's a wireless card. No list of available networks, etc. Too bad.

Okay, skip network configuration. I'll work that out later. Ugh.

Interesting: in text mode, it actually warns you that the partition table is about to be permanently and destructively overwritten. Might be good to put this warning in the GUI as well, guys.

Again with this "No root file system." WTF?

Ah, in text mode, you partition and assign mount points on the same screen. The GUI and the text screens look alike, but don't work alike.

Okay, and I have to tell it not to use the Win2k partition. I'll fix that in the fstab later.

And I have to double-back and tell it to format hda3, the root partition. One more thing that's set up differently in text mode.

Now, I'm bitching about the differences between text and GUI modes. But the truth is that I like the text mode a lot more. See, it works.

Aaaannnddd... It looks like we're installing. I'm going to go bake some cookies or something. Back in a few.

Woah, that was a decoy. Gotta give it HTTP proxy info first. Maybe I'd better keep an eye on this thing. Make sure I don't come back in 20 minutes and find out it's just waiting for a root password or something.

40 minutes later...

Okay, it's installed. But...

  • The screen resolution is stuck in 800x600. I've checked the xorg.conf file, and higher resolutions should be available. Hell, 1280x1024 should be the default. But the screen resolution preference dialog just offers 600x400 and 800x600. This sucks.
  • EMACS is not installed, and I can't seem to install anything without a network connection. I really don't want to have to dig through my closet for some cat5 and go through all that just to get EMACS, which should be installed by default. (BTW: I never got the chance to pick what I wanted installed. WTF.)
  • It seems to have recognized my nVidia video card, but it's not listed in any configuration screen. Likewise with the monitor. So, I can't seem to get any anything that'll tell this blasted machine to crank up the display resolution.
  • Trying to get my WiFi online, there doesn't seem to be a way to tell it that there's another card in the machine. It sees my mobo's built-in ethernet controller, but not my Netgear WiFi card. Evidently, if Ubuntu doesn't see the card on its own, you're hosed. In fact, I was hosed from the moment I decided to configure my network manually. I guess "manually" really means, "YOU ARE ON YOUR OWN, SMART GUY."

This generally bites. I'm killing it, and reinstalling Mandrake 10.1, so I can continue to function this week. I just don't have time to spend all day installing a new OS.

Man, this whole day has been a complete fscking waste of time.

And now I get to repartition my hard drive again, install Mandrake, get my WiFi card working, and restore the contents of my home directory.

Joy.

Final score: $10 and 5 hours spent installing, then un-installing Ubuntu.
title: Installing Ubuntu

intro:
In reading various cycling blogs, I keep finding stories about cyclists killed by inattentive or reckless drivers. So I'm just going to get this out of my system.

During last week's run of the Timbo Biathlon, I found myself sitting in a left turn lane waiting for the light to change. I was right where you're supposed to be: well inside the lane, about where a car's right wheels roll through.

As I'm sitting there, a guy in a Porsche pulled up next to me, squeezing between me and the double-yellow center line.

I tapped on his passenger window, and pointed backward. "You're supposed to stay behind me."

He rolled down the window. "What?"

"You're supposed to stay behind me," I said again.

"What do you mean?"

I was going to have to be blunt. "It's illegal to pass a bike in the left hand turn lane. If a cop sees this, it's a moving violation. Same as running a light. It goes on your license, your insurance, traffic school, the whole thing."

He gave me an "Are you serious?" look, then said: "I didn't think you were in the lane."

"I am. And when this light turns green, I have the right of way. Pass me once we're through the intersection. Have a good one."

Again, he had to think, then said, "I didn't realize you were a cop."

I didn't want to get into a full-blown argument. So I just let it go. But here it is: If you need adult supervision to remind you that getting to breakfast thirty seconds earlier isn't worth risking someone else's life, you shouldn't be driving. You have the moral development of a toddler who steals cookies from the jar when mommy isn't around.

When motorists bend the rules, cyclists end up dead. And it happens all the time.
title: Cyclists Killed

intro:
This is a workout I put together a while back, and has never failed to kick my ass. Here's the deal:

  1. Warmup run: 1 mile to park.
  2. Do the following twice:
    1. 10 "T" push-ups
    2. 20 walking lunges
    3. 10 alternating knuckle push-ups and renegade rows, w/o weights. (pushup, row left, pushup, row right...)
    4. Run along path to first bench (100 yds?)
    5. 10 clap push-ups w/ hands on bench
    6. Run to next bench (100 yds?)
    7. 10 push-ups with feet on bench
    8. Complete lap around the park (~1 mile.)
  3. Run home.

Total distance: about 3.8 miles, broken up into 1-mile chunks.

This took me about 48 minutes last night, which is a huge improvement over the last time, which came in at about 52 min. Woo.

It's a little focused on abs, and upper body "push" mucles: chest, shoulders, and tris. But it's a great compliment to all the heavy "pull" work I do climbing and the un-weighted plyo work I get from Krav.

Maybe next week I'll scrap all the lunging and push-ups in favor of burpees.

So, after work, it was off to The Verity Room in Canoga Park, a hidden performance space behind the Guitar Merchant on Topanga.

I really had no idea what to expect, so I went ready for anything. And that's pretty much what I got. I'm about the farthest thing from a music writer you're likely to find (unless you count, y'know... puppies or phonebooks or moon dust or something), so I'll just run down the list of acts, offer a few thoughts, and try to point you to where you can get a sample for yourself.

The show was a series of five acts, all of which were fantastic. Unfortunately, I can't remember the opener's name, and he's not on the official ticket for tonight, so I'm going to have to ask someone. Omar something, and he was great. Heartfelt lyrics, wonderful guitar.

The second act was Laura's friend Jeremy and his buddy, who did some funny songs about love and poop.

Next up: the She'enedra belly dance troupe. Yep, I was pretty surprised too. But pleasantly. (Beats the hell out of a Sumo exibition, y'know?) Anybody who tells you that being overtly sexy means giving up a woman's power or self-respect just doesn't know anything.

Mystic Defender played a flat-out set of cover tunes, all danceable, all awesome, all hilarious. Technical problems were funny too. These guys are having a great time, and it's infectious. They reminded me a teensy bit of the Minibosses, if you've heard of them. Same attitude. Two keyboards, a guitar, a drumset, and a laptop. Damn geeky, and a fantastic act. I'd love to see these guys again, in a venue where they could put on a full show.

Headliners Negative Blue (who don't seem to exist on the Web) played a straight-up rock-n-roll set in the tradition of Social D and Green Day (damn I'm old). Great stuff, and everyone left with ringing ears and ripped out vocal chords.

intro:
A while back, I posted, then deleted the following rant. I just didn't feel like it was helping anyone.

But with Walter S. Mossberg at the Wall Street Journal laying bare the tradeoffs involved in picking a DVR, I figured I'd post this.

And now, here's my list of most annoying features in Time Warner Cable's Motorola DVR.

1. Auto-on, auto off.

I can't tell you how many times I've sat down with my dinner, seen that "Everest" was recording, and started watching a recorded episode of Mythbusters. What happens when the DVR is done recording "Everest"? It turns off. Even though I'm in the middle of watching Mythbusters.

2. Mute

Again with auto-on issues. If the DVR turns itself on to record a show, it turns on with the sound muted. But the default configuration on the remote has no way to un-mute the sound. I had to dig around online to figure out how to get the "mute" button to apply to the DVR instead of my TV. Then again, this is all moot once the DVR finishes the recording and turns itself off.

3. Where's My Show?

When I first started recording Battlestar Gallactica, I'd missed the first two episodes of the season. So I set it to "record new episodes and repeats." Worked great, since SciFi re-airs everything.

But once I'd seen those episodes, I wanted to switch over to "new episodes only." Whups. There's no way to get directly from a recorded episode to the settings menu for that series recording. You have to go back to the main guide, find the show on the schedule, and edit recording preferences from there.

This is a serious pain in the ass for shows on HBO, which evidently follow no rational schedule. Just because it was on this Tuesday at 11pm, doesn't mean it'll be on next Tuesday at 11pm.

4. I have that already.

In trying to get caught up on Battlestar Gallactica (see above), I ended up with 3 or 4 copies of each new episode, because that ep would air several times on Friday and Saturday.

The options for recording a series have three settings:

  1. Record new episodes only
  2. Record new episodes and repeats
  3. Record all episodes

Where's "Record episodes I don't already have?" All the repeats have the same title and description. How hard could this be?

P.S. What's the difference between #2 and #3? No clue.

5. Can I record one channel and watch another?

I still don't know the answer to this simple question. There are two pieces of information that are confusing me.

  1. Sometimes, after watching some live TV (flipping channels, etc.), I'll try to turn the DVR off, and receive a warning that a recording is in progress, and that turning off the DVR will cancel the recording. This proves that it can record one channel while displaying another.
  2. Sometimes, when I try to change the channel away from something that's being recorded, I get a warning that this will cancel the recording. This suggests that it has only one tuner, and must display the channel it's recording.
  3. Sometimes, when a scheduled recording is about to start, the DVR will warn me that it's about to change the channel, and give me a chance to either a) stay with what I'm watching, and cancel the recording, or b) change to the channel it's about to record. This also suggests that it has to display the channel it's recording.

So what's going on? Do I have upgraded hardware with two tuners, but old software that thinks it has show you what it's recording? Is there just a bug somewhere?

6. Is it recording?

Sometimes, when I hit the "record" button, nothing happens. No "rec" in the front display, and no circular red "record" icon in the guide. Yet if I look at the list of recorded stuff, there's the show that I just told it to record.

7. Start recording now. Stop... when?

I want to start recording a show, and then leave the house and come back in a few hours. How do I tell it, "record this show"? The best solution seems to be to go to the guide and hit "record", but this gets back to #6 above: it doesn't give enough user feedback for me to know what it's going to do.

8. Delayed Reaction

Often (at least once a night), it'll freeze for no reason. Just stop responding to input. Then a few seconds later, it'll do everything at once. This sucks if it freezes on an "Are you sure?" screen, and hit "enter" a bunch of times. When it unfreezes, it'll flash through the guide, the show info, etc. in rapid fire. And you'll never know what you answered to that "Are you sure?"

9. The Remote

And I haven't even started on the remote. The remote that it's impossible to use in the dark, that requires two hands to use, that has buttons in totally random positions.

The Wrap-Up

All of this boils down to a device I'm very, very cautious about dealing with. After every button press, I make sure it's received the signal. If nothing happens, I hit an arrow key or two to test whether the first button press just got blocked by my ottoman, or whether the DVR is frozen again. And when I press "power" or "stop" or "record", I never know for sure what's going to happen. Will I lose a recording? Will it record the show I don't want to miss? Will anything happen at all?

The bottom line is: Time Warner has me over a barrell. The features of this device are what make TV worth having for me. And I know that I just don't want to spend the time building and configuring a MythTV installation and getting a remote control working.

But the interface to this DVR makes me want to chuck the whole package. I can do without TV, and I can certainly do without the cable bill.
title: More DVR Suckage

intro:
I try to have compassion for everyone. I understand guys trying to make their way in crap jobs. But when someone says, "I've repeatedly asked you not to call," and in reply you ask, "Would you like the Daily News delivered to your office or to your home?" I'm going to calmly make you hate me, your boss, your job, and your life, and I will have fun doing it.

I learned how to fight dirty from an ex-girlfriend. I'll be rude and arrogant and entitled. I'll interrupt you, ask you unfair questions, tell you straight out that you're not very bright, and cite your enraged silence and lack of a quick return as proof that you're an imbicile. I'll tell you that not hanging up on me is further proof you're an imbicile. And then I'll remind you that you owe it to me as your customer to stay on the phone and take it. I'll ignore all your defenses, hammer that "you're an idiot" button a few more times, and leave you sputtering and weak and hating me so much you need to take a deep breath and go have a smoke.

Why? Because it's not okay to be actively amoral. It's not okay to try to make a living by bothering people and ignoring their requests that you go away, please. When I tell you that I've asked the Daily News not to call, and you say, "Well, how do I know what you told some other guy?" then you clearly need greater parental involvement, and I don't mind making you call me Daddy for a few minutes.

However.

Maya Angelou was once on the set of a movie, and emerged from her trailer to find two young black men screaming obscenities at each other and getting ready to fight. She walked up to one of them and said quietly, "Can I speak with you, please?"

"This mother(*$%*#@^...--" he started.

"I understand," she said. "But can I please talk with you a moment."

Again he started screaming at the other man.

"Don't you know," she asked him, "that our ancestors lay spoon-fashion in holds of ships, chained to each other, lying in each other's excrement, and urine, and menstrual flow, so that you could live two hundred years later?"

The young man started in again, "Yeah, but he--"

"Don't you know that your grandfathers stood on auction blocks, so that you could be here?"

The man started to quiet down, "You don't understand--"

She said, "When was the last time anyone told you how important you are?"

Tears welled up in the man's eyes, and they talked for a while.

The man was Tupac Shakur, and his mother later called Dr. Angelou to say that she had probably saved her son's life.

So, I'm trying to remember what Dr. Maya Angelou teaches us about compassion, but all I really know today is what my ex-girlfriend taught me about fighting dirty.
title: Attention Telemarketers

intro:
I'm making good progress on the Training Log web app, and it's been a learning experience. Since I decided to push back playing with any AJAX, the technical stuff hasn't been as interesting as the surprising design challenges.

I've found in the past that "dogfooding" is a huge advantage. You don't see the kinds of things a tool needs until you actually use it. So I got a very, very sketchy implementation going on the first day. Nothing fancy: let me enter workouts, and list those workouts blog-style.

What became immediately obvious was that a blog-style listing of workouts doesn't belong on the front page. It doesn't belong anywhere. A training log is not a blog. A blog is a storytelling tool, a training log is a data analysis tool.

The interesting thing about a training log is not the individual entries. It's the relationships. I may enter a data point indicating that I just finished my Monday night "oak tree run" in 43:17, but that's not interesting unless you can compare it to my last run on that route, or of that distance.

But take it a step further. If I did a hard leg workout yesterday, finishing a minute slower today is just fine. But if I've been doing intervals and other speed work, and had a rest day before this run, being slower is cause for concern: am I overtraining?

And, if you're trying to lose weight, or build a running mileage base, you want aggregate as well as comparative data. How many miles did I run this week? What was my average pace? How many calories did I burn?

So just presenting a series of workouts, blog-style, is pretty useless. And even a calendar view only tells part of the story. A truly useful feature would be a graph that shows both my average running pace over time, overlayed with the frequency and intensity of other types of workouts. If I'm training for a marathon, and I see that my pace improves when I lighten my weight training load, I can adjust acordingly. Likewise if I find that working my upper body and core helps.

Just like a metronome helps train a musician's sense of time, a heart rate monitor and GPS helps train an athlete's sense of pacing and distance. I hope this tool will do the same for my sense of what workouts to do and when. Ultimately, I want to train less, enjoy it more, and be more fit as a result.

So, this'll be an adventure for me, both as a programmer, and as an athlete.
title: Building the Training Log

I've spent a lot of time "redsigning" web sites, and it's usually a complete waste if you don't know why the old design needed improvement, and what you're going to do to improve things.

On the other hand, when I have very specific design goals driven by specific usability and functional requirements, I get a lot done very quickly.

body:
I've read about Earnest Shackleton's antarctic expedition, (also at Wikipedia) in which their ship became trapped in polar ice, and was eventually crushed. Shackleton and his men survived for over two years on the antarctic ice, eventually making their way to Elephant Island, where Shackleton and a few key men fashioned their remaining lifeboats into a single covered oceangoing vessel and sailed to South Georgia, where he organized a rescue voyage two years later.

In reading of the Shackleton expedition, I was struck that even the antarctic landscape seemed lush, with ready supplies of seal meat and relatively easy travel. After learning of what happened to Franklin and his men, I can only conclude that Shackleton was an incredible leader, his men extraordinarily diciplined, and his ship's carpenter and navigator both first-rate. Every man that left England aboard Endurance eventually returned. Every single one. Even after four years on the ice pack and Elephant Island.

Franklin, on the other hand, was screwed from the start, and the impression that I get is that it was largely their Victorian optimism that killed them.

They ate almost exclusively from food in cans sealed with soldier, which gave them lead poisioning by the time they reached Greenland. They carried no means of travel over land, and seemed unable to fashion what was necessary from what they had. They carried canned lemon juice to keep scurvey at bay, but in addition to carrying lead from the cans, the vitamin C in the juice lost it effectiveness over time. (And still carried lead.)

As if that weren't enough, they entered the Passage at the start of a 5-year period where the ice along the northern coast of Canada never cleared, even in summer. Once their ships were beset, they never moved again.

And once they abandoned the ships, they took all manner of irrelavent material. Books, personal posessions, niceties of shipboard life that are liabilities traveling on foot. They were weighed down with all this, trying to travel 600 miles south to the nearest outpost, pulling a lifeboat (no small thing in itself) filled with all this junk. In total, it weighed over 1400 lbs.

Some men stayed behind, and fell victim to scurvey, and some to cannibalism. Those that fled didn't know how to use the land, were unwilling or unable to learn from the natives they met, and dropped one by one of cold and starvation.

The Inuit have stories of four survivors still walking south six years after setting out from England, and three years after abandoning the ships. But those men were never heard from again.

What's amazing to me is the ease with which Franklin's expedition propelled themselves into a doomed voyage. They relied on food stores that poisoned them. They carried no means of self-rescue should their ships be lost, and lacked even heavy boots and coats for overland travel. They had no knowledge of arctic hunting methods. And poor judgement led them to weigh themselves down further with useless items instead of the bare necessities. Every advantage they thought they had became, in the end, a liability. They were doomed from the start, yet their assessment was that they could not fail.
intro: I caught a great documentary last night on Sir Franklin's (doomed) expedition to the Northwest Passage, and thought I'd share. Follow the jump if you're interested.
title: Franklin's Doomed Expedition

intro:
Yarn Harlot reports on the goings-on over at Blue Moon Fiber Arts, who supply yarn and knitting patterns, and who recently got totally screwed over by their bank.

Evidently, Blue Moon set up a "Socks Clup" that let people register to be mailed six packages of yarn and patterns (and associated goodies) throughout the year. I'm not into knitting, but if I were, I'd be all over this. I love socks.

Anyway, after taking several hundred registrations for the Rockin' Socks Clup (which translates to several thousand dollars in business), Blue Moon's bank, who handle the credit card transactions, retroactively pulled the plug. They couldn't believe that this many people wanted to knit socks, and concluded that the Socks Club must be a scam. So they stopped accepting new credit card billings, and refunded everyone's money. You can imagine what this means to a small business.

All is well, though. In the fine tradition of practical knitters everywhere, Blue Moon simply switched banks, and emailed everyone who had registed for 2007's Socks Club letting them know that they'd keep their place in line as long as they re-registered. Word is that this is going really well, and everyone is signing up again, and the new bank readily believes that people like to knit.

It makes me angry that a bunch of beancounters were willing to screw Blue Moon solely on the strength of their gut feeling that a knitting-related "club" can't be this popular. But this is the way things are supposed to work: a bank willing to do this to avoid perceived risk (perceived risk!) will lose out to a bank with a more rational attitude. About the only thing that I think is outright wrong was for the bank to refund customers' money retroactively. They are effectively pulling money out of a merchant's pockets when they do that.

I love it that the web is helping scattered communities of hobbyists find each other, and that this will allow more people to make a living doing something wonderful like making yarn and providing the fuel for others' creativity. It's the Long Tail in action, and ultimately I believe it'll make the world more colorful, more accessible, and well... friendlier.
title: The World is Changing

intro:
Okay, kids. Gather 'round, and hear Uncle Chris talk about why you should always use a build script.

Yes, always.

I was a young computer science student, and I was working on a project that happened to be in Java. I'd edit the code, then type: 

%> rm *.class
%> javac *.java

(Yes, javac will re-build all .class files that are older than their source code. But javac isn't smart enough to notice an edit in Foo.java that creates a broken call in Bar.java. Removing all the .class files ensures a springtime-fresh build every time.)

Ahem. Anway, so that's what I'd do. And that worked fine for weeks, until late one night I was very tired, and recompiling and testing about every 90 seconds. At this rate, it was just a matter of time before I typed: 

%> rm *.java

Whups.

If I'd had any sense, I'd have had a build script. In this case, it was simple enough to make into an alias, so that's what I did: 

%> alias build="rm *.java; javac *.java"

I did this before re-typing my source code. Why? Because I don't want to make the same mistake twice. Now I can't type "biuld", and it'll just fail to run. I can't accidentally delete my source code.

And I can already hear you younguns saying, "But I'm smart! I'll be careful to keep backups, or not accidentally delete my source!" That's just youth and inexperience talking. If I'd really been careful, I'd have been fine. But the real lesson here is that the less you have to be careful about, the better. Humans are bad at being careful about repetitive tasks. Computers are really, really good at being careful about repetitive tasks. So staff it out. Building your project is the computer's job, not yours.
title: Programming Basics: Build Scripts

This moring I woke up a little after 7am, dozed until 8, then got up and headed in to work. I feel great, and can't wait to do a little trail biking this weekend.

On Monday, I got paid to write Perl. I feel dirty.

It parsed check-in logs from CVS and cross-posted them to Bugzilla. I started out with this script, which was, as advertised, grotty. Not that Perl is ever ungrotty, but it was just too much for me. I still would've looked the other way if the script had worked with little or no tweaking, but it didn't. And I couldn't read it easily enough to bring it to life, so I rolled my own in no time. It's readable, liberally commented, and works exactly as I need it to.

And I spent much of today with XSL. Turns out that this recursive-by-nature "language" chokes hard on overly deep recursive template calls. Solution: put enough structure in the source data so that XSL can just use the natural recursion, which works fine even for large trees.

I can see that a sample problem might be helpful in illustrating what's going on. I needed to take XML that looks like this: 

<board>
  <coord x="A" y="1" value="X"/>
  <coord x="A" y="2" value="X"/>
  <coord x="A" y="3" value=" "/>
  <coord x="B" y="1" value=" "/>
  <coord x="B" y="2" value=" "/>
  <coord x="B" y="3" value=" "/>
  <coord x="C" y="1" value=" "/>
  <coord x="C" y="2" value=" "/>
  <coord x="C" y="3" value="X"/>
</board>

...and output this: 

  1 2 3
A X X    
B X 
C     X

It's harder than you think. And I couldn't find a good solution that scales. (The data I was working with had about 65,000 coordinates.) But it turns out to be trivial to write an XSL template to do this if your source data has a little more structure: 

<board>
  <row>
    <coord x="A" y="1" value="X"/>
    <coord x="A" y="2" value="X"/>
    <coord x="A" y="3" value=" "/>
  </row>
  <row>
    <coord x="B" y="1" value="X"/>
    <coord x="B" y="2" value=" "/>
    <coord x="B" y="3" value=" "/>
  </row>
  <row>
    <coord x="C" y="1" value=" "/>
    <coord x="C" y="2" value=" "/>
    <coord x="C" y="3" value="X"/>
  </row>
</board>

So I backed up a step, added more flexibility to the code that was creating the output, and I'm home free.

The moral to the story: When formatting with XSL, your source data must contain all necessary information. Trying to compute implied information (boundaries, totals, etc.) with XSL doesn't scale.

Anyway, the rest of my time has been spent monkeying around with Ant, shell scripts, and SQL. Not a lot of Java work this week.

It's been a nice break. I burned out on coding there for a couple of months, but the solution, as always, is to invest more energy, scratch a few itches, and rediscover why I love doing this for a living.

intro:
I've been overscheduled for a long while now, and backing off over the last few weeks has been really good for me. I haven't been running, biking, or going to Krav Maga. And after a few weeks of taking it easier, I think I'm ready to reevaluate and refocus.

So here are the realities:

I'm back to weighing in around 195 lbs., and I know from experience that to lose weight I should get a reliable three or four cardio workouts per week.

I need 3 rest nights per week. A "Rest Night" means 8+ hours of sleep. Less than this doesn't count as a rest night.

I need 8 hours of sleep generally.

Sports/activities, in order of interest:

  • climbing
  • mountain biking
  • road biking
  • Krav Maga
  • hiking
  • running

I mention this not because you'll find it interesting, but because forcing myself to make choices has been enlightening. I'm surprised that I don't miss running that much, or feel like I'm missing out by not doing it more, but there it is. I have more energy and get the rest I need when I don't try to squeeze running into my schedule.

Too much structure takes the fun out of everything. I'm having more fun now just doing what I feel like. But I need to balance this with the demands of my weight-loss goals.

So, the general plan is: no soda or deserts Mon-Fri, get a cardio session every two to three days, get to Krav class more (which counts as cardio), and just have fun with everything else. With the days getting longer, I'll be able to trail run/ride after work, which I'm really excited about.

This puts weight loss front and center, which is great. It'll help me stop spreading myself so thin and focus on what's really important to me: getting healthy, having more fun.
title: The Magic of Doing Less

intro:
I stumbled over an blog entry I wrote about a year ago about the similarities between music and climbing. I talked about how daily sight-reading sessions are key to building skill as a musician:

If you've got the time, the absolute best thing you can do is "perfect" a one-page piece in a single sitting, like this:

  1. Sight read straight through, no stopping.
  2. Go back and take a few minutes (no more than 15) to work up those sections that gave you trouble. If you managed to get through a section, don't work on it. Return only to those sections that you could not sight read.
  3. Play the whole thing through again, no stopping.
  4. If (and only if) you feel like you can really nail the whole thing, go over the trouble spots one more time, then play it again. But only do this if you're confident in moving beyond the notes.

Compare that to Monday's session at the climbing gym, when I worked on and eventually got a new climb:

  1. I started the route, not looking at the grade.
  2. Fell, worked the crux a few times, came down to rest.
  3. Tried again, got the crux, then fell off the last move.
  4. Worked the last move until I got it, then lowered off to rest.
  5. I felt like I had all the moves, so I tried it again, getting the whole thing without falling.
  6. My climbing partner discovered a nicer solution to the last move, so I tied in again, and did the whole thing again, this time using the new finish.

Pretty much identical, eh?

I've been concentrating on new stuff for the last year, and I've become a much stronger climber. I've only moved from 5.10a to about 5.10c/d, but I'm getting climbs in a single projecting session, rather than working on them for weeks before a successful ascent. In short: my sight reading skills have vastly improved, and I've got a lot more tools in my toolbox.
title: Climbing and Music III

intro:
Saturday's ALC training ride was threatened by rain, so I decided to stay in bed. Evidently I needed it: I slept more than 13 hrs, and it didn't leave me groggy.

I woke up around noon, and immediately realized that the ride would have been beautiful. Temps were in the high 60's, and the sun was shining. So I grabbed my mountain bike and headed out exploring on the trails south of Simi Valley.

I headed out from the Long Canyon trailhead, and had a blast. I ended up doing most of the length of the Alberson fire road, which starts at the north end of Westlake Blvd. and runs east-west between Westlake and Simi. The fire road is a long, merciless uphill grind, and several sections forced me to dismount and walk. Even with my lowest gears, my legs and lungs just couldn't keep up. I'll get there, but for now I'm just not going to kill myself trying to get up those sections.

It took me 45 minutes to get to the top of the fire road (or, at least a convenient peak at which to turn around), and once I'd stopped to enjoy the view, I realized that the breeze had gotten much cooler since I'd started out, and that a line of clouds was advancing from the west. So I booked it back down the trail, and was back at the car packing up just as the first clouds were rolling overhead.

Total time: 2h flat, and I covered a little over 11 miles. And here's the Google Map of my ride (one way).

Update 2/15/07: It looks like the hike-a-bike sections took their toll: a spot just to the rear of the ball of my foot, under the first knuckle of my "middle toe" is swolen and hurts when I walk on it without padding. Same spot that always bugs me when I wear dress shoes. So: I need some gel inserts or something for my mountain bike shoes.
title: Training Log: Alberson Fire Road

On Saturday, Deanne and I headed out to Santa Clarita to catch Stage 6 of the Tour of California. We just couldn't stay away: the notion of a world-class race in our backyard was too much to resist.

We arrived early, and had a chance to talk to a lot of the vendors that were there before the real crowds hit. Nearly all the reps were able to talk at length, so Deanne had a great time in the Specialized tent, and I now have a serious jones for the single-speed/fixie offering from Giant. All the booths were fun, but getting there early was definitely key: by the time we'd made it down to the end of the main drag and turned around (maybe an hour), the place was filling up, and every booth were swamped.

Deanne had an uncanny sense of timing, and staked us out some prime seating about 100m back from the finish line, next to the fence, in the shade, where we could watch the race right up close in perfect comfort. The race actually did three laps around the town, so we got to see the peloton pass twice before the final sprint to the finish. Really exciting.

Unfortunately, none of my pictures of the passing riders is more than a blur, so you'll have to go elsewhere for photo coverage. But let me tell you, you really don't appreciate how fast those guys are moving until you see it first hand. Incredible.

(Pro mountain biker Jason Sager was at the race, and snapped some excellent pics.)

This was a great day out. Can't wait for next year!

So it's been great fun reading about riding in the Susitna 100, a bike race across frozen Alaskan wilderness, and 24 Hours in the Old Pueblo, from the perspectives of Chris, of Slip Angle, and pro rider Adam Lisonbee.

Tales of the climbing bum life have reminded me of all the things I want to do with climbing, all the reasons I hit the gym twice a week. And the Dirt Diva is getting in shape to spend three months hiking the Pacific Crest Trail from Mexico to Canada.

And seeing a stage of the Tour of California was fantastic.

All this makes me think that my friends and I have been up to far too little. Time to start making plans.

intro:
Well that was rather more difficult than expected.

My little training log app is up, and can be found here. I'll be posting training stuff there from now on. It's really, really rough, but I have less time to devote to the coding than I expected, and I just want it up so I can stop dumping training log entries here, knowing I'll eventually have to move them and do the data cleanup.

Now, the training log isn't a blog. No way. It may look like a blog, and have very bloggish qualities, but a blog it aint. It's just my spot to track what I've been doing. Really, I don't expect it to be interesting to anyone but me.

Narratives and pictures of hikes, rides, and other adventures will be here. Technical details and notes will be in the training log. (Though I do play to grab the RSS feed from the training log and present it as part of the DMG front page, just for grins.)

The root of the problem turned out to be that I'd somehow rigged my development environment to point to Java EE 5.0.2 instead of 4.1.2, as required by my server. A couple of things masked this. (Obtuse error messages from my IDE, and lack of sleep on my part.)

So, the next thing here at DMG: a front page redesign, which will include the latest Training Log entries.

intro:
Deanne has been getting ready to kick her training rides up a notch, and had been readying a ride over the Santa Susana Pass between Chatsworth and Simi Valley. This morning, I was her guinea pig.

We headed out from Porter Ranch at about 8:45, and rode 30 miles through Chatsworth and over into Simi. This is a fantastic ride. It kicked my ass the exact ammout it needed to be kicked. (GPS Map)

D and I grabbed lunch at Islands (Teriyaki burger, mmm!), and I headed home, planning to spend the afternoon rigging up geocoding for images here. Did it happen? Hell no.

Instead, I stopped home, did a quick change in to hiking clothes, filled my Camelbak, and headed for Wildwood Park in Thousand Oaks to join Laura on a hike. In the parking lot, I got to talking to a guy named Paul from Kentucky who is in town helping out his daughter while she recovers from knee surgery. He and Laura and I ended up wandering around the park for a couple of hours, talking about plants (well, they talked about plants, I nodded as if I understood), and energy policy, and the local ecology. Laura has an incredibly deep and specific understanding of California's ecosystem and geology, and it was a joy to listen to her and Paul talk about that stuff.

Later on, we bumped into a couple who were resting at the base of the trail up to Lizard Rock, and we heard tales of growing up chasing moose in Alaska and untouched "hollers" in Kentucky where logging machines can't get in.

After bidding Paul good luck and leaving Wildwood, it was back home for a few minutes to clean off the trail and road grime, then off to Westlake to have dinner with my parents. We ate at Terri's Cafe over on Cheseboro & Agoura, which has the most laid-back waiters I've seen since college, and some of the best food I've had in a long time.

Terri's Cafe
(818) 707-1934
30135 Agoura Rd
Agoura Hills, CA 91301

And I cheated on my Lenten vow to give up sweets. I had some of the flour-less chocolate cake we ordered for desert. I'm fine with this. I guess I figure that if I don't learn to balance my health goals with enjoying a good meal, then I really am turning Lent into little more than an excercise in pointless self-deprivation. I always say that what you think you're giving up for lent isn't really what you're actually giving up. Maybe this year is more about giving up bullshitting myself about how many sweets I really do eat every day.

And now, it's time for me to get some sleep. G'night, all!

body:
My general plan was to ride a large loop north up Palo Comado Canyon, then east to Shepherd's Flat, and south down Cheeseboro Canyon back to the trailhead.

Unfortunately, I got rolling a little later than I expected to, and had to make some concessions to fading daylight. I cut from the Palo Comado trail over to Cheeseboro Canyon via the Ranch Center trail.

The Ranch Center trail is only 1.2 miles, but it's one hard-ass climb. I walked most of it, cursing the whole way, and praying that I wasn't wrecking my foot all over again. The descent was even steeper, (do not attempt this trail west-to-east) with me squeezing hard on both brakes nearly the whole way down.

That dropped me onto the Cheeseboro Canyon trail, about mid way between the trailhead and Shepherd's Flat. I did a quick check of remaining daylight, and headed north.

I hit Shepherd's Flat just as the sun finally sank below the hilltops, and was treated to a wonderful moment. The cool of night was starting to set in, and the tips of all the hills around were still catching a bit of daylight. Earlier, when I'd stopped to take this picture, I had thought I'd heard a mountain lion growl. Now at the Flat, I spotted what had made that noise: a particular kind of little bird was flitting from bush to bush, and its wingbeats sounded like a cat purring, or a far-off motorbike.

After a minute's rest, it was time to high-tail it back to the trailhead before full dark set in. Not a problem. I know this trail really well, and it's mostly downhill heading home, so it was a fast, smooth ride back over the sandy stretch and down past Sulpher Springs and back to my car.

All in all, I'd spent a total of about 80 minutes on the trail, and covered a little more than 10 miles. Not bad, considering that long hike-a-bike up the Ranch Center trail.

Here's the GPS map, and training log entry.

After packing up my gear I headed over to Boulderdash for a couple hours of climbing. I thought I'd be pooped, but I had a great night. Knocked off a fun new climb, and finally got to the top of a 40-foot .10b that I've been working on for a while. Now I've got the moves, I just need to put them together. I can feel that I'm close to getting this one. I even had enough energy to bust a few push-ups outside while Timbo was having a smoke.

After that it was home again, home again, jiggety-jig for microwaved lazagna and veggies (Stoffer's, yuck), and a wonderful night's sleep.

I cannot wait for daylight savings time. I can do this every day.

intro:
Psychologist Tanya Chartrand of Duke University wanted to understand her husband better.

"My husband, while very charming in many ways, has an annoying tendency of doing exactly the opposite of what I would like him to do in many situations," she admits.

So she enrolled herself and her husband in a study of nagging to try to discover why he insisted on thwarting her.

It turns out that human beings naturally, involuntarily, will undermine the controlling efforts of others. Duh. Evidently, this is called being "reactant."

So, did learning this make Dr. Chartrand realize that maybe she should work on being less controlling, and value her husband's distinct personality? Hell no.

Chartrand says she thinks this knowledge should help her husband "suppress his reactant tendencies."

That makes me giggle every time I read it. Hooo-boy!
title: Nagging is Counterproductive
viaTitle: Psychologists Found Out That Nagging Doesn't Work. (Duh!)

intro:
Okay, I'm finally starting to get caught up. I've run a few errands, fixed a few bugs, eaten, and it's time to post about last week's incredible ride before tomorrow, when I head out on this week's incredible ride.

So, to sum up: the map is here, and the stats are here. ~60 miles, with plenty of climbing, and terrible weather.

Actually, the weather was fantastic. I just wasn't dressed for it. I took the advice of one of the ride leaders, and left my arm warmers in the car, believing that the fog would burn off, the sun would come out, and it would turn into a sunny 75° day. It did not. It stayed an overcast 57° day, and I was pretty cold for most of the ride. (Cold was to be a theme this week. More on that when I post about NYC.)

Bottom line: I did fine on the climb, and I'm really happy with my progress. But I'm still a beginner, and I still have a long, long way to go. I really want to find a group to mountain bike with, but for now I'm sticking with the ALC: I'm really only in good enough shape for one big ride a week. Maybe in the fall I'll be ready for consecutive road/trail days?

I overslept this morning, just long enough to miss the ride out of Santa Monica. So I spent the day doing housekeeping. I fixed some front derailer issues on my road bike, and replaced the old and busted handlebar tape with new, profoundly green tape. (No black or red at the shop.)

Also cleaned the bathroom, and the CDC says I can have people over now. I also have too much beer in my storage closet. Coincidence?

I've been experiencing withdrawal from the New York trip. After five days straight of socializing and big ideas, I'm having a hard time readjusting to my small, quiet world here in Simi Valley.

I keep feeling like I'm about to have some kind of insight about what I'm supposed to do with the next year. But every time, it turns out to be jet lag.

I'm off to sleep, that I may ride tomorrow on my tuned-up bike.
title: Moment of Clarity?

intro:
44 miles of of suffering in Valencia yesterday, more than 20 miles of that was uphill, and I'm starting to love the agony. This was shorter than last week's ride, but the pain is in the numbers:

  Last Week This Week
Time 05:47:01 04:17:18
Miles 58.02 44.18
Top Speed 31.90 35.70
Calories 3267 2631
Avg. Heart Rate 122 136
Max. Heart Rate 157 171

I've found that running and cycling are all about intensity: go fast, and you burn out in a relatively short distance. Keep it mellow, and you can roll along all day.

So, take another look at those numbers: This week I had higher max. and avg. heart rates, which tells me I was working harder over the course of the ride, and spiking near my max heart rate. I'd love to see some Wattage measurements, but that'll have to wait until either I'm rich, or PowerTaps get a lot cheaper.

So my heart rate says I was working about 9% harder than last week, and that jibes with the calorie calculations. Last week's 565 kCal/hr burn jumped about 8% to 615 kCal/hr. (Then again, the link between heart rate and calories isn't a surprise: I'm getting both numbers from my heart rate monitor.)

My average speed also rose a bit, from 10.03mph to 10.32. Not a lot, but I did it without the long, flat return leg of last week's ride.

Bottom line: I'm climbing faster, making the most of the flats and downhills, and I'm having fun doing it. This is everything I got into biking for.

body:
Sunday: Flying Out

After a bike ride and a St. Patty's Day party on Saturday, two coworkers and I hopped a flight to New York City for AJAXWorld East.

Weather worries proved unfounded, but residual backup from a blizzard on the east coast kept our plane grounded for an extra 45 minutes before taking off. I wasn't too bothered by that until I realized that they didn't have the air vents on, and the kid next to me had kicked off his shoes.

Kudos to Luke at Decisive Moments for the book tip: The Rider proved to be a gripping and inspiring read, and perfectly sized for a plane trip. It fit weightlessly in my carry-on, and I finished it about 40 minutes before landing.

We walked around Manhattan for a bit, and followed a recommendation of a passer-by to the Heartland Brewery near Times Square. Very good beer, tasty dinner, and a great table right by the front window, where we could sate our touristy fascination with NYC's street scenes.

Monday: Boot Camp

Dion Hinchcliffe led Monday's "AJAX Bootcamp," and proved he's got the goods, setting the tone for the rest of the week. We got our hands dirty with a carefully-selected set of features combining a bit of DHTML and AJAX (using Dojo and Scriptaculous) that walked us thorugh all the key elements of AJAX. File uploads, Dojo widgets, Scriptaculous eye candy, and all in a DIY packaging that gave me very solid footing to stand on. I've played with AJAX before, but never with any framework, and this was a fantastic introduction to the current state of AJAX methods and tools. Bootcamp alone was worth the trip.

Monday: RENT

After a quick dinner, we headed to Broadway to see RENT, which was wonderful. I'd never seen it before, and had only vague recollections of a soundtrack CD I'd heard in college, so this was something special. If you get the chance, see this. It's amazing.

Tuesday: All Google, all the Time

I'm still processing my notes from the AJAXWorld keynotes and breakout sessions, so this (and all notes from the lectures) will be very abstract.

Google opened big, talking about maps, gmail, Google Talk, and their work with mashups and widgets. Lots of wonderful theoretical stuff about enabling users to surprise you, creating open tools and technologies. First question from the audience: "How do you make money on any of this?" Answer: "This drives search traffic."

Google distinguished themselves at this conference as the smartest guys in the room. I think the industry is going to spend a lot of time chasing them, in terms of tools, techniques, capabiliy, and notions of what's possible.

I had time to look around the floor for a while, and while there were a lot of vendors for such a small conference, I wasn't happy with a lot of what I saw. The big boys want to add new tools to their IDEs to further lock you in, and some of the smaller players think they'll find success producing stand-alone tools. This makes their offerings unsuited for mixing in with existing projects or IDEs from other vendors.

I love the idea of Laszlo: a single project you can export as FLEX or AJAX, but I hate the notion of permanently binding any project to a particular tool or vendor. Web apps are just too long-lived, and require too much maintenance. Surrendering the option of switching tools is just too painful for my taste.

For my money, the standout toolkit at the show was BackBase. They provide tools you can drop into any project, and work within existing standards. I can't wait to play with the sample code they were handing out, and start monkeying with something similar here on my blog.

Dojo is a close second, and will likely be what I start using at home, but I don't like that it breaks XML validation of documents, and that it'll necessarily be a bit behind latest browser changes. Evidently IE7 broke lots of Dojo apps. Ouch.

Wednesday: Struts, JSF, and Hard Choices

The highlight of Wednesday's lectures was a breakout session with Craig McClanahan (of Struts fame). By that time I'd gotten my head around the client-side issues, and was concerned about the need for server-side services to back AJAX apps. His presentation showed that JSF really is the way to go. Making any bean a service endpoint obviates a lot of developer work building all those backing services.

Unfortunately, JSF isn't an option where I work, and I'm not ready to make the jump at home. (Maybe I'll rewrite my training log?)

Maybe my favorite moment of the conference came when an audience member asked Craig, "We have a lot of code written with Struts. What now?" His answer basically amounted to: Well, then you have some hard choices to make." It was a much-needed moment of reality amid all the pie-in-the-sky hype.

Thursday: Empire State Building, Central Park

Our return flight didn't take off 'till 4pm, so we had some time to kill on Thursday morning. We headed over to the Empire State Building, and spend a little time on it's foggy and windblasted observation deck. The pigeons were fearless, and the tourists less abundant than the last time I was there (owing, I think, to the fog and the dire warnings of "zero visibility" by the staff).

The subway took us to the northwest corner of Central Park, and we spend some time wandering southward, just taking in the scenery. Most of the roads were closed to motor traffic, and there were lots of cyclists and runners out and about, and the day was perfect for a spin: 60° and just a little hazy. I'm definitly making time for an hour or so of running in the park next time I'm in the city.

The Roundup

So what do I take away from all this? A desire to spend some real time in NYC (and especially see the other burroughs), a renewed enthusiasm for web development, and for some reason another surge in my nesting instinct. I've been cleaning and organizing since I got back, and I'm planning for more shelving and wall decoration.

On a technical level, I'll be adding AJAX-y features here and to my training log, probably using Dojo. We shall see. For now, I'm putting a little of what I learned to use right away at work, and starting to think about what I can add here that'll let me play with things like JSON and drag-and-drop in conjunction with AJAX. Should be fun!

I'm getting pretty good at this. I rolled my ankle last night at the climbing gym. (That's what I get for bouldering. Feh!) Went immediately home and applied the RICE treatment: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Swelling seems to be under control, but I'm still worried. (Can you blame me?)

I can stand on it, but walking is out of the question, which scares me. Just for grins, I'm checking in with a sports doctor this afternoon to make sure there's no structural damage.

The good news is, I've found a sports doctor close to home, and I have a good feeling about him already: I told the receptionist I rolled my ankle while bouldering, and she asked, "Were you using a crash pad?" These are my people.

I've also got a line on a physical therapist who's also a triathlete. So I think I'm good there if I need PT.

In the meantime, my ankle is wrapped, and I'm staying off it until I head off for my appointment with the doc. Just tracing the alphabet with my toe, to keep things mobile.

A... B... C... D... E...

intro:
Science fiction author Cory Doctorow pointed to an excellent (if freewheeling) essay by Charlie Stross on Why the commercial ebook market is broken. The essay touches on why the eBook market is withering on the vine, and why the publishing industry has little to fear from piracy.

In the pre-internet dark age, there was a subculture of folks who would get their hands on books and pass them around and encourage people to read them for free, rather than buying their own copies. Much like today's ebook pirates, in terms of the what they did (with one or two minor differences). There was a closely-related subculture who would actually sell copies of books without paying the authors a penny in royalties, too.

We have a technical term for such people: we call them "librarians" and "second-hand bookstore owners".

Stross neatly skewers most of the publishing industry's misguided arguments in favor of DRM and their unreasoning panic over piracy.
title: eBooks, and Why Nobody's Reading Them
viaTitle: Why an ebook reader won't displace books

intro:
Ned Batchelder points out LiliPond, music typesetting software. Their article Obsessed with putting ink on paper, is a wonderful exploration of the details that go into making sheet music easy to read, and a pleasure to play from.

Ned said that he couldn't see the difference between their "good" and "bad" example, and I have to admit that I had to really look to see the diferences. But the relative quality was immediately obvious. I found myself thinking, "Well, the one on the left is far better, but I'm not sure why."

From the time I was 11 until I was about 21 I spent many, many hours reading and playing from sheet music, and I can attest that most modern, computer-generated print-outs are absolutely wreched. They're difficult to read, easy to get lost in, and fail to provide so many of the artistic cues musicians rely on. Sight reading from such a print feels degrading, regardless of outcome. If you play well, it's despite the fact that the music is beneath you. If not, then you played badly because the music is beneath you. Either way, you want to pull out something beautiful and sink into a bit of metronomeless art-nuveau self-indulgence just to cleanse the palatte.

That is to say: I'm glad there are people out there that love music and music notation enough to devote real effort to doing it well. It is worthy work.
title: Music Engraving
