intro:
I've shied away from anything DRM-protected, and this is why. Davis Freeberg upgraded to a high-resolution monitor, and that caused the DRM software attached to his Netflix account and Amazon Unbox movies to freak.

Because my computer allows me to send an unrestricted HDTV feed to my monitor, Hollywood has decided to revoke my ability to stream 480 resolution video files from Netflix. In order to fix my problem, Netflix recommended that I downgrade to a lower res VGA setup.

The irony of DRM is that it only affects paying customers. Freeberg puts it better than I could:

The irony in all of this, is that the DRM that Hollywood is so much in love with, is really only harming their paying customers. When you do a DRM reset, it's not your pirated files that get revoked, it's the ones that you already paid for that are at risk.

That's right. All the illegal stuff works perfectly. No problems with high-res monitors or restricted access or revoking privileges. Just high-quality goods you can use however you want, for free. Why do studios think this strategy will work?
title: Netflix DRM Horror Story

body:
My optometrist is a good guy. But on my bad days I believe he has fallen victim to the economic pressures facing all doctors generally, and the temptations placed before optometrists particularly. He sets expiration dates on prescriptions to the legal minimum: one year.

Since it's been 14 months since my last visit, I expected him to stop shipment of the new lenses. I called his office this afternoon, and verified this. Yes, my prescription has expired. Yes, I'll have to come in for a full eye exam to get a new prescription. Yes, the earliest they can see me is next week. 8 days from now. When I only have 15 left on this pair of lenses.

(As an aside: Yes, I can go without contacts. I have glasses, and I look dashing in them. But I'm not crazy about biking without sunglasses or martial arts without clear vision, and both have become rather important to me. But yes, this is, as they say, the problem of a rich man.)

However, I checked on a few things regarding expiration dates, etc. I discovered that the website in question will go ahead and ship me my new contacts if they can't verify the prescription within "8 business hours." In other words, if they don't hear back in a day, they just ship the lenses.

I just received an email saying that my new lenses are on the way. My bet is that my optometrist lagged getting back to them to let them know the prescription has expired. For once a delay worked in my favor. Hip hip hooray!

So, I'm going to call and move my eye appointment to a month from now, when I'll have both more time and more money, and look for my new lenses in the mail.

Update 01/04/08: Just got a call from the optometrist's office: they couldn't have seen me on the 9th anyway. The doctor is in surgery that day. Now I know I got lucky when those lenses shipped.
intro:

So, I hopped on the web and ordered more. And was promptly faced with what I expected to be a real problem: the status on my order was "Verrifying Rx with optometrist."

body:
We dubbed our campsite "Lower Halls Lake", situated as it was slightly south of Halls Lake proper, with water draining into Halls Lake via a rocky stream. While our camp at Long Lake was perhaps the most spectacular, "Lower" Halls Lake combined breathtaking scenery with comfort and ease of living that made it the jewel of our trip. When I think of Wyoming, the first images that come to mind are of Halls Lake.

We gathered the evening we arrived, and weighed our options for the next day. The fish were clearly biting, so fishing was a possibility. But we were also camping just west of the Continental Divide, and so chose to spend the day hiking to the top of Halls Mountain, at 12,473 ft. of elevation.

I'm not typically a peak bagger. I prefer to cover distance and have fun, and getting to the top of some arbitrary rock isn't usually where it's at for me. But this was a chance to do a tough hike at altitude and stand on the Continental Divide, which I thought was pretty cool.

We ascended the western side of Halls Mtn, up a 1100'' scree slope steeper than your average staircase. We practiced switchbacking as a group, and routefinding, and general safety guidelines.

This was certainly the "bunny slope" of peak ascents. But even this put some light on the challenges of mountain climbing. They aren't physical, they're logistical. We each carried just two or three liters of water, and wouldn't have a chance to top up once we started up the mountain. With afternoon storms a possibility, we carried all our clothing layers, which added weight and bulk to our packs. And time was a factor: being caught in a thunderstorm at 12,000 ft, and trying to negotiate a steep, rocky, off-trail descent would be dangerous for a group of beginners like us.

At the top of the scree slope, we spied thunderheads moving in from the Western horizon. But they seemed to be passing north of us, while the skies directly above stayed clear. We debated turning around, but decided that we were making good time, and could reach the summit and get back before any storm caught us. (Plus, we had nearly a 360° view, and would have plenty of warning should a storm head our way.)

A couple members of the expedition elected to stay on the saddle, enjoying the view, rather than make the second leg of the ascent. I have to say that one person particular showed the most courage I saw on the trip. That day, she faced the two toughest challenges of climbing: she faced her fear and climbed anyway, and stopped when she felt she'd hit her limit.

The rest of us continued up, topping out maybe an hour later on the top of Halls Mountain at 12,473 ft. of elevation, standing right on the Continental Divide. Pretty cool stuff. Here's me on the top:

We spent a few minutes on the top, did some quick GPS and map reading lessons, and then headed back down. The clouds we'd been worried about were still skirting the northern horizon, leaving clear skies above us all day.

On arriving back at camp, we discovered that our horsepacker, Nikki, who'd been injured the day before, had passed the time while we were out hiking by making us biscuits. After a long day on your feet, coming home to discover that dinner is already half done is awesome. Nikki kicks ass, and this was just one of the ways she showed it out there. Broken toe, hobbling around, with 4 horses and a dog to care for, what does she do? Makes diner for everyone.

We were famished, and followed up the biscuits with some kind of chilli chese macaroni or something. As we were cooking, clouds rolled in, and the wind picked up, and we knew we were finally going to get rained on. We tightened the lines on our tarps, and got our waterproof gear on, and carried on cooking dinner.

For a couple of hours we huddled under our tarps, enjoying our dinner and the novelty of a rainy evening. And then, as quickly as it arrived, the rain stopped, and the wind faded, and the last rays of the sunset shone in from the west, lighting up the underside of the clouds as they passed, and the peaks above us. Just an amazing reward at the end of the day.

We crawled into my sleeping bag that night well-fed and absolutely exhausted. I think this was the best night's sleep I got the whole trip.

Okay. Day 9.
title: Backpacking: Day 9

intro:
Seth Godin: Music lessons

Most items of value derive that value from scarcity. Digital changes that, and you can derive value from ubiquity now.

The solution isn't to somehow try to become obscure, to get your song off the (digital) radio. The solution is to change your business.

You used to sell plastic and vinyl. Now, you can sell interactivity and souvenirs.

Ian Rogers: Talking To The Music Industry Again, The Aspen Live Conference

Losers wish for scarcity. Winners leverage scale.

There is more opportunity in leveraging the scale of the Web than trying to create scarcity. We've all been engaged in many attempts at creating scarcity in digital music and none of them have worked. Meanwhile, others have been leveraging the scale of the Web with great success. We should learn from this pattern and apply our energy appropriately.
title: Music Business Links

intro:
Brian Whitworth at Massey University in New Zealand is looking into whether we're all just simulations. Here's the abstract for his paper The Physical World as a Virtual Reality (DMG copy):

This paper explores the idea that the universe is a virtual reality created by information processing, and relates this strange idea to the findings of modern physics about the physical world. The virtual reality concept is familiar to us from online worlds, but our world as a virtual reality is usually a subject for science fiction rather than science. Yet logically the world could be an information simulation running on a multi-dimensional space-time screen. Indeed, if the essence of the universe is information, matter, charge, energy and movement could be aspects of information, and the many conservation laws could be a single law of information conservation. If the universe were a virtual reality, its creation at the big bang would no longer be paradoxical, as every virtual system must be booted up. It is suggested that whether the world is an objective reality or a virtual reality is a matter for science to resolve. Modern information science can suggest how core physical properties like space, time, light, matter and movement could derive from information processing. Such an approach could reconcile relativity and quantum theories, with the former being how information processing creates space-time, and the latter how it creates energy and matter.

I honestly don't know whether I want this guy to find anything or not. On the one hand, if reality is hackable, that's awesome. On the other, that's a deep, deep rabit hole...
title: Science Takes the Red Pill

Geoff's comment made me realize that maybe I should not for posterity what I see in that video. I see a woman who's finally just talking, just being herself instead of being who she thinks she has to be to get elected. I hear strength in her voice see experience and passion in her eyes. I think this is the best answer to the "Why do you want to be President?" question I've ever heard.

That said, I was already tipping from Obama to Clinton. I think she's got real foreign policy cojones, and is talking details and real strategy where other candidates are giving answers driven by the presidential race. Asked about building a bike shed, the rest talk about how awesome the bike shed is going to be. She talks about using the right lumber and sinking the posts well below the frost line.

And every time I hear General Wesley Clark talk, I want to stand up and cheer.

They say that you don't always know when you're being lied to, but you do always know when you're hearing the truth. More and more, I hear the truth from Senator Clinton.

intro:
I hit the weights last night, and I'm glad I did. I'd forgotten how great I feel after a good weight session.

After trying partner squats as Jiu Jitsu a couple weeks ago, I've seen the light and permanently replaced dumbell squats with regular shoulder squats. Greatest exercise ever. I could feel every muscle from my back through my heels activating and twitching to keep me in balance. Just awesome.

But I tired very quickly. I've been neglecting high-intensity strength training lately, and it shows. I don't have the explosive strength or raw power I used to. I can go all day at 75% of my strength capacity, but crank it up to 85+, and I gas out quick. Gotta fix that.

I need high-intensity cardio and strength training. This means intervals. This means full-body explosive movements. Sounds a lot like a typical Crossfit workout...
title: Weight Training

intro:
Megan over at From the Archives has once again posted something really interesting. It's about long-term negotiations, and why they tend to break down over time. A combination of two factors is involved:

First, humans tend to value losses more than gains, so the things you give up always feel heavier than what you get in return. Making concessions is always more painful than receiving them is gratifying, and so compromise leads us to perceive our opponents as stronger than ourselves.

Second, once we form an idea, we generally perceive confirming evidence, and unconsciously filter everything else. When others base their opinions on the evidence we've discarded, we regard them as exaggerating or lying.

So, over time, both parties to any negotiation come to regard each other as undeservedly powerful liars. Sound familiar?

I think that first part almost hits the mark. Rather than seeing the other side as powerful, I think compromise leads each party to feel they gave up more than they received. Any requests for further compromise are therefore seen as greedy So my formulation would be "...come to regard each other as greedy liars."
title: Demonizing Opponents

Be careful what you wish for. I said I wanted to turn up the intensity...

I haven't been this sore in a long, long time. Neck, shoulders, back, chest, hams and calves, plus verious burns and bruises from getting beat on in BJJ.

I've cut deserts, and I'm craving protein like I haven't since back in '02 or '03, when I was doing rediculous weight and plyo workouts and gaining a pound a week in pure muscle. My bathroom scale shows I'm up two pounds in body weight, and down 3% in body fat. Now, I don't think the body fat percentage is exact. Not by a long shot. But that's still a hell of a move in just two weeks.

So, I'll be getting a refill on my vitamins* and breaking out my food bible and going to work on what I can do to make sure my body has what it needs. And I'll be making double-sure that I get enough sleep in the next couple of weeks.

* I know everyone says that vitamins are a waste, but I take one that my pharmacist recommended, and though some of it gets flushed, I really feel the difference between getting almost enough nutrition, and getting everything I need and then some. And at $14 for a three-month supply, I'm absolutely getting my money's worth.

intro:
I've been thinking about why this week has been so much harder for me, why I feel so much more drained and sore than I usually do. What changed? I didn't ride my bike last weekend, and the only thing I added this week that I don't usually do was Monday's weight workout. What gives?

What gives is the FITT principle. There are basically four aspects of training that you can change to trigger adaptation:

  • Frequency
  • Intensity
  • Time (Duration)
  • Type

Generally, for a smooth, relatively comfortable adaptation, you change one aspect at a time. I realized that this week I changed three:

  • Frequency: I did three workouts in four days instead of my usual 2-3 workouts in 7 days.
  • Intensity: Both Krav and Jiu Jitsu have both been especially tough this week.
  • Type: I hit the weights, which I don't usually do.

There are plenty of ways to see this, but the FITT principle is a pretty good rule of thumb, and it usually works for me. The bottom line is that by a pretty objective measure, this has been a very big week for me, physically.

So now I don't feel bad about being so tired. I'll ride my bike tomorrow, just to stay loose, and concentrate on getting good food and being ready to hit the weights again on Sunday, if I'm feeling up to it.
title: Pummeled: More Thoughts

Tossed Saturday's bike plans as soon as I woke up, and spent the day seeing friends and eating really, really good food: falafel pita and black bean & veggie soup at Nature's Grill in Ventura and a burger and baked potato at Wood Ranch BBQ in Agoura. My stomach was very happy Saturday night.

I'd thought of repeating my Christmas Eve ride this afternoon, but instead slept late and did my usual Santa Susana to Rocky Peak to Chumash ride. Best ride yet down Chumash-- everything I tried, I got clean on the first try. Zero dabs for the day, and I only walked one short section.

My personal best on this loop is about 1:42:09. I finished today in 1:53:33, which is pretty good, but really shows that I'm not fully recovered from last week. I felt the drag today, and I'm going to make sure I get plenty of rest this week: good food, good sleep.

According to the Financial Times...

EMI, the big music company, spends 25 million pounds a year "to scrap unsold CDs".

That's about $50 million -- a year.

To destroy unsold physical inventory in a world of ubiquitous digital distribution.

Oh my.

Makes me think of a post by Seth Godin:

The marketing you do, the decisions you make, the hurdles you have to go through probably have vestiges of the old [business] model. Sometimes, like the little feet on the back of a whale, it's easy to ignore the vestiges. Other times, it's entirely possibly that they prevent you from achieving your goals.
title: EMI Spends $50M per Year to Scrap CDs

intro:
Ugh. You'd think Apple could get this right. But no.

Piracy still provides a superior service for free. No 30-day or 24-hour deadlines. Whatever you want. Downloaded. Right now. For free.

But... That's if you can find it. And if enough other people are offering it for download. And if the connection doesn't drop. And if...

Apple and all other purveyors of information take heed: only three things make information valuable: freshness, completeness, and convenience.

You can't beat pirate sites for freshness. Not by any meaningful margin. But you can compete on completeness and convenience. Please do so. Right now, it's like you're trying to lose.
title: Apple's Movie Rentals

intro:
Amusing post by Eric Sink, who just wanted to know what the pricing was for a piece of software. The website didn't list any prices, and when he filled in their little "contact us" form asking for pricing, he got an email reply asking for a phone number where a sales person could reach him.

Bottom line: I'm interested in buying your product. The only obstacle in my way is YOU. If your product didn't have such a great reputation, I would give up right now.

When a customer comes looking for your product, that's a gift. Don't think about marginal profit. Don't think about anything. Just get the hell out of the way and let them hand over their money.
title: Obstacles to Making the Sale

intro:
(Update: I talked to Amazon again today, and all is well. I think I just got a surly customer service rep.)

I returned something to Amazon. I was told I would get a full refund. I did not. They charged $30 for restocking. So I called customer service.

  • ME: I was told I'd receive a full refund (minus shipping), but there's a $30 restocking fee on my refund email. Why is that?
  • REP: Perhaps shipping was deducted from the refund.
  • ME: The refund email says that $5 was deducted for shipping, which is fine. But it says that a $30 restocking fee was also deducted.
  • REP: The restocking fee applies to all orders older than 30 days.
  • ME: The item was a Christmas gift, and I was told that the return period had been extended through January 31st.
  • REP: The extended deadline only applies to orders placed after November 1.
  • [LONG pause, while I wait for him to elaborate.]
  • ME: The item was received on November 6th, and I believe all return deadlines are calculated from the date of receipt, correct?
  • REP: Yes, Sir.
  • ME: And when I called to ask for the shipping label, I was told I would receive a full refund. There was no mention of a restocking fee. I have an email here from a "Brandon W" with a shipping label and everything.
  • [Another LONG pause.]
  • ME: Are you still there?
  • REP: Nothing can be done, Sir.
  • ME: Can I please speak to a manager?
  • REP: He will tell you the same information.
  • ME: I understand. Please let me speak with a manager.
  • REP: Nothing can be done, Sir.
  • ME: Let me speak to your manager, please.
  • [I wait for the manager.]
  • MANAGER: Hello, Sir. I need you to verify your shipping address.
  • ME: Do you mean my address, or the shipping address on the order?
  • MANAGER: Sir, I just need you to verify the address we have on file.
  • ME: I understand. This item was a gift, so my shipping address is different to the address where it was shipped. Which address do you want?
  • MANAGER: What was the address, Sir?
  • ME: [I give him what I think is the shipping address.]
  • [Another long silence.]
  • ME: Are you still there?
  • MANAGER: That is not the correct address, Sir.
  • [I try my own address, as well as a third address that might be on the original order. No dice.]
  • MANAGER: I'm sorry, Sir. For security reasons we cannot discuss this without verifying your identity.

I'm going to get the original shipping label out when I get home and get this sorted out. And don't get me started on needing someone else's address as some kind of security measure.
title: Banging My Head Against the Wall

intro:
I just got off the phone with Amazon customer service. The whole conversation took maybe 5 minutes, and the "restocking fee" has been refunded. Awesome.

The rep, who's name was Crystal, did initially say that the restocking fee was correctly applied per Amazon policy, even given the extension of the holiday returns period. But when I told her that the last rep I talked to hadn't mentioned a restocking fee, she relented. She said, "Hmm... let's see what I can do."

This is a striking contrast to yesterday's call.

There are two interesting differences between yesterday's call and today's. First, the customer service representatives I talked to yesterday started out the call trying to make me go away, and things deteriorated from there. Today, the rep was looking for a way to please an unhappy customer.

Second, I provided Crystal with exactly the same information I gave the guys yesterday. Where yesterday's reps stonewalled, Crystal put the puzzle pieces together and could see that I was legit. I don't know what her computer screen looked like, but I suspect she did a little bit of flipping back and forth matching up addresses and order numbers. Kudos to her.

And maybe, just maybe, it helped that I started out the call giving Crystal my account information, which I bet indicates that I'm an Amazon Prime member, and order a metric buttload of stuff from them every year. (Typically $20 - $100 per month.) Spending $30 to keep me happy is a no-brainer, or should be. They're going to make that back by this time next month.

The real weak link in the chain here is communication, and explanation. The email I got from Amazon with the return shipping label didn't say anything about the order, reasons for return, or that I'd received special permission to return this item. The refund email cited an itemized list of fees deducted, but didn't indicate why they were assessed. So both me and the customer service reps are ever quite sure what exactly is going on.

And finally, I'm surprised that Amazon isn't bending over backward to make holiday gifts hassle-free. The "gift" part of the equasion actually caused problems in trying to return it, rather than making life simpler. Take anything back to Best Buy without a receipt, and you get store credit. Why is Amazon any different?
title: Amazon Makes Good

body:
I felt really strong on the initial climb from the trailhead, and I'm sure I put up a personal best for that climb. I only really felt tired in the last hundred meters of the second climb.

Though the time doesn't show it, I can feel that I'm getting stronger. I usually climb exclusively in my very bottom gear, but I'm starting to find that my next gear up is often the better option- same perceived effort, lots more speed. And I'm carrying speed down Chumash much better than I used to, and I'm learning to relax through the technical sections.

All together, a really fun way to spend a couple hours yesterday afternoon.

intro:
I saw Cloverfield, and recommend it, with caveats. Form your own opinion.

But I unreservedly recommend The Descent. It's the best horror movie I've seen in ages. Just awesome. Plenty of sudden frights and repulsive gore to keep horror fans squrming in their seats. And the way the main character just keeps getting stronger and meaner... wow. Awesome. If you can, watch this with the original ending from the European cut, which I'm told is an option on the DVD. (I've already sent the movie back to Netflix, so I can't verify.)

I finally saw Ratatouille last weekend, and loved it. Enough to buy it. It's just wonderful. Unfortunately, the short that comes with it, "Lifted" isn't all that great. But no worries-- Pixar has released a DVD collection of all their short films to date, so you can enjoy all your favorites in one place.

David Cronenberg's Eastern Promises was visually stunning, and features maybe the best fight sequence in any movie I've ever seen. It's classic Cronenberg: the tension is understated, and the pacing deliberate. If you like Cronenberg, you'll love this.

The Kingdom was exciting, but not nearly as brainy as I'd hoped, or as the title sequence suggested. If it had had a little more of Syriana in it's DNA, I'd have been very happy.

Day Watch, the second half of the story that began with Night Watch, is fantastic. The pace picks up from the first movie, and there's plenty of new magical wierdness going on.

intro:
I weighed in last night at 180.6 lbs.

Dude.

That's too heavy. Between Jiu Jitsu and weight training over the last few weeks I'm putting on a noticable ammount of muscle. And my body fat continues to slide slowly downward. (Used to run around 18%, now typically down around 15%.)

So I'm getting stronger and leaner, which is good. But still. Too heavy.

So, it's back on my usual weight loss regimen, which is disturbingly simple:

  • No cola. Ever.
  • No desert unless it's social.
  • At least 3 1-hour cardio sessions per week.

Basically, I eliminate empty calories, and bump my daily burn a bit. Simple and effective.

When I stick to it. Since the plan already incorporates one or two nights a week of "cheating", one or two more will cancel any benefits.

So yeah. Here we go with the weekly weigh-ins again.
title: Heavy, Man

Taking last week off to do some weight work was definitely a good idea, and cranking up my protein intake and taking my vitamins has done wonders for my energy level. Any trainer will tell you that nutrition is half the game, but that's a lesson I keep having to teach myself.

Tonight's Krav class featured a consistent energy level, and Jiu Jitsu followed up with lots of work from the guard, which means I basically feel like I did four thousand sit-ups.

Another student said that he's going to be leaving the school, and moving to the Krav Maga Worldwide Training Center in Sherman Oaks. Evidently he checked it out, and was really impressed with the level of the classes there. So, good luck to him, and now I'm very curious about what's going on over there.

Anyway, I came home tonight and heated up some meatloaf and a giant pile of veggies, and now I'm feeling sane and settled enough to head for bed. G'night all.

intro:
Sony has announced that they will be closing Sony CONNECT and terminating support for the DRM on music bought there.

What does this mean for users?

Like 8-track cassettes, Sony CONNECT music will be playable on old players only; nothing new will play Sony CONNECT music. Even Sony's own stuff won't play it in the future. If you want to listen to it, you have to dig out your old player.

Or, you can burn each album to a regular CD and re-import it into your new player.

So, in a nutshell: the next music player you buy won't play your old stuff, and getting around that is a giant pain in the neck.

Way to go, Sony.

This problem affects only music bought legitimately through Sony CONNECT. As always, DRM bites legitimate users only. Pirates, downloaders, and lawbreakers remain unaffected. (And increasingly prone to saying, "I told you so.")
title: Sony Kills Sony  CONNECT Store, DRM Support

body:
I met up early on with a guy named Fred who's been riding out here for many years. We rode together all they way to the end of my loop, and talked nearly the whole way. Listening to him was like drinking from a firehose of local mountain biking knowledge, and having someone to follow down hills forced me to loosen up and think more about my line and less about the bumps.

I also got a chance to talk with Fred about horse etiquette, and what I can do to make future encounters with horses safer. He told me that it sounded like I'd done everything right, which I found reassuring.

There seems to be some people doing maintenance work on Chumash, but they're clearly not considering mountain bikers. They've placed small speed bump-looking bumps in the trail in an attempt to limit erosion. Unfortunately, they've placed the bumps very poorly (around blind turns, at angles likely to sweep your front tire out), and the erosion has continued, in the form of deep ruts directly in front of the bumps. I don't know what the solution is, but what's there now is clearly doing more harm than good.

And someone put a line of loose stones across the trail, possibly as some kind of speed bump. Fred removed it, and if he hadn't I would have.

But the weather was perfect, the trail quiet, and the company amiable. All in all, a great ride. I didn't manage to clean the whole thing: I fell a couple times, picking up a nasty knot on my shin in the process, and walked the last, nasty climb before hitting Rocky Peak Fire Rd. So there's plenty of fun still to be had on that trail, and I can't wait to get out there and have another go.
intro: Since my first ride up the Johnson Rd. on Christmas Eve, I've wanted to take another shot. I was already pretty tired then, and didn't feel like I gave it my best effort. So today I took a shortcut over Santa Susana Pass, and had a great time climbing one of the toughest trails out here.
title: Johnson Rd. Ride

intro:
The Santa Susana Pass used to be my primary reason for balking at commuting by bike. It's one of the local climbs used by roadies to get and stay in shape, and it's no joke. But Alpe d'Huez it aint, and I'm after riding it frequently over the last few months, I'm not so intimidated any more.

So tonight I swapped the clipless pedals on my road bike for some old platforms, and replaced the ugly yellow bar tape with black, and my road machine is ready to take me to work. It'll probably just be one or two days a week, but that's fine. Now I have no more excuses.

I also got to try my new bike shorts. I took the advice of a couple of friends and picked up a pair of really nice Castelli bib-style shorts. They are better than regular shorts, and I highly recommend them. It's so nice to ride for a couple of hours in a pair of shorts that doesn't ride up, doesn't slip down, and doesn't bind around the waist. Highly recommended.

Unfortunately, I managed to pick up a cold on my travels, so I've dosed myself with NyQuil, and will now be retiring to my bed to pass into blissful unconciousness.
title: Commuting

I was impressed that the managed to give this a satisfying ending, given that the Zodiac serial murderer was never caught. I'm going to put on something with Robert Downey Jr. in it. Restoration? Ah! I've recently realized that I'm hitting the limits of what I know how to do with my training. I'm asking a lot from my body these days, and I have only basic knowledge of training theory and a decent toolbox of different exercises. But I lack what I need to put together a training routine that meets my performance and time commitment goals. I find I'm perpetually wandering between plateauing and overtraining, without really knowing where I'm at until I'm either bored or exhausted.

I've been reading Rippetoe and Kilgore's Practical Programming for Strength Training. I'm just 50 pages in ,but so far it is awesome. Solid theory, clear explanations, and pragmatic guidelines for measuring progress and planning a strength regimen.

body:
I did get off the breaks, which saved me from going over the handlebars into a rock, and no, I did not break anything. I think somehow Krav has gotten me used to painful things happening fast, and gotten my brain to get past the oh shit! and into how do I minimize this?

Of course, once I hit the ground, the fun wasn't over. I lay there for a second, waiting for the pain of broken bones or flayed hips and shoulders, but I was basically fine. Some nasty-lookng scrapes, but nothing serious. Then I heard it: Fssssssss!

My front wheel had pinch flatted when it hit the boulder.

Luckily, I just started carrying a spare tube on my rides. This is the second one I've ever taken a spare tube on. Hoo-rah!

As I was changing the tire, I could hear someone huffing and puffing up the trail, and before long I spotted Fred, the rider I met last time I did this loop. We swapped crash stories for a few minutes (he informed me that the local emergency room charges $1000 to check for concussion), and parted ways once I got my bike back on the trail.

Back on the bike it became clear that I had zero energy left. And while I'd checked my brakes and wheels before setting off again, I'd forgotten to check my chain, which was off the chainrings and totally useless. I found this out the hard way, when I tried to push hard to climb a short rise, and threw myself over the handlebars and tumbled off the trail for my second crash of the day.

I can now attest that the steep, overgrown slopes on the chumash trail offer a soft landing. Just keep your wits about you and roll.

I gathered myself and my bike and climbed back up to the trail where I performed the thorough flight check I should have done after the first crash.

Strangely, I wasn't gun shy the rest of the way. I did walk a couple of sections, but simply because I just didn't have the energy reserves: being sick this week really took a lot out of me, and on hindsight, I think the crash happened mostly because I was overtired. I've nailed that line a dozen times, but today I just got careless and drifted left. Whups.

So I'll make sure I get plenty of protein tonight, and plenty of rest, and get my bike fixed this week. (The front wheel needs to be trued, the right brake lever is bent, and I need a new bracket for my GPS unit.)

And even hurting from the scrapes on my arms, it was such a beautiful day today that I couldn't help enjoying the rest of my ride.
intro:
I wish you could have seen it. It was spectacular. Missed the line on Chumash's toughest rock garden, and ended up endoing badly. From there, I rolled forward for about 15 feet, straight toward a big-ass boulder. I managed to lean left, so my bike hit the boulder and I went around, and crash landed somewhere further down the trail.

During all that, I had time enough for exactly two concious thoughts: Get off the goddamn brakes, and Am I going to break anything?
title: Best Crash EVAR!

intro:
My scraped-up arm annoyed me all night, and was still bleeding a little this morning. I did a quick check for deep cuts, but didn't find any. Actually, this is pretty typical for me. When I was a kid, skinned knees would ooze lymph for days, and that's pretty much what's happening now.

So I hit up the drug store for some real first aid stuff, and bandaged my arm properly. No bad for a one-handed effort!

Everyone's going to think I got tattooed.

Jeez, the things I'm getting good at...

Update: results of bandaging with gauze were unsatisfactory: dry gauze sticks to wounds, even when applied over antibiotic gel, as advised in several first aid resources I found online. Don't believe everything you read, kids.
title: Bandaged

intro:
From Rippetoe & Kilgore:

Fatigue decreases the precision with which motor unit recruitment patters can be managed and has a direct bearing on the skill with which a movement can be executed and practiced.

Yep. More good info from a document on treatment of road rash:

Once the wound has been thoroughly cleaned you are ready to apply a dressing. It is important not to apply a dry dressing, like dry gauze to the wound because this will dry and stick to the tissue, removing healing tissue when it is changed.

This is true, as I discovered earlier tonight, much to my acute discomfort. I'm off to saturate some gauze with antibiotic gel, then get some sleep.

Update: saturating the gauze with Neosporin did nothing to prevent it sticking to the wound. I've switched to non-stick adhesive bandages, which seem to be working a little better. (Though I'm still seeing some evidence that they're sticking to the wound.)
title: Fatigue & Gauze

intro:
I hit a wall yesterday. No energy, no reserves. Just gnawing hunger and the desire to go home and sleep. And that was after sitting on my butt all day at work.

I'm getting over being sick, recovering from last weekend's exciting bike ride, and trying to return to intense two-hour workouts 3 days a week.

So I skipped my workout, called off Lent, and had a chocolate milkshake from The Habit and went to bed early.

I've wanted to do this for a few days, but held off. I figured a stack of cookies was a pretty dumb path to health. But it's tough to argue with results. Today I'm back to my usual mix of high-protein meals and sugar bomb snacks, and I feel great. I feel more like myself than I have in weeks.

I am, however, taking this as evidence that my usual diet is utterly screwed. If cutting sweets results in that kind of strain on my body, then I need to replace them with something. I may be overeating, but not by a lot: I've put on about 4 lbs. in the last 8 weeks. That's just 250 cal. a day or so. That's one Clif bar. Cutting sweets cut a lot more than one Clif bar per day.

But one thing at a time. First, I need to eat well and get properly over this cold, then I'll fix my diet.
title: No More Lent

intro:
I was down in Hollywood last night, walking with my girl from the Pantages over to Musso & Frank Grill for dinner. Up ahead we heard some dude yelling the F-word. "FUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUCK! FUUUUUUUUCK! FUCK YOUR WORLD! FUCK YOU PEOPLE'S WORLD!"

Then I saw him coming our way down the sidewalk: young, big, shaved head, shirtless, bad tattoos across his chest. But he wasn't yelling at anyone in particular. So city S.O.P kicked in: Pretend he doesn't exist. Don't make eye contact, stay relaxed, but be aware.

Once upon a time, I would have simply prayed that he didn't come my way. Last night, I just asked for clarity, and got ready to feed the guy the biggest left hand I could. I reminded myself to go for the first groin or front kick opportunity, then run. Guys like this carry knives.

He kept yelling as we passed each other, and even took an unsteady step nearer (though he was still a good twelve feet away).

Nothing happened. But that moment when he passed out of my peripheral vision gave me quite an adrenaline kick.

I'm really, really glad that the guy didn't get near me. But I'm also really, really glad to have a few options in my toolbox for that kind of situation.
title: Big Left

body:
The difficulty level at Chesebro is dialed down quite a bit from Rocky Peak, so I can concentrate on technique and nailing every move instead of just trying to surf the rocky patches and not die. (Which is thrilling, sure, but...)

Lessons (re)learned:

  • On the technical uphills: pedal in circles, keep your weight focused through the back wheel.
  • On the rocky downhills: easy on the brakes, and stay in "attack" position on the downhills. Push forward through the bars!

I also talked a bit with a couple of guys on the Bike Patrol. Unfortunately, I forgot to get their thoughts on Bike/Horse Etiquette. Oh well.

A lot of the trail near Sulpher Springs was very muddy, and some of it was under water. This area is wet for California (there's a stream running through the canyon), but I've never seen it this green or this muddy.

And I spotted a singletrack line that runs from the Shepherd's Flat connector just above Palo Comado down to a lower spon on P.C. (Now that I've had a chance to check, I see it's marked as "Dead Cow Trail" on the map, not to be confused with the "Dead Cow Road" near China Flat.) Didn't get a chance to ride it, but can't wait to give it a go. I'm really happy to find it, since I always feel that once I finish the leg from Shepherd's Flat to P.C., the fun part's over. This'll add some more interest.

The descent along the Sheep Corral Trail and Sulpher Springs trails has my confidence healthy again, and getting out for a beaudiful dusk ride did me a world of good. Can't wait 'till next weekend, when my scars'll all be healed and my legs'll be strong again, and I can tackle something new!

And with the Wildflower Century coming up in April, it's time to get out once in a while for extended road riding. The only thing that makes road riding interesting is climbing, so I guess I'll be doing a lot of that. Time to dust off my old plans for a big ride that I wanted to do nearly a year ago. Gotta pick an early weekend morning to tackle that one. And maybe I'll rig a camera mount to my handlebars and do a video blog or something. Anything to stave off boredom...
intro:
I took a spin on Sunday through one of my favorite trails around here: Chesebro Canyon. It's a really fun mix of technical riding, smooth singletrack, and fantastic scenery that always does my soul good. After crashing last week, I rode the remainder of the Chumash Trail (it was the only way to get home, after all), but I still wanted a day of confidence-building to get my head back where it should be. Riding's no fun when you're too afraid of getting hurt to push your limits.

And after being sick over the last two weeks or so, I didn't want to do too much climbing. Break a sweat sure, but no hell climb please.

All this made Chesebro the perfect option.
title: Sanity Ride in Chesebro

intro:
Wow! New research! On muscle fatigue! I'm excited about this, as it relates directly to my recent studies.

In The New York Times:

For decades, muscle fatigue had been largely ignored or misunderstood. Leading physiology textbooks did not even try to offer a mechanism, said Dr. Andrew Marks, principal investigator of the new study. A popular theory, that muscles become tired because they release lactic acid, was discredited not long ago.

In a report published Monday in an early online edition of Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Dr. Marks says the problem is calcium flow inside muscle cells. Ordinarily, ebbs and flows of calcium in cells control muscle contractions. But when muscles grow tired, the investigators report, tiny channels in them start leaking calcium, and that weakens contractions. At the same time, the leaked calcium stimulates an enzyme that eats into muscle fibers, contributing to the muscle exhaustion.

The discovery (and the NYT article) is also receiving attention at The Science of Sport, which offers a great nutshell explanation of how calcium plays a part in muscle contraction:

In short, a nerve signal reaches the muscle and stimulates the release of calcium (Ca2+). The calcium is what is actually causing the process of muscle contraction. A special part of the muscle called the sarcoplasmic reticulum, or SR for short, releases calcium, flooding the muscle cells with it. The calcium causes muscle contraction to happen, and when we want to relax the muscle the calcium is then pumped back into the SR, thus causing relaxation of the muscle.

Very cool. I'm sure this understanding will help refine training methods, but we won't see athletes popping anti-fatigue pills; even if they passed FDA approval, they'd quickly join EPO as a banned substance.

So what's the big deal? I'm curious to see how this influences nutritional and training plans.

Runner's World has a few good parting words on the subject:

That still leaves us a proven path to faster marathons: Train long, recover appropriately, run some workouts at your goal pace. When you do this, your body naturally makes all the right biochemistry decisions and adjustments for you. It optimizes your utilization of lactic acid and calcium ions, and you can run longer and faster.

The human body is an incredible machine.
title: Lactic Acid, Calcium, and Muscle Fatigue

intro:
I'm floored by the benefits I'm getting from taking 2g per day of Omega-3 Fatty Acid tablets (fish oil). Both Tuesday and Thursday's Jiu Jitsu classes left me completely spent: I stayed conscious long enough to stretch, stuff myself with food and vitamins, and fall into bed.

And Wednesday and Friday, I've woken up feeling great. This is in stark contrast to several weeks ago where the same effort left me unable to recover in time for the next class. (And I don't think simple adaptation is responsible here: I've been sick, and not maintaining a regular workout schedule during the intervening weeks.)

The weight gain has stopped. However, I'd still like to drop about 7 lbs and return to my goal weight of 175 lbs. I've stopped eating desert in the evenings, and depending on how I feel next week, I'll start either running on my lunch hour or biking to work to burn off the extra me I've picked up.

Chocolate milk is an awesome recovery drink. My formula: 200g milk per hour of work (to a maximum of 400g), plus 10% Hershey's syrup. At 400g 1% milk + 40g chocolate syrup, that's 266 cal, 44g carbs, and 14g protein. Basically, it's a liquid Clif bar with some extra protein and way less fat.

If you're interested in more detail, VeloNews has some great advice on target nutritional values and snack options for recovery meals.

I'm keeping it simple, though. I've got a system that works for me: chocolate milk, a cool shower, a meal and (after especially hard efforts) a short nap. So you can keep your granola and pre-measured pretzel/grape mixtures. I'll have a grilled chicken sandwich with avocado on sourdough, please. Or maybe the portobello mushroom w/ spinach & goat cheese. I love California.

Looking forward to the weekend: bikes, friends, food, music, open windows, good books.
title: Nutrition = Chocolate Milk & Vitamin Pills

This is a great training ride, but I wish I knew of a more interesting aproach to China Flat from the Simi side. Alberson Fire Rd. is just a long uphill slog that I can only motivate myself to do with the promise of something new or fun at the top.

But once I did hit China Flat, the riding was great. The trails are really fun, and because of today's weather, I had them nearly to myself.

I'd set out today planning on riding to Simi Peak, but if I was feeling fresh at China Flat, I'd head down in to Agoura and do a loop around Chesebro Canyon. My legs were not fresh.

The final climb up to Simi Peak is challenging, and after climbing Alberson, my legs just didn't have the juice to keep me moving upward over the rocks. Next time for sure.

The clouds parted just long enough for me to enjoy a bit of sunshine adn a fantastic view from the top of Simi Peak. But before long I was getting cold, and it was time to head down again.

The descent from Simi Peak back to Alberson was great fun. I decided to explore a bit of singletrack I'd spotted on the way up, and it was a really fun ride, and went exactly where I wanted to go, winding up along the west end of China Flat to the connector road to Alberson.

I opted for the easy way back to Simi, and was glad I did-- I was completely gassed by the time I reached the bottom of Alberson, and got home on persistence and granny gears.

intro:
Last night I decided I wanted to see Michael Clayton, and just for grins, decided to "rent" it from iTunes. Mistake.

The iTunes app crashed not long after starting the download. I restarted it, and noticed that Michael Clayton was nowhere to be found.

I went back to the iTunes store, found Michael Clayton, and clicked "rent", thinking that iTunes would be smart enough to say, "Dude! You already rented that! We'll just check on the download status, and resume!" Nope. iTunes advised me that my credit card would be charged. I clicked "cancel".

A quick search for "resume download" in iTunes help led me to click "Store -> Check for Purchases", which caused iTunes to resume downloading Michael Clayton. (Why doesn't it do this when you start iTunes?)

I left it to finish up overnight, and returned this morning.

iTunes had crashed again sometime during the night. Meh. I started it up, clicked on "Store -> Check for Purchases", and saw that it was just a few minutes from completing. Excellent.

Ten seconds later, iTunes popped up an error message: "Some portions of this file appear to be corrupted. Select Store -> Check for Purchases to try again."

I did so. It failed again. I tried resuming the download several more times, only to have the same message pop up each time.

I'm putting Michael Clayton in my Netflix cue. We'll see which arrives first: the DVD or the download.
title: iTunes Movie Rentals

intro:
One of the best lessons I learned from my brief life as a musician: Surround yourself with all the tools you need. Great instruments, music, tuner, metronome, quiet practice space, CDs of the piece you're working on, self-recording setup, and anything else that helps.

But when the time comes to get on stage, you have to forget all of that and just play.

Fat Cyclist this morning has some great thoughts on watches and GPS units and racing, and setting goals for yourself:

"I don't even wear a watch or ride with a bike computer during races," Kenny added. "Just give it everything you've got." [...]

Bry said what I was thinking: "But what if you miss your goal time by just a couple minutes? Won't you wish you had brought a watch?"

Chucky answered with what I see as the crux of the matter: "Look, a watch will never make you race faster. It can only slow you down. If you've got a watch and see you're dropping behind your target, you accelerate for a minute and fry yourself. Then you lose more time than you would have in the first place. Just race as hard as you think you can all the time, and you'll get the best time you can get. If you think you could go faster to pick up a couple minutes at the end of a race, you should do it whether it gets you in under nine hours or not."

Yep. All the tools are for training. On race day, it's time to forget about all the numbers and just ride for all you're worth.
title: Faster

intro:
Just in case you thought that Comcast wasn't a bunch of sleezeballs, I thought I'd pass on Valleywag's report that Comcast admitted hiring people off the street to attend a hearing with the FCC this week. The ringers arrived early to crowd out legitimate attendees and cheered for Comcast. (Also covered at Boing Boing.)

The hearing was on Network Neutrality, and was called in response to Comcast trying to block customers' usage of P2P software in violation of Network Neutrality principles. The basic idea of "Network Neutrality" is that your ISP shouldn't get to tell you what you can do with your internet connection, or give preferential treatment to certain web sites or services. Your phone company can't tell you who you're allowed to talk to, or what about. Why should your internet connection be any different?

Now, as Valleywag notes, Comcast's actions in packing the house with friendly faces wasn't illegal. But employing this kind of deception in a policy debate with a government regulatory body certainly undercuts Comcast's credibility.
title: Comcast Hires Ringers for FCC Hearing

So I headed up into the hills and ran the Sage Ranch Loop Trail, which now that I check the guidebook is more like 2.6 miles. It took all the energy I had, but was definitely good for the soul, and really helped clear my head.

So, when I got home, I decided to get to the bottom of some mysterious OutOfMemoryErrors that have been popping up here on DMG. I put in some extra-strength error handling, and all is well.

I also added a feature that's really should have been included with my overhaul of the GPX mapping code: total time for the ride/run/whatever now appears as part of the route info. (I'll put in total distance another night.)

[Update: There's a obvious bug in the time calculation code. It's so obvious, in fact, that I didn't even have to see it in action to know it was there. I just thought, "Wait, did I really write code that brain damaged?" Yes, yes I did. I plead the NyQuil defense. As a friend once said: "All bugs exist because the programmer is a freakin' moron."]

And I had a dream last night that I had blond surfer hair that went down to just about my jawline. I hated it and cut it off, and it turned red again.

intro:
I'm a big believer in weight training. It is the single best way to build raw strength & power and prevent injury. Your routine can be customized for your needs, from pure strength to power to endurance to cardio training. Knowing what you're doing in the gym is the difference between spending 4½ hours each week for nothing, and getting all you need in two thirty-minute sessions.

The New York Times posted an article titled Does Weight Lifting Make a Better Athlete?

Hell yes it does.

The article implies that there's a lot of debate about whether weight training helps athletes, which is a little misleading. Part of the reason for the "debate" is that different coaches coach different sports, and even if they all agreed that weight training did help their athletes, they'd all have different weight routines to suit the needs of their particular athletes and sports. Another reason that coaches sometimes disagree on matters of weight training is because they're dealing with trained athletes that are already extremely well-suited to their respective sports.

Even if athletes already performing near their genetic potential do receive only limited benefit from weight training, you and I are weak and slow and need all the help we can get. For us, there's really no credible argument against hitting the weights.

Since I started doing my semi-weekly Rocky Peak mountain bike ride, I've taken 20 minutes off the time it takes me to get to the top. That's partly from riding more often, but I saw the biggest performance gains the week I skipped Krav and BJJ and did full-body weight workouts instead.

If you're interested in learning how to get more out of your weight training, I highly recommend Practical Programming for Strength Training. It's a first-rate primer on weight training with applications for everyone.
title: Weight Training
viaTitle: Does Weight Lifting Make a Better Athlete?

body:
I ended up heading up Alberson to China Flat, and playing there a little bit before heading down Palo Comado to Chesebro Canyon. Almost as soon as I hit Chesebro park, I split from the fire road to check out the Dead Cow Trail.

Dead Cow caught my interest the last time I was in Chesebro, I wanted to head out that way and sample a singletrack alternative to the Palo Comado Rd. The guys on the Bike Patrol said it had "a couple of tricky parts", and a website I saw said that it had some drop-offs that could be intimidating. Rubbish. Maybe riding Chumash has gotten me really used to mean drop-offs and technical riding, but I was never worried about getting hurt on Dead Cow. Just good clean fun.

I also got to play a little on China Flat itself, so I took the long way through both heading into Chesebro and on my way back. There's some great singletrack up there, and while the price of entry is high (either a climb up Alberson from Simi, Palo Comado from Chesebro, or the hell climb from King James Court in Westlake), it's worth the trip.

So I spent nearly four hours on my bike this afternoon, and I'm one tired dude. But I can see my bik on the porch, and I can't help thinking it looks like a muddy, happy dog.

Time to go clean my bike and make plans for tonight.

Glassy Eyes, a blog dedicated to all things eyeglass-related (or something) just posted a cool write-up of 39 Dollar Glasses, a mail-order service that can make new lenses for your old frames. Any old frame. For $39.

So yes, my friends, this blog post is here just so I can find 39 Dollar Glasses again.

intro:
I've been watching with interest as CrossFit takes the nation by storm, introducing the masses to the benefits of training like a soldier. I think the foundations are sound: if you want the fitness level of a Marine, you must train like a Marine.

There's an excellent essay at Performance Menu called CrossFit Criteria, talking about the trade-offs in measuring the fitness level of athletes. It's very much a CrossFit specific discussion, but also cuts to the heart of why so many people don't get what they want out of a fitness program. Specifically: what are your goals? How will you measure progress toward them?

That question has a really interesting answer for the "Dirt Diva":

I am planning to come back in a month and have Brian MacKenzie train me for two weeks. He wants to see me cut my running in half and focus on proper running and my crossfit WODS.

Yep: her goal is to train far less than she does, without sacrificing athletic performance.

Elsewhere, the Fat Cyclist discusses how a wrist injury might just make him a happier guy:

[K]nowing that my wrist is messed up ... has made me think about this season. I expect I?m going to have to have surgery and some healing time before I can ride mountain bikes again.

I have to accept the likelihood that I won?t be able to get into great shape by Leadville.

Strangely, I feel very happy about that possibility, because it allows a whole new slew of possibilities.

It's easy to get caught up in fitness goals. "Fatty" was trying for a sub-nine-hour finish at Leadville, a 100-mile mountain bike race. Letting go of that means he's free to measure "success" by other means.

Me, I'm planning on a short workout this weekend (a short fun bike ride just for fun, and a 40-minute weight workout to help my body recover), to give my body time to recover from a tough week of training. My goal is simple: have fun.
title: That Which Gets Measured...

intro:
Food for thought from Seth Godin:

I drove past a hobby shop yesterday. It's hard to make out the awning, but it says, "Hobbies, Trains, R/C Models, Coffee, Lottery."

Bit by bit, on each declining day, it became easier to become more average, to add one more item, to sell a few more lottery tickets or another cup of coffee.

And then, the next thing you know, there's some dusty trains in the back and you're running a convenience store.
title: Getting Lost Along the Way

body:
So I head past the Flat and along the short trail, and up an Edison road I'd never explored before. I know it heads up across a couple of ridgelines to the Alberson Fire Rd, which I certainly know my way around. I thought the full loop around to China Flat (and then back down through Cheesebro) might include more climbing than I wanted to commit to, but a quick climb to the top sounded like fun.

(Yes, I'm a freak. I like riding my bike uphill.)

The road was in good shape, aside from scattered rock fall, and the climbing felt great. So great, that when I hit the top, I just kept going, and decided that I wanted to do the whole loop around to China Flat after all. Unfortunately, I found myself five minutes later at the bottom of the valley with at least one major climb ahead, the sun sinking fast, no food in my pack and no real clear idea of how long it would take to get back into familiar territory. So, reluctantly, I took a picture of "the road not taken", and turned around.

My legs felt super-strong all the way back up to the ridge, and the trail was all downhill from there back to the trailhead.

I'm really happy with how my legs have responded to last week's long ride. My Christmas Eve ride left me averse to big rides for a couple of weeks, but once I was warmed up this afternoon, I felt like I could have gone all day. I did 2½ hours, and felt like I could have done 2½ more if the sun and my growling stomach hadn't called me home.

My work schedule will be a little interesting this week, but I'll have Wednesday afternoon all to myself, and I'm planning to come back this way and do the loop.
intro: I planned on a shortish ride, no more than 90 minutes or so. I headed out to Shepherd's Flat, then out the Sheep Corral trail and down the Dead Cow Trail, and then back up Palo Comado and back to shepherd's Flat. But by then I was warmed up, and I just didn't want to quit.

intro:
I'm trying to make plans to head down to the Staples Center on Friday afternoon to catch the NCAA basketball semis. My girlfriend and I want to head down from Simi at around noon on Friday, and return after the last game, which should be over around 9 or so.

So I headed over to Metrolink's website, and clicked on stations and maps from the top nav menu, and I get... an alphabetical list of stations. I'm not sure which lines I should be taking, so alphabetical doesn't help me. I can find simi just fine, but there's no "Staples Center" stop listed here. I need a map.

So I click on the "Interactive Map." Nearly useless. Where's the Staples Center? No matter. I can zoom in, get an idea where everything is, and... no I can't. There aren't any streets marked on this map. (And nevermind that you can only zoom in on the center of the map. Try it. Try getting a closer look at the Riverside area.)

And the printable map is no better. Major stations only, no streets, no links to schedules. Meh.

This is such a simple question: "Where do I get off within walking distance of the Staples Center?" Yet I've been to two maps and a list of stations, and I can't find the answer.

But, soldiering on, I check the Station Locator. I see a Google map! I see little red point markers! Hoorah!

Oh goddammit. Clicking on the markers gets you the street address of the station. No link to the schedule for that line, or even an indication of which Metrolink line the station serves.

I completely bail on Metrolink, and head for Google Maps. From the map of the world, I type "Staples Center", and hit "Search Maps." It finds the Staples Center first try. Right there where the 10 and 110 intersect. And right there as part of the search results is the Convention Center/Staples Center Metrolink stop, marked on the map right there at Pico and Flower. I click on the icon, and the pop-up dialog says it serves the blue line.

Ah! And there's the 7th Street Metro Center at 7th and Flower, serving the red line. And... looking back at the printable map from Metrolink, I see that the red, blue, and yellow lines (I need the yellow to get back to Simi) all meet at Union Station.

Okay, so now I'm in business. I just need schedules for the red, blue and yellow lines for this friday.

So, back to Metrolink I go. I click on Schedules, and get... a listing of schedules by line. Except, they're not using "red", "yellow", or "blue", it's "91 Line", "Antelope Valley Line", etc. No colors.

Back to the printable map, which provides a key. Ah!

  • RED: San Bernardino Line
  • BLUE: Riverside Line
  • YELLOW: Ventura County Line

Now that I know that, I can get what I need.

Let's check that I can get from Simi to Staples starting at noon on Friday.

Wow. The Riverside Line is useless. It heads south from Union Station at 12:45pm, 1:15pm and then there's nothing until 4:15pm. If the yellow line gets me there by 12:45, I'm cool. Otherwise, the red line had better have something.

As it turns out, the yellow line doesn't even leave Simi until 2:42pm, and takes an hour to get to Union station, whereupon I'd have to wait half an hour to catch the blue line. It's quicker to walk the seven blocks from Union to the Staples Center.

But I'm certainly not waiting until 2:42pm to head out from Simi.

Whups. Just realized: the Riverside line isn't blue, it's purple. Blue is the 91 line. Lemme check the 91 line schedule...

(Now, let's be clear: yes, I was confused because the Google map I looked at used a different shade of blue than the Metrolink site. On the map, there is clearly a difference between the "blue" and "purple" colors. But, the Metrolink site never actually names the colors. So if I tell a friend (or a tourist) "Take the blue line," they may very well match "blue" to the purple on the Metrolink maps. Not good. This is really dumb: don't have blue and purple on the same map.)

Anyway, the schedule for the blue line (AKA: 91 Line) is pretty horrible too: nothing heading south from Union Station until 3:20pm.

So, basically, we're driving. There's a Metrolink station a five-minute walk from my apartment in Simi, and another across the street from the Staples center, and we're heading through the nastiest traffic snarl in the world, and the Los Angeles rail system is still worse than driving. (And yes, I also checked the Rail 2 Rail options.)

I weep for my city. In London, or New York, this would be as simple as "Everything runs every ten minutes, so I just take the yellow line to the blue line, and we're there."
title: Metrolink Still Pretty Much Useless

intro:
Okay, here's the deal. Don't confuse Metro with Metrolink. They both have "red lines", and "yellow lines" and "blue lines", but they're run by different people, evidently, and though their rail systems connect, their web sites do not. Metrolink is something to do with Amtrak filling in as part of L.A.'s extended rail network or something, so their schedule is pretty horrible.

But the Metro system is a genuine subway system, and runs on typical subway schedules such as "every ten minutes" or "every fifteen minutes". We're not down to 2-3 minutes like NYC, but it's pretty good. It's not terribly extensive, but so be it. Here's the map.

So, the upshot of this is that the Metro Red Line goes where I need to go, on a reasonable schedule, but I just have to drive from Simi to North Hollywood to catch the north end of the Red Line. That still skips the worst of the traffic, so I'm happy. And the blue line's Pico stop is the Staples Center stop, which'll save a few minutes of walking.

So, it's off to the basketball games via Metro on Friday!
title: More on the Metro: L.A.'s Rail System

intro:
After a few weeks of weighing options, I'm going to spend my REI divident on new brakes for my mountain bike. Right now it sports Avid SD-3 v-brakes, which are... unsatisfactory. The more I ride, the faster I get, and the less I feel like I'm totally in control on the downhills.

So: discs. This has the advantage of greater stopping power, and opens up the possibility of moving to a full-suspension frame in the future. But it also means new hubs, which means rebuilding the wheels and re-running the cables. Here's the shopping list:

  • Brakes: Avid BB7 disc brakes. (Top-o-th'-line cable disc brakes.)
  • Front Hub: Shimano Deore HB-M525
  • Rear Hub: Shimano Deore FH-M525
  • Spokes: ???
  • Rotors: ???

I'm open to suggestion on the hubs; seems like a shame to spend money just to stay at the same quality level. Then again, my Deore hubs (M510) have been great so far, and show no signs of wear. I'll talk to the tech and see what he says. Ditto for the spokes and rotors.

And I'm hoping to have enough cash left over to switch out my Time ATAC Alium (415g) pedals for egg beaters (Steel @ 266g or Titanium @ 230g).

The steel egg beaters are $109, and the titanium are $199. Spending $90 to shave 36g... bothers me. Way cheaper just to buy a new, lighter CamelBak. But once I apply my 20% coupon, it's only another $72, and I already have two excellent hydration packs, so... who knows. Either way I lose ~150g and gain pedals that are easier to clip in to, which is a good thing.

Update: I visited REI's bike shop yesterday (Tuesday) after work, and they said that I should come back and talk to their head bike tech on Friday.

intro:
There's an astonishingly good piece by Rebecca Solnit which I recommend you read. It's called One Nation Under Elvis. Don't be put off by the title. It's not about The King. Not directly, anyway.

The Sierra Club, which Muir cofounded with a group of University of California professors in 1892, saw nature as not where one lived or worked but where one vacationed. And traditional American environmentalism still largely imagines nature as vacationland and as wilderness, ignoring the working landscapes and agricultural lands, whose beauties and meanings are widely celebrated in European art.

Awesome, awesome stuff. I'd love to meditate on this a while, but I think I'd just get in the way of what Solnit has already said so well.

But, if you're interested in some follow-on thinking, you could do worse than Megan's post at From the Archives.
title: The Things that Divide Us

Since it's short, here's the whole story, from CNN:

NEW HAVEN, Connecticut (AP) -- Contraband candy has led to big trouble for an eighth-grade honors student in Connecticut.

Michael Sheridan was stripped of his title as class vice president, barred from attending an honors student dinner and suspended for a day after buying a bag of Skittles from a classmate.

School spokeswoman Catherine Sullivan-DeCarlo says the New Haven school system banned candy sales in 2003 as part of a districtwide school wellness policy.

Michael's suspension has been reduced from three days to one, but he has not been reinstated as class vice president.

He says he didn't realize his candy purchase was against the rules -- although he did notice the student selling the Skittles on February 26 was being secretive.

Fascists. Did they think that just taking the candy away would send the wrong message?

And schools wonder why students don't take teachers seriously. When teachers behave like this, it's pretty hard for anyone to take them seriously.
title: Student Suspended, Stripped of Honors... over Skittles

The teacher is great, but the Tuesday-Thursday schedule doesn't work for me: those are Krav/BJJ nights.

I'm impressed enough with the benefits that I want to make Yoga a consistent part of my weekly routine, but finding the time will be a challenge. What I need is an early morning (7am) class I can do before work.

There is what looks like a great Yoga studio about a block from my apartment, but the schedule seems tailored for those without day jobs. For reasons beyond comprehension, this seems to be the norm in Simi Valley.

So I just ordered a DVD. It's with Rodney Yee, whom I've seen before, and know is awesome. We'll see if I actually get my ass out of bed and do this. My bet is "no" but so be it. It's $10, so if I don't use it regularly, no biggie.

I just wish there was a real class that fit my schedule. Now that I'm used to getting up early, I'd really like to stick with it through the summer.

intro:
I talked with the head bicycle tech at REI, and found that he really knew his stuff. No disappointment there. But I'm kind of rethinking upgrading from v-brakes to discs. Basically, it's turning out to be a lot more expensive than I thought.

My nieve plan involved swapping out my current hubs for new, disc-compatible hubs. But after talking to the tech, it appears that switching just the hubs (which will require wheel builds) will be nearly as expensive as just buying whole new wheels. He suggested a set of WTB wheels that are about equivalent to what I have, and will run about $250 for the pair. Not a bad plan.

But part of my motivation for switching to disc brakes was to spread out the cost of upgrades (and use my REI dividend to subsidize them!). So if I'm going to get a whole new wheelset, I might as well get something nicer, like the Mavic Crosstrail wheelset. (They usually go for about $475, but I can use my 20% discount to pick up for about $380.)

That'll leave about $85 left in my dividend, which ought to cover most of the expense of the brakes themselves, which run about $120 for both wheels. So the next question is: how much will the installation itself cost?

Of course, the alternative is always to simply stick with what I have, use my dividend to fund the various goodies I'll need for the next year, and pay for a whole new bike when the time comes. But that has the dual drawbacks of spending my own money instead of "free" cash from my REI dividend, and spending a lot all at once, instead of just getting a new frame.

So the Crosstrails seem to be the way to go. But I'll sleep on it before making a real decision.
title: Rethinking

intro:
For some reason, I was thinking about flat tires, and CO2 cartridges vs. pumps. The general wisdom seems to be that CO2 cartridges have the advantage of being smaller, lighter, and more convenient (they inflate the tire in just a few seconds).

I typically carry three cartridges on mountain bike rides, enough to inflate just two tires. Each full cartridge weighs 62g, plus my little Microflate nozzle, which I'm going to guess weighs 15g. That's 201g.

I just put my hand pump on the scale: 125g. So the pump is actually 76g lighter, never runs out of air. Which means it removes any reason not to help a stranded rider. And since we're talking about mountain biking, I'm already carrying a pack with spare tube, snacks, water, etc.

I'll still use the cartridges for road rides. I usually carry just two cartridges on the road, so there's no real weight savings, and a limitless source of air isn't nearly as important when you can just pull into a gas station.
title: CO2 Cartridges vs. Hand Pump

intro:
The instructor at Krav last night tried something new: contact. In the last couple of years, we've done a lot of drills involving pads or focus mitts, but never any sparring. That changed last night.

We introduced some light contact into the night's drills, and wrapped up with "the bull ring". The whole class got in a circle, and one guy got in the middle. For the next two minutes he'd spar with each person for ten seconds. Full contact, body shots only.

It really made me realize that I need to spar regularly if I'm going to move forward. Time to get out of my comfort zone again, and time to start moving toward testing for my orange belt.

Just the opposite is true in Jiu Jitsu. I got pummeled. Hard. Again. I know it's part of learning, but going home every Tuesday and Thursday with bruises and a headache after being a tackling dummy for an hour is sapping my motivation. The nights when things "click" are too few and far between.

I really feel like being in a class with just a few guys, all of whom are much better than me, is making it harder to learn, not easier.

My buck and roll is weak. My sweeps and takedowns are ineffective, and my takedown defenses are non-existant. I'm having some success building offense from the guard, but I'm still weak passing guard. And I've been working on this stuff for seven months.

There's a Wednesday-night BJJ class for beginners in Simi, so I'll try that next week. (I have other plans tonight.) Between moving forward with Krav and BJJ, and trying to drive less, it may be time to really rethink my training schedule.
title: Contact, Progress

intro:
I'm asking a lot of my body these days. I'm doing some kind of workout nearly every day. I'm having fun, but I've got to make sure I'm doing everything I can to help my body recover, or I'll end up just grinding myself into burned-out pulp.

So I've got a new post-workout routine: 440g of chocolate milk, 10-15 minutes of Yoga, and a 2g helping of Omega-3 fatty acids every night.

The net result is that don't get a post-workout crash, I stay limber, and I recover much, much faster and more completely between workouts. Hoo-rah!

The Yoga in particular is good stuff. I've been doing the last 10 minutes of the DVD that I got on Krav/BJJ nights when I get home. Brazilian Jiu Jitsu is especially mentally and physically intense, and Yoga's combination of cool-down, stretching, breathing, and calm concentration really helps bring me back to earth. Net result: I get about another 90 minutes of sleep on Tuesday and Thursday nights. That's what I call a good time investment.
title: Focus on Recovery
