intro:
I finished my last day at my old job on Friday. And tomorrow I start at my new job. I'm really excited, and can't wait to jump in. But I'm smart enough to know by now that truly free weekends are a rare thing, and I wanted to take advantage of being in "limbo:" no leftover work stress from my old job, no new stress from the new job.

Friday was my dad's birthday, so my girlfriend and I joined my parents for dinner. It's great having my girl along; she brings out all new stories in my parents, and vice versa. Everyone had a great time, and I got to know both my parents and my girl even better. Fantastic.

Saturday afternoon my girlfriend went with me apartment hunting. The new gig is 50 miles from my current apartment, and with gas set to march straight past $5/gal, that distance will soon be simply untennable. So I'm going to have to find a new place. I was surprised to discover that the Archstone properties in the area were really unappealing. Poor layouts, odd use of space, and a focus on fixtures rather than features. I found what looks like a fantastic townhouse in Thousand Oaks, but it's in an older, slightly run-down complex, and I'd be worried about noise. So, I'll keep looking.

Saturday night my girl and I caught The Happening at the Arclight in Sherman Oaks. It was so horrible that we immediately went home and watched The Spiderwick Chronicles so that we could just forget about The Happening entirely. (Nutshell review: Spiderwick really moves the plot along, but it's a really fun ride!)

And today we headed up to Ventura for a wonderful afternoon. Good BBQ, used books, great coffee and truffles, and a late-afternoon walk on the beach rounded out a really fantastic weekend.

And now I'm home doing some quick laundry. Tomorrow I start a new job and hit the climbing gym, and Thursday I head out on vacation for ten days. No rest for the weary!
title: Weekend Wrap-up

intro:
I just want to publicly thank all my friends, and especially my girlfriend, for helping me through the last couple of days. I have receded from full-scale freakout.

My God, transitions are hard.

I'm tired. I'm going to get a good night's sleep. Then I'm going to hustle through work tomorrow, and then I'm going to go on vacation for ten days.

And when I get back, I'm going to become a one man army from 7am to 6pm, Monday through Friday.
title: This Has Been a Test...

intro: Well, now I'm stoked. Gracie Jiu Jitsu, three blocks from my new job.
title: Dude, Sweet!

intro: Just got home, and I'm getting settled in. Going to enjoy an easy day, and get set to get back to work tomorrow at my new job. I'll have a write-up and more pictures at some point, but there's lots to do before I'll have time for that.
title: Been Travelin'

intro:
Wow. Lots of email waiting on my return, and I think I blacked out when I saw the accumulation in my RSS reader. Throw in getting settled into a new job and unpacking and catching up on errands and housework, and I'm swamped. (And my girlfriend's birthday is tomorrow.)

I'm declaring a qualified email bankruptcy. I've responded to all the official stuff: Evite invitations, requests for info, etc. I think I've handled everything that has been waiting for my return. But if I missed you, please, please pester me.
title: Catching Up

intro:
Took tonight for myself and got out on my bike for the first time in ages. Wow, did I feel rusty. But I got up and over Rocky Peak and down Chumash and lived to tell the tale, so I guess I'm not too far gone.

Back when I did my little dance over the rock garden, I dropped a tire lever somewhere just off the trail near where I pulled off to fix my flat. Today I finally remembered to look for it again. Lo and behold, it was sitting right where it's been for the last six months, right where I dropped it.

Anyway, great ride, and now I'm going to have a little coffee (decaf) and cookies (finishing off a batch I put in the freezer before leaving town), and go to bed. G'night all!
title: Sunset Ride on Rocky Peak

attachments.title: My Tire Lever!
attachments.description: That thing has been out there for six months, sitting right where I dropped it.  It's now back in my toolkit.

intro:
The vast majority of this trip went really well. I packed very light: just one medium-sized duffel. But there were a few things I'd really like to do better next time.

First, I tried to take a shortcut with chargers for my gadgets, and got burned hard: I couldn't charge anything. My iPod died at the airport, and I ended up paying $20 for a car charger for my phone that I used just once. Ouch. In the future, no more shortcuts. Official chargers for everything.

Second, I want paper copies of all reservations, flight confirmations, etc. Nothing went wrong, but I can't help feeling like I got lucky.

And lastly, I spent the 4th of July shivvering because I didn't bring anything genuinely warm to wear. I had a capilene 3 pullover and a rain shell, but no fleece, and so I froze. Next time, I'll take a fleece and a beanie, so that I have the full range of layering options.
title: Travelling: Lessons Learned

intro:
Remembered my bike & gear, forgot my day planner. Here's tonight's list:

  • laundry
  • pack for Krav/BJJ tomorrow
  • quick bike cleaning (dust & lube)
  • put papers in boxes, start shredding
  • bed by 10pm (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
title: Tonight's To-Do

intro:
Packed my stuff this morning, and took a ride in Wildwood Park this evening on the way home from work. I cleaned a couple of technical sections that I couldn't before, and had a great time riding over the Stagecoach Bluff trail twice: first toward Lizard Rock, then back toward the parking lot.

No pics. I was too busy having fun. (Not that I didn't stop to enjoy the view now and then...)

And I had Bob Dylan's Things have Changed running through my head for most of the ride...

People are crazy and times are strange
I'm locked in tight, I'm out of range
I used to care, but things have changed
title: Quick Wildwood Ride

intro:
I've been juggling a lot of stuff lately. Time management is key.

Staying sane has involved a lot of agressive prioritization. The only way I was going to get to spend time with my girlfriend on her birthday and get a few good workouts this week was to jettison Krav & BJJ. I'm headed back tomorrow night. Can't wait.

I bought a Moleskine daily diary, and keep daily to-do lists. It is awesome. I'm also planning on picking up an iPhone, and we'll see what wins: paper or plastic.

And I've combined Randy Pausch's advice with a couple of techniques from Getting Things Done, and everything's visible and up-to-date, and all my inboxes are empty.

Plenty of fun stuff going on. Movies seen, trips planned, birthdays celebrated. More on that when/if I have time.
title: Quick Update

intro:
I took a ride in Wildwood on Saturday, but have no route data: my GPS kept turning itself off whenever it got jarred. I cracked the case on Sunday morning (the warranty was long dead anyway), and confirmed a loose battery connection. My neighbor Gus soldered it, and I'm back in business. Thanks, Gus!

I flaked on climbing plans with Timbo to get a night to myself. Needed to catch up on some grocery shopping, yoga, call a few friends, fix some NetBeans/CVS issues, and get to sleep early.

Some friends have asked how I'm settling into the new job. Things are great, but the ripples are still bouncing around. I've always been a creature of habit, so I'll only really be comfortable again once things settle into a regular weekly routine.

Tonight I head back to Krav & BJJ classes, and I can't wait. It'll be great to get back in the groove.
title: Housekeeping

intro:
I came back from vacation weighing 188 lbs., which is too much. I'm creeping ever-so-slowly upward again. Most of that's muscle, but the post-vacation pudge is definitely not. So I'm aiming to drop 3-5 lbs in the next month or so. I'll be happy when I'm weighing in consistently south of 185. (Well, I'll be satisfied. I'll be happy when I get back down to 175.)

So, I'm doing the usual: no sweets except on weekends or special events, etc. I've purged the house of any deserts or sugary snacks, and I'm taking my coffee black.

As always, this is driving home the sheer volume of calories I suck down in sugar. I'm hungry every morning when I wake up. My regular breakfast carries me from 7am until about 10am, and then it's a long wait for lunchtime. Same thing after lunch. My stomach starts growling around 3pm, and my regular Clif bar only holds me until 5 or so. Which is a problem, since I typically don't eat dinner on weeknights until 9:30pm or later.

So, time to stock my desk with healthy snacks. Gotta do something about this feeling of always running on empty.
title: Running on Empty

intro:
A friend emailed this morning to let me know that Prof. Randy Pausch, author of The Last Lecture, has died.

Rest in peace, Professor.
title: Prof. Randy Pausch Dies

intro:
Hello,world! I'm typing this on my new iPhone, and a few things are Immediately clear. I typically hand-code the HTML for my blog posts, aside from a few bits that are handled by my software. Hand coding HTML is not happening on the iPhone. Hell, simple punctuation is a problem. And the autocorrect feature keeps "helpfully" munging my slang.

So I'm going to have to implement some support for plain text entry. No two ways about that. But I'm also forced to acknowledge that a tiny keyboard in my palm may not be optimal for blogging. Meh.

So I'll be adding visibility here for my Twitter feed, for which the iPhone is a far more suitable input device. That should be complete shortly.
title: iPhone!

intro:
Just spotted this tweet from Xeni Jardin:

Fell asleep on rock at beach; tide swept in & ate my iphone.

Ouch.

First, I keep thinking about how our notions of the future got everything backwards. We dreamed about flying cars, not realizing that more and more people would work from home in stead of commuting.

And we pictured going into the office and having holographic projectors place you "virtually" at the beach, making your work day more pleasant. Again, backwards: carrying a phone and a laptop can put you really at the beach, and virtually at the office. Moreover, it seems that cellphones and laptops should have been easier to see coming than holographic projectors.

So, really, I'm thinking about blind spots. We were so convinced that we'd all still go to the office that we never considered the office coming to us. What else are we not questioning about work?

Listening to Prof. Pausch's book on my iPod. Time to hit the road and see X-Files.
title: Quick Thoughts

intro: Huge hugs and hearty congratulations to my friends Chris and Meagan, who welcomed their son Sam into the world on Sunday night.
title: Congratulations!

intro:
I got a Black, 8GB iPhone 3G on Saturday. It's still little more than a cool toy, but it is a very, very cool toy. I'm looking at productivity apps that support things like reminders, to-do lists, etc. For now, I'm sticking with my Moleskine day planner for to-do lists and reminders.

My hope is that I'll be able to keep more in touch with friends and relatives now that I have real email and a web browser in my pocket. We shall see. I'm probably going to end up using the iPhone for my personal organization (which is relatively lightweight), and leaving the paper notebook at work, where there's lots more to keep track of, and where losing data would be catastrophic.

Does anyone know of a way to auto-update my blog with what tunes my iPhone is playing? That would be pretty slick.

The downer is that getting the iPhone and getting it set up ate most of my Saturday. I spent two hours at the store, plus another hour at home. I really didn't want to leave the house for the day with two half-functional phones, so I ended up completely blowing plans to climb on Saturday. Meh.

I saw The X-Files: I Want to Believe on Sunday afternoon, and while I enjoyed it, I really can't recommend it. Might be a good rental. But the series clearly ended in a very different place than where it started, and the movie just didn't feel very distincly like The X-Files. The basis was good, but it was stretched out way too far, the creepy/sci-fi aspects got lost, and it turned into just another serial killer flick.

I did get to climb on Monday night, which was great. I'm waltzing overhung 5.9s again, and 10a is very doable, if sometimes challenging. I don't have the endurance I once did, but that's fine. It'll come with time, and I'm certainly leaving climbing in the "just for fun" category; so if I improve, great, but if not, I'm fine with that too. There's lots of great moderates out there.
title: Weekend Notes

intro: We just had a minor earthquake, and the first thing that happened is everyone walked out side (per the company evacuation plan), and pulled out their iPhones, Blackberries, etc. and started looking for the "where and how big?" info. Seems like this is an iPhone app waiting to happen. Could somebody please get on that?
title: Did You Feel That?

intro:
I just saw a very cool presentation by Great Plains Restoration Council founder Jarid Manos. The GPRC is bringing together urban youth, kids growing up on Native American Reservations, and environmental work into a synergistic program aimed at healing plains, kids, and communities. Extremely cool stuff.

From their website:

Out here on the Great Plains, our ecological devastation mirrors our social devastation. By committing to hard work and service now, people can have vital, deep, rich lives again.

See more at GPRC.org
title: Great Plains Restoration Council

intro:
I spotted this graphic in Joel Spolsky's column for Inc., How Hard Could It Be?, and thought it was funny.

I dig Starbucks, and drink their coffee drinks regularly, and the Starbucks I used to frequent was staffed by enthusiastic and friendly people who knew me by name, and knew not just what I like, but what my girlfriend likes.

No corporate policy can do that. Knowing your customers and making them feel welcome happens at the human, face-to-face level.
title: Starbucks

intro:
Well, it should be pretty obvious by now that I haven't been keeping up my training log. The last entry was for an (awesome) bike ride back in early May, just before I moved the site to a new server.

The server switch triggered some odd database connectivity issues that (for reasons I have not investigated) only affected the training log. And it's been so long since I worked on the Training Log code that just getting my IDE to build a new version so I can debug the problem was a time-consuming proposition.

Leave all that to simmer, and add:

  • I already post all my GPS info and ride reports here
  • I can't just upload info directly from my GPS/heart rate monitor, and instead must enter all the data manually
  • I'm not doing anything with my training data; my workouts are driven by a desire to have fun, rather than improve general fitness
  • There are lots of great training log web sites that are free, and far more full-featured than anything I could put together in my spare time.

All together, there just isn't much reason for me to spend the time to get my training log working again. It's just a bad time investment. And lately, my time is scarcer than ever.
title: The Training Log is Dead

intro:
DMG went down sometime early Friday morning, and is now finally back up. I was going to rant and rave here, but in keeping with Chris's Law:

Things are as management has decided they should be.

And given that I'm the management, I have to accept responsibility. When you pay $7 per month for hosting, you get what you pay for. Most of the time, everything's fine. But when it goes bad... watch out.
title: Downtime

intro:
Evidently, whatever my hosting service did also fixed my training log's database issues. Since time to fix this problem was the last straw in deciding to just let it die, maybe I should reconsider.

So, maybe I'll keep posting there.

intro:
A quick update of what happened while I was offline:

Rode my bike up the Chumash trail. In 85° heat. It sucked, and I rested often, but it gave me a feeling of accomplishment. And my GPS, which I thought was fixed, is officially dead. I guess there's more busted up in there than just the battery connection. So I'll be replacing that this weekend.

I also caught The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor, which was great fun. Lots of people think these movies suck. I love 'em.

I had a fantastic birthday weekend with my girlfriend and my parents. We went to Dakota's steakhouse in Westlake Village, and everyone had a fantastic meal. Plus, they server Fat Tire Ale. Nice.

I'm really, really digging Jiu Jitsu. Finally got the footwork for the far arm bar from side control, and now it's pretty smooth. But still kind of useless until I can pass guard effectively.

Tonight I'm headed for a ride in Wildwood, and hope to get home in time to change and head for Jiu Jitsu. Projects for tonight: buck and roll, posture, pass guard.
title: Update

intro:
I abandoned plans for a bike ride last night, and I'm glad I did. Instead, I went to my Krav Maga and Brazilian Jiu Jitsu classes. I figure that if I want to test for my orange belt in Krav soon, I'd probably better show up for class.

And BJJ was fantastic. We worked on passing guard (which is a serious weakness of mine), and there were a few new faces. Free grappling went very well. I just concentrated on fundamentals: posture, buck & roll, and passing guard. Everything's improving, but the biggest is posture: arch my back, keep my head up, sit back. Made all the difference in the world.

And Master Cox also announced an intro-level fight class starting next Monday. No details yet, but that's exactly what I've been looking for to step up my Krav training. Really exciting.

I left all my stuff packed from last night, and I'm headed out for a quick (1-hour) recovery ride tonight.
title: Fundamentals

intro:
The scoring controversy is, to me, maybe the least interesting thing going on here. Look how tense and agressive the top man, Manuel is, while the guy on the bottom, Musah is active and quick, but extremely relaxed.

Manuel also keeps his posture beautifully. On his feet, his stance is wide and Musah's hips are under control. On his knees, even when he's forward, his belly button never gets forward of his knees, so his center of gravity is always under his own control. Pretty amazing. So when Manuel goes for the sweep, it's ineffective.

But mostly, I see that both fighters stick with what's working for them in the short term, and refuse to change strategies. They're both content to stop the other guy from winning, and so that's what happens: the match ends with no score, and goes to a judges' decision. Kind of sad, really.

Anyway, buck & roll and passing guard are my new projects.
title: BJJ: Musah v. Manuel

title: Training Pays, Kids

intro:
I'm recovering from last night's Krav and BJJ classes. I took a beating in Krav (we did some controlled sparring), and had to pace myself through BJJ. Today I really feel the workout, so I'm heading home early to do some stretching and maybe a short run, and I'm looking forward to grilling up some steaks and watching the Olympics with my girlfriend.

Next week starts a four-week stint of Monday-night fight classes. There's a regular Monday night "fight club" at the Krav school, but it's packed with seasoned fighters. Newcomers tend to get their bell rung, and don't return. So Master Cox has arranged an intro-level fight class in Moorpark on Monday nights for the next month.

It's long past time for me to graduate to more contact. And I have to admit that I've been thinking about leaving Krav for a while, and jumping into Brazilian Jiu Jitsu full time. With Krav, I'm really feeling like it's time to get good or get out. So I'm really excited to find a clear path forward.
title: Rough Night

intro:
Wow, jam packed weekend. I spent Friday night with my girlfriend grilling on the porch and watching some of the Olympic opening ceremonies, and 21, the movie about the MIT Blackjack Team. I read the article in Wired a while back, and honestly, the article was more exciting. This movie had all the tired conventions: the ruthless pit boss, the untrustworthy team member, getting in for all the right reasons, then staying in too long, "getting emotional", the love interest, the inevitable caper at the end to put everything right. Bah. In the end, I disliked all the characters, so I really couldn't root for anyone.

On Saturday my girl and I spent the day at the Ventura County Fair. I have lots of pictures of goatlings (Cute Overload, eat your heart out!), chickens, pidgeons, pigs, fish, and frogs. We had a fantastic time: we both took a pass on the rides and fareway games, and instead spent our time seeing livestock, enjoying the arts and crafts exhibits, and sampling some of the great food. (Local tacos, beer & steak sandwiches, kettle corn, and hand-dipped frozen bananas.)

And we lucked into the end of a great set by Four Way Free, and bought both their CDs. They really remind me of a band from my college days called Homunculous (now defunct), but had a much more poppy sound. Where Homunculous drew from jazz, Four Way Free draws from the blues.

Sunday, I rode my usual trail loop, clocking in around 2:05. Not great since my personal best on this ride is 1:42:09, but not terrible either. Looking at my ride history, it seems like I ride around 2:05 on average days, and nail something under 1:45 when everything clicks. Given yesterday's 90° heat and my limited riding lately, I feel pretty good about it.

And last night was a going-away party for a friend of my girlfriend's that is moving to Hawaii. (Poor girl.) The festivities commenced at Medieval Times. The food was good, the show fun, and a good time was had by all.

And today I'm either staying late at work, or heading for an intro-level fight class in Moorpark.

All in all, a great weekend.
title: Weekend Recap

body:
First, she said that I'm too young to have the kind of tightness and knotting that she sees. She guessed correctly that I'm riding the edge of overtraining. She told me to spend some time researching recovery-related dietary supplements, and avail myself of some more opportunities to do some yoga or other restorative activity.

In the past three things have been central to keeping healthy and energized. They are: sleep, stretching, supplements. I will rededicate myself to all three.

I also found recently that staying fueled during my workouts made a huge difference in recovery speed, and benefits gained. So I'm going to invest in some sports drink powder and gel packs, and make sure to keep them handy during Krav/BJJ workouts.

She also mentioned that I have an unusually flat upper back. Nothing dramatic, but she mentioned that I'll have to do a little extra work to keep tension from building up in my shoulders and neck. That jibes with my experience, so I'll be researching some stretches or exercises that will help clear that area. (I remember standing and sitting rows being great for this. One more reason to get back to the gym...)

So, the complete to-do list to get my workout recovery up and my stress levels down:

  • Sleep 8+ hours every night. Get up at the same time every morning.
  • Stretch after every workout. Concentrate on back and neck flexibility.
  • Take my vitamins every night.
  • Stay fueled through every workout.
  • Start doing yoga at least once a week.

And, of course, I've scheduled a follow-up massage for next week, and the place I went offers some great rates on five-massage packages.
intro:
I woke up this morning with my neck in a bind. Knots between my shoulder blades, pain when I try to look down. Typical of me when I get stressed.

Why am I stressed? In a nutshell, because my weekly routine was already pretty packed, and my commute now eats another hour out of each day. I have to make every minute count. I multitask whenever possible. When I'm really rolling, I have three or four things going at once.

So I booked a massage for my lunch hour today. The therapist was very good, and had some interesting comments that I want to act on. I'm putting them here so they don't fall through the cracks.
title: Notes from Today's Massage

body:
Got lots of rest. Slept 10 hours Friday and Saturday nights, and didn't do anything physical. I'd have loved to get out on my bike, but there just wasn't time. Maybe next week.

Caught Kung Fu Panda, which was awesome. Highly recommended.

Also caught Star Wars: The Clone Wars, which was less awesome, but still fun. It's aimed squarely at kids, so don't expect too much. (Ahsoka keeps calling Anekin "Sky Guy." Ugh.) Still, Ahsoka standing on the front of that transport was pretty badass.

My girlfriend and I had a great morning in West Hollywood. We ate an amazing breakfast at Bread and Porridge, and cruised for new clothes. Unfortunately, it seems like Sunday afternoons are pretty quiet. Lots of closed shops. (I imagine everyone's still sleeping after another West Hollywood Saturday night.)

She found some really great new clothes, but came out with zip, so I just treated myself to a new Bikesmiths cycling jersey. It's damn pretty, and reminds me of college, which makes me happy.

I got the drive train on my mountain bike cleaned up last night. Not sure when I'll get to ride next, though. And in any event, the chain has stretched and need replacement. So a new one is on the way.

I'm on the hunt for a good sports drink. I need something with some fuel in it to keep me going through long workouts. I tried CarboRocket a while back, and loved it, but it's not as widely available as the alternatives, and I worry about quality control, actual contents, etc. A coworker recommended Cytomax, so I plan on trying that at some point. But as busy as I am, convenience counts for a lot. So I picked up a canister of Hammer HEED at lunch, and we'll see how I feel with that for a while.

Typical me: I ordered two bottles of vitamins last week online. And then I forgot that I bought them, so I bought two more bottles at the grocery store. Today, the first set of vitamins arrived in the mail. So... y'know, I'm pretty well set on vitamins for a while.

And I've set my phone to remind me to go to bed. At 10:15pm Sun. through Thurs. it plays the sound of crickets.

Provided I stretch after each workout, that takes care of my recent self-care action items, I think. Sleep, stretch, fuel, and vitamins. I've got all the tools I need.

intro:
CEOs publicly demonstrating their technological bewilderment is becoming a genre in itself. Universal CEO Doug Morris called iPod owners thieves, then confessed that he's unqualified to deal with the technology-driven upheaval in the music industry.

Now we have Blockbuster CEO Jim Keyes talking about how their little matrix of consumer use-cases proves that they're built to compete. He's really excited about in-store kiosks, and selling consumer electronics, and he's totally bewildered at why everyone wants to watch anything besides this summer's hit movies.

What [kiosks] do for Blockbuster stores is they allow us to have greater title depth in smaller space. Imagine in the future the ability to have the entire library captured on a kiosk. Some of the stuff is very, very slow moving and it takes a lot of very expensive real estate. So, think of it as a satellite system for stores that extends the reach of Blockbuster and makes it more convenient for our customers to get DVDs.

I'm wetting my pants with excitement!!!

I admit, they've got to do something. But kiosks, home boxes, and consumer electronics is just flailing. Unless they pull of the kind of turnaround that will be studied in business school for the next century, Blockbuster is doomed, and I see no reason for hope in this interview.
title: The Power of Bad Ideas

intro:
It's that time. I've settled in, and have a few gripes with the iPhone.

But first, let me say that I love the thing. I get noticably more done, using time that would otherwise go to waste. I no longer worry about standing in line at the lunch counter. I just chill, and catch up on email.

Likewise with texting. I write more, and reply more quickly. All good.

But.

1. This thing has a WiFi connection. Why do I have to sync with iTunes on my laptop to get the latest podcast episodes?

2. I want to sync my calendar, contacts, and iTunes content via bluetooth. Why isn't this possible?

3. I need Flash support in Safari for iPhone. Too many sites use it as an integral navigation component. Get cracking, Apple!

I'm done.

Wait, no I'm not. Could someone please make a version of Risk, or better yet Railroad Tycoon for the iPhone? Gracias.
title: iPhone Gripes

intro:
I caught a presentation this morning by Erik Knutzen of Homegrown Evolution. Basically, he's putting fun back into self-reliance, gardening, and generally making stuff at home instead of buying at CostCo.

My favorite moment of the talk was when he showed a slide of a woman installing a florescent bulb. "She's not having any fun," he said. The next slide was of a grinning couple in their kitchen... with a still. "These people are making moonshine. They look like they're having a good time."

And that's the idea. Low-maintenance, fun stuff everyone can do at home in whatever space they have, with extra credit for skirting the law at the same time.

I'm so spending time cruising around his site.

Plus, it reminded me that I wanted to research making whiskey at home.

To be continued...
title: Homegrown Evolution

intro:
Another day, another glitch. My hosting service screwed up, and my iPhone went on the fritz. But that's nothing compared to the bad day MySpace had a while back:

And then there was that Sunday night last July when a power outage in Los Angeles, where MySpace is headquartered, knocked the entire service offline for about 12 hours. The outage stood out partly because most other large Web sites use geographically distributed data centers to protect themselves against localized service disruptions. In fact, MySpace had two other data centers in operation at the time of this incident, but the Web servers housed there were still dependent on the SAN infrastructure in Los Angeles. Without that, they couldn't serve up anything more than a plea for patience. According to Benedetto, the main data center was designed to guarantee reliable service through connections to two different power grids, backed up by battery power and a generator with a 30-day supply of fuel. But in this case, both power grids failed, and in the process of switching to backup power, operators blew the main power circuit.

Sometimes you eat the bear, and sometimes the bear eats you.

"You stole my idea!"

intro:
I switched up my routine the last couple of weeks, doing a lot of mountain biking when I normally head for Krav class. The result is that this week my legs and back are recoving from a pretty heavy cumulative workout, and I'm doing a lot of stretching to make sure they stay healthy.

I hadn't been following up on all that by getting enough sleep. I didn't really put it together exactly what was going on until yesterday, when my back really hurt, despite having had several days to recover from last week's bike rides.

The pain really felt like I'd overworked the muscle, rather than a pull or anything else with a single discrete cause.

Overuse injuries are rarely the result of just "overdoing it" on a single run or ride. It's certainly possible, but not usually the case for me.

Overuse injury is usually the result of several workouts (short or long) with insufficient recovery time in between. Doing three rides in a week may or may not have been enough by itself, but adding in insufficient sleep, I was taking away a crucial resource my body needed to repair itself between rides.

After last night's boxing class, I took a few minutes to stretch and do some baby rolls, which are my new favorite thing: part massage, part stretch, part meditation. When I got home, I did a 25-min. yoga session, and got to sleep by 11:30, which gave me about 7½ hours of sleep last night, about 2 hours more than I got on Sunday night. It made a world of difference to my mood, my mental faculties, and to my back: I can feel that it's now in proper post-workout recovery mode, rather than simple damage control.

So, the moral to the story is, once again: I need to sleep a minimum of 8 hours a night. Last night was a good start. I need to get back where I was a few months ago, getting 8+ hours every weeknight, and sometimes more on weekends.
title: Insufficient System Resources

intro:
I'm naturally a gearhead. I want the best I can afford of whatever tool I'm using. My bike, my computer, my phone, my car, my apartment. I eschew quantity, but covet quality.

But, having the budget of a mere mortal, I have to remind myself that it's a poor carpenter who blames his tools, and that the overwhelming factor in the performance of the bike is the rider. So I love the introduction to A No-Frills Kitchen Still Cooks:

Like cookbooks, kitchen equipment is a talisman; people believe that buying the right kind will make them good cooks. Yet some of the best cooks I've known worked with a battered batterie de cuisine: dented pots and pans scarred beyond recognition, an old steak knife turned into an all-purpose tool, a pot lid held just so to strain pasta when the colander was missing, a food processor with a busted switch. They didn't complain and they didn't apologize; they just cooked.

Somehow, I've always believed implicitly that if Alice Waters or Julia Child or John Besch stepped into my kitchen, their food wouldn't taste any different than it does in their own homes. It's not the stove, it's the cook.

Computer programming isn't about computers in the same way that cooking isn't about stoves. And vice versa.

intro:
I love the way that Bruce Sterling thinks. The rest of our heads are all full of warm fuzzy stuff that's meant to make us feel better, but he's got none of it. It's like he was raised by defective parents that always told him the truth.

So he's got some good ideas about why we haven't been contacted by alien races, and why folks doing really clever new stuff will never, ever be rich on the scale of stodgy financial houses:

Okay, you're a gaming guy and a creative guy. You develop games. Are you gonna be as rich as these bankers, even though they're playing inside your games, on platforms that you yourself developed? No, you're not. Because they are money managers and not creatives like you, and they are going to be much, much richer than you. They can easily buy you and maintain your adventure game as a kind of graphic front end, the way old-fashioned banks used to have some marble pillars in the front. Because they're willing to make money and you're not serious about it.

I love that. If you are anything other than a banker you are by definition not serious about making money, and the people who really want to make money are going to own your ass. They will buy and sell the company that has been your life's work, and get richer doing it than you will ever be. Accept that or get in the game and become a banker.

And I had a damn fine ride in Cheeseboro Canyon yesterday. Since riding four days in eight a while back, my legs have been burned out and my back has been deeply annoyed. I've played through, doing a ride each weekend, dutifully ticking off the miles and elevation gain, having fun despite my body not really being in a party mood.

And that seemed to be the way things were going to go yesterday. I rode up from the parking lot to the south tip of the Modelo trail, then down the canyon trail to Shepherd's Flat, and up the Sheep Corral trail to the lookout above Palo Comado. I checked my watch. No time to go all the way to Simi Peak, so I decided to head down Dead Cow, then back up Palo Comado, then back down the Sheep Corral the way I'd come.

Knowing I just had one more short climb before a long stretch of fun downhill put me in the mood to push hard. I was smooth down Dead Cow, then turned and cranked hard up Palo Comado. That seemed to shock my legs awake, and I powered up to the overlook, then continued down to Shepherd's flat, riding smooth and confident the whole way.

My downhilling has radically improved, and I think my legs are finally coming back online. My back is still unhappy, but yoga and stretching help. And, as always, sleep is key.

Then I realized that was stupid, that I'd just learned something about stiff jabs, and that my partner had been kind enough to teach me. I slipped the next one and... threw a completely ineffectual flick jab into open air while getting knocked silly by a big right hook.

No victory for Chris tonight. Not in the sense of "I finally got the only punch that mattered in that bout."

But I learned to keep my hands up, keep moving, keep throwing jabs, and always be looking for the next loopy hook coming at me. I won big in becomming a better boxer.

After over two years slacking in Krav 1 classes, I'm out of my comfort zone. And that's... uncomfortable. But I can feel my brain re-wiring itself when I go to bed every night, and that feels great.

intro:
I've kept on asking the silly question over the last couple of weeks ("WTF!"), because nobody's given me a satisfactory answer. Reason Magazine has put forth the first cogent explanation I've seen.

In brief: everyone used to think (with good evidence) that U.S. housing market was, as Alan Greenspan said, "a collection of only loosely connected local markets." Investment firms believed that they could create very safe investments by packaging mortgages from disparate geographic locations, since the mortgages they placed in a given package would be independent.

The problem is that creating these securities created corelation in housing markets, destroying the actual safety of the packaged securities.

Whups.
title: Mortgage Crisis Analysis

I did some work last night on my home network. I replaced an aging NetGear 802.11g wireless router with an Apple Airport Extreme 802.11n, and attached a 500GB USB drive to the Airport. So I've got speedier transfers between machines, automated backups, and a giant network-accessible storage bin.

Complete backups of all machines are running as we speak, and when that's complete, I'm going to mothball my desktop computers.

And given that I have to stay off my bike for a couple of weeks, I invested in some new running shoes. Nothing fancy. Replacements for my old ones, which are both two years old and completely wrecked from wearing them to Krav.

Tonight I rest up and figure out how to get back to Krav and BJJ with a sprained thumb. Orange Belt testing is coming up in December, and I want to be ready.

Update: After experiencing problems with writing to the USB drive when mounted on the Airport, I found this article, which suggests that the solution might be to reformat the drive without journaling capability.
title: Infrastructure

intro:
Reformatting my USB drive fixed the throughput issues. Writes over the network are on par with FTP. Very happy. Unfortunately, pushing 200 gigs over the network is taking forever. Feels like it's never going to be done.

Three days and counting, mostly because i/o errors keep throwing rsync off its game. And this morning, I had to bounce the Airport Extreme, which I find... troubling. There's no reason I should be seeing i/o errors, let alone the drive and the router dropping off the network and needing a manual bounce.

What I'm saying is: I'm really thinking of returning the Airport and going with a more robust storage system.
title: Infrastructure II

intro:
Quiet weekend. Friday night I went for a run, then chilled at home and watched a bit of HBO's John Adams series, and spent Saturday morning cleaning and running errands. This was made somewhat more exciting by my car battery dying at the worst possible moment: I was on my way to deliver lunch to my girlfriend. The food was in the car, I was ready to go, and poof! No battery. Damn.

Luckily, my girl was nearby anyway, so she came and grabbed the food, gave my car a jumpstart, and was on her way. I went straight to Sears, where they confirmed the dead battery, and installed a new one. (Yes, I'm lame when it comes to DIY car stuff.)

While I was there, I invested in a steam cleaner for my carpet. "Why," you ask? Because a pumpkin rotted and put a nasty stain on my carpet, and because I've always wanted a painless way to clean carpet. Scrubbing just seems so... primitive.

I spent Saturday night with my girlfriend getting caught up on Heroes (which now has more plot holes than we can stand) and baking and eating cake. We put the icing on before it was completely cooled, so it kind of slouched. But that's okay. There are no rules for cake.

My girlfriend and I lamented last week that many of our friends are too far away to be part of a proper pumpking carving party, so we've created a group Halloween blog for everyone to post to. I can't wait to see how it all shakes out as we get closer and closer to Halloween!

And I'm now in the final stages of getting my laptop set up for web app development. Specifically, I'm getting it set up to work on the software that runs this blog. Once that happens, bye-bye desktop. Once I get it running, I'll be checking everything into Subversion, and the transition will be complete.

Sadly, no biking or hiking or biking this weekend. My sprained thumb kept me off my bike (and out of childproof containers, incidentally), and three 5.5-mile runs this week absolved any guilt I might feel about taking a couple of lazy days. Getting back to running feels great, and I'd love to add running to my weekly routine. (Lunch time?)

Just to freak me out, Mother Nature has gone completely to Autumn in about two days. I got home tonight after having dinner with my parents, and discovered that the temperature in my apartment was down around 63. So tonight marks the official first use my heater this season.

And now, it's time for bed. G'night, all!

intro:
In the last few years, Wallmart, Sony, Major League Baseball, and even Microsoft have had to kill off their DRM systems, leaving customers stranded in a painful spot: go through tedious, time-consuming steps to convert the music and video they bought into other formats, or lose that music entirely. (In the case of Major League Baseball, there was no conversion option, and fans lost everything they'd paid for.)

Over and over and over again, loyal customers who've tried to play by the rules have gotten burned while pirates have been completely unaffected. Pirates can play their pirated movies and music on any device they want. They can play them on their iPods, high-definition TV sets, cellphones, and any computer in their houses or cars. They can loan those files to friends, use them as ringtones, and embed them in web pages. And they do it all for free.

Me, Mr. Nice Guy, I have to pay $1 every time I want to use an iTunes track as a ringtone, and I only get to use thirty seconds of it.

intro:
A friend has a theory that "the root cause of any bug is that the programmer is a frickin' idiot."

Consider: 

function formatDate(dateString) 
{
    var d = new Date(dateString);
    var days = ["Sunday","Monday"
        ,"Tuesday","Wednesday"
        ,"Thursday","Friday"
        ,"Saturday"];
    var day = days[d.getDay()];
    var hour = d.getHours();
    var min = d.getMinutes();
    var ampm = (hour >= 12) ? "pm" : "am";
    hour = (hour > 12) ? (hour % 12) : hour;
    min = (min == 0) ? "00" : min;
    
    var s = day + " at "
        + hour + ":" + min + " " + ampm;
    return s;
}

Whups. That line that formats the minutes should read: 

    min = (min < 10) ? "0" + min : min;

Why was I formatting a particular value of min when I should have been zero-padding small values of min? Because I was on NyQuil, that's why.

body:
In my defense, I made a conscious decision to write the software that runs this site without thinking about performance. I tried to avoid the obvious, crashing blunders, but otherwise just kind of did things in whatever way made my work easy and kept the code simple.

I still believe that was the right decision. See, simple code is maintainable code. Simple, well-structured code is easy to change when the need arises.

And by optimizing for performance early on, I would have spent lots of time dealing with the consequences of that optimization rather than adding new features. It's a natural part of a program's lifecycle to reach a point where performance is a problem and some restructuring is in order. If you've done everything else right up until that point, fixing performance issues is a breeze.

In my case, I was making about 10 database calls for every blog entry displayed. On my front page, that's 5 main entries displayed front and center, plus up to 10 more in the "recent comments" sidebar. Several other spots are going to get some attention soon, but it was pretty clear where to start.

My profiler also told me that the query that finds the "recent images" for the sidebar was taking a while to run. It has to search the table based on the Date_Posted field, and I never bothered to add an index to that field. Doh!

So, I've added the index, and changed the database access code so that I now retrieve just the header information for blog posts on the front page, and things are once again pretty snappy. I'm still making too many database calls, but it'd down from hundreds to around thirty or so.

Which brings me to my last bit of advice about performance: when it is acceptable, stop working on it. Once nobody notices any slowdown, speeding things up does not add value to the project, and tends to make the code less maintainable, making the operation a net negative. I'm certainly going to make some adjustments in the future, but, but only as I have time. Working on my website code is pretty far down my priority list.
intro:

In my case, my profiler told me that I was making several hundred individual calls to the database to retrieve all the data on my blog's main page. That's why performance has been in the weeds here for a while.

intro:
As a follow-up to my post on performance, I'd like to point to Strategic Design: 6 Steps For Building Successful Websites, which has some great big-picture advice for designing and building websites.

What I really like about the article is it's emphasis on establishing measurable goals before beginning any work, and following through after the work is done to find out whether you met those goals. Skipping these steps is extremely common, and is a primary reason for project failure.

I also like the notion of "Kaizen", or "focus on continuous improvement using small steps." It's a powerful notion, and one that I've been putting to work for a long time. Every time I go to the climbing gym, I have two missions: climb one route that I couldn't climb last week, and find a new route that's just barely too hard for me. In this way, I improve by one baby step every week. At the end of a year, I'm a whole new climber.
title: Successful Web Design

I was really surprised at how fast my legs got cooked today. Just 35 minutes or so. I'd planned on longer, but my legs were cooked and my thumb had developed a dull ache. I'm clearly not used to turning the cranks any more. Several steep climbs put me well past the red line, and coming back down the steep, winding trail to the trailhead went well (I've retained what technical skill and self-assurance I had a few weeks ago.), it reminded me that staying in "attack position" really does require some leg and low back strength.

I had fun, but really this was just a taste of what I really want to get back to as soon as I can. Today was an absolutely perfect day for a ride, and I'm bummed that a silly injury kept me from making the most of it.

I'm sure that I'll be back in the groove quickly. I know from experience that my body re-acclimatizes quickly to this kind of thing. And it's really not such a fitness leap to go from 35 minutes of tough riding to several hours of more moderate effort. Give me a month or two, and I'll be back to my long weekend rides.

intro:
More performance improvements! The front page should be getting pretty snappy for everyone. The total number of database queries is down from 400 to 20, and most of the queries that are still running go faster than they used to. My profile data now says that talking to the database is emphatically not the major time sink.

What is? My URL rewriting filter. I don't have access to the servers Apache mod_rewrite rules, so I have a Servlet Filter set up that grabs all incomming URLs and does some regexp magic with them. Unfortunately, this has to be done for every request, and the worst case scenario (comparing the URL to a long list of regexps only to find none of them match) is both very bad and very common. In fact, it's the typical case. Ouch.

Oh well. It's exactly the kind of thing that you do when you don't have full access to server configuration. My hosting bill is $5/mo, so I'm not going to sweat this.

And Twitter seems to have a bug, which is why that left-hand column is blank at the moment. I've filed a bug report, and I'm going to add some error-handling code to my end so that I can display a cute little "fail whale" or something when this happens.

And I've just spotted a problem: it looks like the number of comments isn't loading into blog entry header info properly. It's right in the detail pages, but not on the front page. Doh!
title: Two Steps Forward, One Step Back

intro:
I should have known. I changed a lot of things to get performance where it is. (And I'm not done yet.) I thought I'd tested everything, but I forgot one important item: posting photos. Rats.

What's more, I don't know why I can't upload photos. I haven't touched the photo uploading system in ages. I didn't test it because it "shouldn't" be affected at all. But clearly it is.

I've done without automated testing until now because DMG really was pretty simple. But it's reached a level of complexity that leaves me between a rock and a hard place: I don't have time to test properly, but I can't accept breaking stuff.

Automated testing is the way around that dilemma. It will tell me in ten seconds what's broken, which means I can refactor zeal and abandon knowing that there are guardrails that will tell me when I've bulndered.

And I can add it as I have time. This week, I'll add automatic testing for the blog entry creation and editing system. Next week, I'll get around to the comment submission system. And in a few months, I'll have a testing mechanism that saves me huge ammounts of time and ensures that bugs rarely make it to production.

But tonight, it's first things first: create an automated test that catches the bug in photo uploads, then fix that bug.

It's time to plant the seeds of test-driven development.
title: Bugs.

intro:
This video illustrates a great set of movements to build athletic performance. It's all there: balance, explosive power, strength, and lots of functional movement. Great stuff.

The other thing I note here: note all the open space, and the total lack of machines. Big box gyms love machines because they're supposedly safer and give newbies a ready-made format for getting in shape. But past the first few weeks of basic remedial strength building, machines are a crutch.

If you want to be strong, fast, and injury-free, avoid the machines and go with free weights and functional movements. If you don't know where to start, talk to trainers until you find one who can show you.
title: Functional Workout

intro:
Simi Valley Krav Maga has switched their schedule around, and introduced a ground fighting class to their already excellent lineup. (For the hard core, you can follow an hour of ground fighting with an hour of Krav 2/3.)

Tonight's class was great fun: countering sloppy haymakers with nasty chokes and takedowns, then learning the counters for those chokes. It overlapped a bit with some Krav 1/2 stuff, but with the "mean" factor cranked up a bit. Instead of simply taking more favorable positions, we're jumping straight to breaking arms and chokes.

I've dropped about 7 lbs in the last month, and done a lot of running and rebuilding of basic fitness. And it shows. I'm getting around a lot better, and I've got energy for days.

After class let out, I headed home, changed into some warmer clothes, and headed out for a run. I set an easy pace, and breezed through my 5.5-mile "oak tree loop" run, and felt so good down the home stretch that I was tempted to throw in another few miles. But by then it was getting cold, and the wind was starting to bite, and the little voices in my head reminded me that feeling good this workout means I go bigger next time, not this time.

All in all, I feel really good about how my body is building back up. I feel great, I'm sleeping better, and I can't wait to get back on my bike for some long autumn rides.
title: Monday Night Ground Fighting Class

intro:
I have so much to be thankful for this year. An amazing girlfriend, a wonderful family, and a new neice! On wednesday night I drove up to San Francisco where my sister and brother in law hosted a wonderful family Thanksgiving. The new baby was certainly the focus of attention, and is just a magical little girl. I can't wait to see what she gets up to in the lifetime ahead!

On the way up, I got my first listen to the new Guns & Roses album. There's no way that G&R could live up to the pent-up hopes of all the fans, so I'm giving it time to sink in. So far I'm digging everything up until "Street of Dreams", and after that I always feel the need to throw on the Use Your Illusion albums.

I also put on some Indigo Girls (yep, still a fan after all these years), and found that while the old favorites don't mean as much as they used to, I'm finally hearing the newer stuff. All That We Let In and Become You both rock, so I've downloaded Despite Our Differences, and can't wait to have a listen.

On Friday I headed back down the 5 to Simi to spend the weekend with my girlfriend. I did pause along the way for a short run near the highway. It was really nice to break up the long drive like that, and to get out in the weather a bit. It was cold and windy, but a light insulating layer and a wind jacket struck the perfect balance.

My girlfriend and I spent Friday night curled up with Battlestar Galactica, and on Saturday caught the Swedish vampire flick Let the Right One In. (Highly recommended!)

And somewhere in the mix this weekend, I managed to clean my car, do four loads of laundry, vaccuum, clean and maintain my bike, and clear out a bunch of old junk from under the bathroom sink. This year I'm heading into the holidays with my act together.

And Christmas and New Year's eve/day plans are coming together beautifully. It's going to be a wonderful holiday season!
title: Thanksgiving Weekend

intro:
I have a recurring payment scheduled through WaMu's website that pulls a chunk out of each paycheck and pays down my credit card. I realized that with the repairs to my car and several other large-ish expenses last week that "a chunk" was going to badly deplete my checking account.

I tried to cancel the payment on WaMu's website, but couldn't figure out how. So I called customer service. I talked to a nice man who said, "No problem. The payment is canceled, and that change will show on the website once you log out and log back in again."

I did so. The deduction from my account remained. So I called back, and was told that the website isn't "real time," and I should check in the morning.

I checked this morning, and WaMu's website still showed that the payment was about to be deducted from my account.

So I called again, and talked to a nice lady who said that while the payment was deleted, the system kept reinstating it because it was a recurring payment, rather than just a one-time payment. She assured me that the problem was fixed.

At 2 PM, the website still showed the pending payment. I called again. This time, I spoke to a woman who told me that the payment was "in process", and that there is nothing that WaMu can do until tomorrow, when it's "no longer in process." I reminded her that this will leave zero dollars in my checking account, and that I have other payments scheduled for today, including automatic debits from my car insurance company and my gym.

"Those payments are going to go out today, and will cause my account to be overdrawn," I said. "When that happens, who do I talk to to get the overdraft fees reversed?"

She said that nobody in customer service can reverse those fees. "I understand," I said. "Who can I talk to?"

She said she didn't know. "I can wait while you find out," I said.

She returned, and said that there's nobody specifically assigned to adressing bank errors. "So, when this happens, should I call customer service?"

She explained again that nobody in customer service has the authority to reverse overdraft charges. "So who do I talk to if, as a result of WaMu's error, my account becomes overdrawn?"

She repeated that there's no department for that.

We were going in circles. So I repeated her story back to her: "So, you're telling me that after four phone calls over two days, Washington Mutual is still going to make this payment. And when they do, they're going to make me pay overdraft fees that are their fault, and there's nobody I can talk to who can fix Washington Mutual's mistake?"

She put me on hold. When she returned, she said that if there are any overdraft fees as a result of this, I should call customer service, and ask for a supervisor.

To be continued...
title: WaMu Can't Help You.
This made staying up too late worth it.

intro:
For those of you just tuning in, chapter one is here.

On Monday night, as expected, my car insurance company auto-debited my account, triggering an overdraft fee of $33.

I called this morning, and as instructed, I asked for a supervisor. They hung up on me.

I called again, and this time was extra sugary sweet and got through to a supervisor. She explained to me that they've very sorry, but the previous four customer service reps have all been mistaken, and there's no way to stop the payment. Period. I'm out of luck.

The super that even though the payment was scheduled to be initiated on 12/1, that it was actually initiated on 11/28, and therefor I would have had to call on Friday to cancel Monday's payment.

This conflicts directly with everything I've found on the website, which says that the cutoff for cancelling a scheduled payment is 4:00 PM PST on the day the payment is scheduled. Not the previous business day, as the supervisor insists.

The upshot is that WaMu policy grants me forgivness of one overdraft fee per month. I was warned that further overdrafts are on me. I was told that there was no bank error in this case.

I asked to talk to the supervisor's supervisor. I was told that no senior supervisors are available at the moment, but that I could "schedule" a call with one. So they're supposed to call me back sometime tomorrow between 11:00 AM and 4:00 PM EST.

I have been instructed to read the complete Terms of Service on the website so that said senior manager and I can more easily resolve the "misunderstanding."

I can't open a new bank account today. I have work to do. But I'm definitely checking out the local credit union ASAP.

To be continued...
title: WaMu Still Can't Help You

intro:
For those of you just tuning in, chapter one is here, and chapter 2 is here.

The senior manager at Washington Mutual, "Stan" just called. He said that he has no record of my cancellation requests on Sunday night. I said that I'd spoken with a supervisor named "Helen" yesterday, and suggested that he get her on the line. That was "not possible." I suggested we get "Rita", whom I spoke with on Monday, on the line. That was also, "not possible."

Stan just kept telling me that he has no record of what the customer service reps and I talked about on Sunday night, so he can't verify that I asked the rep to cancel the payment.

In other words: Washington Mutual did not make a mistake, because Washington Mutual has no record of making a mistake. My own notes are irrelavent.

If I want Stan to "deem this a bank error", I have to prove:

  1. that I asked on Sunday night for the payment to be canceled.
  2. that Sunday night wasn't too late to cancel the payment
  3. that the customer service rep did something other than what I asked him to do

And I have to do it using Washington Mutual's own records.

I pointed out that I'm looking at my account on Washington Mutual's Web site, and that my "Scheduled Payments" screen shows a cancelled transaction on 11/30. He said that he doesn't see that on his screen, and asked that I fax over what I'm seeing.

I did. He said that my records only prove that there was a transaction canceled on Sunday night. He said they do not show what I asked to be canceled. In other words, they don't prove that the rep made a mistake. The key here is that there's no record of what I asked for, so I can't prove a mismatch between my request and the rep's action.

I expressed to Stan my surprise that Washington Mutual would rather lose me as a customer than forgive a couple of overdraft fees. He said that if I decided to bank elsewhere that I did have that choice.

Stan and I went round and round for a while, and finally I realized that Stan is just a guy who's probably happy to have a job at all at this point, and he works for a giant company that grades him on how effectively he can screw their customers. He has no power to make things right, or give me the benefit of the doubt. It doesn't matter what's true, and he doesn't care what's right. All that matters is what I can prove. Essentially, I'm trying to talk him into hanging WaMu with their own rope. That's not going to happen.

So I decided to ask the obvious question: how do I prevent this kind of problem in the future. How do I make sure that both my request and the action of the customer service rep are properly logged.

Stan told me that I should ask the rep to notate the account to reflect the conversation. Fair enough. I asked Stan to notate my account with the contents of our conversation. "I've already done that," he said. "Good," I said. "Would you read your notes back to me please."

He said that his notes indicated that he'd explained that this was not a bank error, that he'd explained WaMu policy to me, that my fax proved nothing.

"Stan," I said, "Your notes don't say anything about my request for overdraft protection. Given that this whole problem is the result of there being no record of my payment cancellation request on Sunday night, I'd really like you to add something to your notes about what I've asked for here. I'm not asking you to pay my bills, I'm not asking you to reverse the payment. I just want overdraft protection. Please put that in your notes."

He refused.
title: WaMu Has No Record of that Conversation

intro:
With the resolution of my little saga with Washington Mutual, a few things became pretty clear. They're kind of a jumble, but when you really get down to it, the things you learn from any given experience usually are.

First and foremost, I need a new bank. WaMu has made my life harder, not easier, and doesn't deserve my business.

Second, WaMu the most consistent pattern over the course of six phone calls was that each person I talked to told me two things:

  1. the last person I talked to was wrong
  2. the problem is now fixed

This is exactly the pattern that made me swear I'd never deal with UPS again. To this day, whenever there is an option to use the USPS instead, I do.

A WaMu customer service rep can tell you anything, and the next rep will simply say, "I'm sorry you were misinformed." WaMu is not responsible for the information given to you by WaMu representatives. If they're wrong, that's your problem.

It also occurred to me that if I'd lost $100 on a street somewhere, I'd already have forgotten about it. I'm just arguing with Washington Mutual on principal, which is dumb.

Admittedly, I had naively thought that once I got to a senor manager, I'd be talking to a reasonable person who would help. Now I know better.
title: WaMu: Lessons Learned

I have a Capresso MT-500 coffee maker, and it is wonderful. It has a thermal carafe, a timer that lets me set it at night and wake up to fresh coffee, and it makes excellent coffee. The coffee I make in my own kitchen for $.11 is as good or better than anything I can get elsewhere.

I also have a little Italian style espresso maker for weekend mornings when I want to take my time with breakfast. Once again: best coffee, my kitchen. No feeling deprived because I'd rather go out for breakfast.

I've also invested in some really nice bedding. I sleep better because of it. My bed is like a womb. Worth every penny.

I've also spent money on things like Brooks Bros. shirts. I bought three for $200 about 5 years ago, and they still look brand new. So far, each Brooks Bros. shirt in my closet has cost me $13.34 per year.

Investing in nice furniture, TV, Netflix, coffee, etc. means I'm investing in making my apartment a place I want to spend time. These days, I'd rather stay home, cook dinner, and watch a movie with a great cup of coffee than brave the crouds at the theater. I live better, and spend less.

And my credit card bills lately are proof.
intro:
Jason Kottke has a cool post this morning that resonates with my own nesting habits.

My wife and I are ardent upgraders. I rarely buy anything anymore but the things I do buy are usually better versions of things I already have. As things break or wear out, we've been replacing them with items that are nicer to use/wear/whatever and will last a whole lot longer than the cheaper stuff.

A friend from college had a saying: "Buy the best. You'll never be disappointed." I have my own saying: "The good life is cheaper." Buy quality stuff that will last, and you'll spend less time and money shopping, you'll look sharper, eat healthier, and sleep better. I do my research, I buy quality, and I really enjoy the stuff I have.

body:
Okay, now the geek-out gear notes so I remember what I've learned:

The Clothes

I'd completely forgotten how easy it is to stay warm on the slopes, and I hate being cold. So I radically overdressed:

  • super-toasty wool ski socks
  • Capilene 3 zip top and knickers
  • wool t-shirt
  • fleece vest
  • insulated ski pants
  • heavyweight ski jacket

Temps were in the 40's, so I was uncomfortably warm pretty much immediately, and was shedding layers within minutes of getting on the slopes for my lesson. By the time I was done for the day, I was a ripe, sweaty mess.

Next time it'll be Cap 2 just to avoid getting clammy, lighter pants, and no mid layer. The jacket was awesome, and has generous pit zips, and was great later in the weekend with a minimal base layer. If that's still too hot, I'll step down to a Cap 3 top and a lighter jacket.

The Lesson

I originally thought that the lesson was pretty useless, and I still think it wasn't done as well as it could have been. But I also think that I got a lot out of it, and could have gotten even more if I had approached it differently.

This was the first big weekend of the season at Big Bear, and it showed. The instructors were disorganized, and often gave conflicting instructions. But every instructor is genuinely a gem. Huge respect to their skills as teachers. Once they have more structure and get settled in as a team, they'll be awesome.

Bear Mountain has a setup where your first lesson takes place in a roped-off, specially groomed bunny slope, divided into three sections. First you practice gliding straight, and some minor steering. Then you practice your "J turns", then you practice the "falling leaf" technique.

Unfortunately, the section on which you practice gliding and turning is just long enough for one turn, so you never get to link your turns. And every time you want to try again, you have to trudge back to the top of the section.

Me, I'd make the section bigger, and (ironically) steeper. I really found everything much easier with a little speed, and it's tough to get that on too mild a slope.

I also would move through the sections much faster. I was really trying to master each section before moving on, and so got locked into in an un-fun cycle: one ineffectual toe turn, then trudge back to the top, repeat. Once I had the general idea, I should have moved on.

Once I had a little practice in the learners' area, I really should have jumped straight for the bunny slopes. That's where I made the most progress in the shortest time. I still fell spectacularly several times, but by the time I got down the mountain, I was feeling much more in control.

So that's it: dress light, take a quick lesson, then relax and have fun. Can't wait to go back!
intro:
I spent the weekend doing a bit of snowboarding at Bear Mountain in Big Bear, CA. The timing couldn't be better: right after a 30-year storm that dumped 4 feet of fresh snow. Beautiful!

Nutshell Advice for First-Time Snowboarders

Get a lesson, but just pick up a few nutshell bits of advice, get a little practice in a super-safe setting, then head for the bunny slopes where you can get some flow going and concentrate on how your board moves. Keep your eyes up and your knees bent, and find your inner chillness.

If it's in the budget, buy your own boots. I couldn't get my rental boots to fit quite right (serious heel slip), and while I had a great time, I think it would have been even better with well-fitted boots.
title: Snowboarding in Big Bear: Gear Report

intro:
As always, a list of last year's resolutions:

  • Pay down my debt. [check!]
  • Maintain my body weight below 175 lbs.
  • Take at least one 4-day camping trip.
  • Test for my orange belt in Krav Maga.
  • Do fun stuff to stay in shape. [check!]
  • See four big-ticket concerts this year. [check!]
  • Draw regularly.
  • Play music regularly.

I've markedly reduced my debt, I've stayed in shape, and I've had a great time doing it. I've gone to several concerts (NIN, Smashing Pumpkins, the L.A. Phil, and a fantastic gospel choir performance.) I've also found and enjoyed a lot of great recorded music.

Oddly, it's the stuff that didn't happen that I'm really proud of, because the reason it didn't happen is that it got crowded out by more important stuff.

I have an incredible girlfriend. I've spent more and more time on restorative activity like yoga. Instead of testing for my orange belt in Krav Maga, I learned to snowboard. And I have a great new job.

All in all, it's been a great year. I wouldn't change a thing. So I'm going to keep all the same resolutions for next year, with one new one:

  • Buy only what I really need.

Use up, wear out, make due, or do without. Be frugal. Buy only what I really need. I already have everything I need to have a lot of fun. I don't need a new bike, or new clothes, or a fancy car.

And, of course, there are plenty of really important things that are not even on the list. My loved ones, my job, my health. Those are things that I hope I need no reminders for.

Oh, and while I generally hate "life assessment" quizzes, there's one that I actually like: the Clean Sweep life assessment quiz. My current score is 89.
title: New Year's Resolutions for 2009

Here's the low-down:

  • Sept. 1: Buy 2010 day planner.
  • Oct. 1: File vacation forms with HR for the Friday after Thanksgiving and the week between Christmas and New Year's Day. (Total time off: 6 days.)
  • Nov. 16: Start writing Christmas cards, buy stamps.
  • Nov. 26: Thanksgiving

The notion is that by Dec 1, all plans will be booked, and I can relax and get some time off to enjoy the season, and by about Dec 20, I'll have all my shopping done.

I'm not sure whether I'll manage to make all this happen. But at least having a plan seems like a good idea.

intro:
Dictionaries suck, mostly. But they have one thing that most web sites don't: guide words.

Guide words are words printed at the top of each page to let you know what's on that page. There are various arrangements, but my favorite goes like this: the first and last word on each page are printed in the top outside corner of the page. So you can just look at the top corners and know whether you're on the right page, or should keep going.

Now, take a look at TED's alphabetical listing of speakers. At the bottom of the page, what do you find? Page numbers! Why? Those numbers tell me nothing useful about where I might find the speaker I'm looking for.

Rather than this:

1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5   Next »

I'd much rather see this:

A - C | D - G | H - L | M - P | Q - Z   Next »

Same for anything alphabetized.

I'm fine with page numbers when there's no better option, or when they really do describe well what's going on. But the concept of a "page number" is just as much a holdover from print media as "page" is. It's time to really think about guide words, page numbers, calendar dates, and the way in which we help people find things on the web.
title: Page Numbers are Archaic

body:
"So what do you do?" asked the captain.

"Well, I work at Acme Paper, managing a local distribution center."

"Ah. Do you like the work?"

"Well, no," said the businessman. "But if I work hard, and do a good job, I'll get promoted."

"What will you do then?" asked the captain.

"Well, I'll be in charge of a regional distribution center. And I'll have to work even harder, but if I do well, I'll get promoted again."

"I see. What then?" asked the captain.

"I'll have to work harder than ever," said the businessman. "But if I do a good job, I'll get to retire with a really nice nest egg in the bank, and I can relax and enjoy life."

"Ah!" said the captain. "What will you do then?"

"I'm going to live by the ocean, " said the businessman, "And in the mornings I'll go fishing, and in the evenings my wife and I will walk into town and go dancing."

"That sounds wonderful," said the captain.

The young businessman asked, "So, Captain, what do you do with your days?"

"Well, I live by the ocean. And in the mornings I go fishing, and in the evenings my wife and I walk into town and go dancing."

Now, I've been telling that story for years. But I didn't know it was a modern version of an earlier conversation between none other than the philosopher Diogenes and Alexander the Great. The stakes in that earlier conversation were somewhat higher.

Diogenes asked Alexander, "What are you going to do?"

"I'm going to conquor and subjugate Greece."

"Ah. And then?"

"Well, I'm going to conquor and subjugate all of Asia."

"Mmm. And then?"

"I'm going to conquor the whole world!"

"And then?"

Alexander thought a moment. "Well, I guess I'll relax and enjoy myself."

The philosopher said to Alexander, "It seems to me you could save yourself a lot of trouble if you'd just relax and enjoy yourself now."

intro:
Man, I thought I was gaining flexibility. But it's become really clear that I have a long, long way to go.

I can touch my toes easily and hold "Warrior 1" for a while, but my hips are rediculously tight. My hamstrings and groin allow just a minimal range of motion, and I'm compensating with extra flexibility in my low back, which is a bad place to be compensating for anything. And I cannot achieve more than the smallest inward rotation of my thighs.

So, it's good that I went to yoga today instead of running. And particularly good that there are giant mirrors in that room so I can see the ways in which I'm distorting each pose.

Really, it's all about the hips. I've been doing the "Hip Series" on some excellent yoga DVDs I got a while back, and I'm seeing results. But this is going to take time...
title: Today's Yoga Notes

intro:
I took some time this afternoon to ride my bike over in Wildwood park. I wasn't sure how my legs would hold up, or how my technical skills would be, or even how much daylight I'd have. So Wildwood was the place to go: lots of options that feed nicely into each other.

The parking lot was packed when I arrived around 2:45. So I headed out where hikers would be few: up Bik Sky Dr. to the Lower Butte trail. Aside from a single biker, I had the trail to myself all the way up Lower Butte and back along Santa Rosa.

Once I dropped down the switchbacks and got back into the main area of the park, it was a different story. The mesa, tipi and falls areas were pretty crowded, so I tried to keep to the fringes. But, I couldn't stay away from a run over Stagecoach Bluff. Best techie riding in the park! After that it was a careful ride down the switchbacks below Lizard Rock and up the canyon. Lots of beginner riders and hikers along there, so I kept it very, very mellow. But once I was on the Lynnmere trail, I was all alone again, spinning up the countour lines toward the road.

I've done this loop a few times before. My legs definitely burned more than I remember, but my lungs held up, and in the end I did fine. No trouble along Santa Rosa, and cleaned Stagecoach no problem. Good ride.
title: A Sunday Spin in Wildwood
